2a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishnah opens with two primary acts of transferring on Shabbat that expand to four cases for the person inside, and the same count for the person outside.
How do these cases arise?
A poor person stands outside, while the homeowner stands inside.
The poor person reaches inside and places an object into the homeowner's hand.
Alternatively, the poor person takes an object from that hand and carries it outside. In either complete transfer, the poor person is liable and the homeowner exempt.
The homeowner reaches outside and places an object into the poor person's hand.
Alternatively, the homeowner takes an object from that hand and brings it inside. In either complete transfer, the homeowner is liable and the poor person exempt.

If the poor person extends a hand inside and the homeowner takes from it, or the homeowner puts an object in it and the poor person carries it out, neither has performed the full transfer; both are exempt.
Likewise, if the homeowner extends a hand outside and the poor person takes from it, or the poor person puts an object in it and the homeowner carries it in, both are exempt.
The Gemara opens by citing a parallel mishnah in Shevuot: oaths, too, are described as two that become four.

2b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The cited Shevuot mishnah also counts awareness of impurity as two cases that become four.
It likewise counts the appearances of skin affliction as two that become four.
The parallel mishnah lists Shabbat transfers simply as two that become four.
Why does our Shabbat mishnah add separate inside and outside counts, while Shevuot stops at two that become four?
One answer: Shabbat is the main setting for these laws and therefore lists both principal acts and their derivatives; Shevuot lists only principal acts.
But if the principal acts are only acts of carrying out, there are only two such cases.
One might suggest that the four include both liable and exempt cases.
Yet Shevuot groups transfers with the appearances of affliction; just as all four affliction cases entail liability, all four transfer cases should too.
Rav Pappa revises the distinction: Shabbat includes liable and exempt acts, whereas Shevuot lists liable acts only.
If the liable acts are cases of carrying out, there are still only two; how can Shevuot count four?
The four are two cases of carrying out and two of carrying in.
But the mishnah calls them 'acts of carrying out.'
Rav Ashi replies that the tanna also calls carrying in an act of 'carrying out.'
What supports this broad use of the term?
A mishnah calls a transfer from one domain to another 'carrying out' and imposes liability; its language can include bringing an object from the public into the private domain.
Why can a transfer inward be called 'carrying out'?
The tanna uses the term for removing an object from its original place, whichever direction it travels.
Ravina adds a proof from our mishnah: it says 'acts of carrying out' and immediately describes carrying in.
Rava offers another reading: the mishnah speaks of Shabbat domains, two domains generating the listed cases.
Rav Mattana asks Abaye why the mishnah counts eight acts when its divided transfers appear to yield twelve.
Abaye counters that Mattana's counting method would yield sixteen.
Rav Mattana begins to explain why Abaye's countercount is not a difficulty; the explanation continues on the next daf.

3a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Mattana answers Abaye: the first set of exempt, permitted acts is omitted from the mishnah's count.
The second set remains difficult, since those acts are exempt but prohibited and seemingly should be counted.
Can an exempt act on Shabbat really be permitted? Shmuel says exempt acts are generally prohibited, apart from three cases involving a deer, a snake, and an abscess.
Shmuel's rule concerns cases where someone performs an action. Many cases of exemption with no action are permitted.
Even so, why does the mishnah not count twelve acts?
It counts exempt actions that could develop into a complete act carrying liability for a sin offering, but omits exempt actions that could not.
If both participants are exempt, why does their combined performance of the forbidden labor not create liability?
Rabbi cites 'when he does it' to distinguish doing the entire labor from doing only part of it.
Thus one person who completes the labor is liable; two who divide its performance are exempt.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Gamda reports the same interpretation from a group of Sages: a lone performer is liable, two performers exempt.
Rav asks Rabbi whether someone loaded by another person with food and drink becomes liable by carrying them out: does moving his body count as lifting the load?
Rabbi rules that he is liable, distinguishing this from moving an object that another placed in his hand.
Why are the body and hand treated differently?
The body is normally at rest, so moving it lifts the load; the hand is not fixed at rest in the same way.

3b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Hiyya warns Rav that asking Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi about another tractate while he studies this one could embarrass him if the answer is not at hand.
Nevertheless, Rabbi Hiyya says Rabbi answered this question well.
A baraita confirms it: someone loaded before Shabbat who carries the load out after dark is liable, because his body differs from his hand.
Abaye states that a person's extended hand is itself neither a public nor a private domain.
The mishnah's cases involving the poor person's hand and the homeowner's hand show that it takes the status of neither domain.
Abaye asks whether an extended hand instead has the intermediate status of a karmelit, so that the Sages barred pulling it back.
Two baraitot give opposite rulings for a hand holding fruit and extended outside: one forbids returning it, the other permits it.
Might their disagreement be whether the hand has karmelit status?
The Gemara rejects that inference: both can regard it as a karmelit, distinguishing a hand below ten handbreadths from one above them.
Another explanation keeps both hands below ten and denies karmelit status; it distinguishes extension before Shabbat, without a penalty, from extension after dark, with a penalty.
The reverse penalty seems more reasonable: if the hand was extended after dark, forbidding its return might lead to dropping the fruit and incurring a sin offering.
If that concern did not govern the answer, can we resolve Rav Beivai bar Abaye's question whether one may remove bread from an oven to avoid liability for baking?
The proposed resolution is that removal was not permitted; the Gemara allows this inference to stand.
Alternatively, the oven question remains open: the baraitot about the hand can differ between an unwitting act, which draws no penalty, and an intentional one, which does.
A further explanation makes both acts unwitting: the baraitot differ over whether the Sages penalized an unwitting act because of intentional acts.
Yet another explanation rejects that penalty and begins distinguishing return to the same courtyard; the distinction continues on the next daf.

4a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The final distinction from the previous daf is between returning the fruit to the same courtyard and taking it to another.
Rava asks Rav Nahman whether a hand full of fruit extended outside may be brought back to its original courtyard.
Rav Nahman permits returning it there.
May the fruit instead be brought into a different courtyard?
Rav Nahman forbids that transfer.
Why should the two courtyards differ?
Rav Nahman replies that return to the original courtyard does not complete the person's plan, whereas bringing the fruit into a different one does.
The Gemara returns to Rav Beivai bar Abaye's earlier question.
If someone stuck bread in an oven on Shabbat, may he remove it before baking creates liability for a sin offering?
Rav Aha asks whose removal is being considered: if the person acted unwittingly and remains unaware, he would not think to remove it.
If he remembered before the bread baked, he would not incur a sin offering: a cited mishnah requires the whole violation to be unwitting.
If he acted intentionally, the question should instead speak of avoiding a violation punishable by stoning.
Rav Sheila proposes that the actor remained unaware, but the question asks whether others may remove his bread.
Rav Sheshet objects: may one person sin so that another benefits?
Rav Ashi reads the case as intentional and corrects the question to avoiding liability for stoning.
Rav Aha son of Rava transmits the wording explicitly: the Sages permitted removal before the act becomes a stoning offense.
The discussion returns to the mishnah's case of the poor person extending his hand.
Why is the poor person liable if lifting and placing normally require a surface four by four handbreadths, which a hand lacks?
Rabba assigns the mishnah to Rabbi Akiva, who does not require a four by four place.
A cited mishnah has Rabbi Akiva imposing liability when an object flies across a public domain between two private domains; the Sages exempt.
Rabba reads the dispute as whether an object passing through public airspace counts as if it rested there: Rabbi Akiva says yes, the Sages no.
The Gemara begins challenging whether Rabba is certain that this is Rabbi Akiva's reason; the question continues on the next daf.

4b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: How can Rabba confidently locate the dispute below ten handbreadths when he had raised that very issue as an unresolved question?
Perhaps the dispute concerns an object below ten: Rabbi Akiva regards one in airspace as at rest, while the Sages do not; above ten all would exempt.
Or perhaps the dispute is above ten, over deriving throwing from passing, while below ten all would treat an airborne object as at rest and impose liability.
The uncertainty may have been resolved for Rabba later: Rabbi Akiva alone treats an airborne object as at rest.
Even so, perhaps Rabbi Akiva dispenses with a substantial surface for placing but still requires one for lifting.
Rav Yosef instead attributes our mishnah to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Which view of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi supports that attribution? A baraita makes him liable when an object lands on a projection of any size, against the Sages.

That case can concern a branch over the public domain from a tree rooted in the private domain. Rabbi treats the branch like its trunk; the Sages do not. It does not establish a general rule for a tiny surface.
Another baraita supplies the proposed basis: Rabbi imposes liability for a throw from public domain to public domain across a private domain, while the Sages exempt.
Shmuel reports that Rabbi imposes two liabilities there, one for bringing the object in and one for taking it out.
This suggests Rabbi does not demand a four by four surface for either placing or lifting.
The Gemara begins objecting that Rav and Shmuel qualified that case; their statement follows on the next daf.

5a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav and Shmuel limit Rabbi's liability in the cited throw to a roofed private domain, treated as though its space were full; an unroofed one does not establish the proposed rule.
Extending that explanation to our mishnah would require a roofed public domain as well. A cited ruling exempts carrying there because it differs from the uncovered desert encampment.
Rabbi Zeira instead attributes our mishnah to Aherim.
Aherim hold the thrower liable when the recipient stands still and catches the object, but exempt when the recipient moves to catch it.
If the stationary recipient catches it in a hand, where is the required four by four area for placing?
The proposed inference is that Aherim do not require such an area.
Perhaps only placing lacks that requirement, while lifting still needs it; and perhaps the recipient used an outspread garment large enough to count as a place.
Rabbi Abba proposes that our mishnah involves lifting from and placing on a basket large enough to provide the required area.
But the mishnah expressly says 'his hand.'
Read that phrase as 'the basket in his hand.'
A basket in the private domain may fit, but a qualifying basket in the public domain would itself count as a private domain.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda treats a basket atop a pole in the public domain as a private domain: throwing onto it incurs liability.
If that view governed our mishnah, a homeowner placing an object in the poor person's basket would move it from one private domain to another, not incur the stated liability.
The basket on the pole is above ten handbreadths; the basket in our mishnah can be below ten and remain in the public domain.
Rabbi Abbahu returns to the wording: the mishnah says 'his hand,' not 'the basket in his hand.'
He proposes that the recipient lowered his hand within three handbreadths of the ground, making it legally attached to the ground.
But the mishnah says the poor person is standing.
He could be stooping, standing in a hollow, or short enough for his hand to be near the ground.
Rava questions whether the tanna intended all those unusual circumstances.
Rava instead says a person's hand itself counts for that person as a four by four place.
Ravin transmits the same rule from Rabbi Yohanan.
Rabbi Yohanan also rules that a throw landing in another person's hand incurs liability.
Why state that case separately if Rabbi Yohanan already said a hand counts as four by four?
The second ruling shows that a receiving hand counts even when its owner did not deliberately treat it as a significant place.
Rabbi Yohanan rules the thrower liable when the recipient stands still to catch the object, but exempt if the recipient moves to catch it.
A baraita of Aherim teaches the same standing-versus-moving distinction.
Rabbi Yohanan asks about someone who throws an object, moves from his own place, and catches it himself.
What is the precise uncertainty in this case?
Rav Adda bar Ahava frames it as whether two separate efforts by one person count as one person's complete act, with liability, or like two people's divided act, with exemption.
The question remains unresolved.
Rabbi Yohanan states that someone who receives rainwater in a neighbor's courtyard and carries it out is liable.
Rabbi Zeira objects: receiving rain in one's hand seems no different from being handed an object by another; the carrier did not lift it.
Read the case as actively gathering the rainwater, rather than passively receiving it.
But from what four by four surface was the water lifted?
Rabbi Hiyya son of Rav Huna places the water on a wall before it was gathered.
Even there, the falling water may never have come to rest.
As in Rava's explanation elsewhere, the wall is sloped so the water can rest on it.
Where did Rava offer that explanation? The relevant mishnah follows on the next daf.

5b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A cited mishnah lets a reader on a threshold roll back a scroll that has slipped from his hand.
From a roof, the scroll may be rolled back before it reaches within ten handbreadths of the public ground; below that height it must be turned over instead.
Why not roll it back even then, if the scroll has not come to rest?
Rava explained that the wall is sloped, allowing the scroll to rest on it.
That can explain a scroll, but rainwater on a sloped wall keeps flowing and may not rest there.
Rava instead locates the collected rainwater above a hollow filled with water.
Would a hollow not make the case obvious?
The point is that water resting on water counts as at rest, despite a possible doubt about that placement.
Rava elsewhere explicitly says that water on water is at rest.
He contrasts a nut floating on water, which is not at rest.
Rava asks about a nut in a vessel floating on water: does the nut's rest in the vessel control, or the vessel's motion?
The dilemma remains unresolved.
The status of oil floating on wine is linked to a dispute between Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri and the Sages.
A purity mishnah treats contact with floating oil as affecting the oil alone, while Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri considers the oil and wine connected.
Rabbi Yohanan says that a loaded person who continually moves between domains is not liable for carrying until he stops.
Abaye specifies a stop to rest; a pause merely to adjust the load does not count.
A carrying rule distinguishes stopping to rest from stopping to shift a load, both within and beyond four cubits.
What new point does Rabbi Yohanan teach about the original lifting if he already taught that a lift not intended for carrying out does not create liability?
His earlier ruling exempts one who lifts objects to move them within a domain, then changes course and carries them outside.
Two transmitters expressed the same ruling of Rabbi Yohanan in different cases and wording.
A baraita holds a carrier liable for taking an object from a shop to a plaza through a colonnade, while ben Azzai exempts.
Ben Azzai treats walking as a series of stops, interrupting the transfer in the colonnade.
Even if the Sages do not count walking as stopping, what precedent makes a transfer through an intermediate domain liable?
Rav Safra begins transmitting Rabbi Yohanan's response; the explanation follows on the next daf.

6a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yohanan first compares the colonnade to carrying in public: one remains exempt while walking but becomes liable on setting the object down.
The analogy fails because any placement along a public route can complete liability, whereas placement in the colonnade cannot.
He next compares carrying to the end of four cubits: placement before four is exempt, but at the end it is liable.
That too differs: within four cubits is exempt only relative to this carrier, while the colonnade is an exempt place for everyone.
The closer precedent is carrying from private to public through the side of a public domain: placing at the side is exempt, but placing in the public area is liable.
Rav Pappa objects that this works for the Sages, but Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov treats the side as part of the public domain.
Rav Aha limits that view to sides without separating stakes; where stakes intervene, the side remains distinct and the comparison holds.
Rabbi Yohanan says ben Azzai agrees that throwing through the colonnade incurs liability.
A baraita confirms the split: ben Azzai exempts walking an object in or out through the colonnade, but holds throwing or passing it through liable.
A new baraita lists four Shabbat domains: private, public, karmelit, and exempt place.
What constitutes a private domain?
A ditch ten handbreadths deep and four wide, or a raised barrier ten high and four wide, is a full private domain.
What constitutes a public domain?
A highway, large plaza, or passage open at both ends forms a full public domain.
Carrying between those full private and public domains in either direction is forbidden.
An unwitting transfer entails a sin offering; an intentional transfer carries the stated severe penalties.
The sea, valley, and colonnade illustrate a karmelit, neither a full public nor a full private domain.
Carrying within a karmelit is forbidden, though one who does so is exempt from Torah liability.
Transfers between a karmelit and either public or private domain are also barred, but remain exempt from Torah liability.
Shared courtyards and blind alleys permit carrying with an eruv and prohibit it without one.
Someone on a qualifying threshold may exchange an object with the homeowner and likewise with the poor person.
The threshold occupant may not pass an object between the two sides; if that occurs, all three are exempt from Torah liability.
Aherim say a threshold can take the status of the inside when its door is open and the outside when it is shut.
A threshold ten handbreadths high and four wide instead forms its own domain.
What does the baraita's emphatic definition of 'the' private domain exclude?
It excludes Rabbi Yehuda's different rule.
A baraita begins Rabbi Yehuda's case of houses opposite each other across a public domain; its conditions continue on the next daf.

6b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda's case continues: he permits carrying between houses across a public street after placing symbolic posts or beams at its sides.
The Sages reject using those markers to enclose a public domain.
Why did the earlier baraita stress a 'full' private domain?
It rules out treating Rabbi Yehuda's marked street as a private domain even for liability from throwing, not merely for permission to carry there.
What does the baraita's emphatic definition of a full public domain exclude?
It excludes Rabbi Yehuda's view that a public path through a well enclosure must be diverted; the Sages say diversion is unnecessary.
Why call this public domain 'full'?
The wording follows the matching phrase used for the private domain.
Another baraita also lists the desert among public domains; why was it omitted here?
Abaye distinguishes the period when Israel camped in the desert from the present, when it is not similarly trafficked.
The earlier baraita says an unwitting transfer entails a sin offering, while an intentional one may entail excision or stoning.
Why state the obvious liability for an unwitting transfer?
The clause was included to set out the intentional penalties.
But those penalties also seem obvious.
The added point concerns Rav's report of a hidden scroll: Isi ben Yehuda names thirty-nine principal labors and says there is an exception to liability.
That cannot mean only one sin offering for all thirty-nine: Rabbi Yohanan explains that doing them all in one lapse incurs a separate offering for each.
Read Isi as exempting one unspecified labor from the severe intentional penalty; the baraita establishes that carrying is among the labors certainly subject to it.
The baraita again lists the valley with places that are neither full private nor full public domains.
But a purity mishnah calls a valley a private domain for Shabbat in summer and winter, though its purity status varies by season.
Ulla says it remains a karmelit; 'private' in that mishnah simply distinguishes it from a public domain.
Rav Ashi begins an alternative response, continued on the next daf.

7a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Ashi's alternative from the previous daf treats the valley as having partitions.
Ulla cites Rabbi Yohanan: even a very large enclosure not made for dwelling remains a private domain for liability when an object is thrown into it.
Why does such an enclosure count as private?
Its partitions are legally effective, though it lacks residential use.
Why did Ulla not use that explanation for the valley, even if Rav Ashi chose another reading?
Ulla would say an area with partitions should be called an enclosure, not a valley.
Rav Ashi relies on the other mishnah's explicit description of the valley as a private domain.
Why list 'karmelit' separately when the other listed locations already have that status?
Rabbi Yohanan says it includes a corner by the public domain that crowds sometimes enter, but whose awkward use keeps it a karmelit.
Rabbi Yohanan also classifies the area between public-domain pillars as a karmelit.
Even when people walk there, the pillars obstruct direct passage and make its use inconvenient.
Rav Yehuda similarly classifies a bench before the pillars as a karmelit.
One who treats the space between pillars as a karmelit would all the more treat the bench that way.
A view limited to the bench can distinguish the more convenient space between the pillars.
Another version says that space is public because people sometimes pass through it.
Rav Hisda rules that an object striking the side of an upright brick in public incurs liability, but landing on top does not.
Abaye and Rava limit that distinction to a brick at least three handbreadths high, beyond normal foot traffic.
They treat thorny growth as avoided by walkers even below three handbreadths.
Hiyya bar Rav regards low thorns as part of the public area, but excludes filth people avoid.
Rav Ashi says even filth can still be part of the public area.
Rabbi Yohanan states that a karmelit must have at least four handbreadths of area.
Rav Sheshet adds that its extent reaches ten handbreadths.
Does that mean it requires partitions ten handbreadths high, with no karmelit below that height?
A house whose interior height is under ten but roof reaches ten allows carrying across the roof, while carrying inside is limited to four cubits: the interior can be a karmelit.
Thus the ten-handbreadth limit concerns height above the ground: beyond that, an area is not a karmelit.
Shmuel likewise told Rav Yehuda that questions of Shabbat domains need not focus above ten handbreadths.
Could Shmuel mean that private domain itself ends at that height?
Rav Hisda's ruling contradicts that: even a hundred-cubit pole in a private domain has private-domain airspace up to its top.

7b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If Shmuel meant that public-domain airspace stops at ten handbreadths, a mishnah already says so by distinguishing a throw against a wall above and below that height.
His point must concern a karmelit: its status does not extend above ten handbreadths, and the Sages gave it limits drawn from both main domains.
Like a private domain, a karmelit needs an area four handbreadths wide; a smaller place is exempt.
Like a public domain, its special status reaches only ten handbreadths above the ground.
The Gemara repeats the ruling: a low-interior house whose roof reaches ten allows carrying on its roof, but limits carrying inside to four cubits.
Abaye says that digging a four by four area to make ten handbreadths of interior height permits carrying throughout the house.
The remaining interior is treated as ancillary recesses of a private domain.
All agree that recesses of a private domain share its status; Abaye and Rava dispute whether recesses of a public domain share public status.
Rava asks Abaye why an awkward corner next to a public domain was classified as a karmelit rather than as a recess of the public domain.
Abaye distinguishes the inconvenient corner from readily usable public-domain recesses.
A mishnah compares a throw striking a wall below ten handbreadths to a throw landing on the ground, but treats one above ten as in the air.
How can the lower throw count as placed if an ordinary object would bounce off?
Rabbi Yohanan reads the case as a sticky fig cake adhering to the wall.
If wall recesses count as public domain, why not use an ordinary object that rests in a hole, rather than a sticky fig?
One reply is that an ordinary object may rebound instead of remaining there.
Another reply reads the mishnah as describing a wall with no holes.
The clause above ten supports that reading: if there were a hole, an object resting in it would not merely remain in the air.
Even a small hole might matter under Rabbi Meir's rule of treating a cavity as notionally enlarged; the Sages disagree, so hole size alone cannot remove the issue.
The Gemara concludes that the mishnah indeed concerns a wall without a hole.
Rav Hisda says an object resting on a pole in private-domain ground incurs liability even a hundred cubits high, since private-domain airspace rises upward.
Does Rav Hisda therefore follow only Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi?
A baraita has Rabbi impose liability for landing on a projection of any size, while the Sages exempt.
That seems to make the pole ruling depend on Rabbi's rejection of a four by four landing-area requirement.

8a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abaye answers the challenge from the previous daf: all agree with Rav Hisda about a pole within the private domain.
The disputed baraita instead concerns a tree rooted in private ground, with a branch extending into public ground and an object landing on that branch.
Rabbi assigns the branch the status of its trunk and imposes liability; the Sages do not.
Abaye says a ten-handbreadth-high reed basket thrown into public is liable if under six wide, but exempt if six wide, when it forms its own domain.
Rava exempts even a basket under six wide.
Its reed tips necessarily protrude above ten handbreadths, so it never fully enters the liable public airspace.
For an inverted basket, seven handbreadths and a little more incurs liability, while seven and a half is exempt.
Rav Ashi holds even an inverted basket seven and a half high liable.
Its walls are made for the basket's interior and are not legally extended downward to create a domain.
Ulla says an object landing on a nine-handbreadth pillar used by passersby to adjust loads incurs liability.
Below three handbreadths people step on a projection; from three to nine they neither step nor rest burdens on it; at nine they rest burdens there.
Abaye asks whether a hole of comparable depth has the same status.
Rav Yosef says it does.
Rava disagrees because using a hole is awkward; use under strain does not count as ordinary public use.
Rav Adda cites a baraita: a basket ten high and four wide is separate from public ground, a smaller one is not, and it adds 'likewise with a hole.'
Does the comparison apply to the smaller basket, making a shallow hole public?
Rava limits it to the first clause, a deep hole forming a private domain.
Rav Adda begins another objection, continued on the next daf.

8b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Adda's baraita says food for an eruv placed in a pit is valid above ten handbreadths but invalid below that depth.
If the pit itself is at least ten deep, why distinguish where inside it the food sits? It is a private domain throughout, apart from the intended public place of residence.
Perhaps the valid case is a pit under ten deep, implying that awkward use of such a pit still counts as public use.
One response puts both the person and the eruv in a karmelit; 'public' is used loosely to mean nonprivate.
Another puts the person in public and the food in a karmelit, following Rabbi's rule that rabbinic restrictions do not apply at twilight when the eruv takes effect.
Rava insists these are substantive answers and turns to a marsh mishnah for support.
That mishnah twice deems a throw into a shallow marsh traversed by the public liable as a public-domain throw.
Repeating 'marsh' can cover both summer and winter: people might enter for coolness in summer or through muddy conditions in winter.
Why also repeat that the public walks through it?
The repetition distinguishes passage even when awkward, which counts as walking, from awkward use of a place, which does not count as normal use.
Rav Yehuda says repeatedly tipping a bundle of reeds forward does not incur carrying liability until it is actually lifted from the ground.
The earlier threshold teaching permits the person there to exchange objects separately with the homeowner and the poor person.
What sort of threshold is meant?
If it is public domain, taking from the homeowner would be a forbidden transfer from private to public.
If it is private domain, taking from the poor person would be a forbidden transfer from public to private.
If it is a karmelit, even the permitted-looking exchanges would still be prohibited by the Sages.
It must be an exempt place smaller than four by four handbreadths.
Rabbi Yohanan likewise permits people of either main domain to set burdens on a small exempt place, provided they do not pass objects between domains.
The teaching forbids passing an object from homeowner to poor person or vice versa through the threshold, yet exempts all three if it happens.
Could that exemption refute Rava?
Rava's contrasting ruling about carrying across four cubits in public begins here and continues on the next daf.

9a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The previous daf's challenge cites Rava: carrying across four cubits in public remains liable even when the object passes through exempt airspace.
The cases differ: Rava's object never rested in the exempt area; the threshold case includes a stop there.
Aherim say an open doorway makes the threshold like the inside, while a closed door makes it like the outside.
How can an open threshold be treated as inside without the additional side post Rav requires for a doorway?
The problem remains even if the opening is smaller than four by four handbreadths; Rav still requires a separate post.
Rav identifies an alley threshold, half roofed toward the inside and half unroofed.
With its door open it joins the inside; with the door shut it takes the outside status.
Rav Ashi instead posits a house threshold roofed by two narrow beams less than three handbreadths apart, with the door between them.
Opening the door lets the beams combine for inside status; shutting it separates them and leaves the outer section outside.
A threshold ten handbreadths high and four wide constitutes a domain of its own.
The Gemara treats this as support for Rav Yitzhak bar Avdimi's report.
Rabbi Meir forbids setting a burden on a qualifying pillar even inside a private domain, by decree because a comparable mound in public would be a separate private domain.

9b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishnah bars beginning a haircut shortly before afternoon prayer until one has prayed.
It likewise bars starting a bath, work at a tannery, a meal, or a court session then.
Once such an activity has begun, the participants need not interrupt it for the prayer.
They do interrupt for the Shema, but not for the Amidah.
Which afternoon prayer time does 'near mincha' mean?
If it means the earlier time, why prohibit starting when much daylight remains?
The first proposal is the later afternoon prayer period.
But the mishnah's permission not to interrupt a begun meal then would conflict with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who prohibits tasting anything once mincha time arrives.
The mishnah can instead mean the earlier period and a particularly elaborate haircut.
Its bath and tannery examples can likewise mean a full bathhouse visit and a large tannery task.
Its meal can be large and its court case just beginning, so each activity may take much time.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov allows even an ordinary haircut in the case: broken scissors might delay its end.
Even entering the bathhouse merely to sweat is barred, lest the person faint and lose time.
Even inspecting hides can cause a distracting discovery of a loss.
Even a small meal may run long.
Even a case near judgment may be reopened by a new line of reasoning.
When is a haircut considered to have begun?
Rav Avin says when the barber's covering is placed over the customer's knees.
When does a bathhouse visit begin?
Rav Avin says when the visitor removes an outer wrap.
When does work at the tannery begin?
When the worker ties on the apron.
When does eating begin?
Rav says at handwashing; Rabbi Hanina says at loosening the belt.
The Gemara reconciles the practices as applying to different communities.
Abaye considers Babylonian scholars who loosen their belts: if evening prayer is optional, they need not stop eating, but if obligatory, one might impose a stop.
Yet afternoon prayer is obligatory by all views, and the mishnah says a begun meal need not be interrupted; Rabbi Hanina defines that beginning by loosening the belt.

10a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Afternoon meals rarely lead to drunkenness, unlike evening meals, so the prayer cases differ.
Alternatively, mincha has a fixed endpoint that keeps a person alert; the all-night evening prayer can be postponed and forgotten.
Rav Sheshet asks whether retightening a belt is truly burdensome and why one cannot simply pray while it is loose.
Prayer requires suitable preparation, supported by 'Prepare to meet your God, Israel.'
Rava bar Rav Huna dresses carefully for prayer in keeping with that verse.
Rava instead removes his cloak and clasps his hands, approaching prayer like a servant before a master.
Rav Kahana uses a humble stance amid distress, but dresses and wraps himself when conditions are peaceful.
Seeing Rav Hamnuna pray at length, Rava objects that this leaves enduring Torah study for transient requests.
Rav Hamnuna treats the times for prayer and Torah study as distinct.
Rabbi Yirmeya hurries to pray while studying with Rabbi Zeira.
Rabbi Zeira applies the verse warning that turning from Torah renders one's prayer unacceptable.
When is a court case considered begun?
One view starts at the judges' wrapping themselves; another starts when the litigants present their claims.
The views refer respectively to judges beginning a new sitting or continuing from an earlier case.
Rav Ami and Rav Asi study while repeatedly inviting anyone with a dispute to enter for judgment.
Rav Hisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna judge all day and grow faint.
Rav Hiyya cites the verse describing people standing before Moses from morning until evening.
Could Moses really have judged all day and still studied Torah?
Even one hour of truthful judgment is credited as partnership with God in sustaining creation.
The wording 'morning until evening' is linked to creation's 'evening and morning.'
Until what time should judges sit?
Rav Sheshet says until mealtime.
Rav Hama cites Ecclesiastes' praise of leaders who eat at the proper time after the strength of Torah, without drunkenness.
A baraita assigns eating hours to different groups, placing ordinary people's meal in the fifth hour.
Rav Pappa instead calls the fourth hour the ordinary mealtime.
The schedule is revised: ordinary people in the fourth hour, workers fifth, scholars sixth; eating later is compared to throwing a stone into a vessel.
Abaye limits that late-eating concern to someone who tasted nothing in the morning.
Rav Adda bar Ahava says a person may pray in a bathhouse.
A teaching permits prayer and Torah in the bathhouse's fully clothed room, distinguishing it from the other rooms.
In the mixed clothed-and-unclothed room, greetings remain allowed but prayer and Torah are forbidden.
In the fully unclothed room, even greetings are forbidden and tefillin must be removed, sharpening the objection.
The first response says Rav Adda meant an empty bathhouse.
Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina says an established bathhouse remains restricted even when empty, just as an established toilet remains so without waste.
The ruling is reinterpreted as referring to a new, unused bathhouse.
Ravina's unresolved question about a place designated for a toilet raises a parallel doubt for a newly designated bathhouse.
The Gemara begins distinguishing the bathhouse from that toilet question; the distinction continues on the next daf.

10b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A designated toilet differs from an unused bathhouse because the toilet's very function is repugnant.
The bathhouse teaching forbids a greeting of shalom in its inner area.
Rav Hamnuna cites Ulla's prohibition on saying shalom there, since Scripture uses Shalom as a divine name.
Then should the word for faithfulness also be forbidden in a toilet, since God is called faithful?
A transmitted ruling explicitly permits saying that word in a toilet.
Faithful describes God rather than naming Him; Shalom is used as a name itself.
Rav says a gift giver should let the recipient know of the gift.
The rule is linked to the verse about knowing that God sanctifies Israel.
A baraita reads the gift of Shabbat as something God told Moses to announce to Israel.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel therefore says one giving bread to a child should inform the child's mother.
How can the giver make the gift known to her?
Abaye suggests marking the child with oil and eye coloring.
What if such markings raise concern about witchcraft?
Rav Pappa suggests marking the child with some of the same kind of food.
Another teaching says a giver need not inform the recipient, citing Moses' unawareness that his face shone.
The obligation depends on whether the gift will become known on its own.
But Shabbat itself would become known without a separate announcement.
Its reward would not become known, so that aspect needed to be announced.
Rav Hisda offers portions of an ox to anyone bringing him a new teaching in Rav's name.
Rava bar Mehasseya gives him Rav's teaching that a gift giver should inform the recipient, with its verse.
Rav Hisda hands him the promised gift.
Rava asks whether Rav's teachings are so dear to him.
Rav Hisda says yes.
Rava adds another saying of Rav: fine cloth is precious to those who wear it.
Rav Hisda prizes this second saying even more and would have rewarded it too.
Rav warns a parent against favoring one child over the others.
Jacob's extra gift to Joseph aroused his brothers' jealousy and set in motion the descent to Egypt.
Rav recommends settling in a newer city, whose history of wrongdoing is shorter.
Lot's description of a nearby small city is cited in support.
Why point out its visible nearness and smallness if those physical facts were already apparent?
Its nearness refers instead to its recent settlement and comparatively few sins.
Rabbi Avin reads the numerical value of Lot's 'na' as fifty-one years, one less than Sodom; the account continues on the next daf.

11a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The years of service, rebellion, and war in Genesis complete the previous daf's chronology of the cities' history.
Rav warns that a city with house roofs higher than its synagogue will ultimately be ruined.
He connects the warning to the call to raise God's house and restore its ruins.
The comparison concerns houses, not projecting structures such as towers or poles.
Rav Ashi says he kept Mata Mehasseya from this fate.
But the city was destroyed.
Its destruction was not due to this particular failing.
Rav ranks the burdens of subordination, ending with the greater danger of mistreating a Torah scholar, orphan, or widow.
He lists especially painful kinds of illness and distress in a series of comparisons.
Rav describes governmental responsibility as too vast for even boundless writing supplies to record.
Rav Mesharshiya supports the image with the verse that the heart of kings is beyond searching.
Rav says a fast counters a troubling dream as fire consumes chaff.
Rav Hisda specifies fasting on the very day of the dream.
Rav Yosef extends that allowance even to Shabbat.
Visiting Rav Ashi's house, Rav Yehoshua son of Rav Idi is offered a special meal.
He says he is fasting.
His hosts ask why he does not postpone this fast and make it up later.
He explains that it is a dream fast.
He repeats the teachings that such a fast works on that day, even on Shabbat.
The earlier mishnah says begun activities need not stop for prayer, but one stops for Shema.
Why repeat the rule about interruption?
The latter clause addresses Torah study: a baraita says scholars interrupt for Shema but not prayer.
Rabbi Yohanan limits that exemption from prayer to scholars wholly devoted to Torah; others interrupt for both.
Another baraita says such work is interrupted for neither prayer nor Shema.
That exceptional case concerns calendrical intercalation, supported by testimony that the sages at Yavne stopped for neither.
A new mishnah forbids a tailor to carry a needle near nightfall lest he forget and take it out on Shabbat.
A scribe likewise may not go out with a pen.
The mishnah also restricts searching clothes and reading by lamplight.
An attendant may locate the children's reading place by the light, though he may not read himself.
As another precaution, a zav and a zava should not eat together lest it lead to prohibited intimacy.
The Gemara cites a parallel rule: one may not stand in one domain and drink from the other.
It permits drinking after the person's head and most of the body enter the domain of the drink.

11b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The parallel drinking rule ends by extending its ruling to a wine press.
Does the drinking restriction also apply to a karmelit?
Abaye says it applies there in the same way.
Rava objects that this would add a safeguard around a prohibition already created by rabbinic safeguard.
Abaye points to the wine press clause: if it is neither an ordinary private nor public example, perhaps it represents a karmelit.
Rava and Rav Sheshet read the wine press clause as concerning tithes rather than Shabbat domains.
The supporting tithe mishnah distinguishes drinking warm and cool mixtures at a press and whether leftovers can be returned.
The Gemara recalls the mishnah barring a tailor's needle near nightfall.
Could it mean a needle stuck in the garment, whose carrying would itself be only rabbinically prohibited?
The needle may instead be held in the hand, a normal way of carrying.
A baraita explicitly bars going out with a needle stuck in clothing.
Is that restriction on Shabbat eve, implying a safeguard around a safeguard?
The baraita can refer to Shabbat itself.
Another baraita expressly places the restriction on Shabbat eve near dark.
That teaching follows Rabbi Yehuda, who treats a craftsperson's usual carrying method as liable by Torah law.
A baraita lists craftspersons carrying their tools in the distinctive ways used in their work.
Rabbi Meir exempts them from Torah liability while forbidding the practice.
Rabbi Yehuda makes a craftsperson liable when carrying in that customary fashion, but exempts others.
Two teachings disagree whether a zav carrying his pouch is exempt or owes a sin offering.
Rav Yosef attributes the exempt ruling to Rabbi Meir and the liable one to Rabbi Yehuda.
Abaye objects: Rabbi Meir's exemption concerns an unusual manner of carrying, whereas this pouch is normally carried that way; even an unskilled maker can perform a complete labor.
Rav Hamnuna distinguishes a zav after two sightings, who needs the pouch for checking, from one after three.
But after three sightings the pouch can still help track seven clean days.
The exempt case can be the same day as the third sighting, which cannot count as clean.
The pouch still keeps his clothes from becoming soiled.
Rabbi Zeira says this tanna does not treat preventing filth as a legally significant use.
A purity mishnah about placing a bowl in rain begins illustrating the significance of the user's purpose; its contrasting case continues on the next daf.

12a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The prior daf's bowl mishnah says rain collected solely to protect a wall does not count as intentionally placed liquid.
The comparison fails: the wall owner has no use for that water, while the zav wants the pouch to receive an emission.
The closer case is a trough where retained rainwater counts as wanted, although splashed water does not.
Abaye and Rava instead resolve the pouch rulings by assigning them to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon, who differ over labor done for an indirect purpose.
A baraita permits going out with tefillin near nightfall on Shabbat eve.
Why is there no concern that the wearer will forget them?
The wearer is expected to touch the tefillin regularly and remain aware of them.
An a fortiori argument uses the priestly frontplate: if its one divine name requires constant awareness, tefillin with many names do so even more.
Thus the wearer will remember the tefillin.
Hananya requires checking one's clothing near nightfall on Shabbat eve.
Rav Yosef calls this a significant Shabbat precaution.
The discussion returns to the mishnah's prohibition on searching clothes.
Is searching barred even by day lest one kill a louse, as Rabbi Eliezer holds, while reading by lamp is barred lest one adjust it? Or do both rules concern the lamp?
A baraita pairs searching clothes with reading by lamplight.
That wording is no more decisive than the mishnah itself.
Another baraita explicitly places both actions by lamplight; the Gemara concludes both decrees concern adjusting the lamp.
Shmuel extends the precaution even to distinguishing one's garment from one's wife's by lamplight.
Rava limits that case to similar garments in Mehoza, especially those of older women; more distinct clothing needs no close inspection.
A baraita forbids removing lice in the public domain out of regard for dignity.
Likewise, one should not induce vomiting in public.
One teaching permits squeezing and discarding a louse but forbids killing it.
Abba Shaul would allow taking and discarding it but forbid squeezing it.
Rav Huna rules to squeeze and discard it, calling that the dignified course even on a weekday.
The Gemara reports different practices of Rabba, Rav Sheshet, Rava, and Rav Nahman regarding lice.
Beit Shammai forbid killing lice on Shabbat; Beit Hillel permit it.
The houses also differ over arranging children's marriages or education, comforting mourners, and visiting the sick on Shabbat.
A baraita gives words for visiting the sick on Shabbat, with Rabbi Meir adding a different expression of hoped-for mercy.

12b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei give different formulations that include the sick person with Israel's sick in the Shabbat visit.
Shevna greets the patient on entering and offers words of healing and peace on leaving.
Which formulation fits Rabbi Hanina's instruction to include a sick household member among Israel's sick?
It follows Rabbi Yosei.
Rabbi Hanina says visiting the sick and comforting mourners were permitted on Shabbat only with difficulty.
Rabbi Elazar sometimes offers a Hebrew blessing for a patient and sometimes an Aramaic one.
How can he use Aramaic for a request when teachings say ministering angels do not attend to prayers in that language?
A sick person's case differs because the Divine Presence is with the patient.
Rav Anan reads God's support of one on a sickbed as evidence of that presence.
A baraita has a visitor sit respectfully below the patient because the Divine Presence is above the patient's head.
The same verse is also used to describe God's care for the sick person's sustenance.
The discussion returns to the ban on reading by lamplight.
Rabba says the ban remains even when the lamp is far or very high above the reader.
Does the singular wording imply that two readers may read together?
A baraita forbids both one and two readers.
Two studying one topic can remind each other; two studying different topics cannot.
Rav Huna says even ten readers may not rely on a bonfire's light.
Rava allows a person of stature to read, assuming such a person will not adjust the lamp.
Rabbi Yishmael thought he could read without adjusting it, yet the light tempted him to do so.
He acknowledged the force of the Sages' ban.
Rabbi Natan reports that Rabbi Yishmael actually adjusted the lamp and recorded an obligation to bring an offering when possible.
Rabbi Abba distinguishes Rabbi Yishmael, who treated himself simply when studying Torah.
Two baraitot disagree whether a servant may inspect dishes by lamplight.
One distinction is between a permanent servant who checks closely and a temporary servant.
Another distinguishes an oil lamp, which one might adjust, from an unpleasant naphtha lamp.
May a temporary servant inspect by an oil lamp?
Rav permits it in law but declines to teach that permission publicly.
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba says the permission may also be taught openly.
At Rav Asi's home, Rabbi Yirmeya's servant checks by lamplight, and Rav Asi allows him to follow his teacher's ruling.
If the attendant may only see where children read, does that not let him read too?
He may only prepare the beginnings of the passages.
Rabba bar Shmuel also permits arranging those openings.
May the attendant not read the whole passage? The discussion continues on the next daf.

13a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says pupils may arrange passages and read by lamplight, challenging the restriction on reading near a lamp.
One reading limits the permission to preparing the openings of the passages.
Alternatively, pupils fear their teacher and will not adjust the lamp.
The mishnah also forbids a zav to eat with a zava.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar explains that ritual purity was common; the stated concern is that the zav and zava might become accustomed to intimacy.
Likewise, a scrupulous zav should not eat with an unlearned zav, lest closeness develop.
What harm would come from their becoming close?
The proposed concern is that the unlearned zav might serve him impure food.
But a zav is already impure, so why would such food matter?
Abaye instead fears that the other man might serve untithed food.
Rava objects that most unlearned people do separate tithes.
Rava says the concern is continued familiarity: after the scrupulous zav becomes pure, he might be served impure food.
May a menstruating woman and her husband sleep in one bed if each remains dressed?
Rav Yosef cites the dispute about setting fowl and cheese on one table as a possible parallel for keeping distance from a prohibited act.
The table case may differ because it involves one person; two people can restrain each other.
The latter ruling allows two guests to eat meat and cheese at one table, suggesting that two people change the rule.
Shmuel limits the guests ruling to strangers; familiar guests may not share the table, and spouses are familiar.
Unlike the guests, the dressed spouses have both two people and a visible change from their usual conduct.
An alternate version begins by citing the permission for two guests to eat meat and cheese at one table.
Shmuel restricts that permission to strangers, while the husband and wife know each other.
Here the spouses also have the distinctive change of remaining clothed.
The mishnah forbids a zav and zava to eat together lest they become accustomed to intimacy.
Eating together has no distinctive change comparable to remaining clothed in bed.
Ezekiel places the ban on approaching a menstruating woman beside the ban on defiling a neighbor’s wife.
The juxtaposition forbids sharing a bed even while clothed, as with a neighbor’s wife; the question is resolved.
Rabbi Pedat disagrees: he reads the Torah ban on approach as limited to contact leading to forbidden sexual relations.
Ulla would kiss his sisters, with reports differing as to whether on the chest or hands.
Ulla’s conduct conflicts with his own instruction to avoid even proximity to prohibited intimacy, like a nazirite avoiding a vineyard.

A learned student died midway through life. His wife brought his tefillin to study houses and questioned how his many years of study fit the promise of long life; her account continues on the next daf.

13b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The widow finishes her challenge: why did a student who served sages so extensively die in midlife?
No one answered her. The narrator later stayed with her and heard the account.
He asks how her husband behaved toward her during her menstrual period.
She says he did not touch her at all then.
He asks how he behaved during her subsequent clean days.
She says they ate, drank, and slept with bodily closeness, though they did not intend relations.
He attributes the student’s death to disregarding the Torah’s command not to approach a menstruating woman.
Rav Dimi reports that they shared one bed; another report says a belt separated them.
The mishnah recounts that Beit Shammai outnumbered Beit Hillel in Hananya’s upper chamber and enacted eighteen decrees that day.
Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether the mishnah begins “these” or “and these.”
The wording decides whether it points back to the earlier decrees or ahead to those still to be listed.
A baraita joins the lamp restrictions to “and these” among the upper chamber rulings.
The text therefore reads “and these,” referring back to the earlier rulings.
Who wrote Megillat Ta’anit?
Hananya ben Hizkiya and his circle recorded the troubles and deliverances they valued.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says his generation also values such events, but there are too many to record.
One explanation says people fail to recognize the harm that surrounds them.
Another compares their lack of awareness to flesh insensible to a scalpel.
Rav Yitzhak says the dead do feel the pain of worms, citing Job; that challenges the analogy.
The analogy is recast as dead flesh that does not feel a scalpel.
Rav praises Hananya for reconciling apparent contradictions between Ezekiel and the Torah, preserving the book.
The discussion returns to the mishnah and asks which eighteen matters were decreed.
A mishnah lists people and objects that disqualify teruma, including eaters of impure food, drawn water, a scroll, hands, and items touched by impure liquids.
The Gemara begins asking which tanna says eaters of first- or second-degree impure food disqualify teruma; the inquiry continues.

14a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The preceding question distinguishes disqualifying teruma from making it transmit impurity.
Rabba bar bar Hana identifies Rabbi Yehoshua as the tanna behind that distinction.
Rabbi Eliezer assigns the eater the same impurity degree as the food eaten.
Rabbi Yehoshua instead makes eaters of first- or second-degree food second degree, and limits the effect of third-degree food to sacred items.
The discussion returns to people who eat first- or second-degree impure food.
Why did the Sages impose impurity on them?
Impure food remaining in the mouth could disqualify teruma liquid put there afterward.
The next case is one who drinks impure liquid.
Why is that person also subject to the decree?
Impure liquid in the mouth could disqualify teruma food put there.
Why state both versions of essentially the same concern?
The less common sequence might have seemed exempt, so the mishnah teaches that both are included.
The next decree concerns a person who puts head and most of the body into drawn water.
Why was impurity decreed in that case?
Rav Beivai says people washed off foul cave water with drawn water after immersion, then began treating that wash as part of purification.
What does it mean that they made the wash a fixed practice?
Abaye says they thought both cave water and drawn water purified.
Rava objects that they still immersed in the cave water, so that mistaken explanation should not invalidate the act.
Rava says they came to think drawn water alone purified, which explains the decree.
Another decree covers a pure person on whose head and most of whose body three log of drawn water fall.
Why extend the decree to an already pure person?
Without that extension, the decree concerning someone who had just immersed would not endure.
Why did the Sages decree impurity concerning a Torah scroll?
People stored teruma next to Torah scrolls because both were sacred; mice drawn to the food damaged the scrolls, so a decree separated them.
Hands are affected because they frequently touch things without care.
A baraita says even hands that touch a Torah scroll disqualify teruma.
Rabbi Parnakh’s warning against grasping an uncovered scroll explains that added decree.
Does “buried naked” literally mean without clothing?
Rabbi Zeira first interprets it as without mitzvot.
Could one mistake really erase all of a person’s mitzvot?
The warning means losing credit for that particular mitzva.
Which hand-impurity decree came first? The argument begins on the next daf.

14b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If general hand impurity was decreed first, a separate decree for hands touching a scroll would add nothing.
The scroll decree therefore came first, followed by the decree for all hands.
Why count someone who immersed that day among new decrees when Torah law keeps such a person impure until sunset?
Remove that case from the list of new decrees.
Which liquids transmitted impurity to the listed foods? Liquids contaminated by a creeping animal are already covered by Torah law.
The decree concerns liquids made impure by hands, modeled on liquids contaminated by a creeping animal.
Which liquids transmitted impurity to the listed vessels? A zav’s secretions already do so by Torah law.
The decree extends vessel impurity to liquids affected by a creeping animal, by analogy with a zav’s secretions.
Were the students of Shammai and Hillel really the first to decree hand impurity?
A baraita attributes earlier decrees to other sages and the hand decree to Shammai and Hillel themselves.
Shammai and Hillel cannot mean their factions: the eighteen disputes belong to their students, while the teachers disputed only three cases.
A proposed difference between suspending and burning affected teruma fails because Ilfa says burning was required from the start.
The teachers issued the decree but it was not accepted; the students reissued it and people accepted it.
The question remains: Shmuel attributes a hand-washing ordinance to Solomon and cites a heavenly voice praising him.
A response begins here and continues on the next daf.

15a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Solomon decreed impurity of hands for sacred offerings; later sages extended it to teruma.
Shmuel says the sages enacted eighteen decrees amid eighteen disputes.
A baraita instead says they agreed on those matters.
They disputed that day and came to agreement the next day.
Rav Huna says Shammai and Hillel disputed in three places.
First, they differ over the amount of dough requiring hallah; the sages give an intermediate measure and later adjustments.
Second, they differ over how much drawn water disqualifies a mikveh; testimony from two weavers establishes three log.
Third, they differ over retroactive impurity after menstrual blood is found; the sages limit it by the shorter of a day or the last examination.
Was their dispute over laying hands on festival offerings not a fourth case?
Rav Huna counts only disputes that did not also involve earlier sages.
What about their dispute over grapes harvested for the winepress?
Hillel ultimately fell silent before Shammai on that question, so it is set aside.
The earlier baraita credited Yosei ben Yoezer and Yosei ben Yohanan with decrees on foreign lands and glass vessels.
Were those decrees not issued by sages of a much later generation?
Rav Kahana introduces a report from Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei that gives a later date.
The report dates Roman rule, the decrees on foreign land and glass, and the Sanhedrin’s relocation before the Temple’s destruction.
What legal effect did the Sanhedrin’s relocation have?
Rabbi Yitzhak first says fines were no longer judged.
The suggestion about fines is challenged as implausible.
The correction is that capital cases were no longer judged.
The later date still conflicts with the early era of Yosei ben Yoezer and Yosei ben Yohanan, who preceded Hillel’s family by many years.

15b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: An initial answer stages the foreign-land decree: the early sages required burning for contact with its soil, while later sages suspended teruma entering its airspace.
Ilfa’s statement that only the hand decree began at the burning level challenges that sequence.
A revision puts the early soil decree at suspension and the later soil decree at burning, with airspace at suspension.
A further challenge attributes the burning rule to the later gathering at Usha.
A mishnah lists six doubtful impurities, including foreign soil, for which definite contact leads to burning teruma.
Rabbi Yosei and the sages differ about uncertain contact in private and public places.
Ulla says the six doubtful-impurity rules were instituted at Usha.
The final chronology: early sages suspend for soil only; later sages suspend for soil and air; Usha requires burning for soil while air remains suspended.
Why did the sages decree impurity for glass vessels?
Because glass begins as sand, they likened it to earthenware.
Earthenware cannot be purified by immersion, but a mishnah treats adhering pitch or myrrh as an obstruction to immersion of glass.
The immersion case involves a perforated glass vessel repaired with lead; Rabbi Meir follows the repairing material.
A baraita reports Rabbi Meir and the sages differing over glass repaired with lead.
A further difficulty with equating glass and earthenware begins here and continues on the next daf.

16a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If glass is treated like earthenware, why does a mishnah equate earthenware only with natron vessels and exclude glass?
Unlike earthenware, broken glass can be remade, so the sages also compared it to metal.
If glass is like metal, why do remade glass vessels acquire impurity only from now on, while remade metal vessels regain their earlier impurity?
Glass impurity and restored impurity are both rabbinic; the sages did not layer the latter decree upon the former.
Even so, why not decree impurity for flat glass vessels, as flat metal vessels are impure by Torah law?
The sages left that difference visible so people would not burn teruma or sacred food over rabbinic glass impurity.

16b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Ashi keeps the comparison to earthenware: glass has no visible difference between inner and outer surfaces.
The prior baraita credits Shimon ben Shatah with the marriage contract and an impurity decree concerning metal vessels.
Why would metal vessels need a decree when their impurity is explicit in the Torah?
The decree makes remade metal vessels regain former impurity; Queen Shel Tziyyon’s broken and repaired vessels illustrate it.
Why impose that rule?
It protects the required use of purification water for corpse impurity.
That rationale works if the rule applies only to corpse impurity, but what explains its extension to all impurities?
Abaye fears someone may not make a hole large enough to purify the vessel before repairing it.
Rava fears observers will wrongly infer that same-day immersion alone purifies a vessel.
What difference follows from their explanations?
They differ when the vessel was broken completely.
Which further decree belongs to the set of eighteen?
A mishnah addresses rain collected in vessels under a drain: Beit Shammai disqualifies a mikveh even if vessels were forgotten, while Beit Hillel permits the forgotten case.
Rabbi Meir says Beit Shammai won the vote, with an exception for forgotten vessels in a courtyard; Rabbi Yosei says the dispute remained.
Rav Mesharshiya locates the dispute where clouds gathered, dispersed, then returned: did the first intent to collect rain lapse?
On Rabbi Yosei’s account, the rainwater vote does not supply another agreed decree; what fills the count?
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak supplies the decree treating Samaritan girls as menstruants from birth.
What other decree was enacted?
A mishnah about movable objects as wide as an ox goad transmitting corpse impurity is introduced; the argument continues.

17a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Tarfon says the ox-goad ruling was misreported: the goad itself becomes impure when it covers a grave, but that does not prove it transmits impurity onward.
Rabbi Akiva reformulates the rule: movable objects affect their carriers at the ox-goad measure, themselves at any size, and others only at a handbreadth.
Rabbi Yannai explains that a goad’s circumference, rather than its thickness, is a handbreadth; the sages extended the tent rule to it.
If Rabbi Tarfon rejects this as a separate decree, how can the count of eighteen be completed?
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak counts the decree concerning Samaritan girls and follows Rabbi Meir on the rainwater ruling.
Another decree concerns grapes harvested for the press: Shammai deems them susceptible to impurity, Hillel does not.
Hillel asks why grape harvesting requires purity while olive harvesting does not.
Shammai threatens to extend the decree to olives if pressed on the comparison.
The dispute filled the study hall; the later decree was accepted from their students after the teachers’ version was rejected.
What is the reason for the grape decree?
Rabbi Zeiri first says grapes might be gathered in impure baskets.
That explanation depends on whether an impure basket makes its liquid count as intended; one view denies this.
Rabbi Zeiri instead cites pitched baskets, which retain liquid useful for wine making.
Rava attributes the rule to juice squeezed from clusters that cling together.
Rav Nahman describes a grower squeezing a cluster to test ripeness; its intentionally sprayed juice may remain on grapes at harvest.
The discussion asks for yet another decree and continues on the next daf.

17b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Tavi quotes Shmuel: produce grown from planted teruma remains teruma under a decree enacted that day.
Why was that decree needed?
Rabbi Hanina initially fears a non-priest would plant pure teruma to avoid giving it away.
Rava objects that someone seeking to evade the duty could simply separate a single grain, yet people do not do that.
Rava instead fears a priest may keep impure teruma for planting and mistakenly eat it in the meantime.
Ulla adds the rule that someone overtaken by Shabbat while carrying money gives the purse to a gentile.
Bali adds the restrictions on gentile bread, oil, wine, and daughters to the eighteen decrees.
According to Rabbi Yosei’s count, does this leave only seventeen?
Rav Aha bar Adda’s account supplies an additional linked decree between bread, oil, and wine.
Why would oil be a stronger reason for forbidding bread?
The chain is corrected: bread and oil guard against wine, wine against intermarriage, and further restrictions guard against idolatry.
What is the additional unnamed decree in that chain?
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak names a decree treating gentile boys as zavim to discourage sexual familiarity.
Then Rabbi Meir’s count appears to reach nineteen.
He combines the food and vessel decrees involving impure liquids as one.
The new mishnah contrasts Beit Shammai’s required completion of soaking before Shabbat with Beit Hillel’s permission to let it continue.
The same dispute covers heating flax in an oven and allowing wool to absorb dye.
It also covers setting traps before Shabbat when animals may be caught afterward.
It extends to selling or loading for a gentile shortly before Shabbat.
It also covers giving hides to a tanner and clothes to a launderer; the mishnah continues on the next daf.

18a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishnah continues: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel describes an early laundering practice, while both houses permit pressing olives or grapes before Shabbat.
Who treats adding water to ink as the act of soaking or kneading?
Rav Yosef identifies Rabbi, who makes the person adding water to flour liable, unlike Rabbi Yosei who requires actual kneading.
Abaye suggests Rabbi Yosei may require kneading only for flour; ink cannot be kneaded and could be liable on soaking.
A baraita contrasts Rabbi and Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Yehuda even for ash mixed with water.
Perhaps the term for ash actually means soil, which can be kneaded.
Separate baraitot use both words, ash and soil.
The baraitot were not taught together, so their different wording cannot settle the issue.
A Tosefta permits opening a garden channel and starting perfuming, sulfur treatment, or healing before Shabbat so the effects continue.
It forbids starting a water mill unless the wheat is ground before Shabbat.
Why is the mill different?
Rabba says the mill makes audible noise.
Rav Yosef proposes a stronger reason: a biblical duty that one’s utensils rest.
Rav Yosef therefore attributes the mill restriction to the resting of utensils.
If Beit Hillel also requires utensils to rest, why permit sulfur and incense to keep working?
Those utensils perform no action themselves.
Why permit flax left in the oven?
The oven remains stationary while the drying happens.
Why permit animal, bird, and fish traps that appear to act?
The permitted hooks and nets remain still while animals enter them.
Rav Oshaya instead assigns the biblical utensil-rest rule to Beit Shammai alone; Beit Hillel permits even active utensils.
If Beit Shammai forbids even stationary utensils, a new difficulty follows on the next daf.

18b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why does Beit Shammai permit incense and sulfur to act over Shabbat?
They may be set on the ground, so no owned utensil works.
Why permit a tub, lamp, pot, and roasting spit?
The utensils are declared ownerless.
Which tanna forbids leaving wheat or water to cook in an oven at nightfall and delays their use after Shabbat?
The Tosefta seems to follow Beit Shammai rather than Beit Hillel.
It can follow Beit Hillel: the separate concern is that someone may stoke the coals.
Why not apply the same concern to incense and sulfur?
Stoking would create smoke that spoils their effect.
Why not apply it to flax left in the oven?
Opening the oven exposes the flax to damaging wind.
Why not apply it to wool in a dye kettle?
Shmuel places the kettle off the fire.
One might still stir its contents.
The kettle is both removed from the fire and sealed.
A pot of raw meat may be left before Shabbat because it will not be ready that night, so its owner will not stoke the fire.
Fully cooked meat is permitted; partially cooked meat is not, unless a raw bone is added.
Kid meat in a sealed oven is permitted because opening it would be harmful.
Ram meat in an unsealed oven is prohibited.
Rav Ashi and Rav Yirmeya differ about kid meat in an unsealed oven or ram meat in a sealed one.
A baraita requiring meat, onion, and egg to roast before Shabbat challenges Rav Ashi’s permission.
That baraita may concern ram meat in an unsealed oven.
An alternate version permits kid meat in either oven and ram meat in a sealed oven; the sages dispute unsealed ram meat.
The same roasting baraita challenges Rav Ashi’s permission in that version.
The baraita concerns meat roasted directly on coals.
Ravina permits a raw gourd to be left cooking before Shabbat because exposing it to wind is harmful.
A baraita contrasts Beit Shammai’s travel-time limit on transactions with a gentile against Beit Hillel’s shorter limit.
Rabbi Akiva requires only that the gentile leave the Jewish home; Rabbi Yosei says this explains Beit Hillel.
Another baraita contrasts the houses on selling leaven before Passover; Rabbi Yehuda’s view begins on the next daf.

19a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda limits selling long-lasting kutah to a gentile during the thirty days before Passover.
Food may be set before a dog in a courtyard on Shabbat even if the dog carries it out.
The same permission is given when a gentile takes food out.
Why does the baraita need both cases?
One might distinguish a dog, whose feeding is the owner’s duty, from a gentile; both are permitted.
Utensils may not be rented to a gentile on Friday, but may be rented earlier in the week.
The baraita similarly restricts sending letters on Friday, and recalls a sage who never sent his handwriting with a gentile.
Another baraita permits Friday letters with fixed pay; it also reports the houses’ different deadlines for the courier’s arrival.
If pay is fixed, why require the courier to arrive before Shabbat?
Rav Sheshet applies the arrival deadlines to a case without fixed pay.
But the opening clause seems to forbid sending a letter without fixed pay altogether.
The cases differ according to whether an established mail station exists in the destination city.
A baraita restricts optional sea travel within three days of Shabbat, allows mitzva travel with a condition, and permits the short Tyre-to-Sidon voyage.
A siege should begin at least three days before Shabbat, but once begun may continue through Shabbat, as Shammai reads Deuteronomy.
Rabbi Tzadok elaborates the earlier laundering custom: white clothes were sent three days ahead, colored clothes on Friday, since white is harder to wash.
Abaye uses that teaching to reject a launderer’s equal price for a colored garment.
Abaye advises measuring clothing before and after laundering to detect stretching or shrinking.
Why does Beit Shammai permit presses to work over Shabbat while restricting the other activities?
The other acts would incur a sin-offering if performed on Shabbat; operating these presses would not.
Which tanna permits a process that continues on its own?
Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina cites Rabbi Yishmael’s rule on pre-crushed garlic, grapes, and grain; Rabbi Akiva’s view continues on the next daf.

19b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Akiva says the process begun before Shabbat may not be finished after dark.
Rabbi Elazar instead attributes the rule to the tanna Rabbi Elazar, who permits honey to drain by itself from crushed combs.
Why does Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina not use Rabbi Elazar’s parallel?
Honey remains food throughout, while the pressed produce becomes liquid.
Rabbi Elazar cites a baraita that permits even liquid seeping from crushed olives and grapes.
Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina did not know that baraita.
Why does Rabbi Elazar not follow Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina’s reading of Rabbi Yishmael?
Rabbi Yohanan distinguishes produce still needing basic pounding from that needing only further grinding; the mishnah can fit the former.
Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina issued a practical ruling like Rabbi Yishmael.
Rav and Shmuel dispute moving pressers’ oil and mats, cargo covers, and using animals or dates set aside for other purposes; this parallels Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon on muktze.
A student ruled leniently like Rabbi Shimon and Rav Hamnuna excommunicated him.
Why punish him when the accepted ruling follows Rabbi Shimon?
He ruled against Rav in a place under Rav’s authority.
Two students differed over rescuing belongings from a fire with one vessel or several, echoing another dispute.
The new mishnah requires meat, onion, and egg to roast and bread to form a crust before Shabbat; Rabbi Eliezer specifies the lower crust.
It allows lowering the Paschal lamb into an oven and lighting the Temple hearth before Shabbat so they continue afterward.

20a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Outside the Temple, a bonfire must catch on most of its fuel before Shabbat; Rabbi Yehuda makes an exception for coals.
How much must the food roast before Shabbat?
