Rav sets the measure at the partial cooking associated with ben Drosai.
Rabbi Yohanan uses that same measure in a ruling about food finished by a gentile.
Hananya uses that measure to permit leaving food on an unswept stove.
The discussion turns to the mishnah’s bread-in-the-oven rule.
Does Rabbi Eliezer mean the side of the loaf against the oven or the side toward the fire?
A baraita specifies the crust on the side attached to the oven.
The mishnah permits lowering the Paschal lamb into an oven before Shabbat.
The participants in that offering are vigilant about Shabbat.
Why is vigilance necessary when kid meat may ordinarily be left in an oven before Shabbat?
The Paschal lamb is roasted whole, unlike the cut-up kid in that earlier permission.
The next rule concerns lighting the Temple hearth before Shabbat.
Rav Huna derives permission from the Torah’s restriction on kindling in dwellings, as distinct from the Temple hearth.
Rav Hisda objects that this reading would permit lighting it on Shabbat itself.
The verse permits burning sacrificial portions; the hearth may be lit late on Friday because priests are vigilant.
The Gemara returns to the fire outside the Temple.
What counts as most of a bonfire?
Rav requires most of every branch to catch.
Shmuel requires enough burning that no one needs to add kindling.
Rav Hiyya cites a baraita supporting a flame that rises by itself.
What is the measure for one piece of wood?
Two reports of Rav require most of its thickness or circumference; Rav Pappa requires both.
Tannaim offer comparable measures: the wood loses its use for craftwork, or fire grips both ends.
Rav and Shmuel interpret a biblical word for hearth differently; a seller’s use supports the meaning willow.
Rav Huna says loose reeds and date seeds need little kindling, while bundled reeds or basketed seeds need most to catch.
Rav Hisda argues the reverse: loose pieces scatter, while bundled or basketed fuel burns together.
A supporting report begins and continues on the next daf.

20b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Kahana gives the kindling measures for bundled and loose reeds and for date seeds in or out of baskets.
Rav Yosef names four quickly burning bonfires that need not mostly catch before Shabbat; a baraita adds straw and gathered brush.
Rabbi Yohanan says Babylonian wood also needs no majority of flame beforehand.
Rav Yosef asks what wood this means, noting that even the exposed part of a wick must mostly catch.
He identifies a cedar branch; Rami bar Abba proposes hyssop.
The first chapter ends.
The new mishnah lists materials barred as Shabbat lamp wicks and fuels.
Nahum the Mede permits boiled tallow; the sages forbid both boiled and unboiled tallow.
How can cedar wood serve as a wick?
The term refers to the fibers beneath its bark.
Rav Yosef identifies hosen as flax tow.
Abaye cites Isaiah, where hosen is compared with tow rather than equated with it.
Abaye identifies it as crushed but uncombed flax.
Shmuel reports a seafarers’ name for kalakh; Rav Yitzhak identifies it with a silkworm cocoon.
Ravin points to a silk garment as kalakh, but Abaye calls it shira peranda.
A baraita lists shira and kalakh separately, challenging their identification.
The names may distinguish shira from shira peranda, leaving the latter identical with kalakh.
Willow bast is identified by peeling its bark to reveal fibers usable as a wick.
Desert wick fiber is identified as shavra.
Which aquatic growth does the mishnah mean, since growth from a ditch crumbles?
Rav Pappa identifies pliable growth on a ship.
A baraita adds wool and hair wicks; the mishnah may omit them because wool shrinks and hair scorches.
The list changes from unsuitable wicks to unsuitable fuels at pitch; wax belongs to the fuel list.
Why did the mishnah need to state this?
It clarifies that wax may coat a wick even though it is unsuitable as the lamp’s fuel.
Rami bar Avin describes tar as a pitch byproduct and wax as a honey byproduct.

21a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What practical difference follows from the definitions of tar and wax?
The distinction matters when buying and selling those materials.
Materials unfit for a Shabbat lamp wick may still fuel a bonfire for heat or light, on the ground or a stove.
What does the mishnah mean by kik oil?
Shmuel reports a seafarers’ identification with a bird called kik.
Rav Yitzhak identifies it as cottonseed oil.
Reish Lakish identifies the castor plant of Jonah; Rabba bar bar Hana describes its growth, oil, and shade.
Rabba says barred wicks burn unevenly and barred oils are not drawn well through a wick.
Abaye asks whether adding a little permitted oil allows use of an otherwise barred oil, or risks use of the oil alone.
Rabba forbids lighting the mixture.
Abaye cites a baraita in which Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel’s family lit a wick wrapped around a nut.
Rabba points to the first tanna’s prohibition as support for his rule.
The family’s actual practice still appears to permit lighting a combined wick.
The nut may have served only to float the wick.
If so, why does the first tanna forbid it?
The baraita is one incomplete teaching: combining materials as fuel is forbidden, but using a nut merely to float a wick is permitted.
Rav permits adding suitable oil to melted fat or dissolved fish innards, apparently allowing a mixed fuel.
Fat and dissolved innards can be drawn by a wick even alone; their bans guard against unprocessed versions, unlike other barred oils.
Why not also forbid these mixtures out of concern for the versions without added oil?
That would add a decree to guard another decree.
Rami bar Hama applies the lamp restrictions to the Temple menorah and explains that its flame must rise on its own.
Priestly garments containing wool were unraveled for lights at the Water Drawing Celebration.
That celebration used different lights from the Temple menorah.
A report about priestly garments made into Temple wicks raises the same mixed-fiber difficulty.
Those garments could have been linen only.
Rav Huna forbids unsuitable Shabbat wicks and oils for Hanukkah lights both on weekdays and on Shabbat.
Rava explains that Rav Huna requires relighting an extinguished Hanukkah lamp and allows use of its light.
Rav Hisda permits those materials on weekdays but not Shabbat; his reasoning continues on the next daf.

21b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Hisda does not require relighting an extinguished Hanukkah lamp, but permits use of its light.
Rav permits even unsuitable Shabbat wicks for Hanukkah, on weekdays and Shabbat.
Rabbi Yirmeya says Rav neither requires relighting nor permits using the Hanukkah light.
Abaye first rejected that ruling when attributed to Rabbi Yirmeya but accepted it later in Rabbi Yohanan’s name.
Why regret not accepting it earlier if he eventually learned it?
Learning in youth is remembered differently.
A baraita’s lighting window, from sunset until the market empties, seems to require relighting a lamp that goes out.
The window instead limits late lighting or specifies how much oil the lamp should contain.
When does market traffic finally cease?
Rabbi Yohanan says when the late-working Tadmor wood sellers leave.
A baraita gives one household light as the base mitzva, one per person for the meticulous, then contrasts Beit Shammai’s decreasing count with Beit Hillel’s increasing count.
Two explanations compare the counts to remaining and elapsed days, or to festival bulls and the principle of increasing sanctity.
Two elders in Sidon followed the two houses and supplied the festival-bull and increasing-sanctity reasons.
The Hanukkah lamp goes outside the doorway, or by a street-facing window upstairs; danger permits placing it on a table.
Rava requires a separate usable light unless a bonfire suffices; an important person still needs the separate light.
Why is Hanukkah observed?
The account gives eight days from 25 Kislev: after the Hasmonean victory, one sealed cruse supplied the Temple lights for eight days; the next year brought praise and thanksgiving.
A damages mishnah assigns liability for a spark or a camel’s burning flax and shifts it when a shopkeeper sets a lamp outside.
Rabbi Yehuda exempts a shopkeeper whose outside lamp was for Hanukkah.
Ravina infers a duty to place the lamp within ten handbreadths; otherwise the shopkeeper could have raised it above a camel.
The exemption may instead avoid making the mitzva so burdensome that people neglect it.
Rav Kahana introduces a teaching of Rabbi Tanhum that continues on the next daf.

22a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A Hanukkah light placed above twenty cubits is invalid, like a sukka roof or alley beam too high to be seen.
Rav Tanhum asks why the Joseph narrative adds that the empty pit held no water.
It had no water, but did contain snakes and scorpions.
Rabba places the Hanukkah lamp within a handbreadth of the doorway.
On which side of the doorway should it stand?
Rav Aha says right, while Rav Shmuel of Difti says left.
The ruling is left, opposite the mezuzah on the right.
Rav forbids counting money by a Hanukkah lamp.
Shmuel asks whether the lamp has holiness that would forbid use of its light.
Rav Yosef compares covering slaughter blood by hand rather than foot: mitzvot should not be treated contemptuously.
May sukka decorations be used during the festival?
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi analogizes to the ban on counting money by a Hanukkah lamp.
Rav Yosef objects that this uses an unquoted Hanukkah rule to support a rule already stated in a baraita.
The baraita explicitly bars use of sukka ornaments until the festival ends unless a condition was made.
The blood-covering rule is the better source for respecting an object used for a mitzva.
Rav and Shmuel disagree on lighting one Hanukkah lamp from another, moving fringes between garments, and unintended furrows from dragging.
Abaye says Rabba followed Shmuel in these three cases; Rabbi Shimon’s baraita permits dragging without intent to furrow.
One sage explains Rav’s lamp-to-lamp ban as avoiding contempt for the mitzva.
Rav Adda bar Ahava rejects that reason and says lighting from one lamp weakens the first mitzva light.
What practical difference follows?
Direct lamp-to-lamp lighting is allowed if the concern is contempt, but forbidden if the first light is weakened.
Rav Avya begins an objection from a teaching about a sela; it continues on the next daf.

22b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A teaching bars weighing coins against second-tithe money even to redeem other tithe; this challenges any permission to use a Hanukkah lamp through an intermediary.
Rabba distinguishes tithe money: mismatched weights could lead to secular use, a concern absent when lighting another mitzva lamp.
Rav Sheshet cites the western Temple lamp, which lit the others despite fixed lamp positions, apparently requiring an intermediate flame.
This practice challenges both explanations for forbidding lamp-to-lamp lighting.
Rav Pappa says long wicks may have allowed direct lighting.
The weakening-the-mitzva explanation remains difficult even with direct lighting.
What conclusion follows for lighting one Hanukkah lamp from another?
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua makes the rule depend on whether the mitzva lies in kindling or in placing the lamp.
Does lighting or placing the Hanukkah lamp fulfill the mitzva?
Rava says standing while holding a lit Hanukkah lamp does not fulfill the mitzva, seemingly favoring placement.
The real problem may be that observers think the lamp is held for personal use.
Rava also says lighting inside and moving the lamp outside does not fulfill the mitzva, seemingly favoring lighting in place.
Observers may think that indoor lighting was for personal use.
Another proof from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi begins on the next daf.

23a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A lantern that burned all Shabbat must be extinguished and relit after Shabbat; if placement were the mitzva, it would also have to be lifted and replaced.
The blessing says “to light” the Hanukkah lamp, confirming that kindling performs the mitzva.
Consequently, lighting by someone not obligated, such as a minor, does not fulfill the duty.
A woman may light because women too were part of the Hanukkah miracle.
A guest participates in the host’s lamp, unless a lamp is lit on the guest’s behalf at home.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi favors olive oil; Abaye recalls preferring sesame oil’s duration before adopting olive oil for its clear light.
The same sage favors olive oil for making ink.
Is it best for mixing ink or for producing soot?
A teaching says olive oil is best for both mixing and smoke.
An alternate wording favors olive-oil smoke, and Rav Huna praises balsam sap for ink.
Rav requires a blessing for lighting, and Rabbi Yirmeya also requires one for seeing a Hanukkah light.
Rav Yehuda gives three blessings for lighting and two for seeing on day one, then two and one on later days.
Which blessing is omitted, and why not omit the miracle blessing?
The miracle remains relevant on every day.
The lighting blessing describes a command to light Hanukkah lamps.
Where is that rabbinic command grounded?
Rav Avya cites the command not to turn from the sages’ ruling; Rav Nehemya cites asking one’s elders.
Rav Amram asks why doubtful tithes may be separated while naked if every rabbinic obligation requires a blessing.
Abaye distinguishes a definite rabbinic duty from a rabbinic duty based on uncertainty.
The second festival day is based on uncertainty yet receives blessings.
Its blessings prevent people from treating that day lightly.
Rava instead says most unlearned people tithe, so demai is a weaker suspicion.
Rav Huna requires lights at both entrances of a courtyard; Rava limits this to entrances facing different directions.
Whose suspicion explains the two-light requirement, and why do the two directions matter?
Local residents might see only the unlit entrance and assume the other is unlit too.
A teaching about leaving peah at the end of a field includes avoiding suspicion among its four reasons.
Leaving peah only at the end also stops an owner from secretly giving it to one favored poor relative.

23b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Leaving peah at the end of the field saves the poor from waiting and prevents passersby from suspecting that no peah was left.
Do all these reasons not follow from the same Torah command?
Rava says the separate concern is that deceivers could falsely claim they already left peah.
A lamp with two openings can count as two Hanukkah lights.
Separate wicks around a bowl count if covered to distinguish them; otherwise they appear a bonfire and count for no one.
Rava prioritizes the household Shabbat lamp over a Hanukkah lamp or kiddush wine for household peace.
When Hanukkah oil conflicts with kiddush wine, does regularity or publicizing the miracle prevail?
Rava resolves the question in favor of the Hanukkah lamp and publicizing the miracle.
Rav Huna links care in lamps, mezuzah, fringes, and kiddush to fitting rewards.
Rav Huna and Rav Hisda each noticed homes attentive to lamps and foresaw future scholars from those families.
Rav Yosef urges his wife not to delay Shabbat lighting, citing the overlap of the biblical pillars of cloud and fire.
An elder cautions her not to light too early either.
Rava links love, honor, and reverence for sages with scholarly children, sons-in-law, or standing.
What is the mishnah’s “burnt oil”?
Rabba identifies impure teruma oil, destined to be burned.
Why not use that oil for a Shabbat lamp?
Someone eager to burn it may adjust the wick.
Abaye asks why it is also barred on a festival, when tending a flame is allowed.
The festival ban may be a decree guarding the Shabbat ban.
Rav Hisda instead places the mishnah on a festival falling Friday, when impure teruma cannot be burned.
A later clause separately names a festival, suggesting the first clause concerns an ordinary Friday.
Rabbi Hanina reads the later clause as explaining the reason: sacred material is not burned on a festival.

24a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita supports Rav Hisda: unsuitable Shabbat lamp oils may be used on a festival except impure teruma oil, since sacred things are not burned then.
Should Hanukkah be mentioned in Grace after Meals despite its rabbinic origin, to publicize the miracle?
Rav Huna says it is optional; if included, it belongs in thanksgiving.
Rav Sheshet compares it with prayer and places it in the thanksgiving blessing rather than the Jerusalem blessing.
Must the New Moon be mentioned in Grace after Meals because it is biblical, or omitted because labor is permitted?
Rav requires the mention; Rabbi Hanina does not.
Rav Zerika favors Rav, citing Rabbi Oshaya’s rule that days with an additional offering are mentioned in prayer and Grace after Meals.
The teaching next turns to days without an additional offering.
Why are ordinary Mondays and Thursdays listed?
They mean the Monday–Thursday–Monday cycle of communal fasts and watches.
Those fasts are mentioned in the prayer for being heard, without repeating a missed prayer or adding a Grace after Meals mention.
Does Hanukkah belong in an additional prayer that exists because of Shabbat or New Moon, not Hanukkah itself?
Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda say no; Rav Nahman and Rabbi Yohanan say yes.
Abaye relates the no-mention view to Rav’s ruling that a Shabbat haftara blessing need not mention New Moon.
The comparison is imperfect: New Moon has no haftara, whereas Hanukkah is mentioned in other daily prayers.
A closer parallel is Rav’s ruling on a festival during Shabbat: an afternoon haftara blessing need not mention the festival.

24b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The ruling follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: a Yom Kippur Neila on Shabbat mentions Shabbat because the day itself calls for four prayers.
Rava seems to disagree: a Friday-evening prayer leader on a festival that falls on Shabbat does not mention the festival in the added Shabbat prayer.
That added prayer was instituted for safety, not as a duty of the day; Neila is a duty of Yom Kippur itself.
Why do the sages’ tallow ruling and the anonymous first ruling appear identical?
They may differ over cooked fat mixed with oil, but the positions are not specified.
The new mishnah bars impure teruma oil on a festival and records disputes about tar and other Shabbat lamp fuels.
Why may impure teruma oil not be burned on a festival, and what is the source for the broader ban?
Hizkiya reads the repeated “until morning” in the Paschal-lamb verse as delaying burning leftovers until after the festival.
Abaye reads “the Shabbat offering on its Shabbat” to exclude ordinary offerings on Shabbat or a festival.
Rava derives limits from “that alone”: festival labor permits food itself, not every facilitating act or a delayed circumcision.
Rav Ashi introduces another derivation from the festival term shabbaton; it continues on the next daf.

25a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Ashi’s derivation adds a positive festival-rest command to the prohibition; burning sacred leftovers cannot override both.
Why may impure teruma oil be burned for benefit during the week though not on a festival?
Rav says burning impure teruma is a mitzva and its owner may benefit while destroying it.
Where does the Torah permit that benefit?
Rav Nahman reads the plural “My terumot” as including pure and impure teruma; the impure portion may fuel cooking.
Rabbi Abbahu alternatively reads “from it” in the tithe confession as excluding impure teruma oil from the ban.
Perhaps the exclusion instead permits burning impure consecrated oil.
If even the less stringent tithe is barred, consecrated items should be barred all the more.
The same reasoning could also bar the more stringent teruma.
“From it” must exclude something; greater stringencies of consecrated items favor excluding teruma.
Teruma has its own greater stringencies, beginning with death and a fifth-payment rule; the list continues.

25b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Although teruma has its own strict rules, the listed strictures for consecrated items are more numerous.
Alternatively, the karet penalty makes consecrated items more stringent.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak derives from “give him” that impure teruma is fit to benefit the priest as fuel.
Why does Rabbi Yishmael prohibit lighting with tar?
Rava says its foul smell may cause people to leave the Shabbat light.
Abaye asks why leaving would matter.
Rava says Shabbat lighting is obligatory, citing Rav’s contrast with optional hot-water washing.
Rava calls the washing a mitzva even though Rav called it optional.
What is its mitzva value?
Rabbi Yehuda bar Elai prepared for Shabbat by washing face, hands, and feet and sitting wrapped in fringed linen.
His students hid their garment corners; he reminded them that Beit Hillel requires fringes on linen.
The students feared wool fringes on linen might be worn at night, when the command for fringes does not apply.
What do the words about lost peace and forgotten good in Lamentations signify?
Rabbi Abbahu relates the lost peace to Shabbat lighting.
Other sages interpret lost good as bathing, hot-water washing, a furnished bed, or a prepared home.
Four sages give different measures of wealth: contentment, property, a wife of good deeds, or a nearby privy.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar forbids lighting with balsam sap.
Why is that sap forbidden?
Rabba fears its scent may tempt someone to take sap from the burning lamp.
Abaye begins a challenge that continues on the next daf.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abaye suggests volatility as the reason to avoid balsam sap.
The response retains both concerns: volatility and the temptation to draw sap from the lamp.
A story of a daughter-in-law burned after using balsam oil illustrates the danger.
A verse about survivors after Jerusalem’s fall is read as describing balsam gatherers and hilazon trappers.
A baraita forbids lighting with impure untithed produce and with volatile white naphtha even on weekdays.
White naphtha is hazardous, but why bar impure untithed produce?
The plural “My terumot” includes impure teruma; the right to benefit begins only once teruma is separated.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar forbids balsam sap and identifies it as resin from the tree.
Other sages restrict lamp fuel to non-tree sources, fruit products, or olive oil alone.
Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri challenges the olive-oil-only rule from regions with only sesame, nut, radish oil, or naphtha.
He permits any oil not specifically barred by the sages, including fish oil and tar.
Rabbi Shimon Shezuri permits gourd oil and naphtha; Sumakhos allows fish oil among animal products.
How does Sumakhos differ from the first tanna?
They differ over melted fat mixed with oil, though which view permits it is unclear.
A baraita says most tree-derived cloth does not count as a small garment for impurity and may roof a sukka; linen is exceptional.
Abaye begins a comment that continues on the next daf.

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abaye equates Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar’s rule for plant fabrics with the school of Rabbi Yishmael’s garment rule.
The school derives from the Torah’s specified wool and linen that generic “garment” refers to those fibers.
Rava says they differ over a three-by-three-handbreadth cloth of another fabric: one view includes it, the other excludes it.
How do we know a three-by-three-fingerbreadth wool or linen cloth can receive skin-disease impurity?
A baraita derives the small cloth from the extra wording “and the garment.”
Perhaps that wording only includes a three-by-three-handbreadth cloth.
Such a large cloth appears derivable a fortiori from warp and woof threads.
Then the same inference might include a small cloth too.
The larger cloth serves rich and poor and can be inferred; the small cloth serves only the poor and needs an explicit verse.
Perhaps the extra wording includes larger cloth of other fibers instead.
The verse explicitly says wool or linen, excluding other fibers.
Perhaps the exclusion applies only to small pieces of other fibers.
Two wool-or-linen exclusions bar both small and large pieces of other fibers in that reading.
How, then, can Rava distinguish the views about larger pieces of other fibers? The inquiry continues.

27a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava derives impurity for a larger piece of other fabric from the added “or a garment” in the creeping-animal passage.
How does Abaye, who excludes those fabrics, read the added words?
He uses them for a small wool-or-linen piece touched by a creeping animal.
Rava says that small-piece rule is already revealed in the laws of leprosy.
Abaye rejects the comparison: leprosy affects even warp and woof threads.
Rava argues that, if leprosy were stricter, its rule could have been inferred from a verse about creeping animals.
Abaye answers that creeping animals have their own strict lentil-sized threshold, blocking that inference.
Abaye cites a second school-of-Rabbi-Yishmael teaching that “or a garment” includes camel, rabbit, goat, and silk fabrics, seemingly conflicting with the first.
Rava reconciles the teachings by distinguishing small from three-handbreadth pieces of other fabrics.
But Rava earlier said the first tanna excluded even larger pieces of other fabrics.
Rava may have retracted that view, or the earlier attribution was actually Rav Pappa’s.
Rav Pappa proposes a different application of the school’s general garment derivation: mixed fabrics.
Why need that derivation when the ban explicitly names wool and linen?
One might distinguish wearing from merely placing other mixed fabrics on the body.
The distinction fails by an a fortiori inference: if wearing other blends is allowed, mere placement must be allowed; Rav Pappa’s attribution is rejected.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak introduces another reading that continues on the next daf.

27b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak applies the garment derivation to fringes.
Why derive it when the Torah already places wool-and-linen rules beside the fringe command?
Rava’s competing verses might have allowed wool or linen fringes on any garment and matching fringes on other fabrics; the derivation narrows the duty.
Why not use “your covering” to include other fabrics for fringes, as “or a garment” includes them for impurity?
A baraita uses “your covering” to include a blind person’s garment, leaving “you shall see” to exclude a night garment.
Why include a blind person’s garment rather than a night garment?
Others can still see the blind person’s garment; a night garment is not visible to others.
Perhaps “your covering” instead includes other fabrics.
In a wool-and-linen context, it more naturally includes another wool-or-linen garment.
Abaye relates Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar’s fabric rule to Sumakhos’s view.
Sumakhos bars a sukka roof of spun thread because it can become impure from leprosy.
A mishnah disputes when warp, woof, and processed flax acquire leprosy impurity.
The new mishnah permits flax alone among tree products as lamp wick and says flax alone among them becomes impure as a corpse tent.
Why is flax called a tree product?
Mar Zutra cites Joshua’s “trees of flax.”
What is the source for flax alone acquiring tent impurity?
Rabbi Elazar begins a verbal analogy on “tent,” continuing on the next daf.

28a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A verbal analogy between the corpse tent and the Tabernacle tent makes linen the relevant tent material.
Must the linen then be twisted into sixfold threads as in the Tabernacle?
Repeated “tent” wording includes other linen constructions.
Why would that wording not include every material?
That would leave the linen-based verbal analogy without a purpose.
Perhaps the analogy includes the Tabernacle’s wooden beams.
The beams are called supports for the Tabernacle rather than the Tabernacle itself.
That reasoning would also exclude its hide covering, making Rabbi Elazar’s question about non-kosher hide pointless.
A later verse connects the upper hide covering to the lower tent, restoring its status as a tent.
Can the hide of a non-kosher animal acquire corpse-tent impurity?
Rav Adda says Rabbi Elazar’s uncertainty concerns whether Moses’s tahash was kosher.
Rav Yosef cites the rule that heavenly work used only kosher-animal hide.
Rabbi Abba cites competing accounts of the coverings and asks about a comparison to a non-kosher animal.
The comparison concerns its many colors, not its kosher status.
Rav Yosef links the translated name sasgona to those many colors.
Rava begins deriving impurity for non-kosher hide from an added expression in the leprosy passage.
Leprosy may be stricter because it can affect warp and woof threads.
A creeping-animal passage also includes non-kosher hide through “or hide.”
Creeping animals impart impurity at a lentil-sized measure.
The two sources together share a rule for non-kosher hide despite their distinct strictures, suggesting the same for corpse-tent impurity.
Rava of Barnish notes that both sources still impart impurity below an olive-bulk, unlike a corpse.
He begins another derivation that continues on the next daf.

28b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava of Barnish derives non-kosher hide from goat hair: the hair forms an impure corpse tent despite not receiving leprosy impurity.
If non-kosher hide can form such a tent, what remains of the rule that heavenly work used only kosher-animal hide?
It could concern tefillin.
But tefillin already require material permitted for eating by an explicit verse.
Perhaps it concerns their leather boxes.
The box’s form is also a law given to Moses at Sinai.
Perhaps it concerns hair ties and sinew stitching.
A baraita also treats those details as law given at Sinai.
The remaining application is tefillin straps.
But their black color is also a law given at Sinai.
That tradition says black, not that the straps must come from a kosher animal.
What was the nature of the tahash in Moses’s time?
Rabbi Meir describes a unique one-horned animal that appeared for the Tabernacle and then vanished.
The single horn is used as evidence of kosher status, with a verse about Adam’s one-horned offering.
Does that also prove it was a domesticated animal?
No: a one-horned wild keresh leaves its classification open.
The mishnah contrasts Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva on the impurity and Shabbat use of a folded but unsinged cloth wick.
Their impurity dispute is whether folding alone removes its garment status.
What explains the separate dispute about lighting?
The case is an exactly three-by-three-fingerbreadth cloth on a festival before Shabbat; both use rules about broken vessels and lighting most of the wick.
For Rabbi Eliezer it becomes a forbidden broken vessel as it burns; for Rabbi Akiva folding made it non-vessel material from the start.
Rav Yosef recognizes the exact size from an earlier teaching and infers Rav Adda’s view from his explanation.
The Gemara challenges whether Rav Adda actually holds that view; the challenge continues.

29a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Adda permits burning a new vessel carved by a gentile on a festival, apparently against Rabbi Yehuda’s restriction on newly formed objects.
He explained the two tannaim’s views without personally adopting that festival rule.
Rava instead explains Rabbi Eliezer’s wick ruling: an unsinged cloth wick burns poorly.
Why then did Rav Yosef insist on an exactly three-by-three measure?
That measurement concerns cloth impurity and a dispute over whether its hem counts.
Rav reports Rabbi Yehuda barring broken vessels, date pits, and nut shells as festival fuel, while Rabbi Shimon permits them.
All three examples are needed: a broken vessel changes identity, date pits become exposed, and nut shells were already exposed.
The view attributed to Rav was inferred from a story in which Rabbi Hiyya objected to burning date pits on a festival.
Did Rav accept the objection?
Rav later gave date pits to animals on a festival, seemingly rejecting the restriction.
Those may have been pits with fruit still attached, making them usable.
How can Rabbi Yehuda allow burning whole vessels if they become forbidden fragments as they burn and are turned?
As with fallen palm branches, adding enough prepared wood makes the permitted fuel the majority.
Rav Hamnuna offers a different reading involving a cloth smaller than three handbreadths.
A cloth used for household tasks is impure for Rabbi Eliezer, pure for Rabbi Yehoshua, and depends on prior designation for Rabbi Akiva.
A report adds that all agree a small cloth discarded in refuse loses its impurity status.

29b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A boxed scrap retains garment status for everyone; the dispute concerns a scrap hung on a peg or left behind a door.
Rabbi Eliezer treats a scrap kept out of the trash as still intended for use, though less ready than one stored in a box.
Rabbi Yehoshua treats a scrap kept outside the box as discarded, though it is more accessible than actual refuse.
Rabbi Akiva follows Rabbi Eliezer for a hanging scrap and Rabbi Yehoshua for one behind the door.
Did Rabbi Akiva later adopt Rabbi Yehoshua’s position, and how is that known?
Rava reads “the wick of the garment” as implying that it remains a garment, yet Rabbi Akiva calls it pure.
The mishna bars an oil-filled eggshell or earthenware tube dripping into a lamp; Rabbi Yehuda permits it, and a craftsman’s attached vessel is allowed.
The mishna also bars a separate oil bowl feeding the lamp wick, while Rabbi Yehuda permits it.
The eggshell case alone would not establish the Rabbis’ view for a dirty earthenware tube, whose oil is less likely to be taken.
The earthenware case alone would not establish Rabbi Yehuda’s permission for a clean eggshell.
Those two containers alone would not establish Rabbi Yehuda’s view for a separate bowl, where the oil supply can be interrupted.
The bowl case alone would not establish the Rabbis’ restriction for the two tubes; all three cases are needed.
The mishna permits a tube attached by its maker from the outset.
A baraita also permits one attached with plaster or clay.
But the mishna specifies a craftsman’s attachment.
It means an attachment as secure as a craftsman’s.
Rabbi Yehuda cites an eggshell feeder used in Lod before Rabbi Tarfon and other elders without objection.
The Sages answer that the people in that house were careful, so the example does not establish general permission.
Avin dragged a bench across a marble upper floor before Rabbi Yitzhak ben Elazar.
Rabbi Yitzhak warns that silence would mislead others: a marble floor is restricted because ordinary floors can be furrowed.
A community leader dragged a bench before Rabbi Yirmeya, who asks whether he relies on Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Yirmeya argues that Rabbi Shimon’s allowance may apply only to large benches that cannot be carried.
Ulla disagrees: the dispute is over small benches; everyone allows dragging large ones.
Rav Yosef cites Rabbi Shimon allowing a bed, chair, and bench when no furrow is intended, apparently including both large and small items.
Ulla construes the cited bed as small like a chair, retaining a dispute over small furniture.
Rabbi Yirmeya construes the chair as heavy like a bed, keeping the allowance to large furniture.
Rabba cites wool-and-linen merchants, who may carry mixed garments when they do not intend to benefit from wearing them.
They could carry the garments on a pole, yet the ordinary method is allowed; this refutes Rabbi Yirmeya’s limit on unintended acts.
The next mishna exempts one who extinguishes a lamp from fear, an evil spirit, or a sick person’s need to sleep.
It makes one liable for saving lamp, oil, or wick; Rabbi Yosei exempts all but saving the wick because that makes charcoal.

30a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna’s liability clause indicates Rabbi Yehuda’s rule for labor not needed for its own sake.
Why does its first clause say “exempt”? A dangerously ill patient makes extinguishing permissible, while for a patient without danger Rabbi Yehuda would impose liability.
The first clause concerns danger; “exempt” was chosen to parallel the later “liable,” though extinguishing is permitted.
Rabbi Oshaya teaches that extinguishing for a sick person is forbidden at the outset but exempt after the fact.
His case concerns a patient without danger and follows Rabbi Shimon’s rule on labor not needed for its own sake.
Rabbi Tanhum is asked whether one may extinguish a lamp for a sick person on Shabbat.
He opens by challenging apparent conflicts between Solomon’s sayings and David’s, and between Solomon’s own sayings.
David says the dead do not praise God, while Solomon praises the dead yet also favors a living dog over a dead lion.
David means that Torah and mitzvot must be done in life; after death one can no longer perform them.
Rabbi Yohanan likewise reads “free among the dead” as freedom from Torah and mitzvot after death.
Solomon praises the dead because invoking the deceased patriarchs secured an answer to Moses’ prayer.
Moses’ decrees continue to be observed after his death, unlike ordinary rulers’ decrees.
Another explanation begins with David’s request for a sign that his sin had been forgiven; God promises disclosure in Solomon’s lifetime.
At the Temple dedication, Solomon’s prayers and appeals to the gates do not open them.
An appeal to David’s merit opens the gates, exposing his forgiveness and explaining Solomon’s praise of the dead.
The verse about the people returning home joyful after the dedication names God’s goodness to David and Israel.
The Gemara unpacks that joy: family blessing, Divine presence, David’s pardon, and Israel’s pardon for the Yom Kippur celebration.
The living dog and dead lion saying is explained through David’s request to learn when he would die.
God will not reveal David’s lifespan but tells him that his death will occur on Shabbat.
David asks to die on Sunday instead.
God refuses because Solomon’s reign is due then, and reigns do not overlap even briefly.
David asks to die on Friday instead.
God values one more day of David’s Torah study above a thousand offerings Solomon will bring.

30b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: David studies Torah throughout Shabbat; the Angel of Death breaks his concentration with a noise and a broken stair, and David dies.
Solomon asks the study hall how to handle David’s body in the sun while the household dogs are hungry.
They say to feed the dogs a carcass and move David’s body only with bread or a child placed upon it.
The practical ruling illustrates Solomon’s saying that a living dog is better than a dead lion.
Returning to the original question, Rabbi Tanhum says to extinguish the human-made lamp for the sake of a person’s life, God’s lamp.
The Sages considered hiding Ecclesiastes because its statements seem contradictory.
Why was it not hidden?
Its beginning and end teach Torah.
Its opening says labor under the sun has no gain; the school of Rabbi Yannai finds gain in Torah, which preceded the sun.
Its conclusion commands fear of God and keeping the commandments.
What does “this is the whole person” mean?
Three sages explain that such a person is the purpose, equal, or companioned center of the whole world.
Which statements of Ecclesiastes appear contradictory?
It both praises and disparages laughter, and both commends and questions joy.
God’s anger at the righteous in this world differs from divine laughter with the wicked here and the righteous in the world to come.
The commended joy is joy of a mitzva; purposeless joy is the kind questioned.
The Divine Presence rests through mitzva joy, as Elisha receives prophecy after a musician plays.
Rav Yehuda extends joy to teaching law, and Rava to preparation for a good dream.
Rav Giddel’s verse reading requires a student’s lips to drip bitterness or awe before a teacher.
One resolution distinguishes the joyful teacher from the awestruck student.
Another distinguishes a teacher’s mood before beginning from the seriousness of the lesson itself.
Rabba exemplifies this by opening with humor and then teaching in awe.
The Sages also considered hiding Proverbs for apparent contradictions.
Why did they keep it?
They chose to analyze its tensions, as they had done for Ecclesiastes.
One proverb says not to answer a fool according to his folly, and the next says to answer him.
Answer a foolish Torah claim, but do not engage a foolish mundane claim.
Stories of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Hiyya show refusal to debate insulting personal claims, and recall a prayer against insolence.
What is an example of answering a foolish Torah challenge?
When a student mocks daily birth in the future, Rabban Gamliel points to a chicken as a present-day analogy.
When the student mocks daily fruit, Rabban Gamliel points to a caper bush.
When the student mocks future bread and fine garments from the earth, Rabban Gamliel points to fungi and a palm covering.
The next baraita introduces Hillel’s patience and Shammai’s impatience through a story of two people.

31a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Two people wager four hundred zuz that one can make Hillel angry.
On Friday, one contestant interrupts Hillel repeatedly while Hillel is washing; Hillel calmly invites his question.
He asks why Babylonians have oval heads.
Hillel patiently attributes this to their midwives.
After another interruption, Hillel again invites a question.
The man asks why the people of Tadmor have bleary eyes.
Hillel attributes it to the sand where they live.
After a third interruption, Hillel again invites the man to ask.
The man asks why Africans have broad feet.
Hillel attributes it to living among marshes.
The man says he has more questions but fears Hillel will become angry.
Hillel sits with him and invites every question.
The man asks whether Hillel is the leader of Israel.
Hillel says yes.
The man says he hopes Israel will have few leaders like him.
Hillel asks why.
The man admits Hillel’s patience cost him the wager.
Hillel advises self-control and says another such loss would be preferable to his becoming angry.
A prospective convert asks Shammai about Torah; Shammai identifies Written and Oral Torah.
The man accepts only Written Torah and asks for conversion on that condition.
Shammai rebuffs him, but Hillel converts him and teaches him letters, reversing their names the next day.
The convert objects that Hillel gave different letter names yesterday.
Hillel shows that even reading written letters relies on a teacher’s oral explanation.
Another prospective convert asks to learn the whole Torah while standing on one foot.
Shammai pushes him away; Hillel converts him.
Hillel gives the rule against doing to others what one hates, then tells him to study the rest.
A third man hears about priestly garments and wants to convert in order to become High Priest.
Shammai rejects that condition; Hillel receives the man as a convert.
Hillel tells him to study the rules of the office he seeks.
Reading that an outsider approaching the sanctuary dies, the convert asks whom that verse includes.
Hillel says it would include even King David.
The convert reasons that if ordinary Israelites are excluded from priestly service, a convert is certainly excluded.
He returns to Shammai and acknowledges that he cannot be High Priest.
He thanks Hillel for bringing him into the faith.
The three converts later praise Hillel’s patience and contrast Shammai’s response.
Reish Lakish reads Isaiah’s words as the six mishnaic orders, while fear of God remains their treasure.
Rava interprets the same words as questions asked at a person’s final judgment.
The achievements matter only when joined to fear of God.
A parable compares learning without fear to storing wheat without preservative.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael allows adding preservative to a kor of grain.
Rabba bar Rav Huna begins another comparison of Torah without fear of Heaven.

31b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Torah without fear of Heaven resembles a treasurer with inner keys but no key to the outer gate.
Rabbi Yannai compares learning without fear to making a gate for a courtyard one does not own.
Rav Yehuda cites Ecclesiastes to teach that the world was made so people would fear God.
Two sages debate whether to honor Rabbi Yaakov bar Aha as one who fears sin or as a Torah scholar; one ranks fear higher.
Rabbi Elazar is identified as the advocate of fear because his teaching and cited verses call fear of Heaven God’s singular treasure.
Does “do not be overly wicked” permit being a little wicked?
No: prior sin is no reason to add another, just as garlic’s smell is no reason to eat more.
Rava bar Rav Ulla interprets a verse as reproving the wicked for facing death without worry.
Rabba’s reading says they know their fate but continue to speak approvingly of their path.
Why does Rabbi Yosei exempt one who extinguishes to spare lamp or oil but impose liability for a wick, whether he follows Rabbi Yehuda or Rabbi Shimon?
Ulla follows Rabbi Yehuda but treats constructive extinguishing as requiring reuse in the same place; only the wick fits.
Rabba objects that Tabernacle work, the source for Shabbat labor, involved dismantling to rebuild elsewhere.
Ulla answers that divine direction made each new encampment equivalent to rebuilding in the same place.
Rabbi Yohanan instead follows Rabbi Shimon: singeing a wick for later use is a constructive act, so even he imposes liability.
Rava notes that the mishna says one actively makes charcoal, supporting deliberate preparation of the wick.
The mishna lists neglect of menstruation law, separating halla, and Shabbat lighting as three transgressions tied to death in childbirth.
Why is menstruation law linked to childbirth?
Rabbi Yitzhak connects harm in the womb to a wrong involving the womb.
How do halla and Shabbat lighting fit that explanation?
A Galilean begins a broader explanation: God placed a measure of blood in a person and warned about blood law.

32a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Galilean links halla to first fruits and the Shabbat lamp to the soul, which is called a lamp; neglect of the duties imperils life.
Why is childbirth singled out as the time of judgment?
Several sages give proverbs for punishment when a person is already vulnerable or in danger.
When are men similarly examined?
Reish Lakish says when crossing a bridge, meaning any comparable danger.
Rav avoids sharing a ferry with a gentile lest he be caught in another’s judgment.
Shmuel prefers such a ferry, reasoning that accusation does not strike two peoples together.
Rabbi Yannai checks a ferry first and warns against entering danger in reliance on a miracle, which may cost merit.
Rabbi Hanin cites Jacob’s sense of diminished merit after receiving divine kindness.
Rabbi Zeira avoids palm trees on a windy day.
Rav Yitzhak advises prayer before illness, when one would otherwise have to present merits to escape danger.
Mar Ukva reads the parapet verse as requiring the endangered person to supply a defense.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael reads “the fallen” as someone destined to fall, while responsibility still rests with the person through whom harm occurs.
A dying person is urged to confess, as one facing execution confesses.
Increasing danger is compared to arrest, chains, and trial; survival requires strong advocates.
Repentance and good deeds serve as advocates; even one favorable advocate among a thousand can save a person.
Rabbi Eliezer says even a single favorable part of one advocate can suffice.
A baraita contrasts death in childbirth with death when young and records other proposed offenses.
Rabbi Yishmael ben Elazar attributes the deaths of unlearned people to dismissive names for the Ark and synagogue.
Rabbi Yosei describes three potential causes of death tied to menstruation, halla, and Shabbat lighting; two readings match the earlier dispute.
Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel begins to stress the gravity of consecration, teruma, and tithe laws.

32b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: These serious obligations were entrusted even to unlearned people.
Rabbi Natan links unfulfilled vows to a wife’s death through the verse about losing one’s bed.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi links unfulfilled vows to young children’s deaths, reading “the work of your hands” as children.
A baraita disputes whether vows or neglect of Torah study cause children to die.
What verse supports the neglect-of-Torah view?
Jeremiah says children were struck because instruction was not accepted.
Rav Nahman also uses that verse for the vow view, reading “in vain” as a reference to false vows.
How can Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi be linked here to Torah neglect after attributing the outcome to vows?
He changed his position after hearing the other teaching.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Yosei dispute whether missing mezuza or neglected Torah study is responsible.
They differ over how far back to read the verse about children’s long life: the immediately preceding mezuza verse or also Torah study.
Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda differ between mezuza and ritual fringes.
The mezuza view follows adjacent verses; what supports the ritual-fringes view?
A verse speaks of innocent blood found at the corners of garments.
Rav Nahman also finds mezuza in that verse by reading the reference to hidden openings.
Reish Lakish promises a reward associated with 2,800 people grasping the corners of one who observes ritual fringes.
A mnemonic introduces further teachings about sins and their consequences.
Rabbi Nehemya links gratuitous hatred to strife at home, miscarriage, and children dying young.
Rabbi Elazar links neglected halla to failed stores and crops, reading a curse verse through a wordplay on halla.
Ezekiel’s verse promises blessing to a house that gives the first dough to the priest.
Withholding teruma and tithes is linked to drought, high prices, and unsuccessful labor, supported by a verse in Job.
How does that verse imply the claim?
The school of Rabbi Yishmael links neglected summer obligations to lost winter rains.
Malachi promises abundant rain and blessing when the tithe is brought to the storehouse.
What does “until there is no more” mean?
Rami bar Rav says the blessing exceeds one’s ability to say “enough.”
A teaching links robbery with locusts and famine and begins to identify Amos’s “cows of Bashan.”

33a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Verses about damaged crops, locusts, and hunger complete the argument linking robbery to famine.
Delayed or distorted justice and neglected Torah are linked to violence, plague, famine, and measured bread.
Leviticus’s sword and scarce bread, with its covenant and judgments, support that link.
Vain or false oaths and desecration of God’s name or Shabbat are linked to wild beasts and desolation.
The teaching connects these offenses to Leviticus’s curses through verses and shared wording.
Bloodshed is linked to Temple destruction and the departure of the Divine Presence.
Numbers warns that defiling the land prevents Israel and God’s Presence from dwelling there.
Forbidden relations, idolatry, and neglected Sabbatical and Jubilee years are linked to exile.
Leviticus describes the land expelling those who defile it through forbidden relations.
Another Leviticus passage connects idolatry with desolation and dispersion.
The Sabbatical passage says the land will receive its missed rests during exile.
Vulgar speech is linked to harsh decrees and suffering for young people, orphans, and widows.
Isaiah joins wanton speech to unabated anger and withheld compassion.
What does the verse’s still-outstretched hand mean here?
Rabbi Hanan says vulgar talk can reverse even a long favorable decree.
Rav Hisda reads a proverb’s deep pit as punishment for vulgar speech.
Rav Nahman extends blame to one who listens silently.
Rav Oshaya connects preparation for sin to bodily wounds and illness through Proverbs.
Rav Nahman calls that illness a sign of sin.
A baraita distinguishes forms of the illness associated with sin, hunger, and sorcery.
Shmuel HaKatan’s illness is healed after he worries others will misread its cause.
Rava attributes Abaye’s illness to self-denial rather than sin.
Why did Rava himself become ill after warning about bodily neglect?
He was held back from relieving himself while teaching.
A baraita lists signs associated with sin, hatred, arrogance, and slander.
The next baraita begins a dispute over the cause of askara.

33b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: One opinion links askara to neglected tithes; Rabbi Elazar links it to slander.
A verse about closing the mouths of liars is cited for the slander view.
Did Rabbi Elazar mean slander alone, or slander as an additional cause?
A baraita recounts a gathering of sages at Yavne.
They are asked why askara begins in the intestines and ends in the mouth.
Rabbi Yehuda traces the process of speech from inward thought to the mouth that finishes it.
Rabbi Elazar initially attributes the illness to eating impure things.
The Gemara challenges that literal reading.
It refers instead to food not properly tithed.
Rabbi Shimon attributes askara to neglect of Torah study.
Women also suffer askara though they are not obligated in Torah study.
They may interrupt their husbands’ study.
Gentiles also suffer it.
They may interrupt Israel’s study.
Children also suffer it.
They may interrupt their fathers’ study.
Schoolchildren also suffer though they themselves study.
A teaching says the righteous, or in their absence schoolchildren, may suffer for the generation.
A verse about kids near shepherds is read as children taken as collateral for the leaders.
The additional cause confirms that Rabbi Elazar did not limit askara to slander.
Why was Rabbi Yehuda called chief speaker everywhere?
Rabbi Yehuda praises Roman markets, bridges, and baths in the presence of other sages.
Rabbi Yosei remains silent.
Rabbi Shimon says the works serve Roman interests, including taxes and self-indulgence.
After their words reach the authorities, Yehuda is elevated, Yosei exiled, and Shimon condemned.
Rabbi Shimon and his son first hide in the study hall, then move to a cave as the danger grows.
A carob tree and spring sustain them through twelve years of study in the cave.
Elijah announces that the ruler has died and the decree ended.
On emerging, they criticize people who farm instead of studying, and their gaze burns what they see.
A heavenly voice rebukes them for destroying the world and orders them back.
They remain another twelve months before a heavenly voice lets them leave again.
Rabbi Elazar still harms places with his gaze, while Rabbi Shimon heals them and says the two suffice.
Before Shabbat they meet an elder carrying two myrtle bundles.
They ask what the bundles are for.
He says they honor Shabbat.
Why are two bundles needed?
He assigns one to “remember” and one to “observe” Shabbat.
Rabbi Shimon sees Israel’s love of mitzvot and their minds settle.
Rabbi Pinhas tends Rabbi Shimon’s injured skin and grieves; Rabbi Shimon credits the hardship with his growth.
Their later study shows the growth: Rabbi Shimon can now give twice as many answers to Rabbi Pinhas’s questions.
After his rescue Rabbi Shimon resolves to help others, invoking Jacob’s repair of a city through a currency, markets, or baths.
Rabbi Shimon asks what needs repair.
He is told of a place with uncertain ritual impurity.

34a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The uncertain impurity site burdens priests who must walk around it.
Rabbi Shimon asks whether anyone remembers it as presumptively pure.
An elder recalls that ben Zakkai cut priestly lupines there.
Rabbi Shimon tests the ground, declaring firm places pure and marking soft places as suspect.
Another elder mocks him for purifying what he calls a cemetery.
Rabbi Shimon says the elder took part in the ruling and should support fellow scholars rather than undermine them.
Rabbi Shimon’s gaze falls on the elder, who dies.
He later sees Yehuda son of converts, whose report caused the earlier persecution, and the account says his gaze kills him.
The mishna requires a household reminder before Shabbat: tithe, prepare the eiruv, and light the lamp.
At uncertain nightfall, definite produce may not be tithed, vessels immersed, or lamps lit, but demai, an eiruv, and insulation are allowed.
What supports the household reminder?
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cites Job’s instruction to inspect one’s home and avoid sin.
Rabba bar Rav Huna says to speak the reminders calmly so family members will accept them.
Rav Ashi says he followed that practice by his own reasoning.
The mishna first requires asking about the eiruv before twilight, then allows making one during twilight.
A mnemonic introduces the ensuing teachings.
Rav distinguishes a boundary eiruv, which must precede twilight, from a courtyard eiruv, which may be made then.
Rava gives two courtyard eiruv cases: one placed before twilight and eaten during it, the other placed during twilight and eaten later; both take effect.
If twilight is day, only the later eiruv qualifies; if night, only the earlier one qualifies.
Twilight remains uncertain, and doubt in a rabbinic matter is treated leniently in each case.
Why is insulating in material that adds no heat forbidden after nightfall?
One might come to reboil the pot.
Abaye asks why the same concern does not prohibit insulation at twilight.
Pots are ordinarily still hot at twilight.
Rava begins a further ruling about insulation.

34b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why is insulation with material that adds heat forbidden even before Shabbat?
One might use hot ashes containing a live ember.
Abaye asks why using those ashes is itself a problem.
One might stoke the coals on Shabbat.
A baraita treats twilight as uncertain day or night and applies both days’ strictures.
Rabbi Yehuda defines twilight through sunset and the fading colors of the sky.
Rabbi Nehemya measures twilight as the time to walk half a mil after sunset.
Rabbi Yosei regards twilight as an unmeasurably brief transition.
For what legal matter do both days’ strictures apply?
Rav Huna cites a zav whose sightings at twilight make impurity and offering duties uncertain.
The baraita first implies a partly darkened sky is already night, then expressly calls it twilight.
Rabba reads the two descriptions together: twilight includes both red sky and a lower sky that has darkened first.
Rav Yosef reads the red sky as day, partial darkening as twilight, and complete darkening as night.
How long is twilight on these readings?
Rabba reports Shmuel’s measure as three parts of a mil.
Could that mean three halves or three thirds?
Those would be called one and a half or one mil; the intended measure is three quarters.
Rav Yosef reports Shmuel’s measure as two parts of a mil.
The Gemara tests what “two parts” means and continues the calculation on the next daf.

35a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Yosef’s “two parts” means two thirds of a mil.
What practical difference separates the two twilight measures?
They differ by one twelfth of a mil.
Their positions reverse for carrying large wicker vessels: Rabba allows a two-kor vessel; Rav Yosef also allows three kor.
Abaye reports that Rabba forbade moving even a two-kor vessel in practice.
A purity mishna treats a forty-seah container, equivalent to two dry kor, as too large to count as a vessel.
Abaye infers that a heaped dry measure adds one third to the liquid measure.
Abaye challenges Rava for looking west when the twilight baraita mentions the eastern sky.
Rava says it means the western face that reddens the east.
Another version has Rava correct Abaye’s eastward gaze with the same explanation.
Rabbi Nehemya measures twilight as half a mil after sunset.
Rabbi Hanina illustrates that interval by a descent from sunlit Mount Carmel to the sea for immersion.
Rabbi Hiyya describes sighting Miriam’s well from Mount Carmel.
Rav treats Miriam’s well as a movable spring that remains pure.
Shmuel says priests can immerse during Rabbi Yehuda’s twilight.
Rabbi Yehuda himself treats that twilight as uncertain.
The statement applies Rabbi Yosei’s later twilight to Rabbi Yehuda’s earlier period.
Why say so if Rabbi Yosei clearly counts the earlier period as day?
The teaching rules out overlap: Rabbi Yosei’s twilight begins only after Rabbi Yehuda’s ends.
Rabbi Yohanan follows Rabbi Yehuda for Shabbat and Rabbi Yosei for teruma.
Why is Rabbi Yosei’s view used leniently for teruma if priestly immersion also involves Torah-level doubt?

35b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The ruling concerns eating teruma: priests wait until Rabbi Yosei’s twilight has ended.
Shmuel distinguishes day, twilight, and night by one, two, and three visible stars.
A baraita gives the same star count.
Rabbi Yosei specifies medium stars, excluding those seen too early or only late at night.
Labor performed in both Friday and Saturday twilights incurs a sin offering, since one act must have fallen on Shabbat.
Rava tells an unpracticed servant to light when the sun reaches the palm treetops.
How should one judge a cloudy day?
Observe evening behavior of roosters, ravens, or plants.
A baraita assigns the first two of six pre-Shabbat blasts to stopping field and town work, and Rabbi Natan assigns the third to lighting.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi instead assigns the third blast to removing tefillin.
After a short preparation interval, the final sequence of blasts marks cessation from work.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel questions the Babylonian practice of ceasing during a terua, which seems to yield only five blasts.
The account restores an additional tekia and explains the inherited custom.
Rav Yehuda teaches his son that the second blast announces lighting.
That version matches neither named tanna.
It must say the third blast, following Rabbi Natan.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael describes the first blast halting field work and bringing distant and nearby workers home together.
The second blast closes shops while cooking pots still remain on stoves.
The third blast prompts removing pots, insulating food, and lighting; after a brief interval come the final blasts.
Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina infers from the sexton’s time to carry home the shofar that lighting remains possible after all six blasts.
That would make the time depend on each sexton’s distance from home.
The shofar is left in a rooftop hiding place because it may not be carried after Shabbat begins.
A baraita permits moving a shofar, though not trumpets.
Rav Yosei distinguishes a privately usable shofar from a communal one.
Abaye asks what permitted use a private shofar has.
It can be used to give someone water.

36a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The shofar can give water to a child.
A communal shofar too could give water to a child, weakening the private versus communal distinction.
Another baraita allows moving both shofar and trumpets, contrary to the earlier baraita.
The three baraitot can follow Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Nehemya’s distinct muktze rules.
Why mention both instruments if neither may be moved?
Here “shofar” also denotes a trumpet.
Rav Hisda says the names of shofar and trumpet were interchanged after the Temple’s destruction.
What practical difference does this name change make?
It matters for the shofar required on Rosh HaShana.
The names of willow and a different species were also exchanged.
What practical difference follows?
It affects the four species for Sukkot.
Names for large and small tables were exchanged.
What practical difference follows?
It affects buying and selling.
Abaye identifies another exchange between names of two stomach chambers.
Why does that distinction matter?
A needle piercing one or both sides of the second stomach changes an animal’s kosher status.
Rav Ashi adds that the names Babylon and Borsif were exchanged.

36b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why does the Babylon/Borsif name change matter?
It matters when writing a woman’s bill of divorce.
The previous chapter concludes.
A new mishna permits a pot on a stove fueled by straw but requires sweeping or covering coals when fueled by pomace or wood.
Beit Shammai allow hot water but not food; Beit Hillel allow both.
Beit Shammai allow removal but not return of a pot; Beit Hillel allow return.
Does “one may not place” forbid returning a pot, while leaving it over Shabbat on uncovered coals remains allowed?
Hananya’s baraita permits leaving partly cooked food on an unswept, uncovered stove.
Or does the mishna forbid even leaving food unless the coals are swept or covered, and all the more so returning it?
The mishna separately records disputes about which food may stay and whether a removed pot may return.
If the first rule concerns leaving food, the two disputes address distinct questions: what may stay and what may be returned.
If the first rule concerns returning food, its details already state what may be returned, making the later return dispute redundant.
Why would that later clause then be needed?

37a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna can be read as a rule about returning pots, with a missing clause allowing food to remain even on uncovered coals.
On that reading, Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel differ about what may remain and whether a removed pot may return.
Rav says the stove permission applies on top, not inside, apparently favoring a rule about returning.
If the rule were about leaving food before Shabbat, why distinguish top from inside?
Rav’s distinction may refer to the later clause about returning a pot.
A Tosefta compares adjacent stoves and records Rabbi Meir’s and Rabbi Yehuda’s differing accounts of food left on or returned to them.
Reading the mishna as about returning fits neither account cleanly, while the leaving reading fits Rabbi Yehuda.
The mishna’s tanna may agree with Rabbi Yehuda on returning food but differ on whether uncovered coals allow food to remain.
May one lean a pot against a stove whose coals were neither swept nor covered?
An adjoining-stoves case may imply permission despite heat from the unswept stove.
The pot there is elevated and cooled by air, unlike a pot directly against the side.
Rav Safra lists leaning, leaving, removing, and returning food after covered coals reignite.
Does his mention of covered coals imply that leaning is forbidden without covering?
By that reasoning even removing a pot would require covering; the list may include actions only to explain the return rule.
Removing and returning happen at one place, whereas leaning and leaving are distinct actions, so the analogy is weak.
A Tosefta expressly permits leaning a pot against a wood-fired stove while requiring covered or swept coals to leave one on it.
Rabbi Oshaya allows fully heated water and fully cooked food on a stove whose covered coals reignited.

37b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The ruling seems to permit even food that improves as it continues to shrink on the stove.
The coals had been covered with ashes.
If so, why state the ruling?
It teaches that the earlier covering still matters after the coals reignite.
Rabbi Yohanan repeats permission for fully cooked food and hot water after covered coals reignite, even with long-burning broom-tree coals.
That again seems to allow food that improves while shrinking.
Here too the coals were covered.
What new point does the ruling teach?
The case of coals reigniting needed to be stated.
The broom-tree detail itself supplies a new point.
Rav Sheshet reports Rabbi Yohanan permitting incompletely heated food to remain on a wood-fired stove, but requiring swept or covered coals for return.
Rava says the mishna about bread crusting before Shabbat already establishes permission to leave food.
Beit Hillel’s permission to return a pot already covers the second point on a swept or covered stove.
Rav Sheshet makes that implication explicit.
Another report of Rabbi Yohanan allows fully cooked food to remain even if further shrinking improves it.
A sage objects that Rav and Shmuel forbid food that improves by shrinking.
Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda acknowledges their view but says he reported Rabbi Yohanan’s different ruling.
Rav Ukva says his community follows Rabbi Yohanan while Rav Ashi’s follows Rav and Shmuel.
Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether food may remain on the stove.
Rav Yosef cites food kept warm for Rav Yehuda.
Abaye says Rav Yehuda’s illness made his case exceptional and asks for the rule for healthy people.
Rav Yosef cites Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak’s practice in Sura.
Rav Ashi saw fish kept on Rav Huna’s stove but cannot tell whether it improved or deteriorated by shrinking.
Rav Nahman forbids food improved by shrinking and permits food worsened by it.
He sorts flour dishes and turnip dishes by whether meat and continued heating improve them.
Food intended for guests, and dishes of fruit or porridge, are treated as worsened by further shrinking.
The next question is posed to Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba.

38a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What if a forgotten pot remains on a stove and cooks during Shabbat?
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba first gives no answer.
The next day he rules that accidental Shabbat cooking may be eaten but intentional cooking may not, adding “no difference.”
What does “no difference” mean?
Rabba and Rav Yosef read it leniently: leaving a pot requires no act on Shabbat, so even deliberate leaving is allowed.
Rav Nahman reads it strictly: people might falsely claim they forgot a pot, so even accidental leaving is penalized.
A baraita distinguishes accidental and deliberate leaving, then Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda distinguish foods by how further heating affects them.
Rav Nahman can place the baraita before a later decree against claiming to have forgotten.
The lenient reading of Rabba and Rav Yosef conflicts with the baraita either before or after that decree.
The decree arose when deliberate stove users increasingly claimed forgetfulness; the Sages then penalized forgotten pots.
How can Rabbi Meir’s and Rabbi Yehuda’s reports here fit their earlier stove rulings?
Rabbi Meir’s two rulings concern initial permission versus food already left.
Rabbi Yehuda’s rulings concern covered versus uncovered coals.
If someone violated the rule and left a pot, did the Sages penalize the food?
Rabbi Yosei allowed hot water left on a stove but prohibited shriveled eggs.
Was the prohibition for that very Shabbat?
No, it concerned the next Shabbat.
Does the distinction mean shriveled eggs improve with more cooking?
Yes: a story recalls eating many very shriveled eggs served to sages.
The mishna’s permission to return a pot introduces Rav Sheshet’s next ruling.

38b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Sheshet says the permitted return applies even on Shabbat itself.
Rabbi Oshaya recalls returning a hot kettle after serving Rabbi Hiyya, without objection.
Rabbi Tadai allows return only while the pot remains in hand, not after it rests on the ground.
Rabbi Ami says Rabbi Tadai followed a personal stringency.
He reports Rabbi Yohanan allowing return even after a pot was set down.
Two transmitters dispute whether Rabbi Elazar permits return after setting the pot on the ground.
On one reading, a pot held in hand may return only if return was intended when it was removed.
That reading implies setting it on the ground forbids return even with prior intent.
Another reading allows return from the ground if that was the original intent.
It then implies that a pot still in hand may return even without prior intent.
What if the pot was hung on a stick or put on a bed?
What if food was transferred from one urn to another? The question is left unresolved.
The mishna gives stricter rules for an oven and an intermediate rule for a kupah, depending on its fuel.
Rav Yosef initially permits leaning a pot against the oven while forbidding placement inside or atop it.
Abaye argues that the mishna’s contrast between stove and oven makes sense only if leaning against the oven is also forbidden.
Rav Adda reads the comparison as involving swept or covered appliances, leaving the stove more permissive than the oven.
A baraita explicitly forbids even leaning against an oven and distinguishes a kupah by its fuel, supporting Abaye.
Why does a kupah follow stove law with straw but oven law with wood?
Its heat falls between a stove’s and an oven’s.
How are a kupah and a stove shaped?
A kupah holds one pot; a stove holds two.
A purity mishna’s lengthwise and widthwise divisions support that structural difference.
A new mishna bars roasting an egg by an urn or hot cloth or sand; Rabbi Yosei permits the cloth case.
The mishna rejects the Tiberias hot-water channel, treating its water as heated on Shabbat or a festival.
What is the liability if someone lightly roasts an egg?
Rav Yosef says the person owes a sin offering.
Mar son of Ravina begins citing the mishna in support.

39a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A mishna allows reheating previously cooked food but says even rinsing certain fish finishes their cooking, supporting liability for lightly cooking an egg.
The mishna forbids heating an egg in sun-warmed cloths.
Another mishna permits placing cold water in the sun to warm.
Does that ruling follow only Rabbi Yosei and not the Sages?
All permit direct sunlight and forbid fire-heated objects; the dispute concerns objects heated by the sun.
Why does Rabbi Yosei not also permit warming an egg in hot sand?
Rabba says sand insulation could lead to insulating in hot ashes.
Rav Yosef says the act displaces dirt.
What case distinguishes the two explanations?
A baraita allows warming an egg on a sun-heated roof but not hot lime; why does Rav Yosef not fear displacing roof dirt?
Ordinary roofs have no loose dirt.
The Tiberias hot-water pipe resembles insulation, but where is displaced dirt to explain its prohibition?
The Tiberias case can address the earlier dispute over sun-heated cloth, with the Sages citing it against Rabbi Yosei.
Rabbi Yosei answers that the springs are fire derivatives because their heat comes from Gehenna.
Rav Hisda begins an inference from the Tiberias case.

39b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Hisda infers from the Tiberias ruling that insulation in a heat-increasing substance is prohibited even before Shabbat.
Ulla rules like the people of Tiberias.
Rav Nahman replies that they had already broken their pipes and abandoned the practice.
Does the mishna mean a whole-body bath? That would imply hot water heated before Shabbat is allowed.
A baraita permits such water only for face, hands, and feet, not the whole body.
If only partial washing is meant, why does the festival clause prohibit bathing?
That would make the anonymous mishna follow Beit Shammai against Beit Hillel on heating water for one’s feet.
Rav Ika instead interprets the case as rinsing the entire body.
A Tosefta’s three opinions on full-body rinsing with hot and cold water supply the relevant dispute.
Rav Hisda first locates that dispute in vessels and permits ground-collected water for everyone.
The Tiberias water was in the ground yet the Sages prohibited it.
The report is corrected: they dispute ground-collected water, but all forbid water in a vessel.
Rabbi Yohanan rules like Rabbi Yehuda’s distinction between hot and cold rinsing.
Was that ruling heard explicitly or inferred from a general principle?
A general rule follows a third sage who mediates between two positions, with an exception for the cloth-scrap dispute.
One reason for that exception is Rabbi Akiva’s student status; a second reason follows on the next daf.

40a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The cloth-scrap exception rests on Rabbi Akiva later adopting Rabbi Yehoshua’s view.
Why does it matter if Rabbi Yohanan’s bathing ruling was inferred rather than heard explicitly?
The ruling was heard explicitly; the inference might apply to a mishna but not a baraita.
Rav allows washing the body limb by limb with water heated before Shabbat; Shmuel limits washing to face, hands, and feet.
A baraita permits face, hands, and feet but expressly excludes the whole body.
Rav reads that exclusion as whole-body washing at once, not limb by limb.
The text specifically lists face, hands, and feet.
Rav reads that list as an example of separate washing.
A second baraita again limits permission to face, hands, and feet.
Rav gives the same separate-washing reading.
A baraita expressly forbids even limb-by-limb washing of the whole body, supporting Shmuel.
An alternate wording of Rav permits all but one limb and meets the same refutations.
Rav Yosef asks Abaye whether Rabba actually followed Rav’s bathing ruling.
Abaye does not know.
Why is this uncertain after Rav’s view was challenged, unless Rabba did not hear the challenge?
Abaye says Rabba generally followed Rav except three named rulings where he followed Shmuel.
A Tosefta permits a sealed bathhouse after Shabbat and, on a festival, sweating there followed by rinsing outside.
An incident at Benei Berak shows sages permitting festival sweating even without boards covering the hot water.
Later misconduct led the Sages to restrict sweating.
Walking through large city bathhouses remains allowed.
What misconduct prompted the restrictions?
Bath attendants and bathers repeatedly evaded successive restrictions on hot water, sweating, and Tiberias springs; the springs were eventually allowed again.
The restriction on sweating remained.
Rava says a violator of a rabbinic rule may be called a transgressor; what is his source?

40b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita about strolling through city bathhouses supplies the use of “transgressor.”
Rava restricts that permission to large city bathhouses; small village baths produce too much heat.
