A baraita permits warming by a fire then rinsing cold, but forbids rinsing first and warming the water still on one’s skin.
A warm towel may be put on the abdomen; a hot water kettle may not, and is dangerous even on weekdays.
A jug may be placed near a fire to temper cold water, not to heat it fully.
Rabbi Yehuda allows warming a cruse of oil without cooking it.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel allows warming oil on a hand before applying it to a child.
What does the first tanna hold about oil?
Rabba and Rav Yosef read him permissively, while Rav Nahman reads him restrictively.
On the permissive reading, the first tanna says oil is not cooked by heating; the two later sages differ over when warming oil counts as cooking.
On the restrictive reading, even mild warming is cooking for the first tanna, while Rabbi Yehuda and Rabban Shimon dispute that threshold.
How then does Rabban Shimon differ from the first tanna?
The difference is indirect warming on the hand.
Shmuel sets the same rule for oil and water: heating to where a hand recoils is forbidden; less is permitted.
What counts as heat from which a hand recoils?
Heat that would scald a baby’s abdomen.
In a bathhouse, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi tells a student to warm oil in a secondary vessel.
The instruction implies that oil can be cooked, a secondary vessel does not cook it, and merely warming oil can count as cooking.
How could Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi discuss law in a bathhouse where even Torah thought is prohibited?
Using a secular language would not solve it, because sacred content remains prohibited there.
A warning to prevent an imminent violation is different.
Rabbi Meir likewise warned a student against washing or oiling a bathhouse floor on Shabbat.
Ravina infers from the bathhouse incident that cooking in Tiberias hot springs incurs liability.
Rav Hisda says such cooking is exempt from Torah liability.
The “liability” here means disciplinary lashes for a rabbinic violation.
Rabbi Zeira saw Rabbi Abbahu floating and is uncertain whether his feet left the floor.
A baraita forbids swimming even in a pool in a courtyard.
The resolution begins by distinguishing the cases.

41a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Swimming is prohibited in a pool without retaining walls; Rabbi Abbahu’s bath had walls.
Rabbi Zeira saw Rabbi Abbahu cover himself while bathing but could not tell whether he touched his body.
Rabbi Eliezer’s baraita forbids such touching because it may prompt arousal.
Abaye compares the fear of falling in a river to soldiers too preoccupied to pour libations; fear may prevent improper thought.
Another teaching treats covering oneself as apparent denial of Abraham’s covenant.
The ruling differs between entering and leaving the water.
The sages’ contrasting postures when entering and exiting the water illustrate the distinction.
Rabbi Zeira avoids Rav Yehuda because he plans to leave Babylonia, contrary to Rav Yehuda’s reading of Jeremiah.
He nonetheless overhears Rav Yehuda in the bathhouse request natron and a comb, advise exhaling, and advise drinking bath water.
The mundane requests show that secular matters may be spoken there even in Hebrew.
Exhaling follows Shmuel’s claim that breath helps produce sweat.
Why drink the bathhouse water?
A baraita lists bodily harms from eating, bathing, or neglecting aftercare without appropriate drinking, movement, rinsing, or oiling.
A mishna permits drinking from a swept mulyar but not a swept antikhi on Shabbat.
A mulyar has water inside and coals outside.
Rabba and Rav Nahman give different structures for an antikhi and discuss how each ruling includes the other.
A baraita attributes the retained heat to the antikhi’s copper, supporting Rav Nahman.
A mishna forbids adding a little cold water to an emptied urn to heat it, but allows enough to warm it gently.
How should the mishna’s two clauses be reconciled?
Rav Adda distinguishes a small amount that heats from a large amount that only warms.

41b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Does the cold water not temper and harden the hot metal urn?
Rabbi Shimon permits an unintended result of an otherwise permitted act.
Abaye objects that the mishna says the urn was removed, not that its water was emptied.
He reads the first clause as an urn still holding hot water: little cold water would heat, much cold water merely warms.
A wholly emptied hot urn may receive no water because that hardens it; this follows Rabbi Yehuda’s rule for unintended acts.
Rav permits adding water to warm it, not to harden the vessel.
Shmuel is reported as permitting even hardening.
How could deliberate hardening be permitted on Shabbat?
The report is restated: Rav permits only an amount that warms, forbidding an amount sufficient to harden.
Shmuel permits even the larger amount; the reasoning continues on the next daf.

42a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel permits even enough water to harden the vessel when hardening is unintended.
How can Shmuel follow Rabbi Shimon on unintended acts when he allows extinguishing hot metal for public safety but forbids extinguishing hot wood?
Shmuel follows Rabbi Shimon for unintended consequences but Rabbi Yehuda for labor not needed for its own sake.
Ravina therefore allows moving a hazardous thorn in short stages in a public domain, or farther in a karmelit.
The discussion returns to warming water in a vessel.
Beit Shammai permit hot water into cold; Beit Hillel permit pouring in either direction in a cup.
For a bath, hot may be poured into cold but not reverse; Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya forbids even that.
Rav Nahman rules like Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya.
Rav Yosef initially equates a basin with a bath.
Abaye cites Rabbi Hiyya that a basin is not like a bath.
If a basin were a bath and Rabbi Shimon’s restriction applied, how could one bathe in hot water on Shabbat?
Rabbi Shimon’s restriction can instead address the cup rule: he forbids cold water into hot.
Would that make his view identical to Beit Shammai’s?
He reports no dispute between the schools on this point.
Rav Huna observed that Rava was not strict about the vessel distinction.
Rabbi Hiyya’s baraita allows a jug of water into a basin in either hot-cold order.
Perhaps the jug itself separates the waters, so that case is different.
The text actually says to pour the jug’s water into the basin in either direction.
A new mishna forbids adding spices to a boiling pot removed from the fire.

42b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna permits spices in a secondary bowl; Rabbi Yehuda permits them more broadly except with vinegar or fish brine.
Does Rabbi Yehuda relax the first clause or restrict the second?
A baraita allows spices in boiling pots except those containing vinegar or brine, showing he is lenient.
Rav Yosef initially treats salt like spice: a primary vessel cooks it, a secondary vessel does not.
Abaye cites Rabbi Hiyya that salt differs, here meaning even a secondary vessel cooks it.
That reading conflicts with Rav Nahman’s claim that salt takes as long to cook as tough beef.
Another version repeats Rav Yosef’s comparison of salt and spice.
Abaye reads Rabbi Hiyya oppositely: even a primary vessel does not cook salt.
Rav Nahman’s tough-beef comparison supports that reading.
A mishna forbids placing a vessel under a lamp for dripping oil on Shabbat; a vessel placed before Shabbat is allowed, but its oil remains set aside.
Rav Hisda forbids catching a hen’s egg in a vessel but permits covering a laid egg to keep it from breaking.
Rabba says covering an egg in the usual laying place is a common rescue, while catching one on a slope is uncommon.
A baraita permits placing a vessel under an unexpectedly broken barrel of untithed produce.
New earthenware barrels commonly break.
Another baraita permits a vessel under a lamp to catch sparks.
Sparks are also common.

43a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita permits overturning a bowl to keep a lamp from igniting a beam.
Low-ceilinged houses commonly present this danger.
A broken beam may be supported with a bench or bed frame.
New beams commonly break.
A vessel may be placed under a leaking roof on Shabbat.
New houses commonly leak.
Rav Yosef instead explains the hen-egg limit: catching it makes the receiving vessel unusable on Shabbat.
A vessel may catch untithed produce from a broken barrel.
Untithed produce can become usable if someone improperly tithes it on Shabbat.
A vessel may be put under a lamp for falling sparks.
Sparks have no enduring substance to immobilize it.
A bench may support a broken beam.
The support is loose and can still be removed.
A vessel may catch a ceiling leak.
That water is fit for drinking.
A basket may be placed before chicks to climb on and off.
The basket can be moved after they leave.
Baraitot forbid moving it both while the chicks are on it and afterward.
If chicks sat on it at twilight, the basket remains set aside all Shabbat.
Rabbi Yitzhak forbids both catching a laid egg and moving a vessel merely to cover it, because an egg itself cannot be carried.
He answers the earlier challenges as cases where the vessel’s location was needed anyway.
A baraita explicitly permits covering a newly laid egg with a vessel.
Its vessel too was moved because its place was needed.
Another source permits spreading mats over stones.
The rounded stones are suitable for bathroom use.
Mats may also be spread over bricks.
Leftover bricks can be used for leaning.
A mat may cover a beehive against sun or rain without intending to trap bees.
The hive holds usable honey.
How does that explanation work in winter, when there is no new honey?

43b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What about the rainy season, when fresh honey is absent?
Two honeycombs remain in the hive.
Are those not reserved for the bees?
The owner thought to use them before Shabbat.
Would covering be forbidden without that preparation?
Why then does the baraita state a trapping condition rather than the preparation distinction?
Even prepared combs do not permit covering the hive with intent to trap.
Which tanna requires preparation yet appears to allow an unintended trapping result?
It follows Rabbi Yehuda: the mat must leave a gap so bees are not trapped even incidentally.
Rav Ashi offers another reading: the baraita describes rainy or sunny days in spring and autumn when honey remains.
Rav Sheshet says Rav Huna’s rule already permits a partition for a living person near a corpse, but not solely for the corpse.
How is that applied?
Two people sit beside a sunlit corpse, place beds and a mat for their own shade, then leave a shelter standing over the body.
For moving a corpse from the sun, Shmuel allows turning it from bed to bed; Rav uses a loaf or child.
Both permit the loaf-or-child method; they differ on whether indirect movement without one counts as forbidden carrying.
A Tosefta disputes rescuing a corpse from a fire on Shabbat.
With a loaf or child, why forbid rescue; without one, why permit it?
Perhaps the tannaim disagree over whether indirect movement counts as movement.
They may agree it does; the permissive view is driven by a person’s distress over a deceased relative in a fire.

44a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Moving the corpse is allowed here because refusing could lead someone to extinguish the fire.
Rabbi Yohanan rules like Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish on rescuing a corpse.
The fallen lamp oil is unavailable because it was not prepared for Shabbat use.
A baraita forbids remaining lamp or bowl oil; Rabbi Shimon permits it.
The mishna permits moving a new lamp but not a used one.
Rabbi Shimon permits moving lamps except one that is burning.
The baraita attributes the distinction between new and used lamps to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Meir forbids moving a lamp lit that Shabbat.
Rabbi Shimon bars only a burning lamp, permits it after it goes out, yet bars large oil vessels.
Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Shimon even permits taking dripping oil while the lamp burns.
Abaye says the son agrees with his father on one point and differs on another.
Both reject a general ban on set-aside objects.
The father waits for the flame to go out; the son does not require that.
The baraita nevertheless bars moving a cup, bowl, or lantern.
Why are these vessels different?
Ulla assigns this last clause to Rabbi Yehuda.
Mar Zutra asks how the word “however” could fit if the clause changes speakers.
He instead keeps Rabbi Shimon as speaker: a small lamp is expected to go out, but large vessels are not.
A baraita says Rabbi Shimon permits remaining oil from both a lamp and a bowl.
That bowl is lamp-sized; the prohibited bowl here is as large as a cup.
Rabbi Zeira initially distinguishes the permissive and restrictive views for a lit metal candlestick.
Would Rabbi Yehuda then prohibit only repugnant objects and allow objects set aside by prohibition?
A baraita shows that Rabbi Yehuda forbids a metal lamp lit on Shabbat.
Rabbi Zeira’s teaching is corrected: all prohibit a candlestick lit that day and permit one not lit.
Rav says that a bed designated for money may not be moved.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak challenges this from the mishna allowing an unused lamp.

44b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A lamp intended for burning may be moved if unlit; surely a bed not intended for money should be movable.
Rav’s statement is corrected: designation bars a bed only after money has actually been placed on it.
An undesignated bed is barred while holding money, or if it held money at twilight; otherwise it is movable.
Ulla cites the mishna of a detachable wagon undercarriage, which cannot be pulled while carrying money.
The wording implies that without money it may be moved even after holding money at twilight.
That mishna follows Rabbi Shimon, who rejects muktze; Rav follows Rabbi Yehuda.

45a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav permits a lamp on a palm on Shabbat but not on a Festival, supporting his alignment with Rabbi Yehuda.
The difference makes sense if the Shabbat lamp is set aside and will not be moved.
If Rav followed Rabbi Shimon, the lamp could be moved on either day, leaving no distinction.
Rav nevertheless allowed moving a Hanukkah lamp to evade the Persian fire priests.
Rav relied on Rabbi Shimon only in pressing circumstances, without adopting his general rule.
Reish Lakish asks whether Rabbi Shimon still forbids wheat or eggs actively set aside for planting or hatching.
Rabbi Yohanan limits Rabbi Shimon’s muktze to oil in a burning lamp, reserved for its mitzva and subject to prohibition.
A decorated sukka’s food and ornaments remain unavailable until the festival ends, despite being reserved for a mitzva alone.
A related baraita shows Rabbi Shimon allows ordinary sukka wood but agrees festival-sukka material is unavailable unless stipulated.
The earlier lamp example is amended: dedication to a mitzva itself can make the item unavailable.
Another report of Rabbi Yohanan explicitly uses a burning lamp as the model of this restriction.
Shmuel identifies dried figs and raisins as Rabbi Shimon’s exceptional muktze cases.
A baraita also requires advance designation for peaches, quinces, and other fruit put out to dry.
If the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, why state the obvious case of deliberately set-aside fruit; does it follow Rabbi Shimon?
It follows Rabbi Yehuda and teaches that even fruit being eaten is set aside once carried to the roof to dry.
Rabbi Shimon son of Rabbi asks his father a related question, continued on the next page.

45b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Are unripe dates left to ripen set aside according to Rabbi Shimon?
Rabbi answers that Rabbi Shimon restricts only dried figs and raisins.
Rabbi’s festival ruling still treats animals that graze outside town year-round as set aside.
Those animals may be as deliberately unavailable as drying figs and raisins.
Alternatively, Rabbi described Rabbi Shimon’s position without endorsing it.
Or Rabbi argued on the Sages’ terms, urging them to count seasonal grazers as domesticated; they refused.
A report says that the halakha was said to follow Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Yohanan nevertheless forbade moving a hen’s roost, which seems to support muktze.
The roost in question contained a dead chick.
That explanation fails for the view that Rabbi Shimon permits animals that died on Shabbat.
The roost instead contained an egg laid on Shabbat.
Rav Nahman links the ban on newly formed items to muktze, which Rabbi Shimon rejects.
The egg held an embryo and was fit for neither people nor animals.
A later report gives Rabbi Yohanan the ruling of Rabbi Yehuda, while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi follows Rabbi Shimon.
Rav Yosef reads the earlier wording “they said” as a report of others, not Rabbi Yohanan’s own ruling.
Abaye cites Rabbi Asi’s refusal to move a fallen candelabrum as evidence that his teacher Rabbi Yohanan held like Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Yosef distinguishes a candelabrum: Rabbi Yohanan bars it regardless of its size even when allowing an oil lamp.
Why is a candelabrum treated differently?
Its fixed place makes people reluctant to move it.
Abaye begins a challenge from a groom’s canopy, which also has a fixed place.

46a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The canopy may be assembled and taken apart on Shabbat, challenging the fixed-place explanation.
Abaye instead identifies the disputed candelabrum as one with joints.
Why would Reish Lakish then allow moving it?
Its grooves only resemble joints; it does not actually come apart.
Actual joints bar movement at any size; a large grooved stand is barred by decree.
The dispute concerns a small grooved stand and whether to extend that decree.
Rabbi Yohanan ordinarily follows an anonymous mishna, but the wagon mishna appears to permit moving after money falls off.
Rabbi Zeira confines the wagon case to one without money throughout twilight, preserving Rabbi Yohanan’s ruling.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reports that Rabbi issued a ruling about a candelabrum and Rabbi Shimon’s lamp.
The ruling may permit the candelabrum or instead permit only the lamp; the doubt remains unresolved.
Two visitors moved lamps and their hosts objected.
Rabbi Abbahu moved a lamp near Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi but refrained near Rabbi Yohanan.
Why did Rabbi Abbahu act differently in the two places if he followed one consistent ruling?
He followed Rabbi Shimon but respected Rabbi Yohanan’s practice in his presence.
Rav Yehuda permits an oil lamp but forbids a naphtha lamp.
Rabba and Rav Yosef allow moving even a naphtha lamp.
Rav Avya soils Rava’s bed, prompting Rava to challenge him.
Rava asks why Rabba and Rav Yosef allow a naphtha lamp.
It can be used to cover a vessel.
That reason would seem to allow moving ordinary courtyard pebbles too.
The lamp has the standing of a vessel, unlike the pebbles.
A supporting baraita begins and continues on the next page.

46b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Jewelry may be moved in a courtyard because it counts as a vessel, supporting the lamp distinction.
Rav Nahman thanks God that Rav Avya answered without embarrassment.
Abaye contrasts Rabbi Shimon’s permission for leftover oil with his ban on a firstborn whose blemish appeared only on the Festival.
Oil is expected to remain after the lamp goes out; a qualifying blemish and a sage’s approval are too uncertain.
A woman may eat after her husband annuls a Shabbat vow, despite uncertainty whether he will act.
Her vow is made with her husband’s power of annulment in view.
Likewise a person may seek release from a vow on Shabbat despite uncertainty about a sage.
Three ordinary people can release that vow if the sage declines, unlike inspection of a firstborn.
Abaye asks why Rabbi Shimon bars moving a burning lamp if he permits unintended consequences such as a furrow from dragging furniture.
The proposed distinction bars unintended effects by decree when their deliberate form would be a Torah prohibition.
Rava cites garment sellers: carrying mixed fabrics without intent is allowed even though intentional wearing is a Torah ban.
Rava begins a revised explanation, continued on the next page.

47a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A burning lamp supports a forbidden flame, explaining why the lamp, oil, and wick cannot be moved.
A transmitted ruling says Rabbi permitted moving a coal pan containing ashes.
Rabbi Yohanan elsewhere allows carrying a basket with a stone only when fruit is in it; how can ashes alone suffice?
The coal pan also contained usable bits of frankincense.
Abaye objects that scraps have no value in Rabbi’s wealthy household, as a baraita makes significance depend on the owner.
Abaye instead compares removing the pan to removing a foul chamber pot.
Rava objects that the pan neither smells nor stands exposed like such a pot.
Rava recalls moving a pan for its usable ashes despite wood fragments on it.
A baraita bars a lamp containing broken wick fragments.
Abaye places that baraita in the Galilee, where the relevant material was plentiful.
Levi bar Shmuel asks whether a collapsible weaver’s bed may be reassembled on Shabbat.
The first sages he asks permit it.
Rav Yehuda reports that Rav and Shmuel instead make one liable for reassembling it.
A baraita distinguishes candelabrum branches, a plasterer’s pole, and two types of horn by their assembly.
The permissive sages relied on another tanna who treats reassembly of detachable bed parts less severely.

47b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita still bars ordinary reassembly and makes forceful fastening liable, but Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits loose fitting.
Rav Hama’s household assembled a collapsible bed on a Festival.
A sage asks why this escapes even a rabbinic ban on atypical building.
Rava follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel’s permission for loosely fitted parts.
The mishna allows catching sparks in a vessel but forbids putting water there to extinguish them.
Does catching the sparks immobilize the vessel?
Sparks leave no enduring substance in the vessel.
The mishna’s water prohibition is repeated for analysis.
Does this anonymous ruling follow Rabbi Yosei’s ban on indirect extinguishing?
The prohibition applies even to water placed there before Shabbat, where Rabbi Yosei’s indirect-action rule does not fit.
Rav Ashi says even the Rabbis prohibit bringing the spark directly to its extinguishing.
The next mishna lists heat-producing insulation materials and permits certain moist materials only when dry.
Does the ban on pressed residue mean olive residue specifically, or also sesame residue?
A cited ruling bars placing an insulated basket on olive residue, suggesting that olives are the mishna’s case.
The response begins to distinguish direct insulation from placing a basket on residue.

48a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Olive residue produces extra heat beneath a pot; sesame residue does not.
Rabba rebukes a servant for placing cold water over a hot kettle.
Rabbi Zeira asks how that differs from stacking two hot-water urns.
The urn preserves heat, whereas the cold jug gains new heat.
Rabba next rebukes the servant for placing a cup on a cloth over a water vat.
Rabbi Zeira asks why this was wrong.
Rabba predicts that the servant will wring the wet cloth, which then happens.
Why is a different covering cloth permitted?
That cloth is not one whose owner cares to wring it dry.
May stuffing used as insulation be moved on Shabbat?
Abaye says its temporary insulating use does not make valuable stuffing freely available.
A baraita permits insulating in wool and stuffing but says they may not be moved.
The baraita may mean only that unused insulating materials may not be moved.
Why would that obvious rule need stating?
It excludes a proposed use for sitting on those materials.
Rav Hisda allows fallen stuffing to be returned to a pillow on Shabbat.
A baraita forbids putting stuffing into a pillow or cushion even on a Festival.
New pillows are different from old pillows being refilled.
Another baraita explicitly permits replacing stuffing that fell out.
Rav holds one liable for cutting a new neck opening into a garment on Shabbat.
Rav Kahana begins a challenge, continued on the next page.

48b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why does opening a shirt differ from piercing a barrel stopper?
The shirt opening cuts an integral connection; the stopper was already a separate piece.
A mishna treats temporarily attached laundry, keys, and mixed-fabric stitching as connected for impurity.
Another mishna treats an axe handle as connected only during use.
An unused handle may be discarded, while the other temporary attachments remain useful.
The question is transmitted under different names in Sura and Pumbedita.
Which tanna treats an attached component like its host object?
Rav names Rabbi Meir and cites a mishna about receptacles attached to a stove.
If Rabbi Meir treats them as part of the stove, why do they share contact impurity but not airspace impurity?
The receptacles are separate by Torah law; the Sages imposed contact impurity.
Why did the decree not also cover impurity through the stove’s airspace?
The distinction signals rabbinic impurity and prevents burning teruma and consecrated food improperly.
A baraita treats multipart scissors and a plane blade as joined for impurity but not for purification sprinkling.
How can the parts count as connected for one law and separate for the other?
Rava distinguishes Torah law during use, when they are connected for both, from times outside use.

49a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Sages extended the connection rule for impurity and narrowed it for purification sprinkling.
Does the mishna’s ban on moist insulation mean naturally damp material or material wetted later?
The listed materials, especially wool stuffing, suggest moisture from an external source.
Wool from between an animal’s thighs can be naturally damp.
A baraita’s moist garment seems impossible if only natural moisture counts.
It too could be made from wool taken from that area.
The mishna allows several dry insulating materials; Rabbi Yehuda forbids fine material and permits coarse.
Rabbi Yannai requires a clean body for tefillin, like Elisha Man of Wings.
What does a clean body require?
Abaye says avoiding flatulence; Rava says not sleeping while wearing them.
Why was Elisha called Man of Wings?
He hid his tefillin from a Roman officer; on opening his hand, he found dove wings.
Why specifically dove wings?
Israel is likened to a dove whose wings protect it, as mitzvot protect Israel.
The discussion returns to the mishna’s wood shavings.
Does Rabbi Yehuda’s distinction concern wood shavings or flax chaff?
A baraita likens fine flax chaff to manure, identifying the subject of his ruling.
The mishna allows moving hides but not fleece, and records a dispute about replacing a pot in the fleece.
The sages ask whether movable hides include those kept by a craftsman.
Rabbi Yonatan limits permission to a homeowner’s hides because a craftsman protects his stock.
Rabbi Hanina begins a contrasting report from Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei.

49b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yishmael reports that his tanner father used his own hides for sitting.
A baraita forbids moving a craftsman’s boards unless designated for guests.
Boards are different because their owner is particular about damage.
Another baraita permits moving both tanned and untanned hides, apparently including a craftsman’s.
The permission may concern only a homeowner’s hides.
If so, why distinguish them by tanning for impurity rather than by ownership for Shabbat?
The entire baraita speaks of homeowner hides.
A tannaitic dispute explicitly separates homeowner and craftsman hides; Rabbi Yosei permits both.
The sages ask what the mishna’s thirty-nine primary labors correspond to.
Rabbi Hanina ties the count to the Tabernacle’s labors.
Rabbi Yonatan instead ties it to occurrences of the word labor in the Torah.
Does the word “labor” in the Joseph narrative enter that count?
Abaye proposes counting occurrences in a Torah scroll.
Rav Yosef says the choice is between Joseph’s verse and an ambiguous Tabernacle verse; the issue remains open.
A baraita links prohibited work, including sowing and transferring boards, to work done for the Tabernacle.
Why would transferring between two private domains be prohibited?
The transfer crossed the public space between the wagons.
Rava says fleece used for insulation may be moved, unlike fleece left unused.
A new student challenges Rava from the mishna’s ban on moving fleece used for insulation.

50a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna makes the fleece fall from the lifted cover, contradicting permission to move it.
Rava’s statement is revised: prior designation, not one-time use, permits moving fleece.
Another transmitted ruling likewise distinguishes designated from undesignated fleece.
Ravina instead locates the mishna in a merchant’s stored fleece.
A baraita bars merchant fleece unless its owner prepares it for ordinary use.
A baraita disputes whether palm branches cut for wood require tying before they can be used for sitting.
The teacher of that baraita rules like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who needs no tie.
Rav requires a tie, Shmuel requires intent, and Rav Asi accepts prior sitting.
The first two views match the baraita, but which tanna supports Rav Asi?
A wound dressing used briefly before Shabbat may be worn without further preparation.
A mishna also allows moving bed straw by hand after prior use or designation.
Who is the tanna who opposes Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on palm branches?
A report about Rabbi Hanina ben Akiva requiring prior intent for branches at a feast or mourning house identifies him.
That special busy setting implies ordinary sitting would still require tying the branches.
Rav Yehuda permits prepared earth for household use; Mar Zutra requires setting aside a corner.
Does designation alone follow only Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rather than the Sages who require an act?
The Sages require an act only where one can make a preparatory act; loose earth is different.
Conflicting baraitot on cleaning with sand seem to dispute whether preparation by action is needed.
Both may allow designation alone; the dispute instead concerns unintended smoothing under Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon.
The permissive baraita bars washing hair with sand, challenging its assignment to Rabbi Shimon.

50b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A nazirite may wash and separate hair without combing, supporting the challenge about unintended hair loss.
Both cleaning baraitot may follow Rabbi Yehuda, with different views on whether sand scrapes a vessel.
The permissive baraita also allows washing face and limbs, which might remove hair.
It may concern a child, woman, or eunuch without facial hair.
Several sages list powders and mixtures permitted for washing.
What is the washing mixture called berada?
Its ingredients are aloe, myrtle, and violet; aloe must not be a majority.
May olives be crushed for washing on Shabbat?
Rav Sheshet says ruining the olives is barred even on a weekday.
Shmuel permits using bread for ordinary needs despite possible damage.
Bread stays edible, while crushed olives become repulsive.
Mar Zutra declines to use berada although his colleagues wash with it.
They ask why he does not accept Rav Sheshet’s permission.
Rav Mordekhai says Mar Zutra rejects such washing even on weekdays.
He follows a baraita permitting scraping for pain but forbidding it for beautification.
Which teaching supports the colleagues who washed?
A baraita encourages daily washing for the sake of one’s Maker.
The mishna’s concern about tipping a fleece-filled basket is recalled.
Rav rules that all agree a collapsed hollow cannot receive the pot again.
The Rabbis explicitly allow replacement, suggesting they allow it even after collapse.
They disagree only on whether to guard against a possible future collapse.
A flower stem may be withdrawn after its earth opening was loosened before Shabbat.
Shmuel applies the same prior-loosening rule to a knife stored between bricks.
A knife among reeds can be removed without that preparation.
Rav Mordekhai begins a challenge from buried vegetables with exposed leaves.

51a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The buried-vegetable mishna permits removal on Shabbat and conclusively refutes the earlier restrictions.
The mishna forbids starting insulation after dark but permits restoring a cover and sheltering cold water.
Shmuel permits insulating cold food.
Rav Yosef asks what that adds to the mishna’s cold-water jug.
Abaye says Shmuel also allows insulating a cold item normally insulated while hot.
A report that Rabbi forbade cold insulation conflicts with a baraita that he permitted it.
Rabbi first forbade it, then accepted Rabbi Yosei’s permissive ruling reported by his son.
Rav Pappa remarks on Rabbi’s deference to an elder whose son studied under him.
Rav Nahman asks his servant for insulated cold food and water heated by a gentile.
Rabbi Ami objects; Rav Yosef asks why, since Rav Nahman followed his teachers.
Shmuel permits cold insulation, and Rav permits food cooked by a gentile when it is edible raw.
A prominent person is held to a stricter public standard.
A baraita allows adding insulation after dark or exchanging sheets and blankets.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits insulating water transferred to a second urn, since it is being cooled.
A pot under a movable cover may be removed and returned even when other insulation is set aside.
If the cover itself is set aside, return is allowed only if part of the pot remains exposed.

51b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Without an exposed part, the pot may not be removed and returned.
Rabbi Yehuda compares fine flax chaff to heat-producing manure.
The baraita distinguishes safe stacking of vessels for keeping heat from stacking that heats them anew.
A restrictive view bars cold insulation too; Rabbi permits it.
Snow or hail may melt in a cup, but it may not be crushed to release water.
The new mishna lists restraints with which camels, donkeys, and horses may go out and how chains are purified.
What is the mishna’s naka with a hatam?
It is a white female camel with an iron nose ring.
What is a luvdekim with a perumbiya?
It is a Libyan donkey with an iron halter.
A story about Levi illustrates that a donkey’s performance depends on its feed.
The students ask whether restraints permitted for one animal can be switched to another.
A female camel’s insufficient bit would be a burden.
Is a stronger nose ring on an ordinary camel a burden or valid extra restraint?
Rabbi Yosei’s list of four animals with a bit seems to exclude a camel with a nose ring.
It may instead exclude a female camel using a bit.
A baraita allows a Libyan donkey and camel with a bit; tanna’im dispute a wild animal’s collar.
Which animal makes that dispute meaningful if large and small animals present opposite obvious cases?
A cat exposes the issue: is a stronger restraint than needed a burden?
Shmuel rules like Hananya, allowing extra restraint.
A travel story begins when Levi’s donkey moves ahead and Rabba bar Rav Huna feels slighted.

52a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Levi asks whether his unruly donkey may wear a stronger halter on Shabbat.
The reply cites Shmuel’s ruling that additional security is permitted.
A baraita allows a goat to go out with a bit fixed through a hole between its horns.
If the bit passes through the goat’s beard, will it stay secure or fall and be carried? The doubt remains open.
Rav and Shmuel disagree whether a cow’s horn strap is forbidden only as ornament or even as restraint.
Rav Yosef uses Shmuel’s ruling on extra security to identify the permissive view as Shmuel’s.
Abaye cites the four-animal bit list as evidence that Shmuel forbids excessive restraint.
Rav Yosef proposes discarding the conflicting report.
Why discard that report rather than the other one?
Explicit attributions assign the restrictive view to Rav and the permissive restraint view to Shmuel.
A red heifer tied by reins remains fit; if reins are a burden, why is it not disqualified?
Travel, the heifer’s high value, or its unruly nature can make stronger restraint necessary.
Does “go out with a chain” allow a wrapped chain or only a chain used to pull? Rav Huna and Shmuel differ.
A baraita and observed calves support allowing wrapped reins when ready for pulling.
A report of Rabbi’s mules wearing bits leaves open whether their reins were wrapped or used for pulling.
A second report explicitly says the mules went out with wrapped reins.
The sages argue the second report adds nothing if the first report and Rabbi Yosei’s list already establish the case.
Rav Asi says the reports separately establish Rabbi’s acceptance and permission for wrapped reins.
How can the chains in the mishna receive impurity if animal rings are generally pure?

52b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The cited mishna concludes that animal rings are ritually pure.
Rabbi Yitzhak says these were human ornaments later reassigned to animals.
Rav Yosef says a chain pulled by a person counts as a human-used utensil, like an animal prod.
Would rings attached to a chain obstruct immersion?
Rabbi Ami says the rings were widened.
If the rings were altered, Rabbi Yitzhak’s theory of inherited impurity seems to make immersion unnecessary.
Rabbi Ami can follow Rabbi Yehuda: improving a vessel does not remove its impurity.
Another teaching explains that the rings were already well spaced.
A disciple asks Rabbi Eliezer about ring distinctions; he first assigns them to Shabbat, not impurity.
Animal rings and human rings plainly differ for impurity.
The claim concerns only rings worn by people.
A belt buckle and a finger ring still differ for impurity.
The claim concerns only finger rings.
Finger rings of different base materials still differ.
The claim concerns finger rings made wholly of metal.
The disciple similarly asks about needles; Rabbi Eliezer initially assigns the difference to Shabbat.
A needle missing its eye or point is pure, contrary to a broad sameness rule.
The claim concerns intact needles.
Rust on an intact needle can still affect its impurity status.
The claim concerns finished, smoothed needles.
A baraita appears to distinguish eyed and eyeless needles for impurity.
That distinction concerns unfinished needles.
The next mishna lists permitted animal coverings and restraints, with Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda dissenting.

53a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel requires the donkey’s saddlecloth to have been tied on before Shabbat.
The later mishna’s wording supports this: a cloth tied only on Shabbat remains barred.
A baraita explicitly requires prior tying and records a limited dissent about a saddle.
May a saddlecloth be placed on a donkey on Shabbat?
Rabbi Hiyya permits it.
Rav Asi compares the banned saddle and cites a baraita forbidding even its removal by hand.
Rabbi Zeira explains that Rav permits even a feed basket and all the more a cloth preventing cold.
Shmuel allows the cloth but forbids a feed basket and sharply rejects Rav’s broader view.
Rabbi Yohanan permits the saddlecloth, and Rabbi Zeira links the ruling to Aryokh.
Aryokh is Shmuel, but why name him when Rav also permits the cloth?
The fuller report also forbids hanging a feed basket, matching Shmuel specifically.
Why may a cloth be placed when a saddle may not be removed by hand?
The saddle can fall off through walking the animal.
Rav Pappa distinguishes warming an animal in discomfort from removing a saddle merely to cool it.
A baraita bans several animal items in public, including feed baskets, while allowing therapeutic coverings.
The ban specifically names the public domain, seemingly allowing baskets in a courtyard even for larger foals.
The courtyard permission concerns small foals whose feeding basket relieves difficulty.

53b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The wording links small foals to therapeutic amulets, confirming the explanation.
Why ban an effective amulet on an animal when an effective amulet may be worn by a person?
Perhaps this amulet has not proved effective.
The baraita explicitly says it has proved effective.
It was effective for people but not for animals.
Can an amulet succeed for a person yet fail for an animal?
The person has a protective mazal that the animal lacks.
Why then call this an animal-specific stringency?
The stringency refers to shoes, not amulets.
A baraita allows treatment of a person’s wound but not an animal’s, apparently disregarding animal pain.
It concerns pleasure after healing, not treatment of pain.
An overheated animal cannot be stood in water though a similarly afflicted person can.
Ulla attributes the ban to a decree against preparing medicine.
Why would the same decree not bar treating a person?
The person appears merely to be cooling off.
Could the animal not appear to be cooling off too?
People do not ordinarily cool animals in water that way.
A separate law lets an owner call an animal from beyond its limit without a preventive decree.
Ravina places the animal within the owner’s own limit.
Another resolution treats the medicine decree for animals as a tannaitic dispute; Rava permits the treatment.
One baraita bans goats’ udder pouches while another permits them.
Rav Yehuda distinguishes securely tied pouches from loose ones.
Rav Yosef instead invokes the tannaitic dispute over bound udders.
Alternatively, both baraitot can follow Rabbi Yehuda and differ between drying and preserving milk.
An Antioch case reports pouches used to protect unusually large udders.
A baraita recounts a widower miraculously nursing his infant.
Rav Yosef praises the miracle; Abaye objects that nature was altered for the man.
Rav Yehuda and Rav Nahman reflect on the difficulty of providing sustenance.
A story about a one-armed wife prompts competing readings of modesty.
What does the mishna’s “levuvin” mean for rams?
Rav Huna explains it as paired or bound together, supported by a verse about closeness.
Ulla instead describes leather tied over rams’ hearts against wolves.
Why would wolves threaten rams but not ewes?
Rams walk at the flock’s front.
Why would wolves attack only the front?
The rams are plumper.
Wolves cannot reliably distinguish fat rams from ewes.
The rams’ raised heads and searching gait draw the wolves.
Rav Nahman instead explains leather tied beneath males to prevent mounting.
The parallel rule for ewes exposes their tails to encourage mating, supporting the contrast.
What shows that “shehuzot” means exposed?
A cited verse begins the linguistic support, continued on the next page.

54a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The cited verse completes the explanation that shehuzot suggests exposure.
What does the mishna’s “kevulot” mean?
Ewes’ tails are bound down to prevent mating.
How does the word suggest infertility?
The name Kavul for infertile land is offered as linguistic support.
What does “land of Kavul” mean?
Rav Huna describes inhabitants surrounded by wealth.
Rava asks why that wealth would displease the recipient of the land.
Its pampered inhabitants would not work for him.
Rav Nahman instead describes ankle-deep sandy land that does not produce.
What does the mishna’s “kevunot” mean?
The sheep were wrapped from birth to keep their wool clean and fine.
The mishna’s bound-udder case is introduced.
Rav follows Rabbi Yehuda on bound udders; Shmuel follows Rabbi Yosei.
A separate version gives Rav permission for drying but Shmuel a complete ban.
Another version ties the ruling to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, who bans both because the purpose cannot be distinguished.
A report gives Rabbi Yohanan the first tanna’s permissive ruling.
The next mishna bans several camel bindings and permits leading separate camels by ropes held in one hand.
A baraita distinguishes loose saddlecloths from secure attachments to a camel.
Rav Yehuda defines the prohibited bindings called akud and ragul.
A baraita defines akud as binding all four legs, differing from Rav Yehuda.
A second baraita includes both his definition and the four-leg case.
The extra four-leg case still leaves a mismatch.
A narrower baraita matches Rav Yehuda exactly.
Why may one not pull a line of tied camels?
It looks like leading a caravan to market.
The rope rule is tied to mixed fabrics, prompting objections about people and loosely joined ropes.
The prohibition concerns ropes intertwined and then tied together.
Shmuel’s one-handbreadth limit seems to conflict with a two-handbreadth teaching.
Abaye treats Shmuel’s smaller limit as practical guidance.

54b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita instead requires the rope to be raised a handbreadth from the ground.
That ruling concerns the rope segment between the person and camel.
The mishna lists forbidden animal items and records the cow linked to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.
An unsecured saddlecloth may fall, and a bell makes the owner look market-bound.
The neck device prevents rubbing a wound; a leg strap protects the donkey’s stride.
Rooster strings mark ownership or prevent damage, while a small wagon protects a ram’s tail.
One proposed meaning of hanunot is oil-soaked wool on shorn ewes; Rav Hisda objects.
Another proposes oil-soaked wool at birth; Rav Nahman objects.
Rav Huna identifies a hanun wood chip placed in the ewe’s nose to expel worms.
Why not give this treatment to rams too?
Their head-butting dislodges worms without it.
Another sage proposes broom wood, then explains hanunot through merciful care.
What is a calf’s gimon?
It is a bending training yoke; a verse supplies the word’s root.
Hedgehog skin protects a cow’s udder, and the horn strap follows the earlier Rav–Shmuel distinction.
How could Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya have only one cow when his herds were enormous?
It belonged to his neighbor but was attributed to him because he failed to object.
A teaching assigns responsibility to those able to protest wrongdoing in their house, town, or world.
Rav Pappa applies this to the Exilarch’s household and begins a supporting verse.

55a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The elders were judged for failing to protest the princes’ wrongdoing.
A woman cries before Shmuel while he does not attend to her.
Rav Yehuda cites the warning against closing one’s ears to the poor.
Shmuel says the court head Mar Ukva bears greater responsibility.
A verse charges the house of David with rescuing the oppressed.
Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Simon to rebuke the Exilarch’s household despite expecting rejection.
Rabbi Aha cites Ezekiel’s mark on those who mourn Jerusalem’s abuses as a reason to protest.
God initially directs separate protective and destructive marks for the righteous and wicked.
Justice asks why the two groups deserve different outcomes.
God distinguishes the fully righteous from the wicked.
Justice objects that the righteous failed to protest.
God says their protests would not have been accepted.
Justice replies that the people themselves could not know that.
Ezekiel’s verses and Rav Yosef’s reading show punishment beginning with Torah-observant elders.
The six destroyers and a scribe in Ezekiel’s vision are cited.
What bronze altar existed in Ezekiel’s time?
The vision points to the place where Levites sang.
Who are the six figures?
Rav Hisda names six agents of destruction.
What does the letter tav signify?
Several sages read tav as life, death, exhausted merit, mercy, truth, or complete Torah observance.
When did the patriarchs’ merit cease?
Rav places it in Hosea’s time and cites a verse about no rescuer.
Shmuel places it after the covenant’s last explicit protection against Hazael.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi points to Elijah’s prayer saying “this day.”
Rabbi Yohanan points to Hezekiah’s era, when God’s zeal sustains the kingdom.
Rav Ami says death requires sin and suffering requires wrongdoing.
Ezekiel’s verse links a person’s death to that person’s own sin.
A Psalm links affliction to transgression.

55b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita has the angels ask why righteous Moses and Aaron died if death follows personal sin.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says Moses and Aaron did die for their own sin at the rock.
A baraita names four who died only because mortality entered through the serpent, including Yishai.
The source must follow Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, refuting Rav Ami’s claim that death always requires sin.
Rabbi Yonatan says Reuben did not commit the sexual sin ascribed to him; Jacob’s sons remained equal.
The verse is read as Reuben rearranging Jacob’s bed, with Scripture treating that affront severely.
A baraita argues Reuben could not have committed an offense his descendants would later curse.
It explains his act as a protest on behalf of his mother Leah.
Another view says he disturbed two beds, his father’s and the Divine Presence’s.
Tanna’im read the letters of “pahaz” as different judgments of Reuben’s conduct or repentance.
Further readings reverse those letters and emphasize his recoil from sin.
A mnemonic introduces further claims about biblical figures.
Rabbi Yonatan says the sons of Eli were wrongly accused, citing their priestly designation.
Rav infers from the juxtaposition that Pinehas and Hophni were innocent.
How then can Scripture say they lay with women?
Delaying women’s offerings kept them from their husbands and was described in severe terms.
Rav argues Pinehas’ later priestly lineage would be impossible after that grave sin.
A verse about cutting off a sinner’s descendants reinforces the lineage argument.
The wording about lying with women appears to accuse both sons.
Its written form can be read in the singular.
Eli addresses “my sons” in a plural-sounding rebuke.
The written form permits a singular reading.
Another verb also appears plural.
Its written form is again read in the singular.
The sons are jointly called scoundrels.
Pinehas failed to protest Hophni, so Scripture treats him as if implicated.
Rabbi Yonatan begins the next claim, continued on the following page.

56a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yonatan says Samuel’s sons did not follow his ways, but the verse does not say they committed the alleged sins.
They stayed in their own cities to increase attendants’ fees instead of traveling to judge as Samuel did.
Tanna’im give differing accounts of the sons’ improper pursuit of gain.
Rabbi Yonatan argues David did not commit the alleged sin, citing God’s presence with him.
How then does Nathan’s rebuke call David’s action evil?
The text says he sought to do evil but did not perform it.
Rabbi reads the unusual phrase “to do evil” as intention without the act.
David erred in Uriah’s procedure, while the marriage to Bathsheba was legally available.
Soldiers in David’s wars gave conditional divorce documents; a verse about a pledge supports this.
Uriah’s death is treated differently because he defied the king by calling Joab his lord.
Rav names Uriah’s case as David’s sole recorded failing.
Abaye notes that Rav also accused David of accepting slander.
Rav cites Ziba’s first misleading report about Mephibosheth.
Why did David later trust Ziba after seeing his earlier report was false?
David granted Ziba Mephibosheth’s property after hearing Ziba’s new accusation.
Shmuel says David observed suspicious conduct in Mephibosheth and cites their later exchange.

56b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mephibosheth’s words about David’s return are read as a complaint against God, supporting Shmuel’s defense.
His name Meriv-Baal and Saul’s dispute are interpreted as quarrels with God.
A heavenly voice links David’s division of the estate to a future division of the kingdom.
Rav traces the divided kingdom, idolatry, and exile to David’s acceptance of slander.
Rabbi Yonatan says Solomon did not commit the alleged sin, citing a verse that compares his heart with David’s.
How can that fit the verse saying Solomon’s wives turned his heart?
They tried to turn him toward other gods, but he did not follow.
A verse says Solomon built an idolatrous altar.
A proposed reading says he sought to build one but did not.
The same verb says Joshua built an altar, where actual construction is clear.
A baraita compares Solomon with Josiah: acts by others may be attributed to a ruler for blame or praise.
Another verse explicitly says Solomon did evil.
His failure to protest his wives’ idolatry is counted as if he sinned.
Shmuel laments the severity of Scripture’s attribution to Solomon.
Pharaoh’s daughter introduced idolatrous music and Solomon did not object.
A teaching links that marriage to the future founding of Rome.
A baraita similarly links Jeroboam’s golden calves to a settlement in Italy.
Rabbi Yonatan denies Josiah sinned; why then does a verse say he “returned” to God?
Josiah repaid litigants from his own funds for judgments made in his youth.
Rav instead treats Josiah as a great penitent and names another penitent of his generation.
Rav Yosef names Okvan and recounts a dream affirming his repentance.
The chapter closes.

57a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna lists women’s head ties and ornaments barred in public, though wearing them incurs no sin offering.
Why does a Shabbat mishna mention immersion?
Tight ties must be loosened for immersion, so a woman might remove and carry them on Shabbat.
May a woman go out with hollow woven chains?
Rav permits woven ties because immersion does not require their removal.
Rav Huna also says the decree does not cover woven ties.
Another report grounds the permission in his sisters’ practice of leaving such ties on.
What practical difference separates these two explanations?
Dirty ties remain woven but a woman may care to remove them for washing.
A Mikvaot mishna identifies obstructing head ties and Rabbi Yehuda’s exception.
Rav Huna restricts that mishna to girls’ hair.
Rav Yosef asks why neck ties would be less obstructing than ties on hair.
A woman ordinarily will not tighten a neck tie enough to choke herself.
Abaye cites a baraita barring neck straps despite that explanation.

57b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A broad decorative neck strap can be tightened to make the wearer look fuller.
Rabbi Yehuda’s Mikvaot ruling about wool and hair ties is recalled.
Shmuel rules like Rabbi Yehuda for strands of hair.
Abaye questions whether the Sages ever disagreed about hair; Rabbi Yehuda may have cited shared ground.
A revised report says the Sages agree with Rabbi Yehuda about hair.
A baraita distinguishes wool ties from hair strands before recording Rabbi Yehuda.
The mishna allowing a woman’s own or another’s hair supports the Sages’ agreement.
What is the forbidden ornament called totefet?
Rav Yosef proposes a protective spice packet.
An effective protective amulet would be permitted.
It is instead a forehead ornament; a baraita describes it fastened to a hairnet.
Which piece is the totefet and which are sarvitin?
One spans ear to ear; the other reaches the cheeks.
Poor and wealthy women make them from different materials.
Does the mishna’s kavul mean a slave seal or a wool cap?
A baraita about what may be worn beneath a hairnet supports the wool-cap reading.
What is an istema or beizyunei?
It gathers stray hairs from a headdress.
A baraita gives three laws for the istema and begins Rabbi Shimon’s addition.

58a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The istema is exempt from bridal-crown restrictions; Shmuel identifies kavul as a slave seal.
Shmuel elsewhere permits a slave to wear a neck seal.
A master-made seal differs from one the slave made himself.
Why then bar even a master-made seal on the slave’s clothing?
If it breaks, fear may prompt the slave to carry his folded cloak on his shoulders.
Shmuel’s instruction to Exilarch attendants supports the concern about broken clothing seals.
Shmuel’s neck-seal rule is repeated and supported by a baraita.
Another baraita forbids both slave seals and discusses bells and animal attachments.
Both cases can involve the master’s seal; metal is guarded carefully, while clay is not.
The baraita’s impurity wording supports a metal seal, since clay vessels also stay pure.
Why is a neck bell barred but a bell on clothing allowed if either could break off?
The clothing bell is woven in, and woven items are not subject to the decree.
A separate baraita says animal bells can contract impurity, challenging the earlier baraita.

58b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The contrasting baraita says animal bells can be impure and that a change of use alone does not purify one.
A bell with a clapper differs from one without it.
Why should the presence of a clapper alone decide whether the bell is a vessel?
A homiletic reading treats a metal sound-producing object as a vessel.
The baraita’s middle clause and another Tosefta show that an unclappered human bell can be pure.
A child’s bell is for sound; an adult’s bell can also be an ornament without a clapper.
Why does a bell remain impure after its clapper is removed?
Abaye says an ordinary person can reattach the clapper.
Rava cites the connection law for bells and compares multipart tools to challenge mere reattachability.
The multipart-tool rule requires actual connection; rabbinic decrees do not cover detached parts.
Rava begins a different resolution on the next page.

59a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava says the bell can still make sound when struck against earthenware.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina likewise grounds the bell’s status in its ability to sound against earthenware.
Rabbi Yoḥanan instead points to using the bell to give a child water.
Does Rabbi Yoḥanan really accept a new use unlike the vessel’s original use?
The baraita limits seat impurity to things made for sitting, excluding vessels whose main work would require the sitter to rise.
In the dispute over corpse impurity, Rabbi Yoḥanan also applies the original-work test, apparently contradicting the drinking use.
Reverse the attributions in the earlier dispute.
Why reverse that dispute rather than the later one?
Another teaching confirms that Rabbi Yoḥanan requires a use resembling the original one.
A baraita says that a metal animal sandal can become impure.
What human use makes that animal item a vessel?
Rav proposes drinking from it during battle.
Rabbi Ḥanina proposes applying oil with it during battle.
Rabbi Yoḥanan proposes wearing it while fleeing over thorns, preserving its function as footwear.
What practical case distinguishes Rav from Rabbi Ḥanina?
A repulsive sandal cannot serve as a drinking cup but can still apply oil.
What distinguishes Rabbi Yoḥanan from Rabbi Ḥanina?
A heavy sandal can apply oil but cannot be worn while fleeing.
The discussion turns to the mishna’s prohibition on a city-of-gold ornament.
What is meant by a city of gold?
Rabbi Yoḥanan identifies it as a Jerusalem-of-Gold ornament.

59b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Akiva made such a Jerusalem-of-Gold ornament for his wife.
The Tosefta records three rulings for wearing the city-of-gold ornament: liability, prohibition without liability, and full permission.
What underlying disagreement explains the three rulings?
Rabbi Meir treats the ornament as a burden.
The Rabbis call it an ornament but fear its wearer will remove, display, and carry it.
Rabbi Eliezer permits it because only a prominent woman wears one, and she will not display it by removing it.
Rav prohibits a kelila head ornament; Shmuel permits it.
On one account all prohibit a metal kelila, while they differ over whether metal or fabric governs a woven one.
Rav Ashi reverses the scope: all permit the woven one, while the metal one depends on fear that its prominent wearer will remove it.
Rav Shmuel bar bar Ḥana recalls an explicit permissive ruling about a kelila attributed to Rav.
Rav identifies the visiting teacher who permitted a kelila as Levi and infers that Rabbi Afes had died, leaving Rabbi Ḥanina at the academy’s head.
Perhaps Rabbi Ḥanina died instead, and Levi left because he had no colleague outside the academy.
If Rabbi Ḥanina had died, Levi would have submitted to Rabbi Afes.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi had decreed that Rabbi Ḥanina would lead; the teaching about a righteous decree supports its fulfillment.
Levi’s and Rabba bar Avuh’s permissive rulings are followed by women wearing kelila ornaments in Neharde’a and Meḥoza.
Rav Shmuel permits wearing a decorated belt.
One version concerns a fabric belt, compared to a gilded cloak.
Another version concerns a metal belt, compared to a royal belt.
May the decorated belt be worn over another belt?
No: two belts are treated as carrying an extra item.
A short cloak may be worn if it has straps that secure it; otherwise it may not.
The discussion returns to the mishna’s katla.
What is a katla?
It is a neck ornament.
The prohibited nezamim are nose rings.
The mishna prohibits a woman’s ring without a seal.
It implies liability for going out with a sealed ring, treating it as a burden rather than an ornament.
A law of vessel impurity nevertheless lists rings with and without seals among women’s ornaments.
Rabbi Zeira assigns the two rulings to Rabbi Neḥemya and the Rabbis respectively.
A baraita shows Rabbi Neḥemya determining a ring’s status by its seal, unlike the first opinion, and similarly judging a yoke by its rods.

60a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita concludes Rabbi Neḥemya’s functional tests for composite objects; the Rabbis instead follow the supporting component.
Rava reads the two rings separately: a sealed ring adorns a man, an unsealed ring a woman.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak distinguishes vessel impurity from Shabbat carrying: a sealed ring is a vessel yet a burden for a woman.
The mishna also forbids an unperforated needle.
What use does such a needle have?
Rav Yosef says a woman uses it to pin her hair.
Abaye argues that, like a garter, a hairpin should be permitted because she would not expose her hair to display it.
Rav Adda instead says she uses the needle to part her hair.
What use would it then have on Shabbat?
Rava says it has a gold plate: she parts hair on weekdays and wears the plate on her forehead on Shabbat.
The mishna lists articles a man may not wear out on Shabbat, including a spiked sandal, a single sandal, and an ineffective amulet, without sin-offering liability.
Why was going out in a spiked sandal prohibited?
Shmuel recounts hidden fugitives who mistook reversed sandal marks for someone leaving; panic caused fatal trampling.
Rabbi Elai gives another cave account: the sound of a sandal above them caused the deadly panic.
Rami bar Yeḥezkel locates the panic in a synagogue after a sound behind it.
The Sages consequently prohibited going out in a spiked sandal.
If the dangerous sandal caused the decree, why is it not prohibited on weekdays too?
The incident occurred on Shabbat, so the decree followed that circumstance.
Then why does a mishna also prohibit the sandal on a Festival?

60b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A Festival mishna also forbids sending a spiked sandal because it cannot be worn then.
The decree applies when people gather.
A Festival has gatherings, but so does a communal fast; should the fast also be included?
The incident occurred at a gathering on a day when work was forbidden, unlike a fast day.
Even a narrow view of incident-based decrees can equate Shabbat and Festival, which differ chiefly in food preparation.
Shmuel limits the decree to nails that strengthen the sandal; decorative nails are allowed.
How many nails count as decorative?
Rabbi Yoḥanan permits five per sandal; Rabbi Ḥanina permits seven.
Rabbi Yoḥanan explains each count by the placement of side and strap nails.
A baraita permits seven or thirteen nails for a crooked sandal; neither count appears to fit Rabbi Yoḥanan.
His five-nail limit follows Rabbi Nehorai’s ruling.
Ifa says each circle may follow its teacher, Rabbi Yoḥanan or Rabbi Ḥanina.
Rav Huna asks Rav Ashi about a sandal with five nails.
Rav Ashi permits even seven.
What about nine nails?
Rav Ashi prohibits even eight.
A shoemaker asks whether inward stitching changes the rule.
Rabbi Ami permits it but does not give a reason.
Rav Ashi explains that inward stitching makes it a shoe; the decree addressed sandals.
Does bending the nail into a tong-like shape permit the sandal?
Rabbi Abba bar Avina permits it; Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina agrees.
Rav Sheshet permits a sole wholly covered in nails to prevent wear.
A Tosefta supports this exception and describes limits and other permitted nail forms.
The Tosefta seems inconsistent: most nails may fall out even if many remain, yet it permits only four or five.
Rav Sheshet distinguishes broken nail heads from nails entirely pulled out.
The Tosefta’s four-or-five-nail allowance is reconsidered.
If five remain allowed, why mention four?
Rav Ḥisda assigns four to a small sandal and five to a large one.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi allows up to seven nails.
Another baraita permits thirteen according to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
A sandal whose sole needs straightening is different.
That distinction also removes the earlier objection to Rabbi Yoḥanan’s five-nail count.
Rav Mattana rules against Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon’s ban on moving the sandal.
Why state the majority ruling explicitly?
His stricter reasoning might have seemed persuasive; the ruling rejects it.
Rabbi Ḥiyya says social criticism kept him from allowing many more nails.
How many would he have permitted?
Pumbedita reports twenty-four, Sura twenty-two, with a travel mnemonic for the difference.
The discussion returns to the mishna’s restriction on a single sandal without a foot wound.

61a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna permits a single sandal when a foot is wounded.
On which foot should the sandal be worn?
Rav Huna chooses the wounded foot, since a sandal protects against pain.
Ḥiyya bar Rav chooses the sound foot for comfort; the other foot’s wound explains its lack of a sandal.
Rabbi Yoḥanan’s exchange over which sandal was handed to him appears to support Rav Huna.
The exchange could instead fit Ḥiyya bar Rav if Rabbi Yoḥanan meant the unshod left foot.
Rabbi Yoḥanan compares putting on shoes to placing phylacteries on the left.
A baraita says the right shoe is put on first.
Rav Yosef accepts either order because both have authoritative support.
Abaye argues Rabbi Yoḥanan might have retracted after hearing the baraita, or knowingly rejected it; the conflict cannot simply be ignored.
Rav Naḥman describes a practice that starts with the right shoe but ties the left first, satisfying both views.
Rav Ashi reports that Rav Kahana was not strict about the order.
The baraita instructs putting on the right shoe first and removing the left first.
It similarly gives the right precedence in washing and applying oil, with the head first when anointing the whole body.
The discussion returns to the mishna’s prohibition on going out with phylacteries.
Rav Safra says even one who treats Shabbat as a time for phylacteries forbids wearing them out, lest they be carried.
In another version Rav Safra says even one who excludes Shabbat from phylacteries exempts the wearer from a sin-offering.
Why is there no sin-offering?
Phylacteries are worn like clothing.
The mishna restricts an amulet that is not from an expert.
Rav Pappa says an expert writer suffices even if this particular amulet is not proven.
The mishna specifies the expert maker, not the amulet’s demonstrated effectiveness.
A Tosefta defines a proven amulet as one that has healed three times, whether written or made of roots and regardless of illness severity.
It may also be worn preventively and tied or untied in public, subject to a qualification continuing on the next page.

61b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The amulet should not be attached to a bracelet or ring, where its healing purpose may appear to be mere adornment.
Another baraita calls an amulet proven when it heals three different people, unlike the previous three-healings test.
Three people establish the writer’s expertise; repeated healing establishes a particular amulet’s efficacy.
Rav Pappa says three amulets healing three people three times prove both the writer and the amulets.
Three amulets healing three people once prove the writer but not each amulet.
One amulet healing three people proves the amulet but not the writer.
Do three amulets used for one person establish the writer’s expertise?
The cures may instead reflect that patient’s fortune rather than the writer’s skill.
The dilemma remains unresolved.
Do amulets carry sanctity?
Is this relevant to rescuing them from a fire on Shabbat?
A teaching says blessings and amulets are not rescued from fire even when they contain scriptural words.
Perhaps the issue is whether an amulet requires burial.
A divine name must be removed and buried even when written on ordinary furniture.
The remaining issue is whether an amulet may be taken into a bathroom.
The mishna permits an expert amulet outside; if it had to be removed for the bathroom, that could lead to carrying it.
Perhaps the mishna refers only to herbal amulets, which contain no writing.
The baraita equates written and herbal amulets.
Perhaps it concerns a dangerously ill person.
The baraita equates dangerous and ordinary illness.
Because the amulet heals, holding it in hand is permitted too; the bathroom concern need not bar wearing it.

62a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Oshaya’s baraita forbids carrying an amulet by hand four cubits in public, challenging the prior answer.
Perhaps the permitted amulet is covered in leather.
Phylacteries are leather-covered yet must be removed before entering a bathroom.
Phylacteries differ because sacred letter shapes appear on the boxes and straps themselves.
The Gemara identifies the mishna’s armor terms as mail, a helmet lining, and leg armor.
The mishna lists women’s items that incur liability if carried, while the Rabbis exempt the scented bundle and perfume flask.
Ulla applies the ring rules in reverse to men, treating a gender-specific ornament as a burden for the other sex.
Rav Yosef cites sack garments: what shepherds usually wear can still count as clothing for anyone.
Rav Yosef distinguishes women as a separate group for these wearing conventions.
Abaye cites a woman permitted to bring found phylacteries in by wearing them, though a time-bound command would exempt her.
On Rabbi Meir’s view phylacteries apply at night and on Shabbat, making the command non-time-bound for women too.
Why would wearing another person’s ring be ordinary carrying rather than an unusual manner?
Rabbi Yirmeya proposes a woman treasurer who regularly wears a seal ring for her work.
That explains the woman but not a man wearing an unsealed ring.
Rava says either spouse may put the other’s ring on a finger while transporting it for storage or repair, making this a normal way to carry it.
The discussion returns to the mishna’s kulyar and kovelet.
What is a kulyar?
Rav identifies a garment fastener and, with Rav Asi, identifies the kovelet as a fragrant bundle.
A baraita records liability, exemption, and permission for going out with the fragrant bundle.
What explains the three rulings?
Rabbi Meir treats it as a burden.
The Rabbis treat it as an ornament but fear she will remove and display it.
Rabbi Eliezer permits it because a woman masking an odor will not remove it to show others.
Another baraita says Rabbi Eliezer only exempts the wearer, apparently still prohibiting it initially.
His word “exempt” answers Rabbi Meir’s liability claim; against the Rabbis’ prohibition he permits it outright.

62b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Which statement of Rabbi Meir was Rabbi Eliezer answering?
A baraita forbids a woman to carry a key and then records Rabbi Eliezer’s exemption for scented items.
The scented bundle was not mentioned in the baraita’s opening clause.
Supply the omitted clause: Rabbi Meir also makes one liable for the bundle and perfume flask, which Rabbi Eliezer exempts.
That exemption applies when perfume remains; an empty flask incurs liability.
Rav Adda infers from the flask that carrying a vessel with less than the liability measure of contents still incurs liability.
Rav Ashi distinguishes a completely empty flask from a vessel holding a sub-threshold amount.
Shmuel identifies Amos’s “chief ointments” with balsam oil.
Rav Yosef notes the Sages rejected a decree against balsam; why would they if Amos condemned this pleasure?
Abaye compares wine vessels condemned in the same verse yet used without protest by a sage.
The decree concerns pleasure joined with celebration; balsam brings pleasure without that celebration.
Rabbi Yosei reads Amos’s description of reclining as naked urination by the beds.
Rabbi Abbahu objects that such conduct would not explain Amos’s severe exile punishment.
He instead reads the verse as condemning shared feasts followed by exchanging spouses.
A teaching lists three acts said to bring poverty: improper urination, neglecting handwashing, and a wife’s curse.
Rava narrows the urination case to facing the bed and using the floor rather than a vessel.
Rava initially limits negligent handwashing to not washing at all.
Rav Ḥisda’s practice links generous water use with prosperity, challenging that narrow limit.
The wife’s curse concerns ornaments he can afford but refuses to provide.
Rava son of Rav Ilai interprets Isaiah’s phrases as proud posture, attention-seeking steps, eye signals, and conspicuous pairings.
Rabbi Yitzḥak reads the foot imagery as perfumed shoes stamped near young men to entice them.
What punishment followed this conduct?
Rabba bar Ulla maps Isaiah’s images of stench, wounds, baldness, sackcloth, and sores to punishments matching each adornment.
Rabbi Yosei reads the head scab in Isaiah as disease, using a parallel word in Leviticus.
Rav and Shmuel offer two interpretations of Isaiah’s phrase about exposed secret parts.
Rav begins an account of Jerusalemites’ arrogant euphemistic speech, which continues on the next page.

63a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The account of Jerusalem’s coded talk ends; Rav Ḥisda says its contrasts allude to illicit sex.
A tradition describes Jerusalem’s fragrant cinnamon firewood and a surviving remnant after its destruction.
The mishna makes a man liable for going out with weapons on Shabbat.
Rabbi Eliezer considers weapons ornaments.
The Rabbis call weapons disgraceful and cite Isaiah’s future conversion of swords into farm tools.
The mishna distinguishes a permissible, ritually pure garter from prohibited, impure ankle chains.
What is the mishna’s alla?
It is a club.
If weapons are ornaments, why should they disappear in the messianic era?
Rabbi Eliezer says they will no longer be needed because war will cease.
Could they still serve only as decoration?
Abaye compares a weapon without its function to a lamp lit in daylight.
This account conflicts with Shmuel’s view that only political subjugation changes in the messianic era.
It supports Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba’s distinction between prophetic visions of that era and the unseen World-to-Come.
Another version has Rabbi Eliezer say weapons remain in the messianic era, matching Shmuel’s view.
What source lets Rabbi Eliezer call weapons ornaments?
A psalm calls the girded sword a warrior’s glory and splendor.
Rav Kahana objects that the verse speaks metaphorically of Torah.
The verse still retains its plain sense.
Rav Kahana recalls learning the Talmud before grasping that rule of plain meaning.
What does that recollection teach?
Learn the material first, then pursue its reasoning.
A mnemonic introduces further interpretations.
Verses are read to promise success to scholars who sharpen each other in sincere, humble study.
Proverbs is read to distinguish sincere Torah study, rewarded with long life, from lesser study rewarded with wealth and honor.
Malachi and Psalms are read to praise scholars who discuss law calmly and agreeably.
What does thinking on God’s name mean in that verse?
Rabbi Ami says an unfulfilled mitzva intention thwarted by circumstances is credited as an act.
Ecclesiastes supports the teaching that proper mitzva performance wards off bad tidings.
An adjacent verse is read to say a righteous person may avert even a divine decree.
Song of Songs is read to praise scholars who listen to one another.
Failure to listen is read as driving the Divine Presence away.
Another verse says God loves scholars who make mistakes while learning together.
Rava limits that praise to scholars who know the law’s basis and lack a teacher in town.
A teaching ranks partnership support above a loan and a loan above charity.
A teaching urges closeness to a Torah scholar despite flaws and warns against relying on an unlearned neighbor’s piety.
A teaching says keeping a dangerous dog deters kindness from one’s home and begins a verse citation continued on the next page.

63b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The dog teaching finishes its verse and adds that keeping a dangerous dog can erode fear of God.
A pregnant visitor is frightened by a barking dog; the owner’s later assurance comes too late to prevent the harm.
Rav Huna divides a verse in Ecclesiastes between the evil and good inclinations.
Reish Lakish instead divides it between Torah study and good deeds.
Rav Yehuda identifies the garter with an arm bracelet.
Rav Yosef objects that the mishna calls a garter pure while an arm bracelet is susceptible to impurity.
A garter has the bracelet’s shape or position on the leg, not its status.
