Ravin distinguishes one-legged garters from two-legged ankle chains.
Rav Huna says both use two legs; a connecting chain creates the ankle-chain vessel.
Can a sound-making chain be a vessel under the derivation for metal objects that make sound?
A sound-producing vessel has a useful action; what useful action does this chain perform?
The chain limits the wearer’s stride, as illustrated by a Jerusalem family’s use of ankle chains.
Rav Yirmeya confirms that Rabbi Yoḥanan taught the same point.
Rav Dimi initially derives impurity for any size of woven fabric from the priestly frontplate.
Abaye cites descriptions and eyewitness testimony showing the frontplate was gold, not woven fabric.
Rav Dimi corrects himself: the frontplate proves small ornaments, while “or a garment” proves small woven cloth.
A baraita includes tiny woven items, ornaments, combinations of both, and sack material among susceptible objects.
Rava assigns separate scriptural sources to tiny cloth, ornaments, and mixed items.
A sage objects that the mixed-item verse concerns Midian and corpse impurity.
Rava begins a response using a verbal analogy on the next page.

64a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava finishes his verbal analogy between the two impurity passages using their shared word for vessel.
The baraita says a sack is additionally susceptible as a woven item.
Is an ordinary garment not also woven?
The rule includes even an unwoven sack made from goat hair.
What use does so small an item have?
Rabbi Yoḥanan says a poor person can braid three hairs into a daughter’s neck ornament.
A baraita uses “or sack” to include reins and saddle bands but limits the category to spun and woven work.
The corpse-impurity verse also includes reins and saddle bands as goat-hair work.
Would that verse include ropes and cords too?
A comparison to creeping-animal impurity would limit corpse impurity to spun and woven materials.
Corpse impurity is more severe, so that comparison alone may be too weak.
The repeated “garment and leather” establishes a verbal analogy limiting both categories to spun and woven work.
The same analogy extends goat-hair work from corpse impurity to creeping-animal impurity.
How are horse-tail and cow-tail materials included?
The phrase “or sack” includes them.
Was that phrase not already used for reins and saddle bands?
The verbal analogy now supplies those items, freeing “or sack” for the tail materials.
Where is corpse impurity for horse-tail and cow-tail work derived?
A comparison to creeping-animal impurity initially extends the same treatment to corpse impurity.
The two kinds of impurity differ in how broadly they apply, weakening that comparison.
The repeated “garment and leather” transfers the treatment through a verbal analogy.
Unless those words are extraneous, the analogy can be challenged because a lentil-sized creeping animal causes impurity.
The creeping-animal words are extra because its rule can already be learned from adjacent seminal-impurity verses.
That frees only one side of the analogy; some authorities still allow a logical objection.
The corpse-impurity words are also extra because its garment rule can likewise be learned from seminal impurity.
The discussion turns to the jewelry offered after the war with Midian.
Rabbi Elazar identifies two intimate forms of ornament mentioned in that verse.
Rav Yosef and Rabba support the reading of kumaz through translation and a wordplay on the verse.
A verse records Moses’s anger at the returning officers.
Moses asks whether the soldiers repeated the earlier sin.
They answer that no one among them was lost to wrongdoing.
Why then did they bring an atonement offering?
They say they avoided acts of sin but not sinful thoughts, and therefore offered the jewelry.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael asks why that generation needed atonement; the response continues on the next page.

64b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The previous question is answered: the soldiers sinned through looking at forbidden nakedness.
Rav Sheshet reads the pairing of outer and inner ornaments as a warning against lustful looking.
The mishna permits strands from her own, another person’s, or an animal’s hair, and securely sewn ornaments.
It permits a cap or wig in a courtyard and certain protective cloths.
It permits items placed in the mouth before Shabbat but bars first placing or replacing them on Shabbat.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi permits a false or gold tooth; the Rabbis prohibit it.
The three hair cases each matter: own hair might be less embarrassing, while another person’s hair differs from an animal’s.
A Tosefta restricts exchanging hair between young and elderly women.
Why mention a young woman wearing an elderly woman’s hair when it would be unflattering?
The Tosefta mentions it for symmetry with the plausible reverse case.
Rav extends public-domain ornament restrictions to courtyards except for a cap and wig.
Rabbi Anani bar Sason permits all ornaments in a courtyard.
The mishna explicitly permits only the cap and wig, apparently against Rabbi Anani.
His authority is Rabbi Yishmael bar Yosei, a tanna who can disagree with the mishna.
Why does Rav single out the cap and wig?
Ulla says the exception keeps a woman attractive to her husband.
Rabbi Akiva rejected older menstrual restrictions on adornment that could alienate spouses; immersion remains required.
Rav says a prohibition based on appearances applies even in private rooms.
A plugged animal bell is barred in public for appearance yet allowed in a courtyard.
The two rulings reflect a tannaitic dispute introduced on the next page.

65a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita contrasts drying clothes privately with a dispute over even private action barred for appearances.
A cloth in the ear may be worn when tied securely.
A cloth in the sandal likewise must be tied.
The mishna also permits a cloth used for menstrual flow.
Rami bar Ḥama considers requiring that cloth to be tied.
Rava permits it untied because embarrassment makes her unlikely to carry it if it falls.
Does adding a handgrip to that cloth change the ruling?
Rabbi Abba permits it, supported by a report in Rabbi Yoḥanan’s name.
Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Yannai wore ear cloths outside despite colleagues’ objections.
Rami bar Yeḥezkel required the ear cloth to be tied.
The sages’ cloths were held tightly in the ear; the tying rule covers a loose cloth.
Pepper treats mouth odor, salt a toothache, and the broader mouth-item rule includes ginger or cinnamon.
The mishna records a dispute over a false or gold tooth.
Rabbi Zeira limits the dispute to gold; everyone permits a silver tooth.
A baraita explicitly confirms that distinction.
Abaye groups three sages who say a woman will not display an item if removing it would embarrass her.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi’s tooth ruling and Rabbi Eliezer’s fragrant-bundle ruling illustrate the principle.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar permits items beneath the hair net but not removable ornaments above it.
The mishna permits a coin over a foot wound, ear-hole strings, customary veils and fasteners, and prefastened cloak buttons.
What is the tzinit treated by a coin?
It is a wound on the sole of the foot.
Why specifically use a coin rather than any hard shard, metal plate, or engraved disk?
Abaye says its hardness, metal, and image all contribute to the treatment.
Shmuel’s father restricted his daughters’ strings and sleeping arrangement and prepared immersion sites for them.
Why bar their strings when the mishna permits girls’ strings?
Their strings were colorful and might be removed for display.
He also kept his daughters from lying beside one another.
Does that practice support Rav Huna’s teaching about women who rub against one another?

65b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Huna’s statement concludes that such contact disqualifies the women from priestly marriage.
The father may simply have wanted to prevent his daughters becoming accustomed to bodily intimacy.
His springtime ritual baths support Rav’s view that increased Euphrates flow reflects winter rain.
He feared rainwater would outnumber natural flowing spring water and invalidate river immersion.
That differs from Shmuel’s claim that the river gains water from its own bed.
Shmuel’s own limit to Tishrei for flowing-water immersion also conflicts with that claim.
The discussion returns to using a stone, nut, or coin to fasten a cloak.
Why does the mishna first permit fastening and then forbid doing it initially on Shabbat?
Abaye limits the final prohibition to a coin.
May a woman fasten on a nut as a pretext to carry it to her young child?
The question arises under both views about using artifice during a Shabbat fire.
Even if artifice is allowed in a fire, that may be only to keep someone from extinguishing it.
Even if fire artifice is barred, carrying a nut as a fastener might be permitted because that is an unusual way to transport it.
The dilemma remains unresolved.
A new mishna begins: Rabbi Meir permits an amputee to go out wearing a wooden leg.

66a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yosei bars the wooden leg; a pad receptacle makes it susceptible to impurity.
Knee supports are susceptible to treading impurity and may be worn outside or brought into the Temple courtyard.
A seated amputee’s chair and hand supports are impure by treading but cannot be taken out or into the courtyard.
Loketamin are pure but may not be worn out.
Which sage is assigned the permissive ruling in the mishna?
Rav Naḥman does not know the received reading.
What is the practical ruling?
Rav Naḥman does not know that either.
Shmuel and Rav Huna read Rabbi Meir as prohibiting the wooden leg, a reading Rav Yosef adopts.
Rava bar Shira cites Rav reversing that attribution: Rabbi Meir permits and Rabbi Yosei prohibits.
A mnemonic links Yosei to the Hebrew word for prohibition.
Shmuel later identifies Rabbi Meir with a valid wooden sandal in halitza, confirming that he reversed his earlier reading.
A baraita about a plasterer’s sandal supplies another test for the attribution to Rav Huna.
Another version says the Sages did agree with Rabbi Akiva.
Rav Huna assigns agreement to Rabbi Meir and disagreement to Rabbi Yosei.
Rav Yosef instead identifies the dissenter as Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri, who excludes straw and reed objects from vessel status.
How can a plasterer’s sandal be impure by treading if it is not made for walking?
The plasterer sometimes walks home while wearing it.
The mishna says a wooden leg with a pad receptacle becomes impure.
Abaye limits it to corpse impurity; Rava also includes treading impurity.
Rava cites a child’s walking wagon as an object susceptible by treading.
Abaye distinguishes the wagon because the child puts full weight on it.
Abaye cites the purity of an elder’s walking stick to support his limit.
Rava begins distinguishing the stick on the next page.

66b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava distinguishes an elder’s stick, used for posture, from a wooden leg that bears the wearer’s weight.
The mishna bars the seated amputee’s supports from Shabbat use and Temple entry.
A reciter taught that the supports could enter the Temple courtyard.
Rabbi Yoḥanan corrects him: if the support counts as a shoe for halitza, it cannot enter the courtyard.
What are the mishna’s loketamin?
Three sages identify them as a donkey-shaped toy, stilts, or masks.
A new mishna permits children’s therapeutic knots and bells associated with princes, without limiting either custom to those groups.
What are these knots?
One tradition identifies them as knotted madder plants.
Abaye and Rav Aḥa transmit elaborate conditions claimed for the plant remedy.
Rav Naḥman says so many conditions make the remedy practically useless.
If it heals, why would the mishna single out boys rather than girls or adults?
The knots are instead a right-shoe strap tied on a homesick son’s left arm; reversing it was considered harmful.
A teaching allows placing an inverted cup on the navel on Shabbat.
Another teaching permits smearing oil and salt.
A chain of reports describes oil, salt, or wetted clay used with words meant to sober someone.
A teaching permits a tight neck bandage for a displaced vertebra.
Another permits swaddling a newborn on Shabbat.
The Gemara compares the differing attributions of the child-knot and swaddling teachings.
Abaye’s foster mother says incantations use the patient’s mother’s name and healing knots are tied on the left.
She gives a repetition count for incantations with and without an explicit number.
A baraita permits wearing a preservation stone or matching weight even as a precaution against a future miscarriage.
Rav Yeimar limits the matching weight to one found equal by chance.
Does the weight of that counterweight also qualify?
The question remains unresolved.
A reported fever remedy uses salt weighed against a coin and bound near the neck.
A second reported ritual transfers the fever to an ant in a sealed copper tube.
Rav Aḥa worries the ant might already carry another person’s illness.
He changes the words so both burdens stay with the ant.
A third reported ritual addresses a river and returns a jug of water to symbolize a fever leaving.
A new teaching from Rav Huna begins on the next page.

67a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Huna’s reported ritual for a recurring fever collects seven kinds of items and binds them with hair thread.
Rabbi Yoḥanan describes an iron knife and bush used in another reported fever ritual.
The ritual pairs three days of cutting the bush with verses about Moses and the burning bush.
Rav Aḥa suggests using the next verse, “Do not come close,” as more fitting.
He redistributes the verses across the three days to include that line.
A further incantation compares the bush’s humility and the flight of fire with the hoped-for departure of fever.
The text records an incantation for boils that invokes names and asks that the sores stop spreading.
A short wound incantation is reported.
A formula against a named demon is reported.
A separate formula addresses a bathroom demon.
Which tanna permits any person to wear the bells associated with princes?
Rabbi Oshaya attributes it to Rabbi Shimon’s view that all Israel are like princes.
Rava instead says the bell is woven into the garment, allowing it under every view.
The mishna records a dispute over wearing three folk-healing objects, which the Rabbis classify as Amorite practice.
The Gemara describes the traditional purposes assigned to the locust egg, fox tooth, and nail.
Abaye and Rava say a practice regarded as therapeutic is outside the Amorite-custom prohibition.
A baraita permits painting a fruit-dropping tree red, though the paint itself provides no physical treatment.
The red paint alerts others to pray, like the public announcement of a person’s distress in the cited verse.
Ravina links a similar palm-tree marker to that baraita.
A teaching excludes a spoken formula for a stuck bone from the Amorite-custom prohibition.
A second formula is reported for a fish bone lodged in the throat.

67b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A fortune-invoking phrase is classed as Amorite practice.
Rabbi Yehuda says its reference to Gad is idolatrous, citing Isaiah.
Exchanging a husband’s and wife’s names for luck is also classed as Amorite practice.
Another fortune phrase about barrels is prohibited.
Rabbi Yehuda links its invocation of Dan to idol worship in Amos.
An omen-seeking formula addressed to ravens is prohibited.
Ordering slaughter of a rooster or hen for an unusual call is prohibited as an omen practice.
Repeating a drinking phrase to increase wine is prohibited.
Cracking eggs or stirring a pot in front of chicks as an omen is prohibited.
Dancing and counting chicks to prevent their death is prohibited.
Dance, silence, or shouting meant magically to affect cooking is prohibited.
Urination in front of a pot to speed cooking is prohibited.
Wood and glass pieces are allowed as practical cooking aids, though the Rabbis bar glass because of danger.
A Tosefta permits salt in a lamp for brightness and clay beneath it for longer burning.
Rav Zutra calls wasteful handling of oil or kerosene lamps a violation of the ban on destruction.
A blessing of wine and life for sages is permitted; Rabbi Akiva used it at his son’s banquet.
The chapter on women’s Shabbat ornaments closes.
A new mishna says total ignorance of Shabbat produces one sin-offering for many labors on many Shabbatot.
Knowledge of Shabbat but confusion about which day it is produces one offering per Shabbat.
Knowledge that today is Shabbat but confusion over prohibited labors begins a third rule that continues on 68a.

68a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna finishes its rule: liability is counted by primary labor category, not by every related act.
Why does the mishna call this a significant principle?
One proposal links the wording to a later, smaller principle, as in the Sabbatical Year.
A tithes mishna has two principles yet does not use the same wording.
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin says Shabbat and the Sabbatical Year have primary and derivative categories, unlike tithes.
Bar Kappara also calls the tithes rule significant, though tithes lack such categories.
The word marks relative reach: Shabbat covers attached and detached produce, the Sabbatical Year attached produce, and tithes a narrower class of food.
On bar Kappara’s wording, tithes in turn reach figs and vegetables beyond the scope of pe’a.
The pe’a mishna requires food that is protected, ground-grown, gathered together, and stored.
Those conditions exclude dye plants, ownerless produce, mushrooms, figs, and vegetables in different ways.
The tithes mishna omits the gathering and storage requirements, supporting its wider scope.
Rav and Shmuel restrict the first Shabbat rule to someone who never learned it, such as a captive child or isolated convert.
Does “forgets” not imply prior knowledge?
The phrase can mean Shabbat’s essence was always unknown to him.
What then is the liability of someone who knew Shabbat but later forgot it?
If liable for each Shabbat, why does the next clause say “one who knows” rather than explicitly naming prior knowledge and later forgetting?
Rav and Shmuel read that next clause as someone who once knew and now forgot.

68b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What if the person did not forget Shabbat and knew the day—would liability be per labor?
If so, why does the mishna separately state the case of knowing today is Shabbat?
The first case really involves someone who knew Shabbat and later forgot; the earlier attribution must be revised.
Rav and Shmuel regard even an uneducated captive child or isolated convert as liable like someone who forgot.
Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish instead exempt those who never knew the law.
A baraita explicitly makes such a captive or convert liable for one offering for Shabbat and separate offerings for other prohibitions.
Munbaz dissents, requiring prior awareness even for an unwitting sin.
Rabbi Akiva pushes that analogy: would awareness at the very moment of the act also be required?
Munbaz accepts the extension.
Rabbi Akiva says awareness during the act would make it deliberate rather than unwitting.
The baraita’s captive example still seems to contradict Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish.
They can follow Munbaz’s exempting opinion rather than the first opinion in the baraita.
Munbaz derives his rule from verses placing unwitting and intentional transgressions side by side.
How do the other Sages use the phrase “one law”?
They apply it to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s teaching to his son, begun at the page end.

69a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Rabbis use the comparison to idolatry to require a sin-offering for a violation carrying karet when deliberate.
What can count as an unwitting act for Munbaz if the person knew the ban?
He was unaware of the sin-offering obligation.
The other Sages do not treat ignorance of the offering alone as unwitting.
What ignorance do they require?
Rabbi Yoḥanan requires ignorance of karet even if the ban was known.
Reish Lakish requires ignorance of both the ban and karet.
Rava reads the verse about an unwitting forbidden act in support of Reish Lakish.
How does Rabbi Yoḥanan read that verse?
He uses it for the baraita excluding someone who would not repent upon learning of the prohibition.
A mishna’s count of thirty-nine labors implies separate liability when all are done in one lapse of awareness.
How can one know it is Shabbat yet unknowingly do all thirty-nine labors?
Rabbi Yoḥanan can say the person knows the prohibition but not its karet penalty.
Under Reish Lakish, ignorance of every labor leaves no evident Shabbat law the person knowingly violated.
He may know the boundary prohibition on Rabbi Akiva’s view.
A baraita counts several combinations of awareness as unwitting liability, including ignorance only of the offering.
That final case follows Munbaz.
Abaye says all agree an unwitting oath violation requires ignorance of the prohibition itself.
Whom does “all” include?
Rabbi Yoḥanan’s agreement seems obvious because an oath lacks a karet penalty.
The oath offering is exceptional, so one might have counted ignorance of the offering alone; Abaye rules otherwise.

69b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abaye’s oath rule excludes ignorance of the offering alone.
A baraita nevertheless makes one liable for a false oath while knowing the ban but not its offering.
That baraita can follow Munbaz.
In another version, attributing it to Munbaz is trivial; taken as the Rabbis’ view, it refutes Abaye.
Abaye says the added fifth for unwittingly eating teruma requires ignorance of its prohibition.
Which sage is included in “everyone agrees”?
Rabbi Yoḥanan’s agreement seems obvious when there is no karet.
One might equate death at Heaven’s hand with karet; Abaye rejects that extension.
Rava does equate death with karet and the added fifth with an offering.
Rav Huna says someone who loses track of Shabbat counts six days, then observes one.
Ḥiyya bar Rav reverses the order.
What is the basis of their disagreement?
One follows creation’s six days then Shabbat; the other follows Adam’s first Shabbat.
A baraita’s wording seems to support counting six before the observance day.
It might also mean observing one day and then counting six.
That reading strains the wording, and a second baraita explicitly says to count six first.
Rava first proposes making food daily except on the designated Shabbat, with double preparation the day before.
The day before might itself be the actual Shabbat.
Therefore he prepares only that day’s food every day, including the designated day.
How is the designated day distinguished?
By reciting kiddush and havdala.
If he recalls his departure day’s position in the sequence, Rava allows labor on that corresponding day.
What is new in this ruling?
One cannot also permit the next day: he might have departed on Friday with a caravan.
What scriptural basis supports the differing Shabbat liabilities?
Rav Naḥman contrasts singular “Shabbat” with plural “Shabbatot” to derive one offering across many days or one per day.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak says the same verses could be assigned the opposite way.
The discussion returns to one who knows the day is Shabbat.

70a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why does the mishna count liability by Shabbat in one clause but by labor in the next?
Rav Safra distinguishes whether learning the day or learning the labor’s ban would make the person stop.
Rav Naḥman says awareness of the day and of the prohibited labor are intertwined.
He instead counts lapses of knowledge: one mistaken day versus many mistaken labor categories.
Where is separate liability for each labor derived?
Shmuel reads repeated death language as multiplying liability for one Shabbat desecration.
The verse concerns deliberate violation, not an unwitting offering.
A separate verse already covers deliberate death; Shmuel applies this one to multiple offerings.
Why not use Rabbi Natan’s derivation instead?
Rabbi Natan reads the Shabbat passage as alluding to thirty-nine primary labors.
Plowing and harvesting suggest separate liabilities for two named labors.
That still might leave every other labor grouped in one offering.
Kindling is singled out to model separate liability for each primary labor.
Shmuel follows Rabbi Yosei, who says kindling was singled out as a lesser prohibition, not to divide liabilities.
Why then does Shmuel not use Rabbi Yosei’s own source for divided liabilities?
Rabbi Yosei reads “from one of them” as allowing either one offering for many acts or one per act.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina explains the extra wording as supporting both directions of liability.
A finer reading of “one” and “from one” begins and continues on the next page.

70b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yosei’s wordplay distinguishes a partial written name, primary and derivative labors, and one versus multiple offerings.
Shmuel does not derive the one-to-many and many-to-one clauses from that wording.
How many offerings if both the day and the prohibited labors were forgotten?
Rav Naḥman treats it as forgetting Shabbat, requiring one offering.
Rava notes that the same case also involves ignorance of each labor.
Rav Ashi proposes classifying it by what information makes the person stop.
Ravina replies that awareness of the day and awareness of the labor depend on each other.
The proposed distinction does not hold.
The mishna’s count of thirty-nine labors shows possible separate liability for all of them in one lapse.
If simultaneous ignorance of Shabbat yields only one offering, how can someone be knowingly observing Shabbat yet ignorant of every labor?
Rabbi Yoḥanan can say the person knew the labor ban but not its karet penalty.
On Reish Lakish’s view the person may know the Shabbat boundary law, according to Rabbi Akiva.
Rava presents successive reaping and grinding episodes with different lapses of awareness, then staggered discovery of them.

71a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava says offerings for the first reaping and grinding draw atonement to matching later acts, with one grinding case left separate under a different discovery order.
Abaye says the second grinding should also be drawn in because both acts are grinding.
Does Rava even accept atonement by drawing another act along?
A forbidden-fat case records Rava’s limits: offerings cover acts sharing a lapse, and an offering for the middle act covers all three.
Abaye allows any one offering to cover all three through further drawing.
Rava later adopted Abaye’s basic principle.
Then why does the second grinding not follow the first?
Rava accepts one drawing step, not drawing again from an act covered only through drawing.
A similar overlap that Abaye and Rava resolved remained a question for Rabbi Zeira.
Can half-measures of reaping and grinding under different kinds of ignorance combine for liability?
They belong to separate offering units and do not combine.
Does separate offering liability always prevent half-measures from combining?
A mishna contrasts one and several forbidden foods and says halves of one type combine while halves of different types do not.
Why state the obvious rule that halves of one type combine?
Reish Lakish applies it to two dishes, which Rabbi Yehoshua separates for offerings but, on this reading, not to reduce liability.
Thus separate offerings and combined half-measures can coexist.
Rabbi Zeira says that argument depends on placing Reish Lakish’s explanation in the first clause rather than the last.
On his reading, one food served in two dishes is called “two types,” showing Rabbi Yehoshua separates them even to exempt.
The argument turns to what the final clause implies, continuing on the next page.

71b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If the second clause uses one food in two dishes, why state the obvious first-clause case of one food in one dish?
Rav Huna inserts awareness between two half-measures; Rabban Gamliel says awareness does not split a half-measure.
Rabbi Yoḥanan requires two offerings for two fat portions learned about separately; Reish Lakish requires one.
Each cites a different phrase about an offering for, or atonement from, one’s sin.
How does Reish Lakish handle the phrase that seems to require another offering?
It applies when the second sin becomes known only after atonement for the first.
How does Rabbi Yoḥanan handle the verse that seems to allow partial atonement?
It prevents two half-portions from combining after a whole portion was discovered.
Do the sages disagree before designating an offering, so later designation would split liability for both?
Or do they disagree after designation, agreeing that earlier awareness still leaves one offering?
Or do they disagree in both timing cases?
Rav Ashi favors a dispute in both cases.
Otherwise Reish Lakish could have placed his limiting verse after designation instead of after atonement.
Likewise Rabbi Yoḥanan could have used awareness before designation rather than the elaborate half-portion case.
Ravina allows that the precise dispute may remain uncertain; each scriptural explanation may be conditional.
Ulla begins a new comparison to a definite guilt-offering that continues on the next page.

72a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ulla says five acts with a designated maidservant require one guilt-offering when prior awareness is unnecessary.
Rav Hamnuna asks whether even a new act after designating the offering would be covered.
Ulla excludes acts after designation from his ruling.
Rav Dimi says a view requiring awareness for a definite guilt-offering would count each act separately.
Abaye notes that even with required awareness, Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish dispute whether it splits offerings.
Did Rav Dimi mean only an act after designation, as in Rav Hamnuna’s case?
Rav Dimi confirms that reading.
Ravin reports two agreed cases and one disputed case concerning the designated maidservant.
Without required prior awareness, many acts before designation need one offering.
Acts after designation need separate offerings.
Where prior awareness is required, Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish dispute whether intervening knowledge divides liability.
A new amoraic case begins on the next page.

72b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Intending to lift a detached plant but cutting an attached one incurs no offering.
For intending to cut a detached plant but cutting an attached one, Rava exempts and Abaye obligates.
Rava says the person never intended prohibited cutting.
Abaye says the person did intend cutting as an act.
What supports Rava’s view?
A baraita contrasts separate Shabbat labor offerings with nonintentional acts that can incur liability in other commandments but not on Shabbat.
The Gemara restates the baraita’s claim that two Shabbat acts can bring separate offerings where other commandments do not.
Reaping and grinding match eating forbidden fat and blood: both examples bring two offerings.
Repeating one forbidden food matches repeating one labor: both bring just one offering.
The comparison is to idolatry, where several rites in one lapse bring one offering under Rabbi Ami.
Does the baraita’s second clause also work if “other commandments” means idolatry?
Mistaking an idol for a synagogue and bowing with intent to worship Heaven is no transgression.
Bowing to a statue either deliberately worships it or does not worship it at all.
Bowing from love or fear fits Abaye’s liability view, but Rava exempts that case.
A final proposal compares thinking idolatry is permitted with thinking Shabbat labor is permitted.
That would fully exempt the Shabbat case, contrary to Rava’s earlier question, which assumed some liability.

73a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita can contrast idolatry with Shabbat in one clause and other prohibitions with cutting an attached plant in the next, as Rava reads it.
Abaye instead uses swallowing forbidden fat mistaken for saliva and a Shabbat case of intending to lift, which he also exempts.
For a throw intended to travel two cubits but reaching four, Rava exempts and Abaye obligates based on intent for a prohibited distance versus intent to throw.
They likewise differ when someone throws while mistaking a public domain for private property.
The short-throw case is needed because covering four cubits includes two, which might have led Rava to concede liability.
The mistaken-domain case is needed because the intended distance itself was four cubits, which again might have changed Rava’s ruling.
The mishna’s count of thirty-nine labors implies separate liability for all of them in one lapse.
Abaye can explain a person who knew the bans but misjudged the prohibited measures.
How can Rava find such a case if a mistaken measure is exempt?
Under Rabbi Yoḥanan, knowing the labor ban but not karet suffices for unwitting liability.
Under Reish Lakish, the person can know the Shabbat boundary ban on Rabbi Akiva’s view.
The mishna begins its thirty-nine categories with agricultural and food-preparation labors.
It continues through wool preparation, weaving, tying, sewing, and constructive tearing.
It lists trapping, slaughter, and processing hides.
It adds writing two letters and erasing to write two.
It ends with building, demolition, fire, finishing a vessel, and moving between domains, for thirty-nine total.

73b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why state that there are thirty-nine primary labors?
Rabbi Yoḥanan says the count teaches possible separate liability for all in one lapse.
The mishna names sowing before plowing.
Why reverse the usual farming order?
In Eretz Yisrael they could sow before a further plowing that covered the seed.
A baraita groups sowing, pruning, planting, layering, and grafting as one labor category.
What does the grouping add?
Several related acts under one primary labor still bring only one offering.
Rabbi Ami classifies pruning with planting and other growth acts with sowing.
Does that exclude planting liability for tree work?
The point is that sowing applies too.
Pruning for needed wood incurs both reaping and growth liability.
Rav Yosef likewise assigns two liabilities to cutting alfalfa.
Abaye assigns two to cutting beet leaves.
Plowing, digging, and furrowing are classified as one labor.
Removing a mound is building in a house but plowing in a field.
Filling a hollow has the same location-based distinction.
Digging only to obtain dirt is exempt because it damages the ground without constructive purpose.
Reaping and several forms of fruit picking are one labor.
Rav Pappa assigns both severing and extracting to dates knocked from a palm by a clod.
Rav Ashi says that unusual method is not the normal performance of either labor.
Rava includes collecting salt within gathering.
Abaye limits gathering to growth from the ground.
Threshing, beating flax, and removing cotton seed belong to one labor.
Why separately list winnowing, selecting, and sifting if all separate food from waste?
Abaye and Rava begin an answer based on work done in the Tabernacle.

74a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The prior discussion counts a similar labor separately.
Why is pounding omitted from the list?
Abaye says the poor can eat bread without pounding grain.
Rava proposes that the fixed count of thirty-nine precludes another labor.
Why not replace one listed labor with pounding?
The Gemara returns to Abaye’s explanation.
A baraita gives conflicting permissions and liability for selecting foods.
How can the clauses of the baraita be reconciled?
Ulla distinguishes selecting for Shabbat from selecting for the next day.
Rav Ḥisda objects that Shabbat use does not permit baking or cooking.
Rav Ḥisda instead distinguishes less than a liable measure from a full measure.
Rav Yosef asks whether baking below the liable measure is permitted.
Rav Yosef distinguishes hand selection, baskets, and sieves by their liability.
Rav Hamnuna objects that the baraita says nothing about those vessels.
Rav Hamnuna distinguishes removing food from waste from removing waste from food.
Abaye objects that the baraita does not mention food and waste either.
Abaye permits selection for immediate use but treats selection for later as storage.
Rava approves Abaye’s reading when the Sages present it to him.
A case involving two foods receives opposing rulings from Rav Ashi and Rav Yirmeya.
Rav Ashi’s exempt ruling is repeated.
A baraita seems to say the selector is liable.
The exemption concerns a basket or plate; liability concerns a sieve or sifter.
Rav Dimi reports fruit served unsorted, but cannot tell whether the reason was law or generosity.
Ḥizkiya holds one liable for selecting lupines from their waste.
Does this mean selecting food from waste is generally forbidden?
Lupines are a special case; the explanation continues on the next amud.

74b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Repeated boiling makes unshelled lupines spoil, so removing them resembles removing waste.
Rav Pappa assigns chopping beets to the grinding labor.
Rav Menashe likewise assigns chopping wood chips to grinding.
Measured cutting of the chips also incurs liability for cutting.
Why does the mishna list baking instead of the Tabernacle’s spice cooking?
The mishna follows the sequence of bread preparation.
Heating a wooden peg in an oven is cooking.
Why is that ruling needed?
The wood softens before it hardens, so the heating is cooking.
Boiling pitch is also cooking.
Why is this ruling needed?
It counts despite the pitch hardening again afterward.
Making a barrel entails seven labors and making an oven eight.
Making a reed receptacle entails eleven labors, or thirteen if its opening is sewn.
Rabbi Yoḥanan counts shearing, combing, and spinning wool on an animal as three labors.
Rav Kahana says none of these are done in the ordinary manner.
The Tabernacle account describes spinning hair while still on goats.
That unusually skilled work does not establish the ordinary method.
A baraita holds one liable for three distinct acts on a feather.
Reish Lakish identifies them as shearing, cutting, and smoothing.
Where did tying occur in the Tabernacle?
Rava first points to tying tents to their pegs.
Those knots were tied with the intent to untie them.
Abaye proposes knots used to repair torn curtain threads.
Rava asks where untying then occurred.
Untying one of adjacent knots would leave an unsuitable curtain.
Rava, or Rav Elai, cites tying and untying the ḥilazon trappers’ nets.
How could two stitches count if they would not hold?
The stitches count when their ends are tied.
Where did tearing for later sewing occur in the Tabernacle?
Rabba and Rabbi Zeira introduce an answer continued on the next amud.

75a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A worm damaged a curtain, so they enlarged its tear before sewing it.
Tightening a loose stitch on Shabbat incurs liability for sewing.
Rav also warns against learning from a magosh and neglecting astronomical calculation.
Rav and Shmuel dispute whether magosh means sorcerer or heretic.
Rav’s severe ruling about learning from a magosh points toward heretics.
The verse permits learning about sorcery to understand and teach, so Rav cannot mean sorcerers.
The proposed identification of Rav is accepted.
A verse censures those who can calculate the heavens but do not.
Another verse is cited to establish the mitzva of astronomical calculation.
Which publicly visible wisdom does the verse mean?
It means calculating astronomical seasons and constellations.
A baraita records a dispute over whether breaking a ḥilazon adds threshing liability to trapping.
Why do the Rabbis exclude breaking the shell?
They limit threshing to products that grow from the ground.
Should taking the creature’s life add liability?
Rabbi Yoḥanan places the case after the creature died.
Rava says even a living ḥilazon was handled without intent to kill it.
An inevitable death normally incurs liability even without intent.
Here the trapper prefers the creature alive for better dye, so the death is adverse to his purpose.
Under which labor is slaughter on Shabbat prohibited?
Rav identifies dyeing with blood; Shmuel identifies taking a life.

75b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Does Rav’s dyeing classification exclude liability for taking a life?
Rav means liability for dyeing as well.
Rav explains why his additional dyeing claim should stand.
Why would the slaughterer want the bloodstain?
The visible blood helps attract buyers to the meat.
Are salting and tanning actually separate labors?
Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish would replace one with marking lines.
Rabba bar Rav Huna treats salting meat as tanning.
Rava denies that tanning applies to food.
Rav Ashi limits the earlier ruling to heavily salting meat for travel.
Rubbing a hide between pillars counts as smoothing.
Three examples assign planing, spreading a bandage, and chiseling to their labors.
Engraving a vessel or blowing glass completes work and counts as striking with a hammer.
Removing cloak threads counts when their removal matters to the wearer.
A baraita contrasts writing one large letter with erasing room for two.
Rabbi Menaḥem notes that erasing is stricter here than writing.
Completing a work, whatever the act, can count as the final hammer blow.
These primary labors excludes Rabbi Eliezer’s separate liability for a derivative.
The count of thirty-nine excludes Rabbi Yehuda’s two proposed additional weaving labors.
The next mishna sets liability for carrying items according to ordinary or personal storage value.
Which items are excluded by fit for storage?
Rav Pappa names menstrual blood; Mar Ukva names wood of an ashera.
The two exclusions differ on whether the blood has a use as cat food.
One view rejects that use because feeding it to a cat weakens the person.
Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina says the mishna differs from Rabbi Shimon’s storage based rule.
The gemara returns to the mishna’s rule for items unfit to store.

76a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Elazar says the previous mishna differs from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.
A baraita makes another carrier liable through the first person’s decision to store an unusual item.
The mishna specifies distinct minimum carrying amounts for animal feeds and leaves.
What is etza?
Rav Yehuda identifies it as legume straw.
Rav Dimi reports a dispute about carrying a cow’s mouthful of straw for a camel.
Rabbi Yoḥanan later reversed his ruling.
Rav Yosef supports reversal because the amount does not suffice for a camel.
Abaye prefers the first ruling because it is sufficient for a cow.
Ravin relocates the dispute to legume straw carried for a cow; ordinary straw for a camel is agreed liable.
The reported positions are reversed: Rabbi Yoḥanan exempts and Reish Lakish obligates.
Rabbi Yoḥanan does not count eating under duress as eating.
Reish Lakish does count eating under duress as eating.
The mishna gives a lamb’s mouthful as the grain measure.
A baraita instead gives a dried fig bulk.
Both descriptions name the same amount.
The mishna gives different amounts for moist and dry leaves, and says the materials do not combine.
Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina allows combining toward the larger measure, but not toward the smaller one.
Can substances with different minimum measures combine at all?
A mishna and baraita combine different fabrics only because they share a use as a seat.
Without that shared use, the fabrics would not combine despite their different measures.
Rava begins his response, continued on 76b.

76b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava says the materials can combine because merchants use them together as a sample.
The mishna allows edible foods to combine to a dried fig bulk but excludes inedible parts, apart from lentil shells.
Why do bran and coarse bran not count with the food?
A mishna includes them in the flour measure for separating ḥalla.
Abaye says poor people eat bread made with bran mixed in.
Rabbi Yehuda’s lentil shell exception is restated.
Are bean shells excluded?
A baraita includes both bean and lentil shells.
Fresh bean shells count; old ones do not.
Why do old bean shells not count?
Their fragments resemble flies in the dish.
The chapter on the great principle concludes.
The next mishna gives distinct carrying measures for wine and other liquids, with Rabbi Shimon’s dissent.
A teaching defines the wine measure by a significant cup, the cup of blessing.
Rav Naḥman states the undiluted wine needed to make a quarter log cup.
Rava introduces corroboration that continues on 77a.

77a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava cites the mishna’s wine and other liquid measures to support a quarter log diluted cup.
Rava says wine must tolerate three parts water to one part wine.
Abaye cites a color test using only two parts water.
Abaye also asks how water still in the jug can add to the wine measure.
Rava says Sharon wine is weaker, or the color test differs from dilution for taste.
For carrying on Shabbat, undiluted wine is significant because it can yield a cup.
A teaching sets an olive bulk as the measure for congealed wine.
Rav Yosef equates Rabbi Natan’s view with Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda.
A baraita describes a quarter log of carcass blood as capable of forming an olive bulk.
Abaye says viscous blood may congeal into an olive bulk from less than a quarter log.
Alternatively, thin wine may need more than a quarter log; the two rulings need not match.
Is the mishna’s word for a gulp spelled with alef or ayin?
Rav Naḥman cites a Torah verse with the alef spelling.
A further spelling question begins on the next amud.

77b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Is the word for seeds spelled with alef or ayin?
Rava bar Ulla cites a verse using the ayin root.
Is the word for dimmed coals spelled with alef or ayin?
Rav Yitzḥak cites a verse with ayin.
Which spelling describes closing the eyes of the dead?
Rabbi Yoḥanan cites a verse with ayin.
A baraita gives differing carrying measures for animal milk, human milk, egg white, and an eye bandage.
Does the bandage measure include the part held during application?
The question remains unresolved.
A teaching refines the mishna’s honey measure to the opening of a sore.
Does the honey cover the whole sore opening or only its primary protrusion?
The question remains unresolved.
Rav lists purposes for several creatures and their use as remedies.
He describes preparing a remedy for a scorpion sting from two geckos.
A baraita lists five small creatures feared by larger ones.
Rav cites a verse about the weak overcoming the strong.
Rabbi Zeira finds Rav Yehuda in a cheerful mood and begins asking him questions.
Why do goats lead sheep?
They mirror darkness preceding light.
Why are ewes covered and goats exposed?
The ewes provide wool used to cover people.
Why does a camel have a short tail?
A longer tail would catch in thorns.
Why does an ox have a long tail?
It uses the tail against insects in the marsh.
Why are grasshopper antennae soft?
Hard antennae would break in grass and impair the grasshopper.
Why is the chicken’s eyelid raised?
Its eyelid shields the eyes from household smoke.
Rav Yehuda plays on the names of doors, stairs, spices, houses, and barrels.
He continues with names of bricks, fences, water vessels, and washing and pounding tools.
He derives meanings from the names of clothing, a bed, a pit, a head covering, and a palace.
A baraita says fish, snakes, and pigs become stronger with age.
The mishna measures oil by the amount needed for a small limb.
Rabbi Yannai’s school specifies the small limb of a day-old child.
A baraita could imply either a small adult limb or a larger newborn limb.
The school reads the baraita as referring to a newborn’s small limb.
Is this a dispute between tannaim?
A baraita gives seemingly different oil measures in two tannaitic rulings.
Do they dispute whether oil for a newborn’s small limb suffices?
The proposed reading is rejected; the clarification continues on 78a.

78a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The prior tannaitic dispute concerns oil for an adult’s small limb versus a newborn’s large limb.
What conclusion follows?
An explicit baraita gives the oil needed for a newborn’s small limb.
The mishna’s water measure is restated.
Abaye sets a principle favoring common uses when measuring carried liquids.
Wine is commonly drunk rather than medicinally used, so its drinking measure governs.
Milk likewise follows its common food use.
Honey commonly has both uses, so the smaller medicinal amount governs.
Why does water follow its small medicinal measure despite common drinking?
Abaye locates the rule in the Galilee.
Rava extends it elsewhere because water commonly heals the eye without clouding it.
A baraita gives a quarter log for blood and other liquids.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar gives an eye application as the blood measure.
Which blood is used?
The blood of a wild chicken.
Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel also uses an eye application for a different condition.
Which blood is used in that case?
Bat blood is used; a mnemonic distinguishes the two treatments.
The Tosefta distinguishes ordinary carriers, storers, and Rabbi Shimon’s different threshold.
How can the Tosefta contrast a storer with a carrier when liability still requires carrying?
Abaye describes a student carrying out his teacher’s stored item while clearing a room.
The Rabbis agree waste water requires a quarter log.
What use does waste water have?
It can be used to knead clay.
A baraita gives a much smaller minimum for clay itself.
Prepared clay can serve a small task; one would not knead fresh clay for so little.
The next mishna lists carrying measures for rope, reed grass, paper, and a tax receipt.

78b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna continues with carrying measures for paper, hides, parchment, and ink.
It gives practical minimum uses for eye shadow, glue, tar, wax, and clay.
It records differing measures for clay and lime, and gives a measure for bran.
Why is rope not measured by the loop used for a sieve?
Rope is too rough and would score the vessel.
A baraita specifies uses that set the measures for palm leaves and bast.
Fat sufficient to smear beneath a small cake is measured as a sela.
Another baraita gives the measure as a dried fig bulk.
The two descriptions amount to the same measure.
Soft material is measured by enough for a small ball the size of a nut.
The mishna measures paper by a tax receipt.
A teaching identifies the receipt’s writing as two letters.
A baraita gives a two letter measure for plain paper, apparently smaller.
Rav Sheshet reads the letters as the large letters of a tax receipt.
Rava includes regular letters plus a margin for holding the paper.
A baraita about erased paper or a repaid note gives two letters without that margin.
The baraita fits Rav Sheshet’s reading.
It remains difficult for Rava because this paper needs no extra holding margin.
The difficulty is left unresolved.
A baraita disputes whether a tax receipt retains value after being shown.
What practical case divides the opinions?
Abaye points to follow-up tax inspectors.
Rava points to junior and senior collectors.
Rav Ashi says a receipt can still prove good standing even with one collector.
A baraita disputes whether a repaid debt note still has carrying value.
What principle divides the opinions?
Rav Yosef makes it depend on whether retaining a repaid note is permitted.
Abaye says all forbid retention but dispute whether an admitted note needs validation.
How should the baraita’s before and after repayment wording be read?

79a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The earlier before and after wording means before or after the debtor claims repayment.
Rava instead locates the dispute in whether a receipt is written after repayment.
Rav Ashi says a repaid note can demonstrate reliability to another creditor.
Rava asks Rav Naḥman the minimum hide carried on Shabbat.
The measure is hide enough for an amulet, including when tanning it.
What if the hide is carried in order to tan it?
The same measure applies, by analogy to processing and weaving wool.
What if the carrier does not intend to tan the hide?
Rav Naḥman again gives the same measure.
Can raw and tanned hides truly have the same carrying measure?
Unsoaked dye materials require more than prepared dye, suggesting preparation matters.
People would not soak herbs merely to dye a tiny sample.
Garden seeds and fertilizer appear to have different measures before and after sowing.
A person would not carry just one seed to sow, explaining that special threshold.
Waste water before mixing clay and prepared clay have different minimum amounts.
A person would not knead clay just to make a tiny furnace opening.
A teaching distinguishes bare hide and its minimum use for wrapping a weight.
It gives different uses for salted and further treated hides.
The bare hide measure differs from the amulet measure.
The bare hide case concerns wet hide.
A mishna and Tosefta give much larger hide measures for impurity and carrying.
That hide is a type unfit for writing or wrapping.

79b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna gives parchment enough for a small tefillin passage.
A baraita seems to give parchment and dokhsostos the larger mezuza measure.
What does mezuza mean in this baraita?
It refers to a tefillin passage.
Can tefillin passages be called a mezuza?
A baraita uses mezuza for the sacred writing inside tefillin.
The baraita’s later clause separately specifies a short tefillin passage, so its earlier mezuza must be literal.
The two hide types have separate measures: mezuza for dokhsostos, tefillin passage for parchment.
Rav permits tefillin writing on dokhsostos as on parchment.
The mishna names parchment alone for the tefillin measure.
That names the preferred practice.
A Sinai tradition assigns parchment to tefillin and dokhsostos to mezuza.
That too may describe the preferred practice.
A baraita declares a changed material invalid.
It may concern a mezuza.
Another baraita invalidates a change in both cases.
Both changes can refer to writing a mezuza on the wrong side of hide.
Alternatively, tannaim dispute whether switching the materials invalidates the writing.
Rav Pappa cites a teaching allowing several hides but excluding paper and cloth.
Does that teaching concern a mezuza?
It appears to concern tefillin.
But tefillin are not written on gevil either.
The teaching concerns a Torah scroll.
An old tefillin or Torah scroll cannot be repurposed as a mezuza because of sanctity.
If sanctity were no obstacle, would that imply tefillin are written on dokhsostos?
The tefillin could be written on parchment.
Can a mezuza be written on parchment?
Rabbi Meir used parchment for mezuzot to preserve them.
Rav’s equivalence can instead mean that parchment, like dokhsostos, may bear a mezuza.
The discussion turns to the mishna’s ink measure.

80a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A teaching requires ink for two letters in each of three forms.
Can ink for one letter in each form combine toward liability?
The question remains unresolved.
Writing two letters while walking counts as placing the carried ink.
Carrying and writing one letter twice is exempt.
The first quantity is no longer present when the second is carried.
Rava states an exemption for carrying two half-figs separately.
Why, if both halves were placed?
The exemption applies when the first was lifted before the second was placed.
Passing the second half close over the first incurs liability.
How can it count without the second half coming to rest?
It passes within three handbreadths of the first.
Rava elsewhere requires actual resting even within three handbreadths.
That ruling concerns throwing; here the object is carried by hand.
A baraita distinguishes one or two lapses and, for Rabbi Yosei, one or two domains.
Rabba requires a private domain between the two public sections.
Abaye includes a karmelit but excludes separation by a beam.
Rava even counts a beam as separating the areas.
Rava compares Shabbat domains to domains for divorce documents.
Why is eye shadow measured for one eye when people adorn both?
A modest woman may cover her face and adorn only the visible eye.
A baraita requires enough for two eyes when used for adornment.
The baraita concerns village women who do not veil their faces.
A teaching specifies sealing a small hole in a wine vessel with wax.
A teaching specifies glue for the board on a hunter’s rod.
A teaching clarifies the tar and sulfur measure for a small hole.
Does Rabbi Yehuda require more clay than the Rabbis, unlike his smaller reed measure?
He means enough clay to plaster a small tripod, not build one.
The mishna’s bran measure is repeated.

80b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita gives minimum uses for carried hair and clay.
A teaching measures lime by enough to apply to a young girl’s finger.
Rav describes depilatory treatments by wealth and cites Esther for myrrh oil.
What is myrrh oil?
Two explanations name stacte or oil from unripe olives.
A baraita explains that such olive oil removes hair and softens skin.
An anecdote contrasts gradual lime application with a fatal one-time application.
Rav Naḥman explains why Rav Beivai’s daughters needed the treatment.
Rabbi Yehuda’s lime measure is restated.
What are kilkul and andifi?
Rav identifies parts of the temple area.
Does that make Rabbi Yehuda’s threshold larger than the Rabbis’?
His threshold lies between those of the Rabbis and Rabbi Neḥemya.
A baraita distinguishes dissolved and solid lime, which Rav’s two locations do not explain.
Rabbi Ami’s school interprets andifi as lime applied to a wine vessel.
Rav Kahana asks why one would spoil wine with lime.
The lime makes measurement marks on the vessel, as in a Temple mishna.
Alternatively, andifi means forehead, supported by an anecdote using that word.
The next mishna sets minimum carrying amounts for earth, manure, sand, and reeds.
A teaching identifies the plasterer’s trowel for the sand measure.
Who holds that adding sand improves plaster?
Rav Ḥisda attributes it to Rabbi Yehuda, who treats sand as making white cement.
Rava says the Rabbis too can value sand because it dulls plaster’s appearance.
A teaching measures a reed quill by finger joints.
Which finger joint determines its length?
The question remains unresolved.
A teaching specifies a beaten egg mixed with oil in a pan.
Which egg is most easily cooked?
The son suggests a turtledove egg.
A sparrow egg is smaller, undermining that reason.
The son falls silent.
What other explanation has the father heard?
Rav Sheshet identifies a chicken egg as easiest to cook.
Why use an egg measure when food labor measures are dried fig bulk?
The measure is a dried fig bulk of that egg, not a whole egg.

81a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna sets carrying measures for bone, glass, and a stone.
Would Rabbi Yehuda’s bone measure be larger than the Rabbis’?
Ulla means only the teeth of a key.
A baraita distinguishes detachable key teeth from teeth fixed to a ground attached lock.
A teaching measures glass by enough to cut two threads at once.
The competing stone measures are restated.
The stone for an animal must be heavy enough that it feels the throw.
What weight is enough?
A baraita sets ten zuz.
Zunin asks the size of bathroom stones permitted to move on Shabbat.
The Sages first name olive, nut, and egg sizes.
Zunin objects that one cannot bring scales into the bathroom.
They settle on a handful instead.
A baraita preserves both the three sizes and the handful rule.
Another baraita disputes nut versus egg size for three sharpened stones.
Rafram links this dispute to the minimum citron size.
The familiar mishna on citrons should serve as the comparison point.
The comparison is therefore reversed.
Rav Yehuda excludes payis from the movable stones.
What is payis?
It means soft Babylonian earth clods.
Rava restricts ordinary manipulation with a stone on Shabbat.
Mar Zutra objects that this could endanger the person.
He can use an unusual manner.
Rabbi Yannai ties the permitted quantity to whether the bathroom place is fixed.
Rav Sheshet permits a previously used stone.
A teaching lists used wiping stones among practices believed to cause hemorrhoids.
A moist used stone is forbidden; a dry one is permitted.
Alternatively, use the clean side rather than the used side.
Alternatively, the concern applies to another person’s stone.
If rain obscures the sign of use, may the stone still be moved?
It remains permitted when the sign is still recognizable.
A further question begins and continues on 81b.

81b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: May bathroom stones be carried up to a roof?
Human dignity permits moving them despite the prohibition.
Mareimar teaches this ruling.
Ravina cites the ban on taking an undesignated wood chip for tooth cleaning.
A meal place can be planned, but a bathroom place cannot always be planned.
Rav Huna forbids relieving oneself in a plowed field on Shabbat.
If the issue is trampling furrows, why only on Shabbat?
If the issue is weeds on a wiping stone, Reish Lakish permits that use.
The concern is filling a hole with a clod, which is plowing in a field.
Reish Lakish permits using a weedy stone but makes actual detachment liable.
Rav Pappi infers that a perforated flowerpot can be moved.
Rav Kahana distinguishes necessary wiping from unnecessary pot moving.
Abaye says moving a perforated pot away from or onto ground can count as detaching or planting.
Rabbi Yoḥanan forbids wiping with an earthenware shard on Shabbat.
If due to danger, why not prohibit it on weekdays?
If due to witchcraft, why only on Shabbat?
An unintentional removal of hair should be permitted.
Rav Natan explains that the shard remains forbidden despite its utensil status on Shabbat.
Rava says the hair explanation conflicts with Rabbi Yoḥanan’s acceptance of unintentional hair washing.
Rav Natan’s explanation is preferred.
What witchcraft danger was meant?
A boat story describes an attempted spell and the Sages’ response; it continues on 82a.

82a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The woman names practices that prevent her witchcraft from harming the Sages.
Rav Huna asks why his son does not study with Rav Ḥisda.
His son says Rav Ḥisda discusses ordinary bodily matters.
He quotes Rav Ḥisda’s warning about straining in the bathroom.
Rav Huna calls this a matter of life and urges him to study there.
Rav Huna and Rav Ḥisda disagree whether to use a stone or shard for wiping.
A baraita prefers the shard, apparently against Rav Huna.
Rafram reads that shard as a smooth vessel rim.
Rav Ḥisda and Rav Hamnuna disagree between a stone and grass.
A teaching warns against wiping with flammable material.
Moist grass differs from dry grass.
Rav Ḥisda and Ravina describe harms from suppressing the need to relieve oneself.
A baraita supports the view that it brings an odor of filth.
What should someone do when unable to relieve himself?
Rav Ḥisda advises repeatedly standing and sitting.
Rav Ḥanan advises moving to another place.
Rav Hamnuna advises manipulation with a stone.
Other Sages advise a change of attention.
Rav Aḥa objects that distraction could make relief harder.
The advice means clearing other thoughts to focus on relief.
Rav Yirmeya reports someone helped by standing and sitting.
A baraita advises walking before a long meal and relieving oneself.
The mishna gives three thresholds for carrying a pottery shard.
Rabbi Meir cites a verse mentioning a shard for raking fire.
Rabbi Yosei cites the same verse’s mention of drawing water.
Which of their minimum shard sizes is larger?
The verse suggests Rabbi Meir’s size is larger, since a curse progresses to a smaller vessel.
Abaye says Rabbi Meir means a shard for a large fire.
How can Rabbi Meir answer Rabbi Yosei’s use of the verse?
The verse says that even a less valuable shard for water will not be found.
The chapter on carrying wine concludes.
The next mishna derives carrying impurity of an idol from a comparison with a menstruating woman.
A mishna bars rebuilding a shared wall with an idolatrous shrine.
One must move four cubits into one’s own land before building.

82b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A shared wall is counted halfway for rebuilding on one’s own land.
The Rabbis compare the shrine’s debris to a creeping animal for impurity.
Rabbi Akiva compares idolatry to a menstruating woman for carrying impurity.
Rabba explains the verse as a demand to cast idols away.
Rabba says both sides accept carrying impurity but dispute impurity through a heavy stone.
Rabbi Akiva applies the menstruating woman analogy to the stone.
The Rabbis apply the creeping animal analogy to exclude the stone.
Why does Rabbi Akiva also need the creeping animal comparison?
It applies to accessories of the idol.
Why do the Rabbis need the menstruating woman comparison?
It establishes carrying impurity.
Why not compare idolatry to a carcass instead?
The menstruating woman comparison also excludes impurity through severed limbs.
Rav Ḥama’s question about limbs would then already be resolved for the Rabbis.
His question instead follows Rabbi Akiva.
Rabbi Elazar offers another account: all exclude heavy stone impurity, disputing carrying.
Rabbi Akiva derives carrying impurity from the menstruating woman.
The Rabbis derive no carrying impurity from the creeping animal.
What does the creeping animal analogy teach Rabbi Akiva?
It concerns accessories.
What does the menstruating woman analogy teach the Rabbis?
It excludes impurity through severed limbs.

83a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why compare idolatry to a menstruating woman rather than a carcass?
The comparison also excludes impurity through separated limbs.
That would answer Rav Ḥama’s question for both sides.
Rav Ḥama instead asks under Rabba’s account of Rabbi Akiva.
A baraita compares idols to creeping animals and seems to oppose Rabba.
Rabba limits the creeping animal analogy to impurity through a heavy stone.
Another baraita seems to deny carrying impurity for idols, again against Rabba.
Rabba notes that the baraita also seems wrongly to deny carrying impurity for gentiles.
Rabba supplies an amended reading distinguishing carrying from heavy stone impurity.
Rabbi Elazar supplies an alternative amended reading based on his account.
Rav Ashi asks what the baraita’s emphasized word they then adds.
Rav Ashi distinguishes what happens when gentiles, idols, or accessories move others or are moved.
Rabbi Akiva extends the idol’s moving impurity while leaving accessories pure.
How could an idol move other objects?
Rami cites a balance scale where a zav tips food and drink on the other side.

83b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: When food tips the zav’s scale, it remains pure.
How can a baraita say only a zav imparts impurity by moving another object?
Rabbi Akiva says an idol also does so.
The baraita can include a zav and comparable sources.
Can a detached part of an idol impart impurity?
An easily restored idol is treated as joined.
If ordinary repair cannot restore it, is the part broken or still whole enough?
Another version assumes an unrestorable idol is broken.
If it can be restored, does present separation still matter?
Both formulations remain unresolved.
What is the law for an idol smaller than an olive bulk?
Its prohibition is clear even for a fly sized idol, as a baraita describes.
For impurity, is the minimum like a creeping animal or a corpse?
A baraita excludes impurity below an olive bulk by analogy to a corpse.
What do the other comparisons teach the Rabbis?
The creeping animal, menstruating woman, and corpse analogies each limit impurity.
Why not use every analogy to impose a stricter form of impurity?
Idolatry impurity is rabbinic, and uncertain analogies are read leniently.
A new mishna derives a ship’s purity from a verse about a ship at sea.
What does that verse add beyond the obvious location of a ship?
Like the sea, the ship is ritually pure.
Ḥananya instead compares a vessel to a sack that can be carried full and empty.
What practical difference follows from the two derivations?
They differ for a ship of earthenware, to which the sack analogy may not apply.
They also differ for a Jordan boat carried on land while loaded.
Rav urges attendance at study because a long taught rule gained a late explanation.
Rabbi Yonatan cites a verse to urge Torah study even at death.
Reish Lakish says Torah endures through complete personal devotion.
Rava’s further teaching begins on 84a.

84a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Does a wagon pulled by oxen count as carried for Ḥananya’s rule?
A mishna makes a stone wagon with a receptacle susceptible to impurity.
The mishna also classifies side opening, top opening, and very large chests.
A baraita says earthenware vessels resist treading impurity and mentions ships.
How is the baraita to be read?
Rav Zevid reads it as a dispute about whether an earthenware ship becomes impure.
Rav Pappa asks why Rabbi Yosei would say even if he were disagreeing.
Rav Pappa reads the vessel cases and Jordan ship differently, making Rabbi Yosei’s addition coherent.
What is the source for earthenware’s exemption from treading impurity?
Ḥizkiya compares a zav’s bed to a person who can purify in a ritual bath.
Rabbi Yishmael’s school uses the same comparison for a menstruating woman’s bed.
Rabbi Ila begins an objection about a reed mat and corpse impurity.

84b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A reed mat acquires corpse impurity by inference despite having no ritual bath purification.
Rabbi Ḥanina says other vessels of the mat’s kind can be immersed.
The two Sages sharply reject each other’s view.
Why should purification of the broader kind matter?
One verse compares a zav’s bed to him; another includes every bed.
The verses are reconciled by whether other vessels of the kind can be immersed.
Rava instead derives earthenware’s exemption from a verse about a sealed vessel.
A mishna describes planting five seed types in one six by six handbreadth bed.
How does the verse indicate five types?
Rav Yehuda counts two singular expressions, a plural expression, and one more singular.

85a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Sages knew that five seeds in six handbreadths would not draw sustenance from one another.
Why is this inherited agricultural knowledge reliable?
Rabbi Yoḥanan reads a verse as protecting the planting boundaries established by early generations.
What did the early generations establish?
A verse about the Horites dwelling in the land introduces their expertise.
Why say they dwelled in the land when everyone does?
They knew which land suited each crop and could sense the soil’s qualities.
Rav Pappa links Hivites to tasting the earth like snakes.
Rav Aḥa offers another explanation of the name Horites.
Rav Asi says the bed’s six handbreadths exclude its border.
A baraita confirms that the interior alone measures six.
How wide is the border?
Rabbi Yehuda gives the width of a foot.
A verse about watering a garden with the foot supports a handbreadth border.
Rav limits the five seed arrangement to an isolated garden bed.
Why not use its corners for more seeds?
Rav’s school says the existing planting already fills the corners.
Why not plant farther outside instead?

85b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav’s restriction guards against later filling the corners.
A triangular planting can enter another field when its boundary remains visible.
That triangular exception does not apply to a small garden bed.
Shmuel allows the arrangement even among neighboring garden beds.
Would adjacent seeds not become mixed?
The rows incline in different directions.
Can one furrow across the beds maintain their separation?
Rav Sheshet says mixing nullifies the row.
Rav Asi says the mixing does not nullify it.
A mishna permits pairs of crop rows but forbids one row of each.
Those vines and branches can entwine, making that case different.
Rabbi Yoḥanan describes five circles in a six handbreadth bed with planted corners.
What about the spaces between the circles?
Rabbi Yannai’s school leaves those spaces empty.
Rav Ashi instead crosses the planting directions between circles.
Ravina raises a six handbreadth spacing rule against this arrangement; the argument continues.

86a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A square bed rule seems to bar Rav Ashi’s crossed rows.
The square condition instead permits a triangular protrusion from the bed.
What is the source for impurity from semen discharged on the third day?
The three day separation before Sinai is cited.
Why may a circumcision be washed on its third day even on Shabbat?
The verse describes pain on the third day.
What supports tying scarlet wool on the scapegoat?
The verse compares scarlet sins turning white.
What alludes to applying oil being like drinking on Yom Kippur?
A verse juxtaposes water within the body with oil in the bones.
The mishna’s first ruling conflicts with Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya while its later ruling follows him.
One tradition reads the first ruling as pure and attributes the whole mishna to him.
Another attributes the first ruling to the Rabbis and the latter to him.
A baraita records Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya’s purity ruling.
Rabbi Yishmael measures the interval by calendar days, yielding four to six periods.
Rabbi Akiva requires five complete periods, extending into a sixth if needed.
Which Sinai separation chronology supports Rabbi Akiva’s interval?
He follows Rabbi Yosei and the tradition that Moses descended early in the morning.
Verses support morning ascent and, by analogy, morning descent.
Why command separation in the morning if relations are avoided by day?
Relations remain possible in darkness or under a covering.

86b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Were some recipients of the Torah still awaiting sunset after immersion?
Two Sages say revelation could occur even to people who had immersed that day.
Mareimar repeats the ruling.
Did he mean it actually happened or merely could have happened?
He meant only that it could have happened.
Why not immerse and receive the Torah at twilight?
A verse indicates the revelation was not concealed in darkness.
Why not immerse and receive the Torah on Shabbat morning?
The whole people should approach revelation together, rather than some still immersing.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says the Rabbis require six full periods before discharged semen ceases to defile.
Rav Ḥisda limits this timing dispute to semen discharged from a woman.
A verse excludes foul semen and appears to include semen discharged by a man.
The exclusion is read as semen discharged by a woman.
Rav Pappa asks about semen of a Jew within a gentile woman and the effect of bodily heat.
He next asks whether semen within an animal differs from semen within a woman.
These questions remain unresolved.
A baraita disputes whether the commandments were given on the sixth or seventh of Sivan.
Rava derives agreement that arrival at Sinai was on the New Moon.
He also derives agreement that revelation was on Shabbat.
The dispute concerns which weekday began the month; Rabbi Yosei starts it on Sunday.

87a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yosei’s chronology places boundaries on Tuesday and separation on Wednesday.
The Rabbis date the New Moon a day later and separation to Thursday.
A verse says sanctify today and tomorrow, challenging Rabbi Yosei’s three days.
Moses added a day of separation on his own initiative.
A baraita lists three independent actions by Moses that God accepted.
How did Moses derive the extra day?
He read today as requiring a preceding night like tomorrow, so two full days remained.
How is divine approval shown?
The Presence waited until Shabbat morning.
How did Moses derive his separation from his wife?
He reasoned from Israel’s preparation for a one time revelation to his ongoing revelations.
What shows divine approval of that separation?
The verses distinguish Israel’s return to their tents from Moses’ continued standing with God.
How did Moses justify breaking the tablets?
He reasoned that Israel’s idolatry barred them from the whole Torah as apostasy bars Passover.
How is divine approval of breaking them shown?
Reish Lakish reads God’s reference to the broken tablets as praise.
A verse says preparation for the third day, challenging Rabbi Yosei.
Moses’ added day resolves that challenge.
A baraita equates the third day with both the month and the week, against the Rabbis.
The Rabbis assign that baraita to Rabbi Yosei.
Third day of which reckoning?
A baraita brings the two reports by Moses to God.
What message passed among God, Moses, and Israel?
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda identifies it as setting the mountain boundary.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi reads punishment first and reward later.
Another reading reverses reward and punishment.
A baraita puts the sixth of the month on Friday, against the Rabbis.
The Rabbis again assign it to Rabbi Yosei.
Sixth of what reckoning? Rava’s answer follows on 87b.

87b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava and Rav Aḥa explain the sixth day as encampment or travel.
Their disagreement turns on whether the Shabbat boundary rule was already commanded at Mara.
A baraita dates the Exodus sequence to a Thursday.
Could the firstborn have been struck after the Exodus?
The plague occurred the preceding evening.
