Ordinary month lengths then put Sivan’s New Moon on Sunday, against the Rabbis.
They can say Iyyar had an added day.
Another baraita explicitly gives the Exodus date and a thirty day Nisan.
It calls Iyyar short and places Sivan’s New Moon on Sunday.
The Rabbis assign this baraita to Rabbi Yosei.
Rav Pappa cites the manna narrative to date Iyyar’s fifteenth to Shabbat and Sivan’s New Moon to Sunday.
The Rabbis again add a day to Iyyar.
Rav Ḥavivi cites the Tabernacle’s Sunday opening in the following Nisan.
A year length baraita would place Sivan’s New Moon in the Exodus year on Shabbat.
That conflicts with both Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis.
Rabbi Yosei’s adjustment of month lengths begins the reply continued on 88a.

88a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Rabbis’ chronology requires eight short months.
Seder Olam dates the Exodus Friday, yielding a Monday New Moon of Sivan against Rabbi Yosei.
Rabbi Yosei attributes that baraita to the Rabbis.
A baraita gives Moses’ ascents and descents in early Sivan.
How could Moses descend Wednesday without first ascending?
The wording is corrected: he ascended and descended Wednesday, then prepared an altar Thursday.
Was Friday occupied with receiving the Torah?
He could instead have been preparing for Shabbat.
A Galilean homily of threefold features follows the Rabbis’ third day reckoning.
A verse underlies the homily that God held the mountain over Israel at Sinai.
Rav Aḥa says coercion gives a claim against binding acceptance.
Rava says Israel accepted the Torah willingly again in the days of Ahasuerus.
Ḥizkiya cites a verse in which the earth feared and became still.
How could the earth be both afraid and still?
It feared first and was still afterward.
Why was the earth afraid, and why the extra letter in the sixth day?
Creation was conditioned on Israel accepting Torah, or else returning to chaos.
Angels crowned Israel twice for placing doing before hearing.
After the calf, destroying angels removed those crowns.
A verse is read as saying the ornaments were received and removed at Horeb.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says Moses received those crowns.
Reish Lakish cites a verse for their future restoration.
A Divine Voice and a verse link doing before hearing to the angels’ order.
An apple tree image likewise explains Israel’s declaration before hearing.
A heretic sees Rava studying so intensely his fingers bleed unnoticed.
The heretic calls acceptance before hearing rash.
Rava begins his reply, continued on 88b.

88b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava says integrity guides Israel, while deceit destroys those who practice it.
A verse compares acceptance of Torah to one eye and its fulfillment to both.
Ulla likens the Golden Calf sin to betrayal under the wedding canopy.
A verse about fragrance while the king sits alludes to that betrayal.
Rav finds continued divine affection in the verse’s gentle wording.
A baraita praises those who bear insult without retaliation.
Rabbi Yoḥanan reads a verse as seventy languages in every divine utterance.
Rabbi Yishmael’s school derives the same image from a hammer splitting stone.
Why are Torah’s words likened to a ruler?
Like a ruler, they have power for life or death.
Rava links life or death to how one approaches Torah.
An alternative reading gives two crowns to each utterance.
A myrrh image portrays God remaining close despite bitterness.
A cluster of henna image alludes to forgiveness for the calf.
How does the word karmei imply gathering?
A mishna uses a related word for gathering garments.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says each utterance filled the world with fragrance.
Where could fragrance from the second utterance go?
A divine wind cleared each fragrance before the next utterance.
A verse is read as Israel’s souls leaving at every utterance.
How could they hear the next utterance after the first?
The dew of future resurrection restored them.
Each utterance drove Israel back and angels led them forward again.
The angels ask why a human is among them.
God says Moses has come for the Torah.
The angels say a treasure kept in heaven should not be given to humans.
God tells Moses to answer the angels.
Moses fears their fiery breath.
God shelters him at the throne, supported by a verse.
Moses asks what the Torah says.
God cites the commandment about deliverance from Egypt.
Moses asks whether angels were enslaved there.
God cites the ban on other gods.
Moses asks whether angels live among idol worshippers; his argument continues.

89a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Do angels live among idol worshippers?
Do angels perform labor and therefore need Shabbat rest?
Do angels trade and risk false oaths?
Do angels have parents to honor?
Do jealousy and an evil inclination make the remaining prohibitions relevant to angels?
The angels accept that Torah belongs among people on earth.
Each angel befriends Moses and gives him a gift.
The Angel of Death teaches the incense remedy that later stopped a plague.
Satan asks where the Torah went, and God says it was given to earth.
Earth, sea, depths, destruction, and death do not yield the Torah’s location.
Satan reports that he searched earth without finding it.
God directs him to Moses.
Satan asks Moses where the given Torah is.
Moses modestly denies deserving such a gift.
God challenges the apparent denial.
Moses says he would not claim ownership of God’s treasured Torah.
God names the Torah for Moses because of his humility.
Moses sees God tying crowns to the letters.
God asks why Moses offered no greeting.
Moses says a servant does not greet his master.
God says he should at least have offered support.
Moses responds with a blessing for divine strength.
The word for Moses’ delay is read as six hours arriving.
Moses had promised to return at the start of the sixth hour after forty days.
Satan confuses the people and shows a death image, prompting their appeal to Aaron.
Why is the mountain called Sinai?
Rav Kahana first associates the name with miracles.
That would suggest another name.
He next proposes a good omen.
That too would suggest another name.
The Sages connect Sinai with hatred descending upon those who refused Torah.
Rabbi Yosei begins explaining several names of the wilderness.

89b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The wilderness names conclude, and one view names the mountain Horeb.
Rabbi Abbahu calls Sinai its real name and derives Horeb from destruction.
Why does the scarlet sins verse use a plural form?
Even sins accumulated since Creation can become white as snow.
Why does the verse say go and the Lord will say?
God will send Israel to the Patriarchs for rebuke in the future.
Israel asks why it should go to ancestors who did not plead for mercy.
God promises cleansing because Israel turned to Him.
A verse calls God the Father when Abraham and Israel do not acknowledge the people.
Abraham responds to the people’s sins by invoking God’s name.
God turns to Jacob, hoping parental experience will bring mercy.
Jacob gives the same harsh reply.
God finds neither ancestral response satisfactory.
Isaac reminds God that He called the people His children at Sinai.
Isaac narrows the time of culpable sin and offers to bear part or all of it.
Isaac redirects the people’s praise to God, whom they call their Father.
A verse describes Jacob’s descent to Egypt as softened by his merit.
The mishna returns to carrying measures for wood, spices, dye materials, and washing agents.
Why repeat the wood measure when the reed mishna already gave it?
Wood might have been valued as a tiny key tooth, so the fuel measure needs stating.
The spice measure is restated.
A different teaching on combining spices seems inconsistent; the question continues.

90a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The earlier spice combination ruling concerns sweeteners usable in one pot.
Does that imply other spices cannot combine?
The mishna too concerns spices fit to sweeten together.
The mishna’s measure for dry dye materials is restated.
A baraita sets a smaller measure for soaked dye.
People do not begin soaking dye merely for a tiny sample.
A teaching limits the useful urine to forty days of age.
Another specifies Alexandrian natron.
Rav Yehuda identifies borit as sand.
A baraita lists borit separately from sand.
Sulfur is suggested instead.
Borit is subject to seventh year plant rules, unlike sulfur.
Aloe is suggested.
A baraita lists borit and aloe separately.
There are two varieties of aloe.
Rav Yehuda identifies cimolian earth.
Shmuel reports seafarers’ identification of eshlag.
The mishna assigns any amount to pepper, tar, perfumes, metals, sacred debris, and idol accessories.
What use has a tiny amount of pepper?
It treats mouth odor.
What use has a tiny amount of tar?
It serves as a treatment.
The perfume measure is restated.
A baraita adds odor materials, perfumed oil, purple dye, and a rosebud.
The metal measure is restated.
What can a tiny metal piece make?
It can make a small nail.
A baraita sets a cubit square minimum for an unspecified iron donation.
What Temple use needs that amount?
Rav Yosef names an iron raven deterrent.
Another version defines the minimum by that deterrent and gives its size.
Copper donations have a minimum value or a small hook measure.
What Temple use has the hook?
It cleans the lamp wicks.
Rabbi Yehuda lists harmful insects in books, cloth, and fruit.
A fig eating student’s complaint illustrates the danger.
The next mishna covers a merchant’s basket and the minimum garden seed measure.

90b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna adds seed and locust carrying measures, with Rabbi Yehuda’s live locust case.
A mishna values enough manure to fertilize one plant, seemingly at odds with several seeds.
Rav Pappa distinguishes an already planted seed from one not yet planted.
A baraita gives date pit measures according to planting, food, fuel, or counting.
Another teaching gives small measures for animal hairs and palm material.
The special locust measure is restated.
What is tzipporet keramim?
Rav identifies it as palya biari.
Abaye describes its location and a traditional use as a wisdom talisman.
Why does the first tanna omit the non-kosher play locust?
A child might eat it.
A live kosher locust also should not be eaten, as Rav’s warning shows.
The concern is that a non-kosher locust might die and then be eaten.
Rabbi Yehuda thinks the child will mourn the dead plaything instead.
The chapter concludes.
The next mishna distinguishes a personal stored amount from the ordinary carrying measure.
Why mention storing rather than simply carrying for a chosen purpose?
Abaye says the person stored it for a purpose, forgot why, and carried it out generally.

91a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The earlier case retains the person’s original storage intention.
Shmuel says Rabbi Meir obligates for carrying even one seed intended for sowing.
Is this not already clear from the mishna’s any-amount measure?
The ruling clarifies that any amount really includes a single seed, not merely less than a fig-bulk.
Rav Yitzhak challenges intention-based measures with someone intending to carry his whole house.
Such an unusual intention is disregarded against ordinary practice.
The mishna’s ordinary measure for others is identified as differing from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.
His baraita makes a second person liable because the first person deemed the object worth storing.
Rav Nahman obligates for a fig-bulk carried despite a change between eating and sowing intentions.
Why state this when either intention supplies a sufficient measure?
The ruling teaches that lifting and placing need not share the same intention.
Rava asks whether a half fig-bulk carried for sowing remains liable after swelling and a switch to eating.
He next asks about a fig-bulk carried for eating that shrivels before the intention changes to sowing.
He asks whether temporary shrinkage disqualifies a later restored fig-bulk; the dilemmas remain unresolved.
Rava asks about throwing an olive-bulk of teruma into an impure house.
The Gemara asks which legal measure the dilemma concerns.
It concerns Shabbat where the thrown olive-bulk completes an egg-bulk of food for impurity.
Does joining for impurity also create Shabbat liability, despite the usual fig-bulk measure?
Rav Nahman cites Abba Shaul’s fig-bulk measure for the two loaves and showbread.
The Gemara begins challenging why that measure applies; the objection continues on 91b.

91b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The challenge suggests an olive-bulk sacred food measure should also set Shabbat liability.
The two-loaf case is different: disqualification precedes Shabbat liability, while impurity and Shabbat occur together in the teruma case.
The mishna requires the ordinary measure when the person returns the stored object.
Why is this not obvious?
Abaye explains that even a recognizable place in the storehouse does not preserve its earlier special status.
The mishna exempts a staged transfer through a threshold and a basket still partly inside.
If the threshold is public domain, why is the first transfer exempt?
If it is private domain, why is the later transfer exempt?
The threshold is a karmelit, where the food rests between the two transfers.
A baraita contrasts ordinary liability through a colonnade with ben Azzai’s exemption.
Hezekiah limits the basket exemption to long produce and treats individual mustard seeds as removed.
Rabbi Yohanan exempts even mustard seeds because the vessel binds its contents together.
Rabbi Zeira says neither interpretation precisely fits both phrases of the mishna.
The entire-basket phrase appears to contradict Hezekiah by binding even fruit already outside.
The most-fruit phrase appears to contradict Rabbi Yohanan by allowing liability once all fruit is outside.
How can these opposing inferences be reconciled?
Each sage reads the mishna according to his own distinction.
Hezekiah reads the whole-basket rule as applying to long cucumbers and gourds, not mustard.
Rabbi Yohanan reads the exemption as applying even when all fruit has left but the basket remains partly inside.
A merchant’s basket baraita seems to exempt loose items despite Hezekiah’s view.
Hezekiah reads that case as long stalks extending through the basket.
The dragged purse case challenges vessel fusion because theft would precede the Shabbat prohibition.
The purse is dragged bottom first, so access to its contents coincides with full removal.
The Gemara asks whether the seam would still allow earlier access.

92a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The contents could be taken through a torn seam before the whole purse leaves.
Would the purse opening and its laces allow theft before the whole purse leaves?
Either it lacks laces or its laces are wrapped around the purse.
Rava holds that a basket binds long produce but not loose mustard seeds.
Abaye exempts even mustard seeds because the vessel binds its contents.
Their other rulings appear to reverse their views of binding in a vessel.
In the other case Abaye obligates fruit carried by hand, while Rava obligates fruit carried in a vessel.
The Gemara reverses the attribution of those positions.
The opening mishna exempts a transfer made through the homeowner’s extended hand.
That hand was above three handbreadths; the present case is below three.
The mishna distinguishes ordinary carrying by hand, lap, or shoulder from unusual methods.
Rabbi Elazar obligates for a load carried above ten handbreadths, like the sons of Kehat.
How is the height of the sons of Kehat’s loads established?
A verse links the altar to the ten-cubit Tabernacle.
What establishes the Tabernacle’s height?
The boards and Moses’s spreading of the tent support a ten-cubit height for the carriers.
The traditional pole-loading proportions then place the burden high above the ground.
Alternatively, the Ark and its cover, together with pole-loading proportions, establish a height above ten handbreadths.
Why not rely on Moses’s height?
Moses may have been exceptionally tall, as the teaching about prophecy suggests.
Rav initially obligates for head-carrying based on the custom of Hotzal.
Can one town determine ordinary practice for everyone?
The ruling is restated for a resident of Hotzal, where carrying on the head is customary.
Even that local custom should be set aside against general practice.
The final restatement exempts one who carries a burden on the head.

92b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Hotzal’s head-carrying custom does not override ordinary practice elsewhere.
The mishna distinguishes changed carrying positions and special belts or couriers.
If a change from front to back defeats intention, why does a change from back to front incur liability?
Rabbi Elazar initially attributes the two rulings to different teachers.
Rava distinguishes a loss of intended protection from an improvement over intended protection.
The Gemara identifies the actual difficulty in the mishna’s implied cases.
Opposing inferences seem to make back-to-back carrying both liable and exempt.
Rabbi Elazar again assigns the clauses to different teachers.
Rav Ashi says the mishna need only teach that improved protection incurs liability despite changed intention.
The discussion proposes a tannaitic dispute over back-to-back carrying.
A baraita contrasts Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis on a money belt facing downward, with each citing an analogous carrying case.
Does Rabbi Yehuda’s appeal imply that the Rabbis exempt back-to-back carrying?
The reverse inference would wrongly make Rabbi Yehuda liable for backhanded carrying, which all exempt.
All agree on back-to-back liability and backhanded exemption; they dispute which analogy fits a downward-facing belt.
A teaching treats the mishna’s “in truth” formula as an undisputed rule.
Royal scribes commonly carry notes on either side of their belts.
The mishna gives liability for one carrier and disputes two carriers when one cannot carry alone.
The sages distinguish pairs who each can carry, pairs who cannot, and a pair with only one capable carrier.
A baraita confirms Rabbi Meir’s, Rabbi Yehuda’s, and Rabbi Shimon’s positions on two carriers.
What is the scriptural basis for these distinctions?
“By performing it” excludes a person who performs only part of a prohibited labor with another.

93a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita applies “by performing it” to exempt two who carry even a load one cannot carry alone, according to Rabbi Shimon.
How do the sages derive their differing rules from the verse?
Rabbi Shimon reads three exclusions, including two carriers who each cannot carry alone.
Rabbi Yehuda uses the third exclusion for someone acting on a mistaken court ruling.
Rabbi Meir reads only two exclusions and obligates two capable carriers.
When one carrier is capable and the other is not, which one is liable?
Rav Hisda assigns liability to the capable carrier.
Rav Hamnuna says the incapable carrier still assists.
Rav Hisda replies that mere assistance is legally insubstantial.
Rav Zevid cites garments beneath an animal’s feet that remain pure despite each foot helping support a zav.
Rav Yehuda of Diskarta suggests the animal fully lifts one leg, so that leg does not assist.
The shifting lifted leg would resemble a zav turning over and render all the supports impure.
The animal case instead supports the rule that assistance is insubstantial.
Rav Pappi begins a second supporting teaching, continued on the next daf.

93b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The horse-and-donkey teaching treats legs that merely assist the main support as insubstantial.
A priest can stand on the Temple floor with one foot while the other merely assists on a vessel or stone.
A priest’s left hand may assist his right during service, confirming that mere assistance is insubstantial.
The discussion returns to Rabbi Meir’s liability for two capable participants.
Must each participant have a full measure, or is one measure shared by both enough?
Rav Hisda and Rav Hamnuna disagree over the required measure.
Rav Pappa cites one zav whose weight makes several garments beneath a bed impure.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak cites two people who jointly trap one deer.
Ravina cites partners who jointly slaughter one stolen animal.
Rav Ashi cites two people liable for carrying one weaver’s reed.
Rav Aha suggests the reed may contain an ordinary carrying measure for each person.
Rav Ashi asks why the teaching then specifies a weaver’s reed.
A larger reed could supply each person a weaving measure, so this proof is inconclusive.
Rav Nahman corrects a reversed version of the reed baraita: the first opinion obligates, Rabbi Shimon exempts.
The mishna exempts a subordinate vessel and a living person’s bed, and disputes carrying a corpse or impurity source.
A baraita separates liability for food from liability for a vessel needed in its own right.
Would this imply two offerings for two acts of the same prohibited labor in one lapse?
Rav Sheshet begins limiting the baraita to a particular case, continued on 94a.

94a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Sheshet first distinguishes unwitting food carrying from intentional vessel carrying.
Rav Ashi objects that the baraita says liability applies even to the vessel.
Rav Ashi instead distinguishes the separate times when the carrier learned of the two unwitting acts.
The mishna exempts one who carries a living person on a bed.
A baraita on live animals raises whether the mishna follows Rabbi Natan alone.
Rava says even the Rabbis agree that a live person helps carry himself, unlike an animal.
Ben Beteira’s horse ruling seems to make Rabbi Natan’s view special even for a human rider.
Rabbi Yohanan’s comparison concerns a horse designated to carry fowl.
Are horses actually designated for birds?
A falconer’s horse provides such a case.
Rabbi Natan agrees that a bound person cannot help carry himself.
Persian riders seem effectively bound, yet the horse ruling still applies to them.
They can dismount; pride alone keeps them mounted, as an officer’s run illustrates.
The discussion returns to the mishna’s corpse and impurity carrying measures.
Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish begin explaining Rabbi Shimon’s exemption, continued on 94b.

94b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Shimon exempts even carrying a corpse for burial.
Rava says Rabbi Shimon obligates carrying a hoe to dig or a Torah scroll to read.
Why must this be said, if otherwise no carrying would count as needed for its own sake?
The ruling excludes a stricter requirement that the object itself also benefit from being carried.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak permits moving a corpse into a karmelit.
An interlocutor objects that Rabbi Shimon’s exemption still leaves a rabbinic prohibition.
Moving into a karmelit is rabbinically prohibited and human dignity permits it here.
A mishna prohibits removing leprosy signs to change a person’s impurity status.
Rav Nahman and Rav Sheshet disagree whether removing one of three hairs is a consequential act.
Rav Sheshet compares carrying half an olive-bulk that leaves an impurity source intact.
Rav Nahman distinguishes a large corpse from smaller quantities whose status the removal changes.
The mishna disputes nail and hair removal and several grooming acts on Shabbat.
Rabbi Elazar says removal with a tool incurs liability for all opinions.
Why state this when the mishna speaks of removal by hand?
The teaching clarifies that the Rabbis do not also exempt removal with a tool.
Rabbi Elazar says removal of another person’s nails is exempt for all opinions.
Is that not explicit from “his fingernails”?
The clarification rules out liability under Rabbi Eliezer even for removing another’s nails.
A teaching sets the Shabbat hair-removal measure at a scissors’ opening.
How much hair fills that opening?
Rav Yehuda says two hairs.
Another clause also gives two hairs for prohibited baldness.
The two clauses share the same measure.
A baraita confirms two hairs, with exceptions for Rabbi Eliezer and plucking one white hair.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar gives different rules for a mostly detached nail or skin shred.
How could tool removal incur a sin-offering while hand removal is freely permitted?
The baraita is restated with separate rules for mostly detached and still-attached tissue.
The halakha follows that teaching when the detached part faces upward and hurts.
Which prohibited labor could braiding, eye shadow, or blush constitute?
An initial account likens these acts to weaving, writing, and spinning.
The sages object that these are not the ordinary ways of performing those labors.
Rabbi Abbahu begins a revised explanation, continued on 95a.

95a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The revised account links eye shadow to dyeing and braiding or blush to building.
Is grooming an ordinary manner of building?
A reading of “built” regarding Eve and a term for braiding support that analogy.
A baraita distinguishes grooming oneself from grooming another person.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar forbids facial rouge as dyeing.
A baraita contrasts Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis on dairy work, sweeping, sprinkling, and honeycomb removal.
Rav Nahman bar Gurya initially answers dairy-labor questions with the acts’ own names.
The study hall identifies extracting, selecting, and building as the corresponding labors.
The discussion restates Rabbi Eliezer’s liability for sweeping, sprinkling, and removing honeycomb.
The verse’s forest-and-honey wording is used to compare taking honeycomb with picking from a forest.
Ameimar permits sprinkling in Mehoza where stone floors have no holes to smooth.
A baraita describes washing in several corners so the floor becomes sprinkled indirectly.
The sage acknowledges that he had not considered that method.
A further teaching and the accepted view of Rabbi Shimon permit sprinkling directly.
The mishna distinguishes picking from perforated and unperforated pots and records Rabbi Shimon’s exemption.
A contradictory statement of Rabbi Shimon about the two pots is introduced and continues on 95b.

95b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The contradictory pot ruling appears to allow a difference for seed impurity only.
Rabbi Shimon otherwise treats a perforated pot as detached; a verse extends purity to its seeds.
An elder asks whether a root aligned with the pot’s hole changes Rabbi Shimon’s ruling.
The elder challenges Rabbi Zeira’s later statement about a larger hole after the earlier question went unanswered.
Abaye restates the exception as a hole below the vessel’s quarter-log holding level.
Rava begins five earthenware-hole measures: seepage ends shard impurity but leaves the vessel fit for purification water.
A hole admitting liquid ends use for purification water but leaves the pot relevant to seed impurity.
A small-root hole changes the seed ruling while the vessel can still hold olives.
An olive-sized hole ends that use while the vessel can still hold pomegranates.
A pomegranate-sized hole ends ordinary vessel impurity; a sealed vessel has a further condition.
Rav Asi recalls a pomegranate-sized hole as the earthenware measure.
Rava suggests Rav Asi heard that measure only for a vessel with a sealed cover.
That seems inconsistent with Rava’s requirement that most of a sealed vessel be broken.
The Gemara begins resolving the distinction on 96a.

96a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The two hole measures concern large and small vessels respectively.
Rav Asi distinguishes the liquid-entry measure for a vessel from the smaller leakage measure for a shard.
Why does the shard have a different measure?
A leaking shard is discarded because another shard is not placed beneath it.
Ulla reports two views, a pomegranate-sized opening and a small-root opening.
Rabbi Eliezer gives the intermediate olive measure and compares the pierced vessel to materials that do not contract impurity.
A sealed vessel has a separate majority-breakage rule.
The previous chapter concludes.
The new mishna gives liability for throwing between public and private domains and a dispute over crossing public space.
Across opposite balconies, both passing and throwing are exempt.
For balconies on the same side, passing is liable by analogy with Levite wagons, but throwing is exempt.

96b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Where does the Torah state the primary labor of carrying out, of which throwing is a subcategory?
Rabbi Yohanan reads Moses’s proclamation as barring transfers from Israel’s private camps to the Levite public camp.
Perhaps the proclamation was on a weekday because the Tabernacle had enough materials.
A verbal analogy to the Jubilee proclamation places this announcement on a day when labor is forbidden.
What is the source for carrying in?
The direction of a domain transfer makes no logical difference, though carrying in is a subcategory.
Why distinguish primary and derivative labors if both incur liability?
The distinction determines whether combined acts bring one offering or two.
What does the distinction mean for Rabbi Eliezer, who obligates for a derivative alongside its primary labor?
A primary labor was significant in the Tabernacle or expressly written, unlike its derivative.
A mishna distinguishes a four-cubit throw against a wall above or below ten handbreadths.
What establishes liability for a four-cubit throw in public domain?
Rabbi Yoshiya first cites tapestry workers throwing needles.
Weavers do not need needles.
The example is corrected to tapestry sewers.
They might have sat close enough for throws under four cubits.
Rav Hisda instead cites weavers throwing a shuttle through the tapestry.
The thread remained bound to the weaver’s hand.
The proposed case is the final throw.
That throw travels through an exempt domain.
The proposal shifts to throwing the shuttle to a borrower.
The workers might have sat close or staggered, and a teaching says they used their own tools.
The four-cubit carrying and throwing rules are instead received by tradition.
Three sources identify the wood gatherer’s labor as carrying, detaching, or gathering.
Why identify his particular labor?
A hidden scroll names thirty-nine labors but seems to exclude liability for one.
The mishna’s count teaches separate liability for every labor in one lapse of awareness.
The scroll must mean that one of the labors lacks the relevant punishment.
Each identification of the wood gatherer treats that specific labor as certainly punishable.
Rabbi Akiva uses matching desert language to identify the wood gatherer as Zelophehad.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira objects that the identification either reveals a concealed name or slanders a righteous person.

97a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Did Rabbi Akiva not derive Zelophehad’s identity by verbal analogy?
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira did not accept that verbal analogy.
How did he then understand Zelophehad’s desert sin?
He associates it with the group that presumptuously ascended the mountain.
Rabbi Akiva reads God’s anger at both Aaron and Miriam as implying that Aaron was also afflicted.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira objects to revealing a concealed punishment or wrongly accusing Aaron.
Does the plural “them” not support Rabbi Akiva?
It can refer to a rebuke alone.
Another teaching reads Aaron’s turning as recovery from his own affliction.
Reish Lakish warns against suspecting the innocent and supports it with verses about Moses and Israel’s faith.
Moses’s afflicted hand is cited as bodily punishment for that suspicion.
A comparison of Moses’s hand teaches that restoration comes faster than punishment.
Aaron’s staff swallowing the other staffs is described as a miracle within a miracle.
The mishna’s dispute over a throw across public space is recalled.
Rabba asks whether the dispute concerns a throw below ten handbreadths and whether airspace counts as rest.
Alternatively, perhaps they dispute a throw above ten handbreadths by analogy with passing.
A baraita describing travel through the public domain itself points to a throw below ten handbreadths.
Passing is liable even above ten, so the baraita appears to concern throwing and the airspace-rest dispute.
Rabbi Elazar instead obligates under Rabbi Akiva even above ten, reading the baraita as stressing the Rabbis’ exemption.
Rav Hilkiya limits the dispute to heights from three to ten handbreadths.
A baraita supports universal liability below three, exemption above ten, and dispute in between.
The permission for transfers between one owner’s domains seems to contradict Rav’s ban between two houses.
Rav’s case has unequal heights, creating a risk that an object falls into public space.
What is the source of the rule joining gaps under three handbreadths?
One suggestion invokes unavoidable irregularities in the public thoroughfare.
That explanation does not account for the precise cutoff or its use in a sukka wall.
A gap under a wall might differ because goats cannot pass through it.
That does not explain the same rule for upper gaps.
The joining rule is a received tradition.
A baraita and Rav and Shmuel distinguish a roofed private domain traversed by a public-to-public throw.
Shmuel attributes two liabilities to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi for the entry and exit.
Rav Hana begins questioning this ruling; the discussion continues on 97b.

97b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Can Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi obligate for a derivative labor alongside its primary labor?
His derivation of the thirty-nine labors seems inconsistent with that reading.
Rav Yosef says the two-offering claim was taught about Rabbi Yehuda, not Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
A baraita disputes throwing from private into public domain across four cubits.
Shmuel initially infers two liabilities from Rabbi Yehuda’s ruling and the Rabbis’ exemption.
Perhaps only one liability is at issue, if the thrower intended the object to rest immediately on entering public airspace.
Rabbi Yehuda’s added weaving activities are offered as evidence that he separately counts related labors.
They may be independent primary labors in his view rather than derivative acts performed alongside their primaries.
The baraita’s word “adds” and another report support reading Rabbi Yehuda as assigning only one liability here.
If two liabilities had applied, how could the thrower intend the object to rest both early and late?
He could declare any eventual landing place acceptable.
The discussion initially compares a throw intended for eight cubits that lands at four with writing part of a longer word.
If the intended throw was four cubits but went eight, does the different landing place defeat liability?
Is this not the earlier question Ravina put to Rav Ashi?
Rav Ashi had answered it for a thrower who accepts any landing place.
The writing analogy fails because a throw can pass four cubits without landing there, leaving the issue unresolved.
A baraita begins a case of a throw across a private domain between two public areas.

98a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A throw totaling less than four cubits across public areas is exempt.
What does that baraita add?
Separated public areas join for distance, while passage through private airspace is not treated as rest.
Rav exempts carrying four cubits in a covered public domain, unlike the desert camp.
The Tabernacle wagons seem to have been covered, yet their surroundings counted as public domain.
The beams were arranged in separate stacks.
The remaining gaps between widthwise stacks appear too small to defeat a covering.
The beams were stacked on their narrower depth instead.
Even so, the gaps between four stacks seem too small.
Tapered beams solve this, but uniform-thickness beams leave the covering problem.
Rav Kahana invokes the wagon’s open frames.
Where could those frames be placed when the wagon itself was covered?

98b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel says the open wagon space concerned narrow stakes.
A baraita and verse support Rabbi Yehuda’s view that the beams tapered to a fingerbreadth.
Rabbi Nehemya instead reads “together” as requiring full thickness at the top.
How does his view explain “complete”?
It requires whole beams rather than boards joined together.
How does Rabbi Yehuda explain “together”?
The beams must be aligned rather than staggered.
The corner-beam arrangement seems to protrude if the beams taper.
Their widths were also pared into slopes.
A teaching describes the middle bar’s passage through the beams as miraculous.
The twenty-eight-cubit curtains leave different portions exposed across the Tabernacle under the two beam views.
The same curtains’ lengthwise spread also differs in how much of the sockets it covers.
The longer goat-hair curtains cover the sockets under Rabbi Yehuda but leave a cubit exposed under Rabbi Nehemya.
A baraita applies the extra cubit in the verse to sockets or beams according to their respective views.
The forty-four-cubit total yields twelve cubits after the roof and folded front are accounted for.
How can Rabbi Nehemya explain the verse saying the remainder hangs down?
It hangs farther than the other curtains.
A teaching compares the trailing curtain to a woman’s trailing skirt.
The beam bases were grooved to fit hollow sockets.

99a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The clasps joining the curtains resembled stars.
A baraita and verses describe the curtains and the exceptional skill of spinning goat hair while still on the goats.
The spaces beneath, between, and beside the Tabernacle wagons count as public domain.
Abaye sets the gap between wagons at a wagon’s length.
Why must that length be five cubits?
Extra space prevents the beams from pressing together.
Rava sets side space according to the wagon’s width.
Why require two and a half cubits of width?
The wider support prevents the beams from teetering.
How does this yield the standard sixteen-cubit public thoroughfare if the wagons total fifteen?
A remaining cubit held a Levite ready to catch a slipping beam.
The mishna defines liability for transferring from a pit bank or boulder with private-domain dimensions.
Why mention the bank of a pit rather than only a pit?
It supports Rabbi Yohanan’s rule that the pit and bank together supply ten handbreadths.
A baraita on drawing water from a deep, wide pit supports the private-domain status.

99b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The pit baraita requires a partition or entry of most of the body and confirms that pit plus bank supply ten handbreadths.
Rav Mordekhai asks whether a throw onto a tall column is liable after passing through exempt airspace.
Rava, Rav Yosef, and Abaye each cite the mishna as the answer.
They point to the mishna’s express liability for placing an object atop the column.
Rav Mordekhai suggests the mishna may involve a needle.
Even a needle must rise slightly through the exempt airspace.
It could instead enter a protrusion or groove below ten handbreadths.
Rabbi Yohanan asks whether the top of a narrow wall enclosing private space is itself a private domain.
Does its lack of four-handbreadth width matter, or does the enclosed domain confer its status?
Ulla argues that a wall making another area private must itself be private.
Parallel reports explicitly obligate a throw onto that enclosing wall.
Rabbi Yohanan asks whether removing dirt that makes a pit ten deep is liable when removal and partition arise together.
He also asks whether adding dirt to a ten-deep pit is liable when placement and loss of partition coincide.
His earlier ruling on a sticky fig cake against a wall is offered as a possible resolution.
The cake seems to reduce the measured four-cubit distance at the moment it lands.
Unlike pit dirt, the cake is not permanently incorporated into the wall.
Rava asks about a thrown board landing atop narrow stakes.
Would that merely repeat Rabbi Yohanan’s simultaneous-partition dilemma?
Rava instead asks about a separate object atop the thrown board; whether it lands after the board remains unresolved.
Rava begins distinguishing water placed on water from a nut placed on water, continued on 100a.

100a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A nut floating directly on water is not considered at rest.
Rava asks whether a nut in a floating vessel counts as resting in the vessel or moving with it; the issue remains open.
A mishna disputes whether oil floating on wine is joined to it for impurity.
Abaye distinguishes a mat landing in a wide pit from a mat dividing it into two narrow spaces.
The mat ruling is compared with Rabbi Yohanan’s unresolved question about dirt changing a pit’s status.
Abaye treats water in a pit differently from fruit: only the fruit eliminates its private-domain status.
A baraita about throwing between sea and street supports the water distinction.
The mishna distinguishes a throw against a wall above and below ten handbreadths.
How can a hit against a wall count as a completed placement?
Rabbi Yohanan specifies a sticky fig cake that remains on the wall.
A small hole high on the wall leads to Rabbi Meir’s and the Rabbis’ dispute over conceptual completion.
A baraita directly confirms their opposing rulings for a throw into a small hole.
Rav obligates for landing atop a steep mound rising ten handbreadths within four cubits.
A baraita on a sloping alley and Rabbi Hanina ben Gamliel supports the mound rule.
The mishna distinguishes a throw rolling beyond or back inside four cubits.
How is liability possible if the object rolls back without resting?
Rabbi Yohanan requires a brief rest on some surface.
A baraita distinguishes an uninterrupted windblown return from a pause before the return.
Rava requires actual rest even within three handbreadths, under the Rabbis’ view.
Ravina begins challenging Mareimar’s account, continued on 100b.

100b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ravina cites the mishna’s requirement that the rolling object actually rest.
Mareimar distinguishes a rolling object from one that will eventually stop, explaining Rava’s added ruling.
The mishna treats a sea throw differently from a throw into a shallow swamp crossed by the public.
Why does the mishna repeat both passage and swamp?
The two swamp cases cover summer and winter, when different reasons might lead people to avoid the water.
Abaye suggests the repetition includes swamps of both narrow and four-cubit width.
Rav Ashi instead includes swamps narrower than four handbreadths that people may step over.
His bridge-beam ruling similarly counts a narrow surface that people still cross.
The mishna exempts transfers between sea, land, and boats and distinguishes tied boats.
Rav Huna allows a small projection for drawing water; Rav Hisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna require a four-by-four frame.
Rav Huna measures the karmelit from the sea floor and requires the projection as a reminder.
The other sages measure from the water surface and require the frame to avoid transfer from a karmelit.
Rav Nahman asks whether shallow water would undermine Rav Huna’s permission.
A navigable boat is assumed to be over water at least ten handbreadths deep.
A boat’s protrusion may make that assumption uncertain.
Depth measurers go ahead of the boat.
How do those requiring a frame dispose of waste water without fouling their drawing spot?
They pour it onto the boat’s side.
That still sends water into the sea by the person’s action.
Indirect action into a karmelit was not prohibited.
A baraita begins distinguishing direct transfer between ship and sea.

101a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda permits casting from a low boat into the sea but not drawing from the sea into it.
Why distinguish the two directions if each crosses between a private domain and a karmelit?
The outward act can be indirect, confirming that such force in a karmelit was not prohibited.
Rav Huna limits carrying in narrow-bottomed boats unless their width reaches four handbreadths near the bottom or the base is filled.
Rav Nahman invokes a basket precedent to extend the boat’s upper partitions downward.
Rav Yosef replies that the Rabbis exempt in the basket case.
Abaye cites a narrowing column whose upper partition still establishes liability.
A notional partition crossed by goats differs from one they cannot pass through.
Could fish pass through the boat’s projected partition?
Fish passage is not treated like visible passage by goats.
A teaching on a hanging partition is introduced to support this distinction, continuing on 101b.

101b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A water-only allowance for a hanging partition confirms that fish passage does not invalidate it.
The mishna permits carrying between tied boats.
Why must this obvious rule be stated?
Rava proposes that it also permits passage through a small boat between them.
Rav Safra notes that the mishna says only from one boat to the other.
He instead says the rule requires an eiruv before carrying between different owners’ boats.
A baraita permits tied and joined boats, suspends permission when untied, and restores it when retied.
A parallel rule applies to mats used as partitions, including those restored on Shabbat.
Rav Nahman says a partition made on Shabbat may count for throwing yet not permit carrying.
That restriction concerns a partition deliberately erected on Shabbat.
Shmuel permits even a cloak string as the tie between boats.
If the string holds them this is obvious; if it cannot hold them, why permit it?
It can hold them; Shmuel distinguishes the Shabbat rule from his iron-chain requirement for impurity.
The sword-impurity verse explains the iron requirement, while Shabbat needs only a holding tie as a sign.

102a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna exempts a throw interrupted by recollection and another catcher, a dog, or fire.
It also exempts a wound intended on Shabbat if the thrower remembers before injury.
A sin-offering requires both the start and finish of the act to be unwitting.
If the object lands, why would the thrower be liable after remembering the prohibition?
Rav Kahana first limits the final rule to a bolt and cord still held in the hand.
He then applies that to an intended wound.
The mishna already explicitly exempts an intended wound remembered before injury.
Rava proposes that the final rule concerns carrying.
But the rule appears in a mishna about throwing.
Rava reads the mishna as two cases: later recollection, or an interrupted throw without recollection.
Rav Ashi instead requires the thrower to forget again before landing for liability.
Rabba and Rava dispute a six-cubit act with unwitting, intentional, then unwitting stages.
Rabba exempts because the four-cubit measure is completed during intentional action.
His analysis concerns carrying, which remains under the actor’s control.
Rava obligates because awareness during an irreversible act does not split the measure.
His analysis concerns throwing rather than carrying.
Rabba obligates when a thrown object lands in a dog’s mouth or furnace.
The mishna exempts when a dog catches it or it burns.
Rabba’s case involves intending that exact destination.
A mishna’s food-carrying case includes Rabbi Meir’s liability for carrying it in the mouth.
Intention makes an otherwise unusual mouth placement significant, as with the dog’s mouth.
The chapter concludes.

102b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: How much building creates Shabbat liability?
The mishna gives any amount for building, chiseling, striking, or drilling when the work endures.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel also obligates a work-related blow on an anvil.
What use can a minute amount of building serve?
Rabbi Yirmeya compares a coin-hiding pit with needle storage by Tabernacle workers.
Abaye objects that stored needles would rust in the ground.
He instead compares a small stove with a small dye-cooking need in the Tabernacle.
Rav Aha objects that a wealthy public project would not work on such a poor scale.
He compares sealing a small house hole with repairing a worm hole in a Tabernacle beam.
Shmuel obligates for setting a stone in place.
A teaching appears to require the addition of mortar for liability.
The needed act differs between bottom, middle, and upper rows of stonework.
Which primary labor covers chiseling?
Rav says building; Shmuel says the finishing blow.
The same dispute applies to a hole made in a chicken coop.
It also applies to securing a hoe handle with a pin.
Different similarities to ordinary building make it necessary to report all three disputes.
Rav Natan bar Oshaya asks Rabbi Yohanan which labor covers chiseling.
Rabbi Yohanan indicates the finishing blow.
The mishna lists chiseling and striking separately.
The wording can be read as identifying chiseling with the finishing blow.
The Gemara introduces a further proof on the next daf.

103a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The prior mishna obligates drilling a hole of any size.
Why would Shmuel count a drilled hole as completed work?
The drill bit remains in the hole, making the work complete.
What does the mishna’s general rule add?
It includes carving a usable half-kav vessel from material for a larger vessel.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel’s anvil strike is recalled.
What productive work does that blow do?
Rabba and Rav Yosef say it trains the worker’s hand.
Learning by watching would then also seem to incur liability.
Abaye and Rava instead cite metalworkers in the Tabernacle who struck the anvil.
A baraita explicitly connects the anvil strike with those metalworkers.
The mishna gives measures for plowing, tending plants, and gathering wood or grass by purpose.
What can a tiny amount of plowing serve?
It suffices for a pumpkin seed or one dye-plant stalk.
The plant-tending cases are recalled.
A baraita sets different measures for food, fodder, fuel, and improving land.
Does uprooting not improve the land in every case?
Rabba and Rav Yosef place the baraita in swampland.
Abaye alternatively says the worker did not intend land improvement.
Inevitable improvement should still create liability under the agreed rule.
Abaye’s case is work on another person’s land.
The mishna obligates two written letters across hands, forms, signs, and languages.
Rabbi Yosei links writing liability to marking matching Tabernacle beams.
Rabbi Yehuda gives short names written as part of longer names.
Why does writing with the left hand incur liability?
Rabbi Yirmeya first proposes a left-handed writer.
That would exempt the same writer’s right hand.
Abaye instead proposes an ambidextrous writer.
Another explanation assigns the first clause to Rabbi Yosei’s broader marking rule.
The later explicit attribution to Rabbi Yosei seems to exclude the first clause.
The whole mishna can still follow Rabbi Yosei.
The discussion returns to Rabbi Yehuda’s short names.
Does he exclude two identical letters from liability?
A baraita begins deriving partial-labor liability from “from one,” while considering a single letter or thread.

103b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita reconciles the verses by requiring a short name within a longer one.
It also quotes Rabbi Yehuda as obligating for two identical letters.
Rabbi Yosei treats writing as marking, including scratches used to match Tabernacle boards.
Rabbi Shimon reads the verses as requiring a partial act that still produces enduring work.
Rabbi Yosei derives one or several offerings from the verse’s paired terms.
Rabbi Yehuda’s identical-letter ruling seems at odds with the earlier account.
The identical-letter rule is attributed to his teacher Rabban Gamliel.
What distinguishes Rabbi Shimon from the first teacher; could amulet letters make him stricter?
A baraita instead shows Rabbi Shimon requiring completion of an intended physical task.
His writing rule may require the whole word.
Another version of his teaching explicitly excludes a requirement to finish the whole name.
That exclusion can refer to finishing an entire verse rather than a word.
Rabbi Yosei’s one-versus-many offering rule is recalled.
The verse’s “one,” “from one,” “these,” and “from these” supply both restrictions and extensions.
The extensions cover partial names, derivative labors, and different kinds of unawareness.
The discussion returns to a short name within a longer name.
How can Shem be part of Shimon when the mem forms differ?
Rav Hisda infers that changing a closed mem to an open one can still be valid.
A baraita requires exact letter forms and paragraph layout in sacred writing, challenging that inference.
A different teacher derives the water-libation hint from extra letters despite a closed mem.
That reading is offered to extend validity from one changed mem form to the other.
The Gemara begins rejecting the equivalence of the two changes on 104a.

104a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Closing a mem can be treated as elevation, while opening a closed mem diminishes its form.
A report attributes the five alternate letter forms to prophets.
Prophets cannot create a new Torah rule.
Perhaps they assigned already existing forms to the middle and end of words.
Even assigning those positions would appear to create a new rule.
The positions had been forgotten and were restored.
Rav Hisda describes the miraculous letters and two-sided reading of the tablets.
Children interpret alef through dalet as learning and discreetly pursuing charity.
Their next letters teach divine reward for that conduct.
The forms of mem and nun represent open and hidden teaching and humble faithfulness.
Samekh through tzadi teach support for the poor, wise speech, and humility in Torah.
The shapes of kuf and reish portray holiness, wickedness, and the possibility of repentance.
Why must repentance enter through a separate opening?
Reish Lakish’s teaching distinguishes an opening for sin from active help for purification.
The shapes and spacing of letters illustrate truth’s stability and falsehood’s instability.
A reverse-alphabet reading describes the conduct of the wicked.
The same reading describes the righteous and their protection.
The minister of Gehenna requests a share of humanity.
God refuses the righteous, describing their purity and honest conduct.
The minister asks to be sustained with the descendants of Seth.
God sends the righteous to the Garden of Eden.
The minister says he is weary.
God promises other groups while identifying the protected descendants of Isaac.

104b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna obligates two enduring letters written with marking materials in positions that can be read together.
It obligates writing on skin and disputes letters scratched into skin.
Writing in liquid, dust, or another impermanent medium is exempt.
Unusual methods, incomplete letters, overtracing, and separated marks are exempt.
The mishna disputes a single letter used as an abbreviation.
The Gemara identifies the writing materials named in the mishna.
What does the rule for any marking substance add?
Teachings on durable materials for divorce documents supply examples.
Rabbi Eliezer cites a skin-scratch example; the Rabbis reject it as atypical.
An inserted parentage discussion explains the nickname in that example.
The mishna’s single-letter exemption is recalled.
Rava bar Rav Huna says it differs from Rabbi Eliezer’s liability for one added thread.
The mishna’s exemption for writing over writing is recalled.
Rav Hisda contrasts Rabbi Yehuda’s view that retracing a divine name can count as fresh writing.
A baraita obligates one letter or thread when it completes a book or garment.
Rava bar Rav Huna attributes that rule to Rabbi Eliezer.
Rav Ashi says completion can distinguish it even under the Rabbis.
Rabbi Ami obligates two letters written in different cities when only proximity is missing.
The mishna exempts marks on surfaces that cannot be read together.
Those surfaces require an additional physical act to bring the marks together.
A teaching obligates for correcting one letter.
How can correction of one letter incur liability when writing one letter does not?
Rav Sheshet says one correction turns a het into two zayin letters.
Rava proposes turning a dalet into a reish as completion of the text.
A further case of intending one letter begins on the next daf.

105a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A teaching obligates when an intended single letter results in two.
The mishna appears to exempt that case.
The cases differ according to whether the letters still require crowns.
The mishna’s dispute over a one-letter abbreviation is recalled.
Rabbi Yohanan finds abbreviated meanings in the verse naming Abraham father of nations.
The word “anokhi” receives several abbreviation readings.
Readings of “yarat” and “karmel” give further scriptural examples.
“Nimretzet” is read as several accusations.
“Nitztadak” receives another abbreviated reading.
The mishna disputes two letters written in separate lapses of awareness.
Rabban Gamliel and the Rabbis differ over whether awareness separates half-measures.
The chapter concludes.
The new mishna gives measures for weaving, making meshes, sewing, and tearing for repair.
Why does Rabbi Yitzhak report two threads when the mishna gives three?
The number may vary with thread thickness, whether strands unravel, or how visible they are.
A baraita supports Rabbi Eliezer’s weaving measure and gives a special hem measure.
Another baraita supports the Rabbis’ two-thread rule and the hem exception.
What does the mishna mean by making meshes in the nirin?
Abaye describes the needed thread attachments.
What is the keiros?
Rav identifies a loom component.
Why repeat the two-stitch sewing measure?
It prepares for the rule on tearing in order to sew.
Why repeat tearing as well?
It leads to the later case of tearing in anger or mourning.
Where is tearing specifically needed to permit two stitches of repair?

105b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Tearing a seam to flatten a protrusion makes repair sewing possible.
The mishna exempts destructive tearing and gives measures for textile work.
A baraita obligates tearing for a mourner even on Shabbat.
The first distinction is between one’s own dead relative and an unrelated person.
The mishna also says “his dead”; the proposal shifts to someone not subject to mourning duties.
A Torah scholar still warrants tearing by all, as a teaching explains.
The exempt case can concern someone who was not a scholar.
A teaching also urges mourning an upright person.
The exempt case can concern someone who was not upright.
Someone present at death must tear, as another teaching states.
The exempt case excludes someone present at that moment.
How can the mishna and baraita still differ on tearing in anger?
The initial answer assigns liability to Rabbi Yehuda and exemption to Rabbi Shimon.
Would Rabbi Yehuda obligate for a destructive act?
Relief of anger could make the act constructive for its actor.
A teaching likens uncontrolled angry destruction to idolatry and interprets the inner “strange god” as the evil inclination.
The case instead involves a controlled display to impress a household, illustrated by small acts of several sages.
A teaching and psalm value tears shed for an upright person.
Teachings and Joshua’s burial verse condemn neglecting a scholar’s eulogy.
Rabbi Yohanan states a measure-for-measure loss of longevity for such neglect.
The elders after Joshua are described as living many days.
He distinguishes many days from many years.
Would that narrow reading also apply to the blessing of long life?
A blessing is interpreted differently.
A further teaching about the death of a brother begins on 106a.

106a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A death within a family or group prompts concern among its other members.
The mishna exempts destructive labor.
Rabbi Abbahu reports exceptions for wounding and kindling.
Rabbi Yohanan rejects that reading or limits it to useful blood or ashes.
How can the baraita fit the mishna’s general exemption?
The two sources are assigned to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon.
For Rabbi Shimon, the special circumcision permission and prohibition of execution fire imply ordinary liability.
Rabbi Yehuda treats those cases as constructive: repairing a child or heating an execution wick.
Two sages demonstrate the textile measure called a double sit.
The next mishna begins comparing spaces that complete the trapping of a bird or deer.

106b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita completes the enclosure cases and gives Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel’s test: liability depends on whether further pursuit is needed.
A Festival mishna distinguishes fish in enclosures from animals and birds that may already be caught.
A conflicting teaching forbids taking animals and birds from enclosures too, creating two contradictions.
The animal rulings can initially be assigned to Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis.
The bird rulings still conflict: even a roofed house does not trap a free bird under the earlier rule.
Rabba bar Rav Huna identifies the free sparrow, which evades capture indoors as it does outdoors.
The animal rulings can likewise be reconciled by distinguishing a large enclosure from a small one.
What makes an enclosure large or small for this purpose?
Rav Ashi offers practical tests: a single lunge, overlapping wall shadows, or corners where the animal can evade capture.
Shmuel rules according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel’s enclosure distinction.
Abaye asks whether that ruling implies the other sages disagree.
Rav Yosef asks what practical difference that inference makes.
Abaye insists that a transmitted legal teaching must be understood, not merely recited.
A baraita distinguishes catching a blind or sleeping deer from one that is lame, old, or ill.
Abaye asks why the two groups receive different rulings.
The first group can still escape; the second ordinarily cannot.
Another baraita nevertheless makes one liable for catching an ill deer.
Rav Sheshet distinguishes an animal with fever, which can flee, from one weakened by exhaustion.
Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis differ over whether trapping a species not ordinarily hunted incurs liability.
Another baraita distinguishes locusts in dew and heat and cites Elazar ben Mehavai on swarming locusts.
Does Elazar ben Mehavai qualify the dew case or the heat case?
A fuller version explicitly says his exemption for swarming locusts applies even during heat.
The mishna assigns liability when one person closes a deer in a house, with a dispute when two must close it together.
Shmuel says a lion is not fully trapped until placed in its cage.
The next mishna assigns liability to the person who first completes the doorway trap, comparing a later occupant to guarding a deer already confined.

107a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav permits guarding a bird that entered beneath one’s clothing until Shabbat ends.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak challenges this permission from the second person’s exemption in the doorway mishna, which may still imply prohibition.
The exemption may instead mean the second person’s act is permitted.
The mishna’s comparison to locking a house around an already secured deer supports permission.
An alternate tradition introduces the same doorway mishna as support for Rav’s ruling.
The wording of the exemption alone could still mean prohibited.
The house locking analogy establishes that this exemption permits the act.
Shmuel identifies three Shabbat exemptions that are permitted, unlike ordinary exemptions.
The deer case is permitted because the mishna compares it to locking one’s own house.
Draining an abscess only to release fluid is exempt; making an opening incurs liability.
Permission to use a needle to remove a thorn supports permitting relief of the abscess.
Catching a snake to prevent a bite is exempt, while trapping it for medicinal use incurs liability.
The permission to cover a threatening scorpion with a bowl supports permitting protective capture.
The chapter concludes.
The next mishna distinguishes trapping and wounding the eight listed creeping animals, other creatures, and animals already controlled by a person.
The wound ruling seems to imply that all eight creeping animals have skins; whose view does the mishna follow?
Shmuel attributes the mishna to Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri, who says all eight have skins.
Rav allows the mishna to follow the Rabbis too: their disagreement over the animals’ skins concerns impurity, not the Shabbat wound rule.
A baraita appears to show that the Rabbis do dispute the skin distinction for Shabbat as well; its citation continues on the next side.

107b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The wording about which creatures the Sages counted seems to imply the opposite of their supposed position.
Abaye reads the wording as saying that only creatures the Sages did not count have skin distinct from flesh.
Rava objects that the transmitted wording explicitly says those they did count.
Rava construes the count as identifying skins that transmit impurity like flesh.
That reading would wrongly imply Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri treats even the uncounted skins as impure.
Rav Adda bar Mattana limits the Sages’ statement to impurity, preserving the distinction.
A second baraita appears to make skin status relevant to the Shabbat law of wounding as well.
Rav Ashi assigns that baraita’s first view to Rabbi Yehuda; the other Rabbis can still agree about Shabbat.
If the Rabbis agree, why does the baraita name Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri alone?
The attributed statement should be read as including those who dispute him on impurity.
Levi asks Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi for the source that a wound must be lasting.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi cites the verse comparing enduring skin and a leopard’s markings.
Why read the leopard’s marks as wounds rather than mere colors?
The parallel to unchanging skin supports an irreversible wound as the intended meaning.
The exemption for wounding other creatures seems to imply liability for killing them; whose view is that?
Rabbi Yirmeya initially attributes it to Rabbi Eliezer, who makes killing even a louse liable.
Rav Yosef says the Rabbis may agree about creatures that reproduce and differ only about lice.
The dispute turns on how to compare creatures to Tabernacle rams: any loss of life or only reproducing species.
Abaye questions the claim about lice by citing a saying that mentions their eggs.
Rav Yosef says “lice eggs” names another kind of creature.
Abaye cites a second teaching that mentions lice eggs.
The same expression is again explained as a species name.
A flea reproduces, yet a baraita exempts its captor according to Rabbi Yehoshua.
Rav Ashi separates trapping from killing: their flea dispute concerns whether its kind is normally trapped.
Who supports the mishna’s exemption when trapping a creature without need for it?
Rav attributes it to Rabbi Shimon’s exemption for labor not needed for its usual purpose.
Another tradition applies the same issue to draining an abscess for relief rather than forming an opening.
Whose view supports that exemption?
Rav again identifies Rabbi Shimon’s rule about labor not needed for its usual purpose.
A further tradition frames the issue as catching a snake for safety rather than medicinal use.
Whose view supports the exemption for protective capture?
Rav again assigns the distinction to Rabbi Shimon.
Shmuel gives the drying threshold for liability after taking a fish from water.
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin locates the decisive drying between the fins.
Rav Ashi clarifies that a film of mucus suffices without complete dryness.
Shmuel rules that detaching a fetus inside its mother incurs liability.
What is the basis for that liability?
Rava analogizes the detachment to uprooting hops from the plants on which they grow.
Abaye begins a related ruling about detaching another growth, continuing on the next side.

108a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abaye completes his ruling that detaching a mushroom from a pitcher uproots it from its place of growth.
Rav Oshaya objects from the exemption for uprooting a plant in an unperforated pot.
A pot is not the plant’s usual growth site; a mushroom can normally grow where found.
Rav Huna permits writing phylacteries on the skin of a kosher bird.
Rav Yosef asks what is new if the mishna already treats bird skin as capable of being wounded.
Abaye explains that the bird’s feather holes could have invalidated writing, but holes bridged by ink do not.
Rabbi Zeira challenges calling bird skin true skin from a verse that includes it in an offering.
Abaye says the verse can expressly include actual skin.
In another version, Rabbi Zeira argues that explicit inclusion is needed precisely because it is skin.
Abaye says the verse could instead overcome concern that its many holes make it unfit.
Mar asks whether phylacteries may be written on the skin of a kosher fish.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak makes the answer depend on information Elijah would bring.
The Gemara asks what remains uncertain when fish visibly have skin and a mishna mentions it.
The uncertainty is whether the fish skin’s odor can be removed.
Shmuel sees murky rising water, anticipates Rav’s arrival, and sends Karna to test him.
Karna asks Rav why phylacteries require hide from a kosher animal.
Rav derives the requirement from “God’s Torah in your mouth,” linking the material to permitted food.
Karna asks for a source that blood is red.
Rav cites a verse comparing red water to blood.
Karna asks for the source of circumcision at the bodily site in question.
Rav links foreskin terminology to a fruit bearing tree.
Karna proposes the heart, also described with foreskin language.
He similarly proposes the ear, also called uncircumcised.
Rav relies on the matching complete form of the term to exclude those alternatives.
Rav asks Karna’s name and responds with a wordplay after being tested.
Shmuel’s treatment of Rav’s stomach pain leads Rav to curse his tormentor; the narrative records its effect.
A baraita sets Rabbi Yoshiya’s fruit bearing analogy beside Rabbi Natan’s proof from the wording about a male.
A baraita lists permitted kosher hides, hair, and sinews for phylacteries and excludes those from nonkosher species.
A Boethusian asks Rabbi Yehoshua HaGarsi for the exclusion of nonkosher hide.
He cites the rule that the material must come from a species permitted as food.
The questioner asks why hides of kosher animals that died improperly remain permitted.
A parable distinguishes death administered by the king from death administered by an executioner.
The questioner presses whether such animals should then be eaten.
Rabbi Yehoshua invokes the separate explicit prohibition on eating carcasses.
The next mishna begins with a restriction on making brine on Shabbat.

108b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna permits small quantities of salt water; Rabbi Yosei questions that distinction and gives an oil first method.
What does the first ruling mean?
Shmuel explains it as a contrast between making much salt water and making a little.
Rabbi Yosei calls either quantity brine.
Does Rabbi Yosei intend to prohibit both quantities or permit both?
Rav Yehuda initially infers permission from the absence of an explicit prohibition.
Rabba points to the mishna’s separate description of salt water that is permitted.
Rabba and Rabbi Yohanan conclude that Rabbi Yosei prohibits ordinary preparation in either quantity.
A fuller baraita explicitly forbids both quantities and permits adding oil before combining salt and water.
A mnemonic introduces the next three topics.
Rabbi Yehuda bar Haviva forbids making concentrated salt water.
What counts as concentrated salt water?
Rabba and Rav Yosef bar Abba define it by whether an egg floats.
What is the mixture’s proportion?
Abaye specifies two parts salt to one part water.
What is this mixture used for?
Rabbi Abbahu identifies its use in fish brine.
A teaching forbids salting radish and egg on Shabbat.
Rav Hizkiya distinguishes radish, which remains prohibited, from a permitted egg.
Rav Nahman revises his earlier practice of salting radishes after learning that salting preserves them, while allowing dipping.
A related teaching describes the difficult digestion of citron, radish, and egg without their outer covering.
Rav Dimi states that people do not drown in the highly saline Sea of Sodom.
Rav Yosef challenges the wording as if it implied a plank would sink instead.
Abaye explains that planks float everywhere and Rav Dimi emphasizes that even people float there.
What practical question follows from this discussion?
The Gemara introduces a conversation at the shore of the Sea of Sodom.
Ravin asks whether one may wash with its water on Shabbat.
Rabbi Yirmeya permits washing with it.
Ravin asks whether opening and closing the eyes in that water is permitted.
Rabbi Yirmeya knows analogous rulings distinguishing wine in the eye from wine on it and restricting even external use of bland saliva.
Shmuel’s permission to put wine soaked bread on the eye seems to identify his father as the source of the wine ruling.
Shmuel also repeats the saliva ruling, so his agreement alone cannot identify which teacher said which.
He learned one from his father and one from Levi; the attribution remains unresolved.
Shmuel permits preparing an eye salve before Shabbat and applying it on Shabbat.
Bar Livaei objects when Mar Ukva repeatedly opens and closes his eyes while applying salve.
Mar Ukva offers to send Rabbi Yannai salve but reports Shmuel’s preference for simple water and evening washing.
A baraita transmits a matching recommendation from Rabbi Mona in Rabbi Yehuda’s name.
The teaching continues with cautions against touching sensitive parts of the body with a hand.

109a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The prior teaching continues its warnings about hands touching a vessel, eye, ear, and nose.
Rabbi Natan attributes the hand related concern to a spirit said to persist until three washings.
Rabbi Yohanan describes effects he attributes to eye shadow.
A baraita transmits the same eye shadow description from Rabbi Yosei.
Shmuel says leaves placed on the eye are not treated as medicine.
Rav Yosef says coriander is not treated as medicine.
Rav Sheshet says hops are not treated as medicine.
Rav Yosef says coriander is harmful even to him.
Rav Sheshet says arugula benefits even him.
Shmuel permits various hops but excludes a kind reserved for medicinal use.
Rav Hisda distinguishes a permitted melon preparation from a prohibited egg preparation.
Zeiri’s wife questions Hiyya bar Ashi for refusing food she had also served Zeiri.
Zeiri treats this food as ordinarily consumable, comparing it to filtering already clear drinks.
Mar Ukva permits stopping bleeding from a hand or foot with wine on Shabbat.
Does the same permission extend to vinegar?
Rav Hillel reports that vinegar was prohibited in Rav Kahana’s house.
Rava adds that even wine acts as medicine for especially sensitive people.
Ravina sees Rav Ashi applying vinegar to an injured foot.
Ravina objects from Rav Hillel’s prohibition of vinegar.
Rav Ashi distinguishes an injury on the back of the hand or foot.
Another version says Rav Ashi applied wine.
Ravina objects that even wine is medicinal for sensitive people like Rav Ashi.
Rav Ashi invokes the danger of such wounds and a ruling that Shabbat may be overridden for them.
A baraita lists waters allowed and waters forbidden for bathing on Shabbat.
A second baraita permits the Great Sea, contrary to the first.
Rabbi Yohanan initially attributes the conflicting rulings to Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda.
Their dispute over whether all seas or only the Great Sea count as a ritual bath supplies the proposed distinction.
Rabbi Yosei adds his rules for purification in seawater.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak begins an objection to applying that purity dispute to Shabbat.

109b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A disagreement over purity does not itself establish a disagreement about bathing on Shabbat.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak instead distinguishes prolonged bathing from a brief dip.
A further baraita permits even medicinal waters when one does not linger, undermining that distinction alone.
The Great Sea rulings distinguish pleasant from unpleasant waters; the flax water rulings distinguish lingering from not lingering.
The mishna distinguishes foods and drinks used only as remedies from things ordinarily consumed, even when taken for relief.
Several sages offer names or identifications for the hyssop and eizoveyon plants.
Rav Pappi offers another identification of hyssop.
Rav Yirmeya supports Rav Pappi from the three branched form specified by a mishna.
For what condition is the plant eaten?
The text identifies intestinal worms.
With what is it eaten?
The text gives seven dark dates.
What causes the stated condition?
The text attributes it to barley flour left in a vessel for forty days.
The discussion turns to the mishna’s permitted yo’ezer.
What is yo’ezer?
It is identified as potnak.
For what is it eaten?
The text identifies liver worms.
With what is it eaten?
The text gives seven white dates.
What is said to cause the condition?
The text lists foods eaten on an empty stomach and water drunk afterward.
A series of fallback remedies and preparation instructions is recorded for the same ailment, including a disagreement about vinegar.
The discussion turns to the mishna’s permitted abuvroa.
What is abuvroa?
It is named humtareya.
What is humtareya?
It is called the solitary staff.
For what purpose is it used?
The text identifies suspected venom in exposed water.
An alternative preparation using flowers and beer is recorded.
A story recounts another preparation and its reported effect.
Rav Avya gives another historical remedy for suspected venom.
Rav Huna bar Yehuda gives a citron and honey preparation.
