Rabbi Hanina lists several uses he attributes to aged urine.
Rabbi Yohanan lists other substances he regards as effective for the reported conditions.
The text records a remedy for someone said to have swallowed a snake.
A story reports the remedy’s application and outcome.
An alternate account identifies Rav Shimi himself as the patient.
The text begins another remedy for snakebite and limits it to a particular animal condition.

110a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A story continues the search for an uninjured donkey after a snakebite and reports that the last available animal was lost.
Abaye asks whether the bite followed a breach of a rabbinic restriction, citing a verse about a snake biting one who breaks a fence.
The others confirm an earlier violation of a decree about wedding music and report the man’s death.
The text records a historical method for removing a snake coiled around someone.
Further instructions concern a snake said to be pursuing a person.
The text adds running on sand in a pursuit.
A procedure is given for testing whether a snake has turned toward a woman.
What action is proposed if the snake has turned toward her?
One initial suggestion is recorded.
An alternate view says that suggestion would worsen the situation.
The alternate view proposes a different response.
The text records another historical snake related treatment and its stated rationale.
What does the mishna’s phrase “all foods” include?
It includes spleen and vetch despite their medicinal uses.
What does “all drinks” include?
It includes caper water mixed with vinegar.
Ravina asks whether urine may be drunk on Shabbat.
Rava excludes it because people do not ordinarily drink it.
The phrase for palm water has two readings, explained as a piercing effect or a spring between palms.
Rabba bar Beruna describes the spring water and the effects attributed to successive cups.
Ulla compares Babylonian beer, qualified by whether the drinker is accustomed to it.
Rav Yosef and Rav Pappa give different Egyptian zitom recipes and the text describes its use.
What is the mishna’s cup of roots?
Rabbi Yohanan gives its ingredients and distinguishes the reported effects of two preparations.
The text repeats one preparation and begins an alternative if it fails, continuing on the next side.

110b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The previous page’s fallback preparation for a woman with a discharge continues.
A second described procedure uses a crossroads, wine, and a startling voice.
Another preparation combines three plants with wine.
The text next describes a preparation from barrel seals.
A boiled herb is proposed as another fallback.
The next method specifies burnt thistle and different cloth according to season.
Another procedure uses pits, vine shoots, and a repeated phrase.
The text proposes flour on the lower body as another fallback.
An ostrich egg preparation is specified for different seasons.
Another fallback opens a barrel of wine for her.
The final proposed procedure uses a grain found with a white donkey and gives different claimed durations.
The discussion returns to the jaundice mixture and gives a fish based alternative.
Several further historical treatments are listed, including brine and heating.
Rabbi Yohanan describes warming the patient; a story reports its use by Rav Kahana.
A later fallback combines dates, wax, and aloe in beer.
The text records a donkey related procedure and cautions about the eyes.
A pickled ram head is proposed as another fallback.
The next recorded procedure uses a pig.
Leeks are given as a further option.
A story about a patient, gardener, leeks, and cloak follows.
The stated jaundice treatment causes sterility, apparently conflicting with a baraita prohibiting castration.
The Gemara distinguishes intended castration from a side effect of treatment.
A rooster example is offered to support that distinction.
Rav Ashi’s explanation of the rooster undermines that example.
The proposed response shifts to an already sterile subject.
A further objection from Rabbi Yohanan begins and continues on the next side.

111a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Separate verses establish liability for additional acts of leavening after a meal offering has already been leavened.
The castration verse similarly establishes liability for further damage after an earlier act.
The proposed allowance for an elderly man is challenged because fertility may return.
The discussion first shifts the treatment to a woman.
Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka also obligates women to reproduce, undermining that broad answer.
The case is narrowed to an elderly or infertile woman.
The mishna distinguishes ordinary eating and oiling from conspicuous treatment of teeth and loins, with Rabbi Shimon’s view of rose oil.
Rav Aha contrasts the mishna’s implied benefit of vinegar for teeth with a verse portraying it as harmful.
One answer distinguishes fruit vinegar from wine vinegar.
Another answer distinguishes damaged teeth, which the text says benefit, from undamaged teeth.
The Gemara returns to the mishna’s rule about sipping vinegar.
A baraita allows sipping and swallowing while forbidding sipping and spitting.
Abaye reads the mishna as addressing only sipping and spitting.
Rava distinguishes sipping before a meal’s vinegar dip from doing so afterward.
Rava’s broader “since” principle seems to require permission in both cases.
The Gemara proposes that Rava retracted that principle here.
How do we know he retracted this case rather than the immersion rule?
A baraita permitting required immersion on fast days supports retaining his immersion ruling.
Rav rules like Rabbi Shimon on using rose oil.
Another report of Rav’s view appears to conflict; its example continues on the next side.

111b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav’s prohibition on tightening a barrel stopper seems to conflict with his permission for rose oil.
Even Rabbi Shimon forbids an action whose prohibited result is inevitable, such as wringing here.
Other transmitted rulings place Rav with Rabbi Yehuda and Shmuel with Rabbi Shimon.
Rava and Rabbi Hiyya bar Avin distinguish agreeing with Rabbi Shimon’s result from accepting his reasoning.
How can the result agree while the reasoning differs?
The suggestion that Rav denies rose oil has medicinal effect conflicts with the mishna’s reference to wounds.
Rav permits rose oil where it is common, whereas Rabbi Shimon permits it even where it is rare.
The chapter ends and the knot chapter begins.
The mishna identifies permanent camel and sailor knots as liable and gives Rabbi Meir’s one hand test.
Do those names mean temporary rope attachments, despite their being regularly untied?
They mean the permanent knots fastening the rings themselves.
The discussion returns to Rabbi Meir’s one hand test.
Rav Ahadvoy asks whether a bow qualifies because it is easy to undo or fails because it is tightly tied; the issue remains unresolved.
The next mishna distinguishes nonliable knots from permitted garment, vessel, and animal restraint ties.
The opening suggests a prohibition, but the following list permits tying some knots from the outset.
The Gemara begins to distinguish the classes of knots, continuing the explanation on the next side.

112a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The preceding mishna is resolved by distinguishing prohibited temporary attachments from knots expressly permitted at the outset.
Why mention tying the robe opening?
Even with two fasteners, neither is assumed to be left permanently tied.
Why mention tying a hairnet?
Even a loose hairnet is untied to avoid pulling hair, so its tie is temporary.
The discussion turns to shoe and sandal straps.
Three baraitot assign liability, prohibition, and permission to untying shoe or sandal straps.
Shoes are distinguished by a shoemaker’s permanent knot, a sage’s tie, and a daily tie.
Sandals are distinguished by permanent construction, an intermediate tie, and a tie adjusted by two wearers.
A shared pair of sandals worn alternately by Rav Yehuda and his child supplies a practical example.
Rav Yehuda asks Abaye for the status of this shared sandal.
Abaye initially declares liability.
Rav Yehuda says even a lesser prohibition would be surprising for his case.
Abaye asks why.
The adult and child both wear the sandals on weekdays.
Abaye then permits undoing the strap from the outset.
Rabbi Yirmeya’s sandal strap breaks while he is walking in a karmelit.
He asks Rabbi Abbahu what to do with it.
Rabbi Abbahu tells him to wrap it with a moist reed usable as animal food.
Abaye’s strap breaks in Rav Yosef’s presence.
Abaye asks what to do with that sandal.
Rav Yosef tells him to leave it.
Abaye asks how his case differs from Rabbi Yirmeya’s.
The first sandal would be unguarded outside; this one can be left safely.
Abaye argues it remains a usable article if the sandal is switched to the other foot.
Rav Yosef invokes Rabbi Yohanan’s explanation according to Rabbi Yehuda.
Which teaching of Rabbi Yehuda is meant?
A baraita distinguishes broken sandal parts and cites Rabbi Yohanan applying the impurity dispute to Shabbat, but apparently not to halitza.
Attributing that distinction to the Rabbis conflicts with a mishna validating a left shoe on the right foot for halitza.
Attributing it to Rabbi Yehuda initially seems to explain impurity and Shabbat while treating halitza differently.
A torn outer strap makes the sandal unfit for ordinary use, undermining that halitza distinction too.
The statement is corrected so halitza follows the same rule: switching sides helps only a still usable sandal.

112b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The corrected rule excludes a sandal no longer fit for its normal use.
Rabbi Yohanan’s preference for an unattributed mishna seems to conflict with his reported reliance on Rabbi Yehuda.
Does that mishna treat inner and outer sandal parts alike?
The mishna may address only an inner part.
If an outer break differs, why does the mishna discuss a second break rather than state that distinction?
Rav Yitzhak ben Yosef preserves the explanation by positing a sandal with four ears and four straps.
A later report explicitly has Rabbi Yohanan rule against Rabbi Yehuda.
His earlier explanation in Rabbi Yehuda’s terms seems to imply agreement instead.
The two reports come from different transmitters of Rabbi Yohanan’s view.
A mishna sets the breakage threshold of household utensils at a pomegranate sized hole.
Hizkiya asks whether multiple repaired olive sized holes accumulate to that threshold.
Rabbi Yohanan invokes a sandal whose two ears broke and were repaired at different times.
Why does the second repaired break change the sandal’s impurity status when one repaired ear still functions?
The repaired object is treated as newly formed; the same reasoning is applied to the utensil.
The exchange ends with praise of Rabbi Yohanan in two versions.
Rabbi Zeira records a reflection on the stature of earlier sages.
The discussion returns to tying wine and oil jugs.
Why must this obvious permission be stated?
Even a vessel with two openings does not make one tie permanent by abandoning an opening.
The discussion turns to tying a covering over a pot.
Why mention that permission?
Even a pot with a flap does not make the covering tie permanent.
The Gemara returns to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov’s animal restraint tie.
Why must its permission be stated?
The answer begins with an entrance having two ties and continues on the next side.

113a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The previous case concludes that neither of two animal restraint ties is treated as permanently abandoned.
Shmuel rules in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.
Abaye asks whether announcing a ruling implies that others disagree.
Rav Yosef asks why that inference matters.
Abaye insists that a ruling should be understood rather than merely repeated.
The mishna permits tying a bucket with a belt, disputes a rope, and states Rabbi Yehuda’s nonpermanent knot principle.
A normal rope would make a lasting knot, so the rope in the dispute must be a weaver’s rope.
Does the dispute turn on whether to prohibit the weaver’s rope by analogy to a regular rope?
A baraita about a broken bucket rope seems to reverse both sides’ attitudes toward a bow and a knot.
The Rabbis distinguish easily confused kinds of rope from a bow, which is not confused with a knot.
Rabbi Yehuda regards the bow itself as a knot, so his baraita does not rely on a preventive decree.
Rav permits bringing a rope from home to tie a cow to its trough.
A baraita explicitly bars bringing a new rope from home for both attachments.
The permitted case uses a weaver’s rope rather than an ordinary rope.
Shmuel permits moving a weaver’s tools on Shabbat.
Does that permission include the loom’s upper and lower beams?
Rav Yehuda’s response remains uncertain.
Another report permits moving the beams but not the posts.
Rava asks why posts are excluded if the holes formed on removal arise by themselves.
A mishna permits lifting stored vegetables from the ground on Shabbat despite the resulting hole.
A hole in a house may be smoothed afterward, unlike one in a field.
Rabbi Yohanan separately asks about moving the loom beams.
Rabbi Yehuda bar Liwai forbids moving beams because they are not normally lifted.
The mishna sets rules for folding clothes, preparing beds, and offering festival fats across Shabbat and Yom Kippur.
The school of Rabbi Yanai limits permissible folding by number of people, garment age, color, and availability of a replacement.
Rabban Gamliel’s household did not fold white garments when replacements were available.
Rav Huna advises changing garments or arranging current garments to honor Shabbat.
Rav Safra objects that the latter practice can appear haughty.
Doing it specifically for Shabbat makes its purpose apparent.
A verse about honoring Shabbat supports distinct clothing, reinforced by Rabbi Yohanan’s description of garments as his honor.
The verse is further applied to walking and personal business on Shabbat.
The final phrase about speech begins and continues on the next side.

113b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The verse is applied to weekday speech on Shabbat, while private thought remains permitted.
What does it mean for Shabbat walking to differ from weekday walking?
One view treats a jump across a wide stream as the prohibited form of walking.
Rava says detouring adds exertion and wading risks wet clothing and wringing.
Jumping the stream is permitted when the alternatives are impractical.
The walking rule is instead connected to large strides, discussed with their stated effect on eyesight.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asks whether eating earth is allowed on Shabbat.
Rabbi Yishmael says it is disallowed even on weekdays because of harm.
Rabbi Ami gives severe comparisons for eating Babylonian earth and cites a Flood verse.
Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yohanan interpret place names through traditions about the Flood dead.
The bodies in the soil would have decomposed, challenging the comparison to forbidden creatures.
The text grounds the restriction in harm and recounts a fatal incident involving earth and cress.
A verse about Ruth’s clothing is read as referring to garments for Shabbat.
Rabbi Elazar names Ruth and Samuel as people who made wise use of advice.
Ruth’s order of actions differs from Naomi’s instruction, showing her own judgment.
Samuel omits the divine name from Eli’s suggested reply until he knows who is calling.
Ruth’s repeated movement in the field is read as a search for suitable companions.
Why did Boaz ask about this particular young woman?
Rabbi Elazar points to her observance of the gleaning rule for two rather than three stalks.
A baraita instead points to modest behavior while collecting fallen stalks.
Why did Boaz invite Ruth to stay near his women workers?
Her earlier loyalty to Naomi is presented as the reason.
Boaz’s “come here” is interpreted as a hint to Ruth about the future Davidic dynasty.
The invitation to dip bread in vinegar is read as evidence of its use in heat.
A second interpretation reads the vinegar as a hint about a future descendant, Manasseh.
Ruth’s seat beside the reapers is read as a hint to division of the Davidic kingdom.
The words about eating, satisfaction, and remainder are mapped to successive reigns.
Another version maps those words to different historical periods.
A baraita interprets the same words across this world and future eras.
Rabbi Yohanan interprets “under his honor” alongside his use of “honor” for clothing.
Rabbi Elazar offers another reading of what was burned.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani compares the burning to the fate of Aaron’s sons.
A new teaching in Rabbi Yohanan’s name begins and continues on the next side.

114a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What Torah source supports changing garments for an honored occasion?
The priest’s change of garments when removing ashes is cited.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael reads this as etiquette for changing from work clothes before serving.
Rabbi Yohanan says a scholar should not appear in disgraceful patched shoes in public.
Rabbi Aha bar Hanina did go out in patched shoes.
The concern is narrowed to patch upon patch.
Rabbi Yohanan condemns a conspicuous stain on a scholar’s garment through a reading of Proverbs.
Ravina’s alternate wording is assigned to a different kind of garment.
Isaiah’s “naked and barefoot” is read as worn garments and patched shoes.
A mishna distinguishes stain sizes and one or two stained sides for immersion barriers.
Does a stain on a saddle matter on one side or only both?
Rabbi Hanina compares it with the differing standards for a scholar’s and an ordinary person’s garment.
Who are the “builders” mentioned in that comparison?
Rabbi Yohanan identifies them as scholars occupied in building the world.
He describes the scholar trusted to identify a lost article by sight.
He gives a standard for appointing a scholar as communal leader.
He limits communal support to a scholar who sets aside personal work for sacred work.
Which scope of learning qualifies a scholar, and why does it matter?
Expertise in one tractate qualifies locally; broad expertise qualifies for heading the academy.
Reish Lakish gives another identification of the garments called “builders’.”
Rabbi Yannai’s burial request suggests those imported garments were colored rather than white.
The descriptions refer to different types of garments.
The discussion returns to Rabbi Yishmael’s festival ruling.
Rabbi Yishmael reads a verse to allow Shabbat offering fats on Yom Kippur, while excluding the reverse.
Rabbi Akiva reads the same verse to permit them on a Festival but not Yom Kippur.
Their views on voluntary offerings explain why each needs the verse for a different day.
Rabbi Zeira begins a related report, continued on the next side.

114b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Zeira initially regarded the no trumpet, no havdala baraita around Yom Kippur as agreed by all.
In the Land of Israel he heard an argument that Rabbi Yishmael would require a signal about Shabbat fats offered on Yom Kippur.
Rabbi Zeira responds that priests know their duties without the signal.
Mar Kashisha cites ordinary Friday trumpet blasts as a challenge to that claim.
The blasts were for the rest of Jerusalem, not for the priests.
Why not signal the later permission to trim vegetables?
Rav Yosef says a rabbinic restriction is not set aside merely to permit another act.
Rav Sheisha instead distinguishes immediate permission from one that begins later.
A Festival after Shabbat has immediate permission to slaughter yet receives no trumpet blast.
This supports Rav Yosef’s broader reason.
Rav Huna prohibits trimming vegetables when Yom Kippur falls on Shabbat.
A baraita derives an additional rest restriction and applies it to vegetable trimming.
Rabbi Yohanan is reported to permit trimming in that case.
The earlier baraita is raised directly against his ruling.
He reads the extra rest verse as adding a positive command concerning labor.
A supporting baraita for Rabbi Yohanan begins and continues on the next side.

115a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The preceding baraita concludes that vegetable trimming is permitted.
Rabbi Yohanan permits late day preparation of nuts and pomegranates on a weekday Yom Kippur.
Household practice is described, and Rabba stops his household when they begin too early.
The knot chapter closes.
The mishna permits rescuing sacred writings from fire and addresses language, storage, and public reading.
Rav Huna and Rav Hisda dispute whether translations may be rescued.
Their dispute is limited to the view that translated writings may not be read.
Rav Huna ties rescue to permitted reading; Rav Hisda permits rescue to avoid disgrace.
The mishna appears to permit saving even translated Writings that may not be read.
Rav Huna points to a redundancy in the mishna’s later burial clause.
Each sage therefore reads the mishna’s wording according to his position.
Rav Huna limits rescue to Hebrew texts while still requiring storage of translations.
Rav Hisda extends rescue to translations and assigns the storage clause to decayed text.
A baraita expressly permits saving translations, challenging Rav Huna.
Rav Huna assigns it to a view that permits reading those texts.
Another baraita allows rescue of foreign language texts even though they may not be read.
Rav Huna cites a tannaitic dispute on precisely that point.
Rabbi Yosei recounts the handling of an Aramaic translation of Job in the Rabban Gamliel family.
Another version describes a bowl of mortar placed over that text.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi questions the mortar account and rejects deliberate destruction of the writing.
Which tannaim supply the two sides of the dispute?

115b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The earlier first tanna might allow reading translations; the relevant opposing view is the one that saves texts even when unreadable.
A baraita excludes written blessings and amulets from rescue despite sacred names within them.
An incident about a writer of blessings illustrates the severity attached to producing and destroying such pages.
The Exilarch asks whether Hebrew sacred writings in impermanent inks may be saved.
The question tests whether language or durable ink controls the rescue rule under either earlier position.
Rabba bar Rav Huna initially says they are not saved.
Rav Hamnuna reportedly teaches that they are saved.
The contrary teaching is accepted if it is reliably transmitted.
A baraita distinguishes books from the Scroll of Esther in language and ink requirements.
Rav Huna bar Haluv asks whether a damaged Torah scroll lacking eighty five surviving letters may be saved.
Rav Nahman asks why the short Ark passage itself would not pose the same issue.
That passage has divine names and is saved even if shorter; the question concerns an ordinary damaged scroll.
Rav Nahman says the insufficient scroll is not saved.
A baraita saves texts containing Aramaic verses, apparently even with fewer than eighty five letters.
Those verses count toward letters elsewhere in a larger scroll.
Must the eighty five letters be together or may they be scattered?
Rav Huna requires a gathered passage; Rav Hisda accepts scattered letters.
A baraita speaks of collecting letters from a worn scroll, seemingly refuting Rav Huna.
Rav Hisda explains Rav Huna as requiring surviving words, not one uninterrupted passage.
A new baraita begins interpreting the signs surrounding the Ark passage.

116a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Ark passage is variously explained as out of place or as a separate book.
The seven books interpretation of Proverbs follows the view that the Ark passage is a book.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel instead says the passage separates two accounts of wrongdoing.
What is the second account?
The complaint following the Ark passage is cited.
What is the first account?
The departure from God’s mountain is interpreted as turning away.
Where would the Ark passage otherwise belong?
Rav Ashi places it among the banner arrangements.
May blank margins of a Torah scroll themselves be rescued from fire?
A worn scroll with too few letters is not rescued, apparently despite its margins.
A worn scroll may differ because its former sanctity has lapsed.
An erased scroll with too few letters presents the same apparent counterexample.
The question excludes erased writing surfaces and concerns the permanent margins around text and pages.
A trimmed away margin would seem to pose a further difficulty.
A mishna treats the surrounding margins as imparting hand impurity.
That may hold only while the margins remain attached to a scroll.
A baraita about blank folios and sectarian scrolls is offered as another test.
It may refer only to folios of those sectarian scrolls.
That reading seems redundant when the scrolls themselves are not saved.
The baraita compares the sectarian scrolls to blank folios.
The baraita and Rabbi Yosei state different weekday handling of divine names in these writings.
Rabbi Tarfon states an emphatic position on those writings and cites a verse.
Rabbi Yishmael argues by analogy from erasing a divine name to restore peace in the sota rite.
The nonrescue rule is extended to other ways the writings might be destroyed.
Yosef bar Hanin asks whether writings kept at the house of Abidan may be rescued; Rabbi Abbahu is unsure.
Rav and Shmuel differ in which debate houses they visit.
Rava gives an excuse for not visiting the house of Abidan.
Mar bar Yosef says he is unafraid there, though one visit nearly endangers him.
A textual addition records two wordplays on the title of a disputed writing.
The next story introduces Imma Shalom, Rabban Gamliel, and a neighboring philosopher.

116b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Imma Shalom’s gift precedes the philosopher’s ruling that she and her brother share their father’s inheritance.
After Rabban Gamliel gives a different gift, the philosopher reverses the ruling, and the siblings expose the change.
The Gemara returns to the mishna’s limit on reading Writings on Shabbat.
Rav and Shmuel initially differ over whether the study hall’s hours limit that reading.
The known practice in Shmuel’s Nehardea conflicts with a complete ban outside study hours.
The dispute is reformulated around the study hall’s location or the time of its session.
Nehardea’s Shabbat afternoon practice fits the time based reading of Shmuel.
Rav Ashi alternatively keeps the first version and assigns Shmuel to Rabbi Nehemya’s concern about ordinary documents.
The mishna permits rescuing a scroll or phylactery case along with its contents, even with money inside, and disputes the destination alley.
A baraita disputes how far one may flay the Paschal lamb when its offering falls on Shabbat.
Why do the Rabbis permit complete flaying once the altar parts are accessible?
Rabbi Yohanan cites the verse that God’s works should serve His purpose.
What purpose is served by the remaining flaying?
Rav Yosef cites avoiding decay; Rava cites avoiding a degrading appearance.
What difference lies between those reasons?
A golden table or a cold day separates appearance from the risk of decay.
How does Rabbi Yishmael use the same verse?
It permits removing some hide before taking the altar portions.
Why is that needed?
Rav Huna names concern about hairs adhering to the altar portions.
The Rabbis compare the lamb’s hide with rescuing a scroll case alongside its scroll.
Moving a case seems unlike performing the labor of flaying.
Rav Ashi separates the arguments over moving the hide and over flaying it.

117a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A scroll case supports a movable scroll, while the lamb hide supports meat not yet movable.
The analogy is revised to a scroll case containing money as well as a scroll.
That case still combines a permitted and a prohibited item, unlike the hide and meat.
The analogy is revised again to bringing in a case containing money to save a scroll.
Nothing establishes that permission; keeping existing money during urgent rescue differs from bringing it in.
Mar bar Rav Ashi returns to the original analogy where the hide itself is not wanted.
An unwanted result remains prohibited if removing the hide inevitably produces it.
The hide is taken off in strips so the usual skinning result does not occur.
What counts as the closed or open alley in the mishna?
Rav Hisda distinguishes numbers of entrance posts under Rabbi Eliezer’s alley rule.
Rabba objects that an alley with three walls and one post is not really open, and asks about saving food there.
Rabba instead uses two wall alleys and the corresponding view of Rabbi Yehuda.
The Rabbis reject treating the public domain as enclosed that way.
Abaye repeats the food rescue difficulty under Rabba’s explanation.

117b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Ashi distinguishes three walled alleys with or without a post and allows a lesser enclosure for scroll rescue.
The mishna limits rescued food by meals still needed that Shabbat; Rabbi Yosei always allows three meals.
Why not save more food when carrying itself is permitted?
Rava fears a distraught owner may go on to extinguish the fire.
Abaye cites the limited rescue of a broken barrel and asks what comparable concern applies there.
An extra vessel might be carried through the public domain.
A baraita allows extra vessels when guests are first invited and records a dispute over artifice.
Does that dispute match the positions about saving a parent animal and its young from a pit?
A baraita contrasts Rabbi Eliezer’s single rescue with Rabbi Yehoshua’s staged rescue of both animals.
The two situations may differ because the pit animal can be fed and animal suffering is involved.
A baraita ranks bread that may be rescued and excludes preparing on Shabbat for a later holy day.
Another baraita allows rescuing oven bread for three meals and asks that it be removed unusually.
Removing bread is described as a skill rather than prohibited labor, challenging the need to change method.
One still changes the method when feasible.
Rav Hisda reads the manna verse as support for early Friday preparation.
The double manna portion supports using two loaves for the Shabbat meal.
Rav Kahana holds two loaves while breaking one.
Rabbi Zeira breaks enough bread for his whole meal at once.
Ravina asks whether that looks excessive.
Its being done specifically on Shabbat distinguishes it from habitual excess.
Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi favor bread already used for one mitzva to serve another.
The Gemara returns to the mishna’s fire rescue schedule.
A baraita disputes three or four Shabbat meals, with both views interpreting the threefold “today” in the manna verse.
The mishna’s Friday night case is introduced as a challenge to the four meal view.

118a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Friday night fire allowance of three meals seems to contradict Rabbi Hidka’s four meal rule.
The case could follow a meal already eaten.
The morning allowance of two meals again seems to count only three total.
The morning meal could already have been eaten.
The afternoon allowance of one meal raises the same difficulty.
That meal too could already have been eaten.
Rabbi Yosei’s contrast implies both mishnaic views assume three required meals, unlike Rabbi Hidka.
A charity mishna counts fourteen weekly meals, seemingly matching neither the three nor four Shabbat meal view.
For the Rabbis, a Saturday night meal can be taken earlier on Shabbat.
Applying the count to Rabbi Hidka would require the recipient to go without Friday food.
The charity threshold follows Rabbi Akiva’s instruction to avoid dependence even with a plain Shabbat.
A different charity mishna provides a traveling poor person three meals for Shabbat.
That allowance seems to exclude Rabbi Hidka’s fourth meal.
The traveler may already carry one meal.
Would the traveler then leave without any food?
An additional meal is supplied for departure; Rav Pappa explains the lodging provision.
A baraita permits washing meal vessels for later Shabbat use, while drink vessels may be washed throughout the day.
A teaching promises escape from three calamities to one who eats three Shabbat meals.
A shared word in verses is used to connect the meals with the messianic tribulations.
A second verse comparison concerns the day of judgment.
A third comparison concerns the war of Gog and Magog.
Rabbi Yohanan promises a broad inheritance for delighting in Shabbat and begins citing Isaiah.

118b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Jacob’s unbounded blessing is contrasted with the bounded land promises to Abraham and Isaac.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak links Shabbat delight to release from foreign rule through matching verse language.
Rav derives a promise concerning one’s wishes by joining verses about delight in God and delight in Shabbat.
How is Shabbat made delightful?
One answer lists substantial prepared foods.
Another answer says even a small item prepared specifically for Shabbat suffices.
Rav Pappa gives a small fish dish as an example.
Rabbi Yohanan reads a verse as promising forgiveness through proper Shabbat observance.
Rav connects Israel’s first Shabbat lapse with the ensuing attack by Amalek.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai connects two properly observed Shabbatot with redemption through Isaiah.
Rabbi Yosei wishes to be among those eating three Shabbat meals.
He also wishes to complete verses of praise each day.
A teaching criticizes reciting the full Hallel daily.
His daily practice refers to the verses of praise rather than festival Hallel.
Rabbi Yosei praises prayer near sunrise and sunset, with a verse cited for the timing.
He records a wish connected to the deaths of righteous people.
He wishes to die while engaged in a mitzva.
He describes taking in Shabbat early and ending it late by place.
He favors gathering people for study over ending the session.
He favors collecting charity over distributing it.
He speaks of unfounded suspicion, followed by Rav Pappa’s similar experience.
Rabbi Yosei describes his five sons by name.
What about the son called Vardimas?
Vardimas is identified with Menahem, with a reason for the nickname.
The initial wording might imply only five acts of marital intimacy.
The wording is corrected to include repetition.
Rabbi Yosei describes his indirect names for his wife and ox.
He describes a personal practice of modesty.
A similar practice was ascribed to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi as a mark of distinct sanctity.
An additional practice distinguishes Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Rabbi Yosei describes how he kept his garment seams from view.
He describes not opposing the instructions of colleagues even in an unlikely example.
He says he did not retreat from what he had said.
Several sages list practices for which they seek reward, including meals, prayer, head covering, phylacteries, and fringes.
Rav Yosef hears an example of Rabba’s care with ritual fringes.
Abaye begins a report of his response when a scholar completes a tractate.

119a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abaye completes his report of celebrating a scholar’s completed tractate.
Rava describes giving a young scholar a favorable hearing in judgment.
Mar bar Rav Ashi declines to judge a scholar because personal affection could bias him.
Rabbi Hanina ceremonially goes out to greet Shabbat.
Rabbi Yannai dresses and welcomes Shabbat as a bride.
A host explains that ample food was prepared for Shabbat, not for a visitor.
Rabbi Abba buys meat from many butchers for Shabbat and urges prompt preparation.
Rabbi Abbahu personally tends the cooking fire.
Rav Anan wears work clothing for preparation, following an etiquette teaching.
Several sages personally perform different Shabbat preparation tasks.
Rav Nahman or, in another telling, Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi carry supplies to honor Shabbat.
The story of Yosef who honored Shabbat recounts the pearl found in a purchased fish.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asks what accounts for wealth in the Land of Israel.
Rabbi Yishmael attributes it to tithing and a wordplay on the verse.
What accounts for wealth in Babylonia?
He attributes it to honoring Torah.
What accounts for wealth in other lands?
He attributes it to honoring Shabbat.
Rabbi Hiyya recounts a wealthy host’s elaborate table and the verses recited around it.
He asks the host how he attained this prosperity.
The host says he saved the finest meat for Shabbat.
A conversation with an emperor uses a figurative Shabbat spice to explain a meal’s fragrance.
The Exilarch asks how a verse’s “holy one” is honored.
Rav Hamnuna applies it to wearing clean clothing on Yom Kippur.
Rav and Shmuel propose different meal times to mark Shabbat.
Those with meat and wine every day ask how to make Shabbat distinct.
Rav Pappa advises changing their usual meal time.
Rav Sheshet seats students where the weather encourages a shorter session.
A new report about Rabbi Zeira begins on the next side.

119b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Zeira asks scholars in pairs to protect Shabbat’s delight.
A teaching requires the Vayekhullu passage even in individual Friday night prayer.
Rav Hamnuna reads its wording as crediting the speaker with partnership in creation.
Rabbi Elazar cites a verse to connect speech and action.
Rav Hisda recounts a blessing pronounced by accompanying angels for saying Vayekhullu.
A baraita describes the two angels’ response to a prepared or unprepared Shabbat home.
Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Hanina commend a set table before and after Shabbat.
The text praises warm food and drink after Shabbat.
A story about Rabbi Abbahu’s meal contrasts fresh preparation with saving food.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi links wholehearted answering of Amen to annulment of judgment through Judges.
Rabbi Yohanan extends the promise using a verbal link to the Golden Calf account.
Reish Lakish reads a verse as promising entry to paradise for answering Amen.
What does Amen signify?
Rabbi Hanina expands it as “God, faithful King.”
Rav connects destructive fire with Shabbat violation by citing Jeremiah.
What is meant by a fire that is not extinguished?
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak says it breaks out when no one is available to extinguish it.
Abaye attributes Jerusalem’s destruction to Shabbat violation and cites Ezekiel.
Rabbi Abbahu attributes it to neglect of morning and evening Shema, citing passages in Isaiah.
Rav Hamnuna attributes it to interruption of children’s study and cites Jeremiah.
Ulla attributes it to lack of shame over wrongdoing and cites Jeremiah.
Rabbi Yitzhak attributes it to collapsing distinctions between ranks and cites Isaiah.
Rav Amram attributes it to failure to rebuke one another and explains a verse’s stag image.
Rabbi Yehuda attributes it to contempt for scholars, citing Chronicles.
What does the verse’s “without remedy” mean?
Rav applies it to one who disparages a scholar.
Rav interprets “anointed” as schoolchildren and “prophets” as scholars in a verse.
Reish Lakish says children’s study sustains the world.
Rav Pappa asks how adult study compares.
Abaye distinguishes study by those who have not sinned.
Reish Lakish says children’s lessons are not interrupted even for Temple building.
He gives a severe rule for a town without schoolchildren; Ravina gives a variant.
Rava attributes Jerusalem’s ruin to a lack of trustworthy people and cites Jeremiah.
Rav Ketina’s report of trustworthy people even during Jerusalem’s decline is raised against Rava.

120a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Isaiah dialogue is read as showing people who candidly declined leadership for lack of learning.
The refusal is interpreted as a claim to lack mastery of Bible, Mishna, and Gemara.
Perhaps the speaker avoids a test of learning rather than admitting a lack of it.
The two accounts distinguish Torah learning from honesty in commerce.
The mishna permits carrying large units of food, describes others helping, and limits the rescue destination and clothing.
How does this large food allowance fit the earlier three meal limit?
Rav Huna distinguishes rescuing one unit from collecting separate items.
Rabbi Abba distinguishes saving within the same courtyard from moving to another.
Does repeatedly collecting into one spread count as rescue or as gathering?
Rava’s criticism of a reported three meal vessel limit suggests that one large unit is permitted.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak asks what error was in that report.
The baraita limits additional vessels, not the amount caught in one vessel.
Why would helpers later calculate payment for ownerless rescued food?
Rav Hisda calls their return of it an act of piety.
Rava asks whether pious helpers would take Shabbat wages.
The helpers are God fearing and may accept later payment because this is not treated as ordinary Shabbat wages.
Why does the mishna say “for yourselves” for food but “with me” for clothing?
The owner is limited in useful food but can keep wearing more rescued clothing.
A baraita contrasts Rabbi Meir’s repeated garment rescue with Rabbi Yosei’s list of eighteen garments.
The next mishna permits barriers before fire but records Rabbi Yosei’s concern about bursting water vessels.
Rav permits water on the far side of a burning garment, even if the fire then goes out.
A baraita permits handling a burning garment or scroll but appears to avoid adding water.

120b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav’s rule is initially assigned to Rabbi Shimon ben Nannas.
That tanna permitted a singeing hide; did he also permit indirectly extinguishing fire?
Rabbi Yosei’s explicit ban on bursting water vessels implies the first tanna permits them.
A baraita permits shaking a forgotten lamp from a board but not moving a board deliberately made its base.
Another baraita permits ordinary door movement that might put out a nearby lamp.
Why did Rav condemn that ruling when a tanna could follow Rabbi Shimon’s unintentional act view?
Even Rabbi Shimon forbids an act whose prohibited consequence is inevitable.
Rav Yehuda permits opening a door opposite a fire, but Abaye disapproves.
Which wind strength could produce a genuine disagreement?
They differ on whether to prohibit the ordinary wind case because of the stronger wind case.
The mishna’s dispute on indirect extinguishing seems reversed by a baraita about fire barriers.
That baraita lists vessels not expected to break, including kinds Rabbi Yosei adds.
Reversing the mishna’s attribution conflicts with a report expressly naming Rabbi Yosei as the prohibiting tanna.
The baraita is reconstructed as Rabbi Yosei’s own list of vessels that do not normally break.
How can each side’s stance here fit its stance about a divine name written on skin?
That baraita requires covering the name for immersion according to the Rabbis, while Rabbi Yosei allows ordinary immersion without rubbing.
The erasure prohibition may apply to direct action rather than an indirect result.
The Shabbat labor verse likewise speaks of direct action.
A fire creates special concern that a worried owner will extinguish it directly.
That concern makes the Rabbis’ strictness about immersion harder to explain.
The proposed reed covering raises problems about interposition and water, though moist ink itself need not interpose.
Why then insist on a reed at all?
Rava bar Rav Sheila says the concern is standing unclothed before the divine name.
Does Rabbi Yosei allow that exposure?
He can cover the name with a hand.
Why would a hand not suffice for the Rabbis too?
They worry the hand will be removed inadvertently.
The same concern seems to apply to Rabbi Yosei.
Rabbi Yosei also uses a reed when available; the dispute concerns seeking one out.

121a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The immersion dispute is initially explained by whether immersing at its assigned time is itself a mitzva.
A baraita has Rabbi Yosei allow postponing immersion after the afternoon prayer.
That baraita is attributed to Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda instead.
The mishna distinguishes a non-Jew who comes to extinguish a fire from a Jewish child who does so.
Rabbi Ami permits an indirect invitation that anyone extinguishing the fire will not lose.
The mishna’s refusal to give a direct instruction could support that indirect wording.
Its refusal to forbid the action supports the opposite inference, leaving the mishna inconclusive.
A baraita recounts Yosef ben Simai’s fire, the visitors he stopped, and the sages’ correction.
The mishna’s restriction on a child who comes to extinguish is restated.
Does that establish a general duty to stop a child from violating a prohibition?
Rabbi Yohanan limits the case to a child acting for his father.
Would the corresponding non-Jew acting for a Jew then also be permitted?
The non-Jew acts for his own purposes.
The next mishna permits covering a lamp, child’s excrement, or scorpion, with Rabbi Yehuda reporting concern over a scorpion case.
The Gemara begins a visit to Avin’s house, continued on the next side.

121b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: At Avin’s house, Rav Hanan is not given a bed and hears the mishna taught to a child.
He objects that a child’s excrement can itself be moved, citing a rule about newly available water.
How should the mishna be taught instead?
He changes the case to chicken excrement near a child.
Even chicken excrement may be removed as a repulsive object, as a mouse removal incident shows.
The case is narrowed to a refuse heap within the courtyard, where covering the hazard is relevant.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi permits killing harmful creatures on Shabbat.
A baraita names only five creatures, apparently limiting that permission.
Rabbi Yirmeya questions whether the baraita is reliable.
Rav Yosef keeps the baraita but limits the broader permission to pursuing creatures.
A teaching and response disagree over killing snakes or scorpions on Shabbat.
Rav Huna’s reaction to someone killing a hornet shows a stricter position.
A baraita gives a providential reading of encounters with snakes and scorpions.
Rabbi Yohanan limits that reading to creatures brushing against the person.
A story reports a snake killed in the study hall and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi’s ambiguous response.
Was that response praise or disapproval?
Rabbi Yannai says he would kill a hornet and certainly a snake or scorpion.
Perhaps the permission concerns incidental trampling, like rules for spittle and dangerous creatures.
An incident with Abba bar Manyomi illustrates incidental trampling of spittle.
Rabbi Abba bar Kahana transmits a rule permitting movement of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi’s candlesticks.
Rabbi Zeira asks whether that includes candlesticks needing two hands.

122a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The candlesticks are as large as those in Rabbi Zeira’s family home.
Rabbi Hanina permits moving the sedan chairs of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi’s household on Shabbat.
Rabbi Zeira asks whether that permission includes chairs requiring two carriers.
The reply points to the large chairs in Rabbi Zeira’s family home.
Rabbi Hanina allowed wine brought in a gentile’s wagon with one seal; the reason for his leniency is uncertain.
The mishna permits benefiting from a gentile’s lamp, water, or ramp made for himself, but forbids benefit when made for a Jew; Rabban Gamliel used such a ramp.
All three examples are needed: light is shared, water can be increased for a Jew, and the ramp incident confirms the practical ruling.
A baraita gives the same distinction for grass picked or water drawn for a gentile’s animal, and restricts it when the gentile knows the Jew.
The permission to feed freshly picked grass seems to conflict with the ban on placing an animal by muktzeh.
The Jew merely stands the animal before the grass and lets it eat on its own.
If acquaintance makes the gentile’s work forbidden, why could Rabban Gamliel use a ramp made by someone who knew him?
Abaye says the gentile built the ramp outside Rabban Gamliel’s presence.
Rava says a ramp built for one person serves many, like a lamp.
A teaching about the incident explicitly grounds permission in the ramp being made outside their presence.
Rava rereads the teaching as permitting use simply because the gentile made it.
A mixed city’s bathhouse requires waiting when most residents are Jews, suggesting the gentile’s work can be for Jews.
Heating bathwater is directed toward the majority of prospective users.
A banquet lamp is likewise forbidden when Jews form at least half the group, challenging the shared-use rationale.
The response begins by distinguishing the intention behind lighting a lamp for a group.

122b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A banquet lamp is lit with the majority of those present in mind.
Shmuel first avoided a gentile’s lamp, then used its light after seeing that the gentile lit it to read his own document.
The chapter on saving sacred writings concludes.
The mishna permits moving vessels and detached vessel doors, and lists tools that may be used for permitted purposes.
Does the mishna imply that a door detached before Shabbat is certainly movable?
A door detached on Shabbat was prepared while attached at its start, whereas an earlier detached door might not have been prepared.
Abaye rereads the mishna as expressly allowing doors detached during the week.
A baraita permits removing a chest door but not replacing it; a chicken-coop door may neither be removed nor replaced.
A chicken coop is fixed to the ground, where building and dismantling are prohibited.
Why may a vessel door be removed but not replaced, when building and dismantling vessels should be treated alike?
Abaye says both acts are prohibited for vessels, and reads the baraita as discussing doors already removed.
Rava objects that the baraita says one may remove them and contrasts that permission with the ban on replacement.
Rava says ordinary vessel assembly and dismantling are permitted, but replacement is barred lest one fasten the door firmly.
Rav Yehuda limits the mishna’s nut-cracking mallet to one designated for nuts, excluding a blacksmith’s hammer.
That reading treats a tool whose usual work is prohibited as unusable even for a permitted purpose.
Rabba cites the mishna’s winnowing shovel and pitchfork, neither designated for feeding a child, against that limit.
Rabba accordingly allows a blacksmith’s hammer for cracking nuts; his underlying principle continues on the next daf.

123a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A tool normally used for prohibited work may still be moved to perform a permitted task.
Abaye cites a mortar that may be moved only while it contains garlic.
Rabba attributes that restriction to Rabbi Nehemya, who permits moving a vessel only for its usual function.
Abaye cites the ban on moving a meat-cutting pestle after its festival use.
Rabba initially considers assigning that rule to Rabbi Nehemya too.
A teaching about tools whose owners reserve a place for them instead explains why the pestle remains set aside.
Two reports identify the mishna’s nut-cracking hammer as a goldsmith’s or spice merchant’s hammer.
The spice-hammer permission would include a goldsmith’s hammer; the reverse view excludes spice tools because their owners protect them.
The discussion returns to the mishna’s reed and shuttle.
A baraita permits removing food buried in straw or coals when part of it is exposed.
Rabbi Elazar ben Tadai permits lifting it with a reed so the surrounding material falls away; Rav Nahman rules like him.
Rav Nahman elsewhere forbids pulling a radish in a way that displaces dirt, apparently rejecting indirect movement.
Rav Nahman retracted that earlier ruling about the radish.
The discussion returns to extracting a thorn with a sewing needle.
Rava son of Rabba asks whether a needle missing its eye or point may be moved.
Rav Yosef permits it because the thorn can be removed with a needle whether or not it has an eye.
A damaged needle loses its status as a vessel for ritual impurity.
Abaye distinguishes impurity, which requires a finished utensil, from Shabbat, which requires present usefulness.
Rava argues that loss of vessel status for impurity should also make it unmovable on Shabbat.
A baraita permits moving perforated and unperforated needles, distinguishing them only for impurity.
Abaye limits that baraita to unfinished needles that may still be made into tools; a broken finished needle is discarded.
Rav Nahman and Rav Sheshet dispute whether one may align an infant’s limbs on Shabbat.
Rav Nahman begins to support his prohibition from the ban on inducing vomiting.

123b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The ban on inducing vomiting completes Rav Nahman’s support for forbidding treatment of the infant.
Rav Sheshet distinguishes unusual medicinal vomiting from ordinary care for an infant.
Rav Sheshet cites the permitted extraction of a thorn with a needle as support for his ruling.
Rav Nahman replies that removing a lodged foreign object differs from altering the infant’s own body.
The mishna distinguishes whether an olive-turning reed can receive impurity, while permitting its movement in either case.
Why can a knotted reed receive impurity if a flat wooden implement has no receptacle?
The knot creates a cavity whose oil can be inspected while turning the olives.
Rabbi Yosei excludes a large saw and plow blade from the general permission to move tools.
Rav Nahman and Abaye identify other carefully protected trade tools with the same restricted status.
A baraita recounts successive permissions, from only three movable utensils to nearly all utensils.
What were the successive stages of permission?
Abaye describes gradual permission by a tool’s usual work, its intended use, and the number of hands needed to move it.
Rava objects to splitting use of a permitted tool from moving it to clear its place.
Rava offers different stages: permitted-use tools, protection from sun, prohibited-use tools for use or space, then tools needing two carriers.
Abaye challenges Rava with a mortar that may be moved only if it contains garlic.
Rava limits that ban to moving the mortar merely to protect it from the sun.
Abaye again cites the prohibition on moving a pestle after cutting meat.
Rava again limits the case to protecting the tool from the sun.
Rabbi Hanina dates the restrictive mishna to Nehemiah’s response to widespread Shabbat violations.
Rabbi Elazar names four earlier teachings that preceded the later permission to move utensils.
The showbread rods could not be arranged or removed on Shabbat.
The rule for poles used in preparing the Paschal lamb begins another example and continues on the next daf.

124a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The earlier example concludes: two people can suspend and flay the Paschal lamb without poles.
A mishna about a door bolt with a thick end supplies the next case of restricted movement.
The mortar rule discussed earlier supplies the fourth case.
Rabba questions whether these teachings really predate the general permission to move tools.
The showbread rods were unnecessary for the short remainder of Shabbat.
The lamb could be flayed without the poles.
The bolt dispute can concern carrying between a house and an unjoined courtyard, rather than its status as a tool.
The mortar restriction can follow Rabbi Nehemya’s stricter view.
A mishna permits moving vessels with or without a defined need; Rabbi Nehemya requires a need.
What do the mishna’s two kinds of need mean?
Rabba distinguishes using a permitted-use tool from clearing its place and describes tighter limits for prohibited-use tools and Rabbi Nehemya.
Rava asks why clearing space should count as having no need.
Rava instead distinguishes use or space from moving a tool only to protect it from the sun.
The sages ask how empty bowls can be moved under Rabba’s reading of Rabbi Nehemya.
Rav Safra likens empty bowls to a repulsive chamber pot that may be removed.
Abaye puts the same question about empty bowls to Rabba.
Rabba cites Rav Safra’s chamber-pot explanation.
Abaye again challenges Rava with the mortar that may be moved only while containing garlic.
Rava limits that restriction to moving it only to protect it from the sun.
Abaye cites the pestle that cannot be moved after cutting meat.
Rava gives the same limitation: protecting it from the sun.
Abaye cites a festival rule against propping a pot or door with wood that appears available for permitted use.
Wood is unavailable for that purpose on Shabbat, and the festival rule follows a decree based on Shabbat.
The permission for prohibited-use tools applies to utensils; a piece of firewood has no utensil status.
A mishna permits dropping fruit through a skylight on a festival though it is forbidden on Shabbat.
Another mishna says food preparation is the only difference between festival and Shabbat laws.
Rav Yosef assigns the conflicting approaches to Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, citing their dispute about rescuing two animals from a pit.
Rabbi Eliezer might permit lifting the second animal where it cannot be fed in the pit.
Rabbi Yehoshua might allow the second rescue only where it can be framed as preparing an animal for slaughter.
Rav Pappa proposes Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel as the differing authorities; his evidence continues on the next daf.

124b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Beit Shammai bar carrying a child, lulav, or Torah scroll into the public domain on a festival, while Beit Hillel permit it.
The dispute concerns carrying between domains, which may not settle mere movement of an object.
The restriction on moving objects was itself enacted because of carrying between domains.
Rav’s ban on moving a hoe merely to prevent theft supports Rava’s distinction between protecting and using a tool.
Rav’s request for a net on which Rav Kahana could sit seems to allow use of a prohibited-use tool but not clearing its place.
Rav either requested clearing the net’s place or clarified that it was needed for use rather than protection from the sun.
Rava permits moving sun-exposed cushions, but tells Rav Mari, who follows a stricter view, to act consistently with it.
Rav permits moving soft brooms but apparently excludes palm brooms; Rabbi Elazar appears to include them.
If the brooms are needed for use or space, Rav’s exclusion conflicts with his acceptance of Rava’s rule.
If they are moved only to protect them, Rabbi Elazar’s apparent permission is also difficult.
The case concerns protection from the sun, and Rabbi Elazar is reread as agreeing with Rav’s restriction.
The mishna allows useful vessel fragments to be moved; Rabbi Yehuda demands a use like that of the original vessel.
Shmuel initially places the dispute in vessels broken before Shabbat and permits all fragments broken on Shabbat as previously prepared.
Rav Zutrai cites a festival rule barring fuel from broken vessels, which must concern fragments newly broken that day.
Shmuel’s statement is revised: the dispute concerns new Shabbat fragments; all permit fragments broken beforehand.
Three baraitot give conflicting rules for using vessels and their fragments as festival fuel.
The rulings reflect the distinct positions of Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Nehemya.
Leftover building bricks may be moved for sitting, unless stacking them shows they were set aside.
Shmuel, Rav Nahman, and Rava give increasingly broad permissions for moving a useful shard across different spaces.
Rava permits his servant to use a street shard for mud on a shoe, arguing that its usefulness does not vanish outside a courtyard.
Shmuel and a baraita permit moving a broken jug seal but forbid breaking off a new piece or moving one discarded in refuse.
Rav Pappa objects that throwing even a useful cloak into refuse should not automatically make it unmovable.
Rav Pappa begins a revised account, continued on the next daf.

125a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Pappa limits discarded jug seals to those thrown away before Shabbat.
Shmuel permits moving strips that have broken off a mat.
Why are these strips usable?
As the mat can cover dirt, its strips can still cover filth.
Rav forbids moving the remnants of worn cloaks.
Abaye limits this to scraps too small to serve rich or poor people.
A baraita disputes moving old oven fragments and reports that an oven cover needs no handle.
What is the basis of the dispute over oven fragments?
Abaye links it to the earlier dispute over fragments useful for a new purpose rather than their original purpose.
Rava asks why that dispute would be stated specifically for oven fragments.
Rava connects it to a special oven set above a pit, whose status as a vessel Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis dispute.
Their interpretations of the verse about breaking impure ovens explain their different tests for vessel status.
Why do the Rabbis not derive Rabbi Yehuda’s rule from the command to break the oven?
They use that phrase to show an oven remains impure even when fixed to the ground.
How does Rabbi Yehuda understand the verse’s broader declaration of impurity?
He applies it after the oven’s first firing, when it already became a vessel.
Ulla says the Rabbis count even the first firing of a suspended oven.
Rav Ashi asks why the tannaim would dispute oven fragments if they already disagree about the oven itself.
Rav Ashi returns to the original fragment dispute and says Rabbi Meir presses Rabbi Yehuda to recognize a shard used for baking.
Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes baking with a shard from firing an intact, upright oven.
The testimony about moving old oven fragments and covers without handles is restated.
Ravina cites the practice of moving handleless oven covers in Mehasya as following that testimony.
The mishna permits filling with a gourd weighted by a secure stone, but not when the stone falls out.

125b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna allows drawing water with a vine tied to a pitcher and records a dispute over a window shutter.
A mishna says to tilt a barrel so a stone resting on it falls away.
Rabba reports that a deliberately placed stone instead makes the barrel a base for a prohibited object.
Rav Yosef reports the opposite consequence: intentional placement turns the stone into a usable barrel cover.
Rabba considers the weighted gourd, whose secure stone can be moved, as a challenge to his rule.
He distinguishes a tightly fitted stone that becomes part of the gourd’s wall.
Rav Yosef considers the loose gourd stone, which bars use, as a challenge to his rule.
He distinguishes a stone not secured to the gourd, which was not made part of it.
What principle separates the two accounts?
They disagree whether changing the status of a stone requires an action.
A report says Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi allowed students to designate building stones for sitting by thought alone.
Rabbi Yohanan says Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi required an action.
What action did he require?
One report says arranging the stones, and another says rubbing them clean.
Two reports identify the objects in the incident as a stack of beams or a ship’s sounding pole.
Permission for a sounding pole would include beams; permission for beams need not include the carefully protected pole.
Does the requirement to tie a pitcher’s vine contradict Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel?
He permits sitting on previously cut palm branches without tying them.
Rav Sheshet says the pitcher’s vine may still be attached to its plant.
Would that not entail using a plant attached to the ground?
The vine is below three handbreadths from the ground.
Rav Ashi instead allows a detached vine and explains the restriction as a precaution against cutting it.
Rabbi Yohanan says all forbid first making a temporary shelter, but dispute adding to one already present.
The Rabbis’ permission to shutter a window in either case is quoted.
What do the Rabbis mean by “either case”?
Rabbi Abba begins to transmit Rav Kahana’s explanation, continued on the next daf.

126a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Abba explains that a prepared window shutter may be used whether or not it is tied.
Rabbi Yirmeya suggests that the distinction should instead require tying but not hanging.
A linked dispute over a dragged door bolt distinguishes its use in the Temple and elsewhere.
A baraita defines the dragged bolt and contrasts one left untied and detached.
Ulla identifies the stricter view of the dragged bolt with Rabbi Eliezer’s shutter ruling.
Rabbi Abba instead cites a teaching in which Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel allows a prepared bolt even without a tie.
Rabbi Yohanan rules according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in that case.
The Gemara begins challenging that ruling from Rabbi Yohanan’s rule for vessel covers.

126b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yohanan requires movable vessel covers to retain the status of a tool, challenging preparation alone.
The Gemara considers whether Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel also requires the bolt to be a tool.
His permission to use palm branches for sitting without tying shows he does not require making them into a tool.
Rabbi Yohanan agrees with him about the prepared bolt but disagrees about the need for tool status.
Rabbi Yitzhak declares the law on window shutters to follow Rabbi Eliezer.
Rav Amram cites a mishna and incident permitting shuttering a window on Shabbat.
Abaye notes that the stringent dragged-bolt rule also appears as an unattributed mishna.
The recorded practical act nevertheless has greater weight.
A mishna permits covers with handles; Rabbi Yosei allows vessel covers even without handles.
Rabbi Yohanan adds that such covers must retain the status of a tool.
Ground covers need handles, while ordinary vessel covers can be moved without them.
The dispute concerns vessel covers for vessels fixed to the ground and whether to decree against them.
An alternative account makes the dispute specifically about an oven cover.
The chapter on tools concludes.
A new mishna permits moving several baskets to seat guests or students, but restricts clearing a storeroom.
It lists prepared foods and tithes that may be moved, including dry lupines eaten by goats.
It excludes untithed or unredeemed produce and certain foods; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits arum as raven food.
Bundles of straw, wood, or twigs may be moved if prepared as animal feed.
If five baskets may be moved, why mention four?
Rav Hisda limits the number according to the size of the storeroom and how much must remain.
What does the ban on clearing a storeroom mean?
It bars starting on an unused storeroom under Rabbi Yehuda’s rule of set-aside items.
Shmuel begins a different reading of “four or five,” continued on the next daf.

127a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel reads “four or five” as an example, permits beginning a storeroom, but bars emptying it entirely lest one level holes.
A baraita bars first use of a storeroom while allowing a path through it.
How can a path be made if first use of the storeroom is barred?
One makes the path with one’s feet while entering and leaving.
A baraita disputes whether grain from an untouched pile may be used on Shabbat.
The named authorities are reversed so the lenient position belongs to Rabbi Shimon.
A half-kor is given as the measure of a grain pile.
Rav Nahumi asks Abaye for the measure of piled grain.
Abaye repeats the half-kor measure.
Does the basket limit favor fewer trips with heavier loads or smaller loads with more trips?
Baraitot mentioning five versus ten or fifteen appear to support different preferences.
The larger figures count jugs, not trips: several smaller jugs can be carried in each basket.
Does the number of baskets remain fixed even when there are many guests?
If it varies with guests, may one person move all the baskets for them?
A report that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi cleared a whole field for crowded students supports scaling the amount to need.
A parallel report about Rabbi Hiyya supports the same conclusion.
The question whether one person may clear the space for everyone remains open.
The wording that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi cleared the field is offered as evidence.
He may have ordered others to clear it, leaving each person to move for himself.
Rabbi Yohanan equates hospitality with attendance at the study hall based on the mishna’s pairing.
Rav Dimi ranks hospitality higher because the mishna mentions it first.
Rav cites Abraham asking God to wait while he receives guests as support for hospitality’s importance.
Rabbi Elazar contrasts ordinary social rank with Abraham’s address to the Divine Presence.
Rabbi Yohanan lists six deeds whose reward is enjoyed in this world while their principal remains for the next.
A mishna appears to limit that reward to a different list of deeds.

127b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The longer list fits within the shorter list, especially under acts of kindness.
A baraita teaches that one who judges others favorably is judged favorably.
A worker goes home unpaid after his employer says he has no money, produce, land, animals, or bedding to offer.
After the festival, the employer brings the wages and provisions to the worker.
The employer asks what the worker thought when he claimed to have no money.
The worker supposed the money had gone toward a bargain purchase.
The employer asks why the worker accepted his claim of having no animals.
The worker assumed the animals were hired out.
The employer asks what the worker thought about the unavailable land.
The worker assumed the land was leased out.
The employer asks about the unavailable produce.
The worker assumed it had not been tithed.
The employer asks why the worker accepted the lack of bedding.
The worker supposed the employer had consecrated all his property.
The employer confirms that a vow over his son’s failure to study Torah had bound his property, then blesses the worker for judging him well.
A pious man rescues a captive woman, has her sleep by his feet, and immerses the next morning.
He asks his students what they thought of his sleeping arrangement.
They assumed he was protecting her from a student whose conduct was uncertain.
He asks what they thought of his immersion.
They attributed it to a bodily emission caused by travel.
He confirms their charitable judgment and blesses them.
Rabbi Yehoshua volunteers to visit a Roman matron on the scholars’ behalf.
He removes his phylacteries, enters behind a closed door, later immerses, and teaches his students.
He asks what they thought when he removed his phylacteries.
They assumed he would not bring sacred objects into an impure place.
He asks why they thought he closed the door.
They assumed he needed to discuss a confidential government matter.
He asks what they thought of his immersion.
They supposed the matron’s spittle had touched his clothing.
He confirms their judgments and blesses them.
The discussion returns to the mishna’s pure teruma.
Why must its movability be stated?
Even an Israelite may move it because a priest can eat it.
The mishna’s permission for doubtfully tithed produce is quoted.
Why is demai considered usable?
One could become poor and then eat it; the cited mishna and dispute establish the poor person’s access to demai.
The mishna’s permission for first tithe after removal of its teruma is quoted.
Why is that permission needed?
It covers tithe taken while the grain was on stalks, before teruma gedola was separated.
Reish Lakish derives from the verse that early first tithe requires terumat maaser but not teruma gedola.
Rav Pappa asks why the same exemption would not apply when the Levite took grain after it was piled.
Abaye cites a verse requiring teruma from all gifts.
Why distinguish piled grain from grain still on stalks?
Piled grain has been processed, while grain on stalks has not.
The mishna’s redeemed second tithe is quoted.
Why must its movability be stated?
Payment of the principal effects redemption even before the extra fifth is paid.
The mishna’s dry lupine is quoted.
Why does the permission apply only when the lupine is dry?
Wet lupine is too bitter for animals to eat.

128a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna’s ban on moving untithed produce is quoted.
Why is this ban necessary to state?
It also covers produce whose tithing duty is rabbinic, such as growth in an unperforated pot.
The mishna’s ban on first tithe lacking teruma is quoted.
Why is that ban necessary to state?
Even tithe taken after grain was piled still requires teruma gedola, as Abaye answered Rav Pappa.
The mishna’s ban on unredeemed second tithe is quoted.
Why is that ban necessary to state?
It includes invalid redemptions: unminted silver for second tithe or land for consecrated property.
A baraita permits squill for deer and mustard for doves; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits glass shards for ostriches.
Rabbi Natan asks whether that logic should permit vine bundles as elephant food.
Ostriches are relatively common, unlike elephants.
Ameimar limits the glass permission to someone who owns ostriches.
Rav Ashi argues from the elephant objection that suitability as food matters even without owning the animal.
Abaye groups four sages who treat all Jews as fit for items associated with princes, beginning with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Rabbi Shimon permits rose oil for all Jews because he calls them all princes.
Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva say every Jew is worthy of a costly cloak when determining what a debtor may keep.
The discussion returns to prepared bundles.
A baraita repeats the preparation rule; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel distinguishes bundles carried with one hand from heavier ones.
A baraita addresses herbs set aside as fuel or food and permits limited hand picking and crushing for eating.
What plant is called amita?
Names are supplied for amita, sia, hyssop, and koranit.
A seller’s use of koranit for thyme challenges the proposed identification.
The herb names are corrected, identifying koranit as thyme.
Rav Huna and Rav Hisda disagree whether unsalted meat may be moved; salted meat is permitted.
Rav Huna’s permissive view seems to conflict with Rav, his teacher, who accepts muktzeh.
A food may be set aside from eating yet still allowed to be moved.
Rav Hisda’s prohibition on moving unsalted meat is restated.
A visit to Rav Hisda’s house suggests duck meat was moved to prevent it spoiling.
Duck meat is different because it can be eaten raw.
A baraita distinguishes salted from unsalted fish but permits both kinds of meat.
A baraita permits moving bones because dogs can eat them.

128b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita permits spoiled meat for wild animals and exposed water for cats, though Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel warns against retaining dangerous water.
The mishna permits aiding chicks, a fleeing hen, young animals, and a walking child within specified limits.
Rav permits placing cushions under an animal trapped in a water channel to help it out.
A baraita appears to allow only feeding the trapped animal in place.
Feeding suffices when possible; cushions are allowed when the animal cannot be sustained there.
Putting cushions under the animal makes them unavailable for their ordinary use.
Avoiding animal suffering, a Torah concern, overrides this rabbinic restriction.
The mishna permits pushing a fleeing hen but appears to exclude helping it walk.
A baraita likewise permits helping other animals walk in a courtyard but not hens.
Why is a hen treated differently?
It lifts its body, so guiding it would amount to carrying it.
Two baraitot distinguish helping animals walk, lifting them, and merely pushing them.
The second baraita seems to both imply and deny permission to help an animal walk.
The clause denying such help refers specifically to a hen.
Abaye advises securing or lifting a hen during slaughter so its claws do not damage the required cut.
The mishna permits assisting animal birth but allows Shabbat labor needed for a human birth, and states rules for the cord and circumcision.
What counts as assisting an animal’s birth?
Rav Yehuda says catching the newborn; Rav Nahman says pressing the mother’s flesh.
A baraita supports Rav Yehuda and adds ways to help the newborn breathe and suckle.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel reports helping a kosher animal accept its offspring on a festival.
How was this done?
Abaye describes salt and afterbirth fluid used to prompt the mother to recognize its newborn.
That intervention is limited to kosher animals.
Why exclude non-kosher animals?
They usually accept their young; if they reject them, these measures do not help.
The mishna’s permission to deliver a woman on Shabbat is recalled.
What extra permission does the general phrase about desecrating Shabbat for her add?
A baraita permits bringing light and oil, using less usual carrying methods where feasible.
The baraita’s permission to light a lamp is quoted.
Why is that permission necessary to state?
Even for a blind woman, light helps her trust that others can see and respond to her needs.
The rule for bringing oil in the helper’s hair is quoted.
Would extracting the oil from hair violate the rule against wringing?
Rabba and Rav Yosef say hair is not subject to that prohibition.
Rav Ashi says the oil may instead be carried in a vessel tied through the hair, altering the usual method.
Shmuel allows Shabbat labor for a woman in childbirth while the womb remains open, whether or not she requests help.
His rule for after the womb closes begins and continues on the next daf.

129a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Ashi’s version forbids Shabbat labor once the womb has closed, even if the mother requests it.
Mar Zutra’s version allows such labor after closure when the mother says she needs it.
Ravina asks which version governs the law.
Mareimar follows Mar Zutra because doubt concerning danger to life is resolved leniently.
When is the womb considered open?
Three accounts place the start at labor posture, bleeding, or the point when others must support her.
How long does that condition last?
Views give three, seven, or thirty days.
