The Nehardean rule distinguishes the first three days, days four through seven, and the rest of thirty days by the mother’s need.
Rules for asking a gentile to care for a non-dangerously ill person support help during the later period.
Shmuel states a thirty-day rule for a woman after childbirth.
To what law does the thirty-day limit apply?
The Nehardeans apply it to immersion.
Rava limits that concern to a woman without her husband present and cites Rav Hisda’s daughter becoming chilled.
Shmuel permits a fire for a woman after childbirth on Shabbat.
Is that permission limited to childbirth and the rainy season?
No; a fire is also allowed for illness and in summer, as the case of a chilled person after bloodletting shows.
Furniture was broken for firewood to warm Shmuel, Rav Yehuda, and Rabba after bloodletting.
Abaye asks whether destroying Rabba’s bench violated the ban on wasteful destruction.
Rabba places preventing bodily harm ahead of preserving the bench.
Rav urges obtaining shoes, but selling even shoes to secure food after bloodletting.
What food is needed after bloodletting?
Rav names meat and Shmuel names wine, each as a way to restore strength.
A mnemonic introduces the following reports.
Reports describe the foods and wine different sages consumed after bloodletting.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak advises obtaining a substantial meal after bloodletting.
He permits an expedient for someone who cannot afford nourishment, with dates, oil, and sunshine as another recourse.
Ablat questions Shmuel’s sunbathing, and Shmuel attributes it to bloodletting.
The account says Shmuel actually withheld a different explanation tied to the summer solstice.
A mnemonic introduces further cautions about bloodletting.
Rav and Shmuel warn against neglecting food after bloodletting.
They also warn against sitting in a draft after the procedure.
Shmuel noticed weakness when a half-brick was missing from his usual sheltered room.
Rav and Shmuel advise eating before going out after bloodletting; their warning continues on the next daf.

129b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The warning about encounters immediately after bloodletting concludes.
Rav and Shmuel advise resting before rising and list abrupt rising after several activities as harmful.
Shmuel describes longer intervals between bloodlettings as a person ages.
Shmuel gives preferred weekdays and cautions against Monday and Thursday in the language of judgment.
Why is Tuesday also omitted?
Its association with Mars at even hours is offered as the reason.
The same association seems to apply to Friday.
Common practice is invoked under the verse that God protects the simple.
Shmuel warns against certain Wednesdays by their dates in the month.
Further cautions concern the new month and festival eves, especially Shavuot.
Shmuel distinguishes bloodletting after wheat for treatment from bloodletting for relief.
A teaching specifies when to drink and eat after bloodletting.
Does drinking later cause harm, or simply lose the immediate benefit?
The question remains unresolved.
Does eating outside the specified interval cause harm or simply lack benefit?
This question also remains unresolved.
Rav’s saying about barbers’ work explains a remark about an unproductive study day.
A baraita permits tying or, according to Rabbi Yosei, cutting the cord and warming the newborn with the placenta.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel describes different materials used to insulate the placenta.
Rav rules like Rabbi Yosei that the cord may be cut on Shabbat.
The sages agree that twins’ cord may be cut because leaving them attached is dangerous.
Rav derives permitted care for childbirth from Ezekiel’s description of a neglected newborn.
Each part of the verse is applied to delivery, cutting the cord, washing, salting, and swaddling on Shabbat.
The chapter on clearing space concludes.

130a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Eliezer permits bringing a forgotten circumcision scalpel openly on Shabbat, or covered with witnesses during danger.
He even permits preparing wood and charcoal to make the needed iron tool.
Rabbi Akiva distinguishes preparations that could precede Shabbat from circumcision itself, which cannot.
Does Rabbi Eliezer require an uncovered scalpel to honor the mitzva or avoid suspicion?
Would carrying it covered with witnesses reveal which reason applies?
Honor requires public display, while witnesses would remove suspicion even when it is covered.
Which reason is correct?
Rabbi Levi identifies affection for the mitzva as the reason.
A baraita states that Rabbi Eliezer permits only uncovered transport in ordinary circumstances.
Rav Ashi derives the same reason from the mishna allowing a cover only in danger.
Another baraita reports the uncovered rule and the exceptional practice of covered transport with witnesses during danger.
Do the required witnesses mean the carrier plus one other person or two others?
The mishna’s plural wording appears to require two other witnesses.
The carrier and one other person could still be called witnesses because both can testify elsewhere.
The discussion returns to Rabbi Eliezer’s permission to make the tool.
A baraita recounts local practices under Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
Levi declines poultry in milk, then explains why he did not censure a community that may follow its local rabbi.
Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives from the wording of the meat-and-milk verse that poultry is excluded.
Rabbi Yitzhak describes a city that followed Rabbi Eliezer and was spared a decree against circumcision.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel contrasts mitzvot first accepted joyfully with those accepted amid dispute.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar contrasts practices defended at risk of death with those observed less firmly.
The discussion cites the need for a clean body when wearing phylacteries.
What does a clean body require?
Abaye forbids passing wind in phylacteries; Rava forbids sleeping in them.
Why was Elisha called the Man of Wings?
A story describes his defiance of a ban on phylacteries and the dove wings found in his hand.
Why did he name a dove rather than another bird?
Israel is compared with a dove, whose wings protect it as mitzvot protect Israel.
A case begins in which a forgotten circumcision scalpel was carried on Shabbat over roofs and courtyards.

130b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The scalpel incident is described as contrary to Rabbi Eliezer’s wishes.
Rav Yosef objects that Rabbi Eliezer permits even public-domain carrying and the Rabbis might seem to allow the lesser route.
A baraita explicitly forbids the roof and courtyard route too, ruling out that reading of the Rabbis.
Rav Ashi attributes the route to Rabbi Shimon’s treatment of roofs, enclosures, and courtyards as one domain for objects resting there.
Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Asi whether an alleyway without a joint arrangement permits carrying throughout it.
He weighs the courtyard analogy against differences in enclosure and residence.
Rabbi Asi gives no answer at that time.
Later, Rabbi Asi relates the scalpel incident and the sages’ difficulty with apparently following Rabbi Eliezer.
Rabbi Oshaya identifies the route as an unmerged alleyway, crossed from one end to the other.
Rabbi Zeira asks whether Rabbi Asi therefore permits carrying throughout such an alleyway.
Rabbi Asi says yes.
Rabbi Zeira asks why Rabbi Asi had not answered this way earlier.
Rabbi Asi says study had restored the forgotten ruling to him.
A separate report from Rav limits carrying in an unmerged alleyway to four cubits.
Abaye says that report needed clarification from Rabba bar Avuh.
The restriction applies when houses and courtyards were joined; without that joining the whole alleyway is usable.
Rav Hanina asks why joining the courtyards to houses would make the alleyway more restricted.
He begins to connect the distinction with Rav’s requirement for an alleyway to be permitted by sidepole and crossbeam.

131a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav’s rule requires houses and courtyards opening into the alleyway; the joined case seems to lack qualifying courtyards.
If houses are unusable without joining, the unjoined case seems instead to lack qualifying houses.
Residents could relinquish their rights to one householder.
That would leave only one qualifying house.
Rights might be relinquished to different householders during different parts of the day.
At any one time there would still be only one qualifying house.
Rav Ashi says the houses cause the courtyard restriction; without usable houses, that cause is absent.
Rabbi Yohanan says Rabbi Eliezer does not allow preparation for every mitzva to override Shabbat; even the two loaves need a special derivation.
A shared word for bringing links the two loaves to the omer, whose preparation overrides Shabbat.
Unless the shared words are superfluous, the analogy can be challenged because reaping differs between the offerings.
An extra use of “bringing” in the omer passage makes that side of the analogy available.
One free side is insufficient under Rabbi Eliezer’s approach because the analogy could still be challenged.
An extra “bringing” for the two loaves frees the other side as well.
Which mitzva did Rabbi Yohanan exclude, since baraitot include lulav, sukka, matza, and shofar?
Rav Adda excludes attaching fringes and affixing a mezuza.
A baraita says those acts remain liable when performed on Shabbat.
Why are those preparations excluded?
Rav Yosef says neither mitzva has a fixed time.
Abaye objects that a mitzva without a fixed time may be due at every moment.

131b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abaye completes the objection that an ongoing obligation has no exempt moment.
Fringes and mezuza can be deferred by making the garment or house ownerless.
Rabbi Eliezer’s permission for lulav preparations is recalled.
It cannot simply come from the Temple offerings, whose service has a special status.
The verse’s “on the day” is read to include Shabbat.
Would a verse be needed merely to allow moving a lulav?
The verse instead permits its preparations.
The Rabbis use the phrase to require daytime performance.
How does Rabbi Eliezer know lulav is taken by day?
He derives it from “seven days,” excluding nights.
The Rabbis need a separate limit lest “seven days” be compared to the nights of sukka.
Why not derive every other mitzva’s preparations from lulav?
Lulav is distinctive because it requires four species.
Rabbi Eliezer’s permission for sukka preparations is recalled.
What supports it, when Temple offerings and lulav each have distinctive features?
The shared phrase “seven days” links sukka to lulav.
Why not derive the other mitzvot from sukka?
Sukka is distinctive because it applies at night as well as by day.
Rabbi Eliezer’s permission for matza preparations is recalled.
What supports it, when the preceding mitzvot each have a special feature?
The date “fifteenth” links matza with Sukkot.
Why not derive the others from matza?
Matza is distinctive because it binds women and men alike.
Rabbi Eliezer’s permission for shofar preparations is recalled.
How is it derived when each earlier source has a feature that limits comparison?
The verse’s “day of sounding” is read to include Shabbat.
Sounding itself is treated as a skill rather than prohibited labor, so that alone would not need a verse.
The verse therefore covers preparations.
The Rabbis use the word “day” to exclude nighttime.
What is Rabbi Eliezer’s source for excluding nighttime?
He links the sounding to the daytime Jubilee shofar.
Why not derive all other preparations from shofar?
Rosh HaShana shofar invokes remembrance, while Jubilee shofar frees people and returns fields; each has a special effect.
The baraita’s permission for circumcision preparations is recalled.
The Gemara asks for Rabbi Eliezer’s source and begins challenging derivation from the other mitzvot.

132a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The other mitzvot lose their opportunity when their day passes, unlike delayed circumcision.
Rabbi Eliezer instead derives even Shabbat circumcision from “on the eighth day.”
Why not derive the other preparations from circumcision?
Circumcision is distinctive because thirteen covenants are associated with it.
The sages agree circumcision itself overrides Shabbat; what is its source?
Ulla and Rabbi Yitzhak call it a received halakha.
A teaching derives saving life from Shabbat circumcision, yet a fortiori reasoning cannot be built on a received halakha.
Rabbi Elazar proposes a verbal analogy using “sign.”
Phylacteries are also called a sign, which would wrongly extend the rule.
The analogy is instead proposed through “covenant.”
Adult circumcision also involves a covenant but does not override Shabbat.
The analogy is next proposed through “generations.”
Fringes also use “generations,” yet do not override Shabbat.
Rav Nahman requires all three terms together: sign, covenant, and generations.
Rabbi Yohanan instead reads “on the day” as including Shabbat.
Reish Lakish asks why the same wording for atonement offerings would not permit them on Shabbat.
There the wording requires offerings by day rather than night.
Circumcision likewise needs a rule excluding nighttime.
Another verse already gives the daytime rule for circumcision.
A general verse already requires sacrifices by day too.
A separate limit is needed lest the concession of a cheaper offering suggest nighttime atonement.
Ravina asks why that logic would not permit a non-priest or mourner to offer it.
The verse restores the usual restrictions.
Rav Aha offers “eighth” as a different source for Shabbat circumcision.
Is “eighth” needed simply to exclude the seventh day?
Another verse already excludes the seventh.
Both verses may still be needed to distinguish the seventh from postponement to the ninth day.
Rabbi Yohanan’s derivation remains the clearer one.
A baraita ultimately invokes “on the day” to permit circumcision on Shabbat despite the general labor ban.
Rava asks why the baraita first accepts, then doubts, its interpretation.
He reconstructs its initial reasoning: circumcision can override the labor ban by an a fortiori argument.
The argument begins with leprosy’s relation to Temple service and continues on the next daf.

132b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Circumcision overrides leprosy, which obstructs Temple service; since service overrides Shabbat, circumcision might do so too.
Why did the baraita then reconsider?
Shabbat may be more stringent, or leprosy may obstruct service because the afflicted person is unfit.
The baraita therefore relies on “on the day” to establish Shabbat circumcision.
A baraita says circumcision overrides leprosy even when delayed, but a festival only at its proper time.
What is the source for removing a leprous foreskin?
The circumcision verse is read to permit removal despite a bright spot, limiting the leprosy warning elsewhere.
Perhaps circumcision applies only where the foreskin has no such spot.
The extra word “flesh” includes a foreskin bearing the spot.
Rava asks why the baraita first accepted, then questioned, the ruling.
He reconstructs a first proof: if circumcision overrides stringent Shabbat, it should override leprosy.
The tanna could object that leprosy might be more stringent because it obstructs Temple service.
The explicit word “flesh” then resolves the issue.
Another version initially uses the rule that a positive command overrides a negative one.
Leprosy removal carries both positive and negative commands, so the ordinary rule may not apply.
The extra word “flesh” again permits the circumcision.
What proves the rule for a child older than eight days but not yet an adult?
Abaye derives it from what the eight-day child and adult share, despite each having a distinct feature.
Rava says no verse is needed for timely circumcision to override leprosy if it already overrides Shabbat.
Rav Safra asks whether leprosy may be more stringent because it obstructs Temple service.
Rava says the afflicted priest is unfit for service for reasons beyond the ban on removing the spot.
Why not remove the spot and then serve?
The priest still needs immersion.
A pure leprous spot raises the same issue without requiring immersion.
Rav Ashi distinguishes an act that fulfills a positive command while violating a ban from merely preparing for service.
The discussion of Rava and Rav Safra continues on the next daf.

133a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita gives two sources for circumcision overriding a leprous spot: an extra word or an a fortiori inference.
Why is a verse needed when removal of the spot is unintended?
Abaye says the verse is needed under Rabbi Yehuda’s ban on unintended prohibited results.
Rava says even Rabbi Shimon forbids an unavoidable prohibited result.
Does Abaye reject that principle?
Abaye and Rava are both reported to accept it.
Abaye adopted it after hearing Rava.
Another version attaches their exchange to a verse permitting indirect, unintended removal of a leprous spot.
Why is a verse needed for an unintended removal?
Abaye again applies Rabbi Yehuda’s stricter view.
Rava again invokes an inevitable result even under Rabbi Shimon.
Did Abaye not accept that inevitable-result principle?
Both sages are reported to state it.
Abaye adopted it later.
Under Abaye’s earlier view, what work does the extra word “flesh” do?
It covers someone who explicitly intends to cut the leprous spot while circumcising.
How can that apply to a young child with no intention?
The father may intend to remove the child’s spot.
If another circumcisor is available, both the positive duty and the prohibition can be respected.
The case has no other person available.
Why does delayed circumcision not override a festival?
Hezekiah derives from the postponed burning of Paschal leftovers that festival labor is limited.
Abaye derives a distinction between the day’s required service and an ordinary weekday offering.
Rava limits festival permission to food preparation, excluding deferred circumcision.
Rav Ashi notes that a festival has both positive and negative rest commands.
Rav rules in accordance with Rabbi Akiva’s limit on preparations that could be done beforehand.
A parallel ruling for the Paschal lamb distinguishes advance preparations from its time-bound slaughter.
Both rulings are needed because the Paschal lamb carries a karet penalty absent from a child’s delayed circumcision.
Circumcision, however, has thirteen covenants, unlike the Paschal lamb; the second ruling also needs stating.
The mishna permits the required cutting, uncovering, wound care, and medicine on Shabbat.
If medicine was not prepared beforehand, it is chewed or applied in separate parts.
A dressing is not made afresh, but a rag may be worn on a finger and brought from another courtyard.

133b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What does “all requirements” add beyond the mishna’s list?
While engaged in circumcision one may trim all remaining shreds; after stopping, only shreds that invalidate it may be cut.
Which tanna treats stopping as a limit on resuming the optional trimming?
Rabbi Yohanan proposes Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka.
That sage limits flaying a Paschal lamb on Shabbat to what is required for the offering.
Circumcision may differ because beautifying the mitzva matters there.
A baraita derives the practice of beautifying ritual objects from “This is my God and I will glorify Him.”
Abba Shaul reads the verse as a call to resemble God in mercy and compassion.
Rav Ashi instead proposes Rabbi Yosei, who bars extra witnesses from traveling on Shabbat when the new moon is plainly visible.
The moon case may differ because Shabbat need not be overridden there, whereas timely circumcision already overrides it.
The Nehardean sages point instead to the Rabbis’ uninterrupted replacement of the showbread.
Rabbi Yosei allows a gap, highlighting the Rabbis’ stricter sense of interruption.
A baraita requires finishing the circumcision and mentions karet for failing to do so.
Rav Kahana identifies the liable person as the circumcisor.
Rav Pappa asks why he could not say he performed part of the mitzva and others should complete it.
Rav Pappa instead identifies an uncircumcised adult.
Rav Ashi notes that liability for such an adult is already explicit in Scripture.
He returns to a circumcisor who knowingly begins too late to complete the mitzva before Shabbat ends.
The mishna’s requirement to draw blood from the wound is recalled.
Rav Pappa says omitting this care endangers the child and disqualifies the practitioner.
Is that not evident from its being permitted on Shabbat?
The teaching establishes that drawing this attached blood is normally labor, permitted here because it prevents danger.
The mishna’s bandage is recalled.
Abaye and Rava report different ingredients for a wound dressing.
Rava’s public recipe troubles local doctors; he says he kept another remedy to himself.

134a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The preceding remedy concludes with washing in beet water.
A baraita allows grinding cumin and mixing wine with oil on a festival although these preparations are barred on Shabbat.
Abaye asks why wine and oil are barred when such a mixture can serve a sick person on Shabbat.
A baraita records Rabbi Meir permitting that mixture.
Rabbi Meir personally declined it out of respect for colleagues despite maintaining his permissive view.
His personal stringency does not bar others.
The circumcision mixture requires beating, unlike the sick person’s mixture.
Why not make it without beating?
The mishna permits applying wine and oil separately instead.
A baraita bars straining mustard or sweetening it with an ember on a festival.
Abaye compares the mustard strainer to placing an egg in one.
The egg does not look like selecting, while straining mustard does.
Another baraita permits sweetening mustard with an ember.
The permission concerns metal; the prohibition concerns a wooden ember.
Abaye compares mustard on coals with permitted meat on coals.
Cooking meat that way is needed, while sweetening mustard can be done otherwise.
Abaye asks whether cheese may be curdled on a festival.
Rav Yosef prohibits it.
Why does this differ from kneading dough?
Fresh bread requires same-day kneading, while cheese can be prepared earlier.
The Nehardeans praise cheese made that day.
Even same-day cheese is good; older cheese is at least as suitable.
The mishna’s restriction on making a new pouch is recalled.
Abaye reports advice on arranging the infant’s pouch to avoid injury.
He describes using a worn cloth with a hem if no pouch is available.
A reported technique addresses an infant whose bodily opening is obscured.
Another report addresses an infant who cannot nurse.
A further report describes a remedy for an infant who does not urinate.
A further report describes a remedy for an infant who is not breathing.
Abaye reports different handling for a baby considered too small or too strong.
Abaye advises delaying circumcision for a markedly red or pale infant until the condition changes.
Rabbi Natan recounts delaying the circumcision of a red infant, who then survived.
He recounts a comparable case of a pale infant whose circumcision was delayed.

134b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna permits washing around circumcision but specifies sprinkling by hand rather than vessel.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya permits washing on the third day, citing the pain of Shekhem’s men.
The mishna restricts Shabbat circumcision in doubtful cases, with Rabbi Yehuda excepting an androginos.
The permission to wash seems inconsistent with limiting water to hand sprinkling.
Rav Yehuda and Rabba bar Avuh read the latter clause as explaining that “washing” means sprinkling.
Rava objects that the mishna explicitly says washing.
Rava distinguishes normal washing on day one from hand sprinkling on day three; Rabbi Elazar permits washing then too.
A baraita supports Rava’s distinction and states that sprinkling is done by hand.
Why is the verse about third-day pain called only an allusion?
Adults and infants may heal at different rates.
Rava rules on a baby’s washing, then worries that he disputed older sages.
The other sages point out that a baraita supports him.
Rava replies that the mishna’s wording fits the elders’ reading better.
Rav Dimi reports the law follows Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.
Does this permit washing the whole infant or only the circumcision site?
Rabbi Yaakov favors the whole body because hot water may already be placed on an ordinary wound.
Rav Yosef distinguishes water heated on Shabbat from water heated beforehand.
Rav Dimi asks how the dispute is known to involve water heated on Shabbat.
Rav Yosef explains that failing to warm the child is dangerous.
Ravin’s report explicitly permits either kind of water and either extent of washing because of danger.
Rav permits hot water and oil on a wound; Shmuel requires placing them nearby so they flow onto it.
A baraita forbids applying them to a pad before placing it on the wound.
That restriction addresses squeezing the pad.
Another baraita forbids applying them to a pad already on the wound.
The same concern about squeezing applies.
A baraita explicitly supports Shmuel’s nearby-application rule.
A baraita distinguishes dry dressings that may be placed on a wound from those that may not.
Its two clauses appear to contradict each other about rags.
New healing rags differ from old ones.
Abaye infers that the restricted rags have a healing effect.
The discussion turns to doubtful and androginos circumcision and begins a scriptural derivation.

135a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita excludes uncertain and androginos circumcision from overriding Shabbat.
Rabbi Yehuda permits the androginos case and associates its neglect with karet.
The baraita also excludes twilight birth and a child born apparently circumcised, recording Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on drawing covenantal blood.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar relocates their dispute to an already circumcised convert, saying they agree about the newborn.
What further uncertain case does the baraita include?
A child’s uncertain gestational age bars Shabbat circumcision under the cited rule.
The baraita restricts handling a presumed nonviable infant but permits the mother to nurse for her own safety.
Rav follows the first tanna on a child born circumcised; Shmuel follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.
Rav Adda has such a child circumcised on Shabbat, injures him, and regrets departing from Rav’s ruling.
Rav Nahman says even Shmuel’s requirement to draw blood was not stated for Shabbat.
Rav Adda had treated a concealed foreskin as certain.
Rabba considers the concealed foreskin only possible, while Rav Yosef treats it as certain.
Rav Yosef cites a baraita in which the houses agree on drawing blood but disagree whether Shabbat may be overridden.
He infers that the earlier tanna may allow Shabbat circumcision by all opinions.
Perhaps that earlier tanna instead bars it by all opinions.
That would leave Rabbi Eliezer HaKappar merely reporting Beit Shammai’s rejected permission.
The baraita could instead mean the houses do not disagree on this Shabbat issue at all.
Rabbi Asi links eighth-day circumcision to a birth that renders the mother impure, citing the paired verses.
Abaye cites the generations before Sinai, when eighth-day circumcision preceded childbirth impurity law.
Rabbi Asi begins to answer that the Torah later introduced a new rule.

135b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Torah introduced a new law after the earlier generations.
A dispute about a caesarean birth or double foreskin appears to allow Shabbat circumcision without the mother’s birth impurity.
Both sides seem to agree on the eighth day, challenging Rabbi Asi.
The timing and Shabbat permissions are linked in that dispute.
A baraita lists home-born and purchased servants circumcised either immediately or on day eight.
It explains the purchased cases by whether the child was born before or after the purchase.
It gives a home-born eighth-day case where the servant conceives after purchase.
Rav Hama instead makes the home-born timing depend on whether the mother immersed before birth.
The first tanna does not make that distinction and so challenges Rabbi Asi’s link to maternal impurity.
Rava says Rav Hama’s view can account for all four timing categories.
Rava works through birth, immersion, and ownership patterns for each category.
How can the first tanna have a home-born child circumcised immediately?
Rabbi Yirmeya proposes buying the servant only for rights to her fetus.
That depends on whether rights to a product count as ownership of the source.
Rav Mesharshiya uses a purchase conditioned on not immersing the servant.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel gives survival periods after which a human or animal newborn is presumed viable.
Does a shorter survival leave the newborn’s viability uncertain?

136a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: How can a child of uncertain viability be circumcised on Shabbat?
If viable it is a mitzva; if not, cutting the nonviable body is not a Shabbat wound.
A baraita still says not to override Shabbat for a child whose gestational age is uncertain.
That baraita bars preparatory labor under Rabbi Eliezer, not circumcision itself.
A tannaitic dispute asks whether slaughter purifies an eight-month animal offspring from carcass impurity.
Does the dispute concern whether the offspring is legally alive?
Rava asks why the tannaim would then dispute impurity rather than eating the meat.
All treat it as nonviable; the dispute is whether its slaughter works like slaughter of a tereifa.
A tereifa from birth still belongs to a species normally subject to slaughter, unlike the nonviable offspring.
Do the Rabbis disagree with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel’s survival test, and which view is law?
A calf born on a festival may be slaughtered that day.
Its full gestation may be known.
A firstborn born with a blemish is also treated as available on the festival.
Its full gestation may likewise be known.
Shmuel’s ruling for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel shows a dispute exists and favors his view.
Abaye first locates their disagreement in an infant who briefly breathes then dies, rather than one killed accidentally.
What practical difference does this distinction make?
It determines whether the mother is exempt from levirate marriage.
The proposed agreement about an infant killed accidentally is restated.
Sages refused a calf slaughtered on its seventh day, challenging the claim that an accidental death proves viability.
The disagreement is relocated to accidental death; one who briefly breathes and dies is treated as nonviable.
A mourner says he knows the infant who died within thirty days had completed gestation.
Rav Kahana likewise explains mourning an infant’s early death by certainty about completed gestation.
The discussion begins a case of a widow betrothed after her infant died within thirty days.

136b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ravina requires halitza for a woman betrothed to an Israelite, but does not impose it after betrothal to a priest.
Rav Sherevya reports a stricter version requiring halitza in both cases.
Ravina says Rava retracted that version; Rav Sherevya sharply protests the leniency.
Rav Sheizvi limits Rabbi Yehuda’s treatment of an androginos as male to circumcision, not all laws.
How is the limit shown for vows of valuation?
A baraita reads the valuation verses as applying only to a definite male or definite female.

137a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: An unattributed Sifra teaching is ascribed to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Nahman cites the purification-water mishna: Rabbi Yehuda excludes an androgynos, supporting a limited male status.
Why then does Rabbi Yehuda include an androgynos in circumcision?
The verse says “every male,” broadening the circumcision rule.
The mishna holds one liable for circumcising on Shabbat the infant whose eighth day is Sunday.
For an infant whose eighth day was Friday, Rabbi Eliezer imposes a sin offering and Rabbi Yehoshua exempts.
Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda transmit different liability readings of the first case.
Rav Huna cites Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: both tannaim impose liability for circumcising the Sunday infant on Shabbat.
Their dispute instead concerns the overdue Friday infant, whom Rabbi Yehoshua exempts.
Rabbi Eliezer analogizes to unwitting idolatry: violating the prohibition brings liability.
Rabbi Yehoshua distinguishes an act performed in pursuit of a mitzva.
Rav Yehuda cites Rabbi Meir: both tannaim exempt circumcision of the overdue Friday infant.
Their dispute concerns the Sunday infant circumcised too early on Shabbat.
Rabbi Eliezer again derives liability from the idolatry model of unwitting transgression.
Rabbi Yehoshua exempts one occupied with a mitzva.
Rabbi Hiyya transmits another Rabbi Meir version: both tannaim impose liability for the Friday infant.
In that version they dispute the Sunday infant; Rabbi Yehoshua exempts.
How can Rabbi Yehoshua exempt the case without a mitzva yet impose liability when a mitzva was performed?
Rabbi Yannai’s school says the Shabbat infant had already been circumcised on Friday, leaving no timely circumcision for Shabbat.
Rav Ashi objects that Shabbat can still be overridden for other infants.
For this particular circumcisor, no infant remains whose circumcision overrides Shabbat.
The mishna sets circumcision at eight through twelve days according to twilight births and intervening holy days, and delays it for illness.
Shmuel grants a baby seven days of recovery after a fever subsides.
Must the seven days be complete twenty-four-hour periods?
A teaching equating recovery day with birth day seems to allow counting without exact hours.
The inference is rejected: recovery requires full periods even though ordinary birth counting does not.
The mishna defines remaining tissue that invalidates circumcision and requires correction when flesh makes it appear incomplete.

137b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna adds that circumcision without uncovering the membrane does not count.
Rav defines the disqualifying tissue by the height of the corona.
Shmuel assesses a fleshy child by whether he looks circumcised when the organ is erect.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel gives a differently worded test for the same situation.
What practical difference follows from the two formulations?
They differ when he looks partly, but not fully, circumcised.
The baraita prescribes blessings for the circumcisor, father, and people standing nearby.
It gives the additional blessing over the covenant.
It specifies blessings for circumcising converts, including the covenant-blood blessing and its scriptural support.
It specifies parallel blessings for circumcising slaves.
The chapter on Rabbi Eliezer’s circumcision rules closes.
The new mishna disputes hanging a wine strainer on a Festival and filtering through one on Shabbat or a Festival.
How can Rabbi Eliezer permit first hanging a strainer when he bars even adding to a temporary tent?
The shutter mishna and Rabbi Yohanan’s explanation establish Rabbi Eliezer’s strict temporary-tent rule.
Rabbi Eliezer treats hanging the strainer as a food-preparation aid permitted on a Festival, following Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Yehuda permits only preparations impossible before the Festival; the strainer could be hung earlier.
Rabbi Eliezer is more lenient than Rabbi Yehuda on such preparations.
Under the Sages’ rule, what happens if someone nevertheless hangs the strainer?
Rav Yosef says he owes a sin offering.
Abaye challenges that logic by comparing a jug hung on a peg.

138a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abaye instead calls the hanging prohibition rabbinic, to keep Shabbat practice distinct from weekday practice.
Abaye distinguishes rabbinically prohibited temporary tents, liable permanent tents, and prepared folding furniture that may be opened.
The mishna bars straining wine on Shabbat; what is the liability if someone does it?
Rav Kahana imposes a sin offering.
Rav Sheshet objects: could the Sages impose liability where Rabbi Eliezer permits the act outright?
Rav Yosef counters with the city-of-gold ornament dispute.
The baraita has Rabbi Meir imposing liability and Rabbi Eliezer permitting the ornament.
Abaye says Rabbi Eliezer challenges the Sages’ intermediate prohibition, not Rabbi Meir’s liability.
Which prohibited labor supports liability for straining?
Rabba classifies it as selecting; Rabbi Zeira as sifting.
Rabba compares taking the wine and leaving the sediment to ordinary selection.
Rabbi Zeira compares sediment above and wine below the strainer to the layout of a sieve.
Rami bar Yehezkel bars making a doubled-cloak canopy unless a cord was already attached for spreading it.
Rav Kahana asks Rav about spreading a canopy.
Rav initially says even a bed is prohibited.
Rav Kahana asks specifically about a bed.
Rav now says even a canopy is permitted.
Rav Kahana asks for the ruling on both together.
Rav prohibits the canopy and permits the bed.
The responses concern different constructions: folding beds, preattached canopies, and ordinary beds and canopies.
Rav Yosef reports canopies in Rav Huna’s house that were spread and removed.
Rav permits hanging and dismantling a curtain.
Shmuel introduces a further ruling transmitted from Rabbi Hiyya on the next daf.

138b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A sloped bridal canopy may be spread and dismantled on Shabbat.
Rav Sheshet limits this to a canopy without a handbreadth roof, near-roof width, slope, or hanging wall.
Rav Sheshet permits wearing a felt hat.
Another teaching forbids that hat.
The first resolution distinguishes whether the brim is a handbreadth wide.
But an extended cloak of that width would not make its wearer liable for a tent.
The actual concern is whether the hat fits securely or could blow off and be carried.
Rami requests Rav Huna’s three teachings from Rav: two on Shabbat and one on Torah.
Rav permits spreading a large wineskin with two people, but bars one person doing it alone.
Abaye bars spreading a canopy even with ten people because it is inevitably stretched briefly.
The discussion asks for the second Shabbat teaching.
Rav bars moving even a one-legged-damaged stove lest its leg be forcefully reattached.
Rav predicts Torah will be forgotten, reading the threatened astonishment through Isaiah’s loss of wisdom.
The Sages at Yavne cite Amos’s famine for hearing God’s word and an unsuccessful search for it.
God’s word here includes halakha, the end of days, and prophecy.
What would such an unsuccessful search look like?
A woman will ask whether a teruma loaf is impure and find no one able to decide.
The Torah plainly addresses whether food can contract impurity.
Her uncertainty concerns first- versus second-degree impurity.
The oven mishna already says bread inside an oven with a creeping animal is second-degree impure.
The unresolved issue is Rav Adda’s suggestion that an oven’s airspace be treated as filled with impurity.
Rava rejects that suggestion: a baraita distinguishes food from vessels within an impure earthenware vessel.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai counters that Torah cannot be forgotten, citing the promise it will remain in descendants’ mouths.
How then does he understand the prophecy of searching without finding?
His alternative explanation begins on the following daf.

139a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The promised failure is to find a clear halakha and clear teaching together.
Rabbi Yosei ben Elisha attributes widespread troubles to corrupt judges.
Micah condemns bribed judges, paid priests, and prophets who divine for money.
Despite their reliance on God, three calamities answer their three wrongs.
Micah names the ruin of Zion, Jerusalem, and the Temple Mount.
The Divine Presence will not rest until corrupt judges and officers disappear.
Isaiah promises to purge the dross and restore righteous judges.
Ulla says Jerusalem is redeemed through righteousness.
He cites Zion being redeemed through justice and righteousness.
Rav Pappa links the end of arrogant and dishonest officials to the end of oppressive outsiders.
He grounds the paired claims in Isaiah’s purging and Zephaniah’s removal of enemies.
Rabbi Mallai asks how to interpret the wicked staff and rulers’ rod in Isaiah.
He identifies corrupt judges and protective scholarly relatives; Mar Zutra adds scholars who coach ignorant judges.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Mallai asks how Isaiah’s defiled hands, fingers, lips, and tongue should be read.
He assigns them to bribed judges, their scribes, legal advisers, and litigants.
Rabbi Mallai says Joseph abstained from wine after parting from his brothers.
He reads Joseph’s title “separated from his brothers” as an allusion to abstinence.
Rabbi Yosei says the brothers also abstained.
Their later drinking with Joseph implies an earlier absence of drunkenness.
Rabbi Mallai distinguishes earlier drinking from earlier drunkenness.
Aaron’s gladness at Moses’ rise earns the breastplate over his heart.
The people of Bashkar ask Levi about a canopy, hops in a vineyard, and burial on a Festival.
Levi dies before receiving the questions, and Shmuel asks Rav Menashya to answer.
Rav Menashya sends a strict ruling on spreading a canopy.
Why not tell them Rami bar Yehezkel’s permissive method?
They are insufficiently trained to apply that distinction.
He prohibits hops in a vineyard.
Why omit Rabbi Tarfon’s leniency, especially given the rule of leniency outside Israel?
Again, their lack of training explains the strict answer.
Rav openly permits sowing hops there, while Rav Amram lashes for it.
Rav Mesharshiya uses a gentile child to sow hops.
Why not employ a Jewish child?
That child may keep the habit as an adult.
Why not employ a gentile adult?
He may be confused with a Jew.
For a Festival death, Rav Menashya bars Jews and gentiles from burial on either Festival day.
A case brought to Rabbi Yohanan after a death near Shabbat challenges that ruling.

139b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yohanan allowed gentiles to attend to the burial in the reported Festival case.
Rava permits gentiles on the first Festival day and Jews on the second, even at Rosh Hashana.
Rav Menashya ruled strictly for people unable to apply the distinctions.
Rav Hama permits wearing a canopy with its straps in the public domain.
Why are its straps unlike invalid ritual fringes, which count as a carried burden?
Invalid fringes retain significance; canopy straps are insignificant parts of the garment.
Rabba permits hanging a strainer for pomegranates on a Festival and then using it for wine.
Rav Ashi requires actually placing pomegranates in it first.
A baraita permits a brewer to claim he wants fresh beer during the intermediate Festival days without such a visible demonstration.
Brewing purpose is hidden, while a newly hung wine strainer makes the circumvention obvious.
The Sages report a scholar’s contrived storage of garlic in a barrel spout and sleep on a ferry.
Rav Ashi permits a scholar’s artifice around rabbinic rules, trusting him not to disregard them openly.
The mishna allows water over sediment and filtering drinkable wine through cloth or basket.
It permits egg in a mustard strainer and sets differing quantities for preparing spiced wine.
Zeiri permits filtering clear wine and water but bars cloudy liquids.
A baraita permits filtering an entire stirred wine barrel with its sediment.
Zeiri confines that ruling to new wine that remains cloudy between presses.
Rav Shimi requires filtering through cloth without forming a hollow receptacle.
Rav Hiyya bars raising the Egyptian basket a handbreadth above the lower vessel.
Rav permits covering half a barrel with a perforated cloth, but not the whole barrel.
Rav Pappa bars putting straw into a spigot because it resembles a strainer.
Rav Pappa’s household pours beer carefully to leave sediment behind.
Rav Aha asks whether the final drops are impermissibly selected.
Those last drops are not significant to Rav Pappa’s household.
The discussion introduces the mishna’s egg and mustard-strainer rule.

140a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The egg-white is used only to improve color, so it is not waste being selected out.
Rav permits thinning mustard kneaded before Shabbat with a vessel, but not by hand.
Shmuel objects that mixing by hand is never the ordinary food-preparation method.
Shmuel reverses the permission: mix by hand as a change, but not with a vessel.
Rabbi Elazar forbids both methods, Rabbi Yohanan permits both, and Abaye and Rava reject the latter ruling.
After the two sages exchange positions, Abaye and Rava adopt Rabbi Yohanan’s stricter view.
Accounts of Abaye, Rav Hiyya bar Ashi, and Ravina illustrate differing practice with prepared mustard.
Mar Zutra instead permits mixing previously kneaded mustard by hand or vessel with honey, provided it is stirred gently.
Previously ground cress and garlic may receive other ingredients and gentle mixing, but not beating or pounding.
What is amita, the ingredient added to cress and garlic?
It is mint; Abaye infers that mint benefits cress.
A baraita allows making the drink anumlin but bars medicinal aluntit, and identifies their ingredients.
Rav Yosef recalls the powerful effect of the cooled bathhouse drink given by Mar Ukva.
How could Mar Ukva drink it daily without harm?
He had become accustomed to it.
The mishna restricts soaking asafoetida, cleaning vetches, and sifting straw while allowing specified ordinary placements.
What liability follows from soaking asafoetida on Shabbat?
Rav Adda says it brings a sin offering.
Abaye compares soaking meat in water: that would not create Torah liability.
Abaye instead calls the restriction rabbinic, to avoid weekday practice.
Rabbi Yohanan asks Rabbi Yannai about soaking it in cold water.
Rabbi Yannai forbids it.
The mishna mentions lukewarm water, apparently allowing cold water.
Rabbi Yannai identifies the mishna with Rabbi Yosei’s individual leniency; the other sages prohibit cold water too.
What condition is asafoetida used to treat?
It treats heaviness of the heart.
Rav Aha begins a three-day course on Thursday and asks in the study hall about Shabbat.
The study hall permits drinking asafoetida on Shabbat, even in substantial amounts.
Rav Aha clarifies that he asks about soaking it, not drinking it.
Rav Hiyya recounts Rav Huna’s report that Rav permits soaking it in cold water and warming it in the sun.
Does that follow only the view that allows cold soaking?
Even the stricter view permits continuing an already-started course when missing a dose is dangerous.
Rav Aha visits Rav Safra with Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak.
He asks whether rubbing laundered linen merely softens it or impermissibly whitens it.
Rav Safra permits it as softening.
Rav Aha reports the question and answer to Rav Nahman.
Rav Nahman asks why he did not also ask about a scarf.
Rav Aha had already obtained Rav Huna’s permission for a scarf.
Why not infer the linen shirt ruling from the scarf ruling?
Whitening appears to be an issue with the shirt but not the scarf.
Rav Hisda begins a new ruling about a linen shirt, continued on the next daf.

140b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Hisda permits removing the linen garment from its hanging reed, but not removing the reed from the garment.
Rava permits moving the support if it is a weaver’s utensil.
Rav Hisda permits moving a vegetable bundle fit for animal food, but not one unfit for it.
Rav distinguishes a movable meat hook from a fish hook that is not moved.
Rav Ketina’s warning about standing on a bed board is rejected as an authoritative rule.
Rav Hisda advises buying long vegetables because length adds no cost to the bundle.
He applies the same buying advice to reeds.
He advises a scholar short on bread to avoid appetite-stimulating vegetables and explains his own practice.
He advises a scholar short on bread about slicing and sharing it, and describes checking the available supply.
Rav Hisda and Rav Pappa call costly substitutions of wheat bread or wine wasteful.
The Gemara rejects that economy when it harms the body.
Rav Hisda suggests ditch water in place of oil for a scholar without oil.
He recommends buying neck meat for its variety.
He advises buying a durable linen shirt and washing it monthly; a wordplay praises fine clothing.
He warns against sitting on a new damp mat that damages clothing.
He discourages sending clothing to a host for washing because it may be embarrassing.
Rav Hisda counsels his daughters to be modest and avoid eating bread before their husbands.
He adds advice about night foods and private bodily habits.
He advises a feminine form when asking who is at the door.
His pearl and clod demonstration illustrates the appeal of something kept concealed.
The prior mishna’s sieve permission differs from Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov’s sweeping restriction.
The new mishna records Rabbi Dosa and the Sages on moving fodder near animals, and permits transferring fodder between animals.
Do the Sages dispute one part of Rabbi Dosa’s rule or both?
A baraita says they prohibit moving fodder aside in both cases.
Rav Hisda initially locates the dispute in a ground trough and permits a vessel trough.
How could anyone allow moving fodder in a ground trough, where holes might be leveled?
His ruling is corrected: they dispute a vessel trough, while all prohibit the ground trough.
Two baraitot reverse which animal’s fodder may be moved to the other.
Abaye resolves both as allowing transfer from a donkey to an ox, never the reverse.
The donkey is called clean-mouthed because it does not wet the fodder with saliva; the ox is the recipient.

141a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The ox has saliva that affects the fodder left in front of it.
The other baraita calls the donkey indiscriminate and the cow selective in feeding, preserving the donkey-to-ox rule.
The mishna permits body movement of set-aside straw, or hand movement when it was prepared for use.
It distinguishes opening a household clothes press from operating a professional one; Rabbi Yehuda permits one already loosened.
Rav Nahman allows pulling a radish from the ground only when its shape will not displace soil.
Rav Adda cites the straw mishna against a distinction based on indirect movement.
The conclusion is that indirect movement does not count as ordinary moving.
Rav Yehuda permits crushing one pepper at a time with a knife handle, but not two.
Rava permits even several peppers because the method is altered.
Rav Yehuda advises drying after bathing before going ashore, lest water be carried in a karmelit.
Entering water also seems to push it four cubits.
The Sages did not prohibit indirect force in a karmelit.
Abaye or Rav Yehuda permits wiping muddy feet on the ground, but not a wall.
Rava rejects concern over apparent building on the wall.
Rava instead permits the wall and bars the ground lest holes be leveled.
Mar son of Ravina forbids both surfaces, while Rav Pappa permits both.
On the strict view, where may one wipe the mud?
On a beam.
Rava warns against sitting by an alley entrance lest a rolling object lead to carrying.
He bars setting a barrel on dirt lest one level holes.
He bars stuffing a rag into a jug lest it be squeezed.
Rav Kahana permits rubbing mortar from inside a garment, but not from outside.
A baraita permits scraping mortar but says not to rub it; does that bar all rubbing?
The baraita bars rubbing from outside, while leaving inside rubbing permitted.
Rabbi Abbahu reports permission to scrape a new shoe but not an old shoe.

141b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: With what may the shoe be scraped?
Rabbi Abbahu says with the back of a knife.
An elder cites Rabbi Hiyya’s baraita forbidding scraping either a new or an old shoe.
The same baraita bars oiling a foot inside a shoe, but allows oiling it before putting it on and rolling an oiled body on leather.
Rav Hisda initially distinguishes polishing leather from tanning it.
Tanning is obviously barred, and intentional polishing should not be allowed either.
Rav Hisda instead distinguishes an amount of oil fit only to polish from an amount sufficient to tan.
The baraita restricts oversized and damaged footwear, halitza with a damaged shoe, and new women’s shoes on Shabbat.
Bar Kappara permits a new shoe already worn before Shabbat, when its fit has been checked.
Two baraitot conflict over removing a shoe from its last.
They follow Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages, who disagree whether a shoe still on its last is a completed vessel.
Rava’s permission to move a tool of prohibited use for its place fits removal of the shoe.
Abaye permits moving such a tool only for use of the tool itself; how can the shoe be removed?
The shoe sits loosely on its last and can be removed without moving the last.
The baraita’s loose-shoe limit fits Abaye’s distinction.
On Rava’s view, why would a tightly attached shoe be different?
That baraita states Rabbi Yehuda’s version of Rabbi Eliezer, not the Sages’ view.
The chapter on hanging a strainer closes.
The new mishna permits carrying a child with a stone, a basket with a stone, certain mixed teruma, and lifting a neutralized portion.
Rava distinguishes a live baby with a purse, for which carrying the purse is liable, from a dead baby with a purse.
The live-baby-and-purse ruling is repeated for analysis.
Why is the carrier not also liable for the live baby?
Rava follows Rabbi Natan: a living being carries itself.
Why is the purse not secondary to the baby, as a bed is secondary to its living occupant?
A bed is needed for its occupant; a purse retains separate importance.
The dead-baby-and-purse exemption is repeated for analysis.
Why is the carrier not liable for the dead baby?
Rava follows Rabbi Shimon’s exemption for labor not needed for its own sake.
The mishna permits lifting a child holding a stone; why does the attached purse differ?
Rabbi Yannai’s school limits the mishna to a child who longs for his father.
The Gemara begins a follow-up challenge, continued on the next daf.

142a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why does the mishna permit a stone in a child’s hand but Rava forbid a dinar there?
A father may chase a fallen dinar and carry it; he would leave a fallen stone.
A baraita supports Rava: carried garments and jewelry incur liability, worn ones do not.
The same distinction holds when another person wears the articles being carried.
Why may one move a basket containing a set-aside stone?
It also contains fruit, so it supports permitted contents.
Why not empty the fruit and stone instead?
The fruit would be spoiled by being thrown down.
Why not shake out the stone alone?
The stone closes a hole in the basket and serves as part of its side.
Rav Hisda limits moving impure with pure teruma to cases with pure teruma underneath.
Why not throw off the impure produce even then?
The fruit would be damaged.
A baraita permits moving the mixture with either type of teruma on top, refuting the limit.
Rav Hisda distinguishes needing the basket’s contents from needing its place.
Why read the mishna as a case of needing the contents?
Rava cites the next mishna’s coin cushion: shaking is required only for using the cushion itself.
Why may Rabbi Yehuda lift teruma if that seems to make the mixture fit for use?
The first answer associates him with Rabbi Eliezer’s view of teruma as separately present.
A mishna has Rabbi Eliezer treat a portion transferred from a teruma mixture as definite teruma.
That view was stated to impose stringency, not necessarily to permit lifting on Shabbat.
The next proposal associates Rabbi Yehuda with Rabbi Shimon, who permits a mixture after two successive teruma falls.
That dispute may concern successive dilution, without assuming each teruma portion remains separate.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar supplies a stronger basis: mental designation permits eating before physical lifting.
Does Rabbi Yehuda really agree with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar?

142b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita states Rabbi Yehuda’s lifting rule and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar’s designation rule separately.
They agree in principle; Rabbi Yehuda adds the preference to lift even on Shabbat.
The mishna requires tilting a barrel to dislodge a stone, or moving it away from other barrels first.
For coins on a cushion it requires shaking; it also distinguishes wiping a cushion from wetting leather.
Rav limits the barrel rule to a forgotten stone; a deliberately placed stone makes the barrel a base for it.
Which tanna requires exertion with the permitted barrel rather than directly moving the stone?
Rabbi Yohanan identifies Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
His rule for selecting on a Festival favors moving food when waste is more plentiful.
The barrel seems much larger than the stone, so why not move the stone?
The stone blocks access to the wine, making it functionally like the greater waste.
Rabbi Yosei details moving and tilting a barrel when nearby objects might be damaged.
Rav likewise limits the cushion-and-coins ruling to forgotten coins.
Rabbi Yohanan and a baraita allow moving the cushion with coins when its place is needed.
Sages recount moving a forgotten purse or brick with a loaf or baby, including a case referred to Rabbi Yohanan.
Mar Zutra accepts these rulings only for objects forgotten before Shabbat.
Rav Ashi rejects that device even for forgotten objects except in moving a corpse.
Abaye and Rava place a utensil on produce bundles or a young dove to move them.
Rav Yosef asks how they can use this device intentionally when the earlier cases involved forgetting.
Abaye says the bundles are themselves fit for reclining; he uses a spoon only because of his standing.
Rava says the dove is fit as raw food; he uses a knife only because of his standing.
Does Rava thereby bar moving meat unfit for people but fit for animals?
His own instruction to give duck intestines to a cat challenges that inference.

143a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Duck intestines spoil quickly, so their use as cat food was already in mind before Shabbat.
Rava’s strict ruling on a Festival poker and broken utensils supports his alignment with Rabbi Yehuda on set-aside items.
The mishna contrasts clearing bones and shells by hand with shaking them from the table board.
It permits moving crumbs and legume pods fit for animal food.
It distinguishes a sponge with a handle from one without, then addresses their movement and ritual purity.
Rav Nahman aligns Beit Shammai with Rabbi Yehuda and Beit Hillel with Rabbi Shimon.
The crumb rule supports Rabbi Yohanan’s prohibition on destroying even small crumbs.
Whose opinion permits moving the legume pods?
It fits Rabbi Shimon’s treatment of set-aside material.
The sponge rule seems to follow Rabbi Yehuda’s prohibition of an unintended result.
Rabbi Shimon also prohibits an unintended outcome when it is inevitable, as squeezing here is.
Pits of low-grade dates can be moved as prepared animal food, unlike pits of fine dates.
Shmuel moves the latter with bread, consistent with his view that bread may serve many needs.
Rabba uses a water pitcher; Rav Huna treats the pits as repulsive refuse.
Rav Ashi asks whether one may deliberately create such a repulsive container for moving.
Rav Sheshet, Rav Pappa, and Rabbi Zekharya each dispose of the pits without ordinary handling.
The chapter about carrying a child closes.

143b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna permits saving three meals from a broken barrel and inviting others, without soaking up liquid.
It bars squeezing fruit and using liquid that seeps out on its own.
Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes fruit designated for eating from fruit designated for juice.
The mishna records a dispute over honey released from combs crushed before Shabbat.
A Tosefta bars soaking up wine or collecting oil in an ordinary weekday manner.
A baraita allows collecting scattered fruit gradually for immediate eating, but not into a container.
Shmuel says Rabbi Yehuda concedes about olives and grapes because they are normally squeezed.
Ulla reports a broader disagreement, while Rabbi Yohanan rules differently for other fruit and for olives and grapes.
Rabba transmits Shmuel’s version: both sides agree on olives and grapes, and on other fruit.
If so, where do Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages disagree?
Rabbi Abba tells Rabbi Yirmeya to investigate the remaining case.
Rav Nahman identifies mulberries and pomegranates as the likely disputed middle category.
A baraita forbids seepage from olives and grapes, but distinguishes how mulberries and pomegranates were designated.
Does Rabbi Yehuda really forbid seepage from fruit with no stated designation?
A mishna distinguishes involuntary milk from a woman and an animal for susceptibility to impurity.
Rabbi Akiva argues that animal milk should qualify even when expressed involuntarily.
The Sages answer that human milk has a special analogy to blood from a wound.

144a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Sages complete their distinction: involuntary animal milk resembles wound blood that is pure.
Rabbi Akiva argues milk is stricter than blood when both are extracted for treatment.
The Sages counter with olive and grape baskets: only desired seepage gives the liquid significance.
If undesired means unstated intent, even olive and grape seepage is disregarded; surely mulberry and pomegranate seepage is.
The first reply reads “undesired” as an express objection, rather than an unstated preference.
Alternatively, liquid lost from olive and grape baskets is relinquished from the outset.
What proves the Sages concede to Rabbi Yehuda about other fruit?
A baraita about squeezing fruit begins, continuing on the next daf.

144b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita permits squeezing several fruits but bars pomegranates, citing a household that squeezes them.
How do we know the baraita reflects the Sages rather than Rabbi Yehuda?
Even Rabbi Yehuda permitted only juice that seeped by itself, not necessarily squeezing deliberately.
For fruit normally not squeezed, either view can permit squeezing; the pomegranate exception identifies the Sages’ position.
Rav Nahman treats the household’s pomegranate squeezing as halakhically significant.
Rava asks how one household’s custom could determine a rule for everyone.
Rav Nahman compares thorns cultivated for camels in Arabia, which Rabbi Eliezer treats as significant.
A regional custom differs from one household’s unusual practice.
Rav Hisda’s beet-juice case suggests that deliberate squeezing makes even an unusual juice significant.
Rav Pappa explains the bath ruling by the separate rule that non-bath liquids can discolor and invalidate it.
A mishna lists wine, vinegar, and olive discharge that invalidate a bath by changing its color.
Who considers olive discharge a liquid?
Abaye cites Rabbi Yaakov, who calls it liquid but disregards early seepage that its owner does not want.
Rabbi Shimon denies its liquid status and attributes later impurity to traces of oil.
What practical distinction separates them?
They differ over discharge after extensive pressing.
Rava explains bath invalidation without treating olive discharge as liquid.
Shmuel permits squeezing grapes directly into a food pot but not an empty bowl.
Rav Hisda applies that rule to milking into food and infers that liquid entering food counts as food.
Rami challenges from milk obtained by a zav: if it is food, what made it susceptible to impurity?
An initial drop on the teat remains liquid and renders the food susceptible.
Ravina introduces another impurity case involving squeezed olives and grapes.

145a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ravina’s squeezed-fruit case asks why juice entering food can become impure if it counts as food.
Ravina resolves it as juice squeezed into an empty bowl.
Rabbi Yirmeya cites a mishna disputing whether grape juice smoothed on bread prepares it for impurity.
Is that dispute over whether liquid entering food becomes food?
Rav Pappa instead places the disagreement in whether soon-lost liquid retains liquid status.
A baraita distinguishes olives cut for use from olives cut for salting or testing ripeness.
Is the olive dispute likewise about liquid destined to be lost?
Rav Huna separates the olives’ lost juice from juice used to polish bread.
Rav permits squeezing grapes into food but not a bowl, and permits fish brine even into a bowl.
Abaye asks why the fish-brine permission, if attributed to Shmuel, would not conflict with his other ruling.
Rav and Shmuel distinguish squeezing pickled or boiled vegetables for themselves from squeezing for their liquids.
Rav Dimi confirms the fish ruling came through a chain of transmitters from Rav, not Shmuel.
The Gemara restates Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yohanan on squeezing pickled and boiled vegetables.
A baraita permitting squeezing pickled vegetables for Shabbat seems to challenge all three rulings.
Rav reads the permission as squeezing for the vegetables; liquids remain prohibited, while boiled vegetables are permitted.
Shmuel extends the same limitation to both pickled and boiled vegetables.
Rabbi Yohanan also distinguishes purpose, imposing liability when either is squeezed for its liquid.
Rav and Menashe’s school limit Torah liability for pressing to olives and grapes.
Menashe’s school begins a related rule about hearsay testimony, completed on the next daf.

145b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Hearsay testimony is accepted to establish a husband’s death and permit his wife to remarry.
Is hearsay also accepted to permit a blemished firstborn animal? Rav Ami and Rav Asi disagree.
Rav Ami cites the rule limiting hearsay to testimony about a woman.
Rav Asi reads it as testimony in any matter for which a woman may testify.
Rav Yeimar permits it, Mareimar objects, and the Gemara rules that hearsay is valid for a firstborn.
Rav Hoshaya’s baraita extends the leniency for self-released liquid from honeycombs to pressed olives and grapes.
Does the baraita merely add another sage to the mishna’s permission?
Abaye says it teaches permission even when food becomes liquid, unlike honey remaining food.
The mishna permits soaking previously cooked food and rinsing uncooked food, but exempts fish cooked by rinsing.
What previously cooked food needs further soaking?
Rav Safra cites Rabbi Abba’s thoroughly cooked chicken.
Rav Safra recounts eating it and needing aged wine to avoid vomiting.
Rabbi Yohanan and the Babylonian sages exchange reactions to kutaḥ and Rabbi Abba’s chicken.
What if one rinsed the exceptional fish in hot water?
Rav Yosef imposes a sin offering for cooking.
Mar son of Ravina cites the mishna’s statement that rinsing completes their cooking.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Asi converse while Rabbi Yohanan dozes.
Why are Babylonian birds especially fat?
Rabbi Asi points to even fatter birds near Gaza.
Why are Babylonian Festivals especially joyful?
Rabbi Asi attributes their joy to poverty and rare abundance.
Why do Babylonian scholars wear distinctive clothes?
Rabbi Asi attributes it to lack of scholarship.
Why are gentiles described as contaminated?
Rabbi Asi attributes it to their diet.
Rabbi Yohanan wakes and rebukes answers asserted without the clarity required for teaching.
The two sages ask him to answer some of their questions.
He attributes the birds’ fatness to not having undergone exile, citing Moab.
A verse and baraita support the claim that animals and birds in Judea went into exile.
Rabbi Yohanan says all returned except a weak-spined fish unable to ascend the waterways.
He attributes greater Festival joy in Babylonia to their escape from a curse on the land’s festivals.
Rabbi Elazar explains the burden of decrees, and sages recount troops arriving on festivals.
Babylonian scholars dress distinctively because they are not native to their place.
Rav Yosef interprets a verse as praising Babylonian scholars’ contributions to Torah.
Rabbi Yohanan begins his answer about gentiles by saying they did not stand at Sinai.

146a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The prior discussion attributes lingering moral contamination to the serpent, and its removal for Israel to Sinai.
Rav Aha asks how this account applies to converts.
Rav Ashi says their guardian angels stood at Sinai, invoking the covenant with those not present.
Rabbi Abba bar Kahana offers a different account: the patriarchal line became free of the flaw by Jacob’s generation.
The mishna allows breaking a fig barrel without making a vessel and disputes puncturing its stopper.
It bars a side opening and smoothing wax over a hole; Rabbi Yehuda reports concern for liability.
Rabbi Oshaya restricts opening a fig barrel to tightly pressed figs.
Why would loose figs rule out breaking the barrel?
A baraita permits cutting a wine barrel’s top with a sword for guests.
The baraita follows the Sages; Rabbi Oshaya reads the mishna through Rabbi Nehemya’s utensil restriction.
Why force the mishna into Rabbi Nehemya’s narrower view?
Rava says its specific mention of figs points to pressed figs that need a utensil.
Two baraitot disagree on unbraiding or cutting sealed fruit baskets.
They follow the Sages and Rabbi Nehemya, who limits utensils to their designated use.
May one pierce a barrel with a spear for a generous display, or does it create an opening?
Rav Sheshet treats it as making an opening and forbids it.
The permitted sword-cut barrel appears to contradict this.
Cutting off a top breaks the barrel for guests; a spear hole indicates a desired lasting opening.
Rav Huna places the plug dispute on its top and bars side perforation for everyone.
Rav Hisda places the dispute on the plug’s side and reads the absolute side ban as applying to the barrel.
A baraita bars new holes, disputes widening old ones, and permits reopening a sealed old hole.
Why distinguish a new hole from widening an existing one if both create an opening?
Rabba says an outlet-only hole is not Torah-level building; the rabbinic decree concerns a two-way chicken-coop vent.

146b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The coop analogy extends to widening an inadequate vent; Rav Nahman rules like the stricter “some say” view.
Shmuel permits reopening an old hole only when it served straining, not reinforcement.
How are the two types of old hole distinguished?
Rav Hisda distinguishes holes above and below the wine level.
Rava says a hole below the wine also serves straining; reinforcement requires a hole below sediment.
Abaye cites a sealed doorway that retains its legal status until its posts are removed.
Rav and Shmuel agree on cutting and on replacing a prepared reed, but dispute inserting a cut unused reed.
Rav decrees against insertion lest one cut a new reed; Shmuel does not.
A baraita and Rabbi Yoshiya present a parallel dispute about a reed tube.
Where can Rabbi Yoshiya’s leniency fit if cutting is forbidden and replacing is already permitted?
They differ when the reed was cut but not yet fitted.
Rav Sheisha publicly rules in accordance with Rabbi Yoshiya.
Rav and Shmuel dispute sealing a hole with oil, a possible decree against wax smoothing.
Rav Shmuel bar bar Hana cites Rav himself as permitting oil.
Shmuel bars inserting a myrtle leaf as a spout.
Rav Yeimar fears making a real spout; Rav Ashi fears cutting a leaf.
What practical difference follows?
A leaf already cut and available avoids only Rav Ashi’s concern.
Rav and Shmuel dispute wearing medium-stiff felt in public; both agree on soft and hard felt.
Rav’s apparent strictness came from an incident, but he actually permitted the felt and declined to sit out of respect.
The mishna permits cooling or warming food and water and wearing wet clothes, but restricts public drying.
Why state the obvious permission to place food in a pit?
It rejects a decree based on possible leveling of holes.
Why state the permissions for cooling water and warming it in sunlight?
They reject concern that one might instead insulate the water in hot ashes.
Rav’s broad appearance-of-prohibition rule seems to conflict with drying clothes away from the crowd.
A baraita makes it a tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon forbid even that drying.
Rav Huna begins a further statement on the next daf.

147a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shaking dust from a cloak incurs laundering liability only for a new dark garment whose owner insists on cleanliness.
Ulla objects to shaking cloaks, but Rav Yehuda permits it for people who are not particular about the dust.
Rav Yosef likewise tells Abaye to shake dew off his hat because he is not particular about it.
Rabbi Yohanan imposes carrying liability for a cloak folded on the shoulder.
