A teaching about crumbling and mixing feed again appears to permit work on food.
The straw is spoiled and the young animals need the preparation.
The mishna distinguishes ways of feeding animals and adding water to bran.
What is the prohibited overfeeding of a camel?
Rav Yehuda describes packing food into its stomach.
Can such feeding really occur?
An observed case confirms that it can.
Which feeding method is hamra’a and which is halata?
Rav Yehuda distinguishes whether the animal can bring the food back.
Rav Hisda instead distinguishes use of a vessel from use of a hand.
Rav Yosef cites chicken feeding rules that seem to contradict Rav Yehuda’s definition.
Rav Yehuda distinguishes animals whose feeding depends on the owner from those that find food.
Rav Ashi cites the mishna’s distinction in giving water as support.
If owner responsibility alone matters, why single out water?
Water is more readily found in reservoirs.
Rabbi Yona describes the dog’s scarce food and its slow digestion.
The sages discuss feeding a dog and contrast its poverty with the pig’s plenty.
A baraita explicitly defines the feeding methods in support of Rav Yehuda.
Abaye asks whose opinion allows water in bran without kneading.
A baraita distinguishes adding water from kneading according to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda.
Perhaps bran differs from flour because it cannot form ordinary dough.
An explicit baraita permits adding water to bran under Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda.
A new baraita records opposing rulings on kneading parched grain flour.
Rav Hisda begins identifying the permissive opinion.

156a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The lenient view is Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda’s, provided the mixing method changes.
What counts as a changed method?
Rav Hisda prescribes mixing a little at a time.
A baraita permits stirring shatit and drinking Egyptian beer.
How can stirring be permitted after the ban on kneading?
The rule distinguishes thick from thin mixtures, with an altered method.
What alteration is required?
Rav Yosef reverses the usual order of vinegar and shatit.
Levi objects when he sees bran mixed for an ox on Shabbat.
His father cites permission to mix, subject to a changed method.
How is the method changed?
Abaye suggests moving the utensil crosswise.
Would that mix the feed adequately?
Rav Yehuda says it can be poured into another vessel.
Zeiri’s notebook records asking Rabbi Hiyya about mixing.
Rabbi Hiyya forbids it.
He then asks about moving feed between animals.
It is permitted, followed by differing limits on how much feed may be moved.
Levi’s notebook reports Rabbi’s unsuccessful protest against mixing shatit in Babylonia.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s notebook begins predictions by birth day.
Does Sunday birth mean the person has no good traits?
Rav Ashi’s examples show both a leader and a thief born on Sunday.
The saying means a person may be wholly inclined to good or bad.
The notebook assigns characteristics to births on the remaining weekdays.
Rabbi Hanina disputes that the weekday determines character, assigning influence to the birth hour.
He lists supposed traits for planetary hours, with examples and comments from the sages.
Rabbi Hanina says constellations influence wisdom, wealth, and Israel.
Rabbi Yohanan says Israel is not governed by constellations.
Rabbi Yohanan derives his view from Jeremiah’s instruction not to fear heavenly signs.
Rav is also reported to reject a fixed constellation for Israel.
God’s exchange with Abraham is read as a command to leave astrological predictions behind.

156b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: God’s changing Abraham’s planetary position completes the argument against fixed astrology.
Shmuel’s exchange with Ablet begins another case in which a predicted snakebite fails.
The returning man’s bundle contains a severed snake.
Shmuel asks what deed saved him.
He discreetly supplied bread for a companion who had none.
Shmuel interprets charity as saving a person from death itself.
Astrologers’ prediction for Rabbi Akiva’s daughter fails when her hairpin kills the snake.
Her father asks what she did to merit rescue.
She had given her own meal to a poor guest at the wedding.
Rabbi Akiva likewise teaches that charity saves from death itself.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak’s mother counters a prediction of theft by teaching reverence and prayer.
The mishna permits cutting prepared pumpkins and carcass, while Rabbi Yehuda excludes a new carcass.
Ulla rules for Rabbi Yehuda’s restriction; Shmuel is recorded for Rabbi Shimon.
Rav and Levi’s practices support Rabbi Yehuda’s set-aside rule.
Shmuel and Zeiri support Rabbi Shimon’s more permissive rule.
Zeiri limits a mishna’s ban on moving a dead animal to consecrated animals.
Rabbi Yohanan is also reported to rule like Rabbi Shimon.
His rule favoring an unattributed mishna seems to challenge that report.

157a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: An unattributed mishna forbids chopping set-aside beams on a festival.
Rabbi Yohanan attributes that ruling to an individual tanna.
Another mishna permits straw but not wood stored away.
Even Rabbi Shimon agrees about costly timber set aside from use.
A further mishna distinguishes wild and domestic animals for feeding and slaughter.
Rabbi Yohanan can rely on another anonymous mishna favoring Rabbi Shimon.
Rav Aha and Ravina disagree which set-aside exception remains under Rabbi Shimon’s rule.
A mishna about a large saw and plow pin shows even Rabbi Shimon restricts valuable reserved tools.
The final mishna permits Shabbat vow procedures, sealing an opening, measuring, and tying for a purpose.
Does a vow’s nullification require a Shabbat purpose as its dissolution does?
A teaching restricts nullification on Shabbat to a Shabbat purpose.
Another version links the scope of Shabbat nullification to its time limit.
The same teaching seems to support a full twenty-four-hour period for nullification.
Rav Ashi cites a mishna limiting nullification to the day on which the vow is heard.
The timing rules reflect a dispute among tanna’im.
May a vow be dissolved on Shabbat if there was time before Shabbat?
A case of sages dissolving such a vow shows that it may.
The discussion returns to sealing the opening and tying the vessel.
Rav begins explaining the narrow alley and impurity that made the measurements necessary.

157b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A cracked roof and the measured opening determine whether impurity spreads between houses.
The mishna’s case establishes permission to seal, measure, and tie on Shabbat.
Ulla sees Rabba bar Rav Huna measuring a tub of water.
Ulla asks why a non-mitzva measurement is permitted.
Rabba says he is merely occupied casually with it.
The text closes the chapter and tractate of Shabbat.
